An extract selects Cases in a particular resolution status for a quality review sample.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The review sample has been empty since the status picklist labels were rewritten for clarity.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The extract should return every Case in the intended status.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query runs without error and returns no rows at all.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The picklist labels were updated while the stored values were left unchanged, and the extract filtered on the new label text. A query on the stored value returned the expected 1,800 Cases, which confirmed the data was present.

RESOLUTION
The extract now filters on stored values, and the field definition was documented so that future label changes do not imply a value change. A comment in the extract records the label-to-value mapping.

VALIDATION
The review sample returned 1,800 Cases matching a manual count, and a repeat label change in a sandbox left the extract working.

column1: Summary query fails whenever an extra descriptive column is added
column2:
CONTEXT
An analyst maintains a set of aggregate queries that summarize revenue by owner and region.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Adding the owner's department to an existing summary makes the query fail immediately.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Descriptive attributes should be available alongside the summarized figures.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query is rejected with an error stating that the added field must be grouped or aggregated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Aggregate queries permit only grouped fields and aggregate expressions in the selected columns. Every failing variant added a plain field, and every working variant added it to the grouping as well, which confirmed the rule rather than a data problem.

RESOLUTION
The queries now add descriptive attributes to the grouping when the attribute is one value per group, and use an aggregate expression when it is not. The pattern was written up in the analytics guide with both examples.

VALIDATION
Six summaries were extended with descriptive attributes and returned the same totals as before, and a deliberately invalid variant reproduced the documented error.

column1: Row-level restrictions in the reporting warehouse cover accounts but not cases
column2:
CONTEXT
Salesforce data is copied into a reporting warehouse where analysts build their own dashboards.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The warehouse must respect the same regional data boundaries that apply inside Salesforce.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An analyst should see warehouse rows only for the regions they are entitled to.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Account rows are restricted by region, while case and activity rows are visible to every analyst.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Row-level rules were implemented per table, and only the account table carries a region column. Cases inherit their region through the account, which the current model does not resolve, and 14 analysts currently see all case rows.

RESOLUTION
The account region is now denormalized onto the case table during load and enforced by the same rule. This is partial: activity and email tables have no reliable region attribution yet, so they remain unrestricted and are excluded from the analyst workspace until they do.

VALIDATION
Analysts from three regions retrieved only their own account and case rows, while the excluded activity tables are no longer reachable from the workspace.

column1: Weighted scoring cannot be expressed in the report builder
column2:
CONTEXT
The service team ranks accounts by a health score combining case volume, response performance, and renewal proximity.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The score must be produced monthly, but the report builder cannot express the weighted combination.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The health score should be calculable and reportable inside the platform.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The calculation needs values from three unrelated objects at different grains, which report formulas cannot combine.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Report formulas operate within one report type and cannot reach across unrelated objects. A prototype confirmed the score is straightforward once the three inputs are on one row, which the current model does not provide.

RESOLUTION
Three reports are exported monthly and combined in a spreadsheet that applies the weighting. This is a workaround: the score exists outside the platform, is refreshed only monthly, and cannot drive automation or alerts. A stamped score field maintained by a scheduled job is the preferred solution.

VALIDATION
Three monthly cycles produced scores matching the prototype, and the service team confirmed the ranking was usable, though always up to a month behind.

column1: Two reporting tools disagree because they convert currency on different dates
column2:
CONTEXT
Revenue figures are published both from Salesforce reports and from the finance reporting tool.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The two sources disagree by one to three percent every month, which undermines confidence in both.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both tools should report the same converted figure for the same period.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Salesforce converts using the rate effective on the deal close date, while the finance tool applies the month-end rate.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both methods are internally consistent and defensible, and the difference tracks currency movement during the month. Reconciling one quarter showed the gap closes entirely when the same rate basis is applied to both.

RESOLUTION
A published rate table is now applied in a parallel report set so the two tools can be compared on the same basis. This is a workaround: the primary Salesforce reports still convert on close date, so two figures circulate and the comparison set has to be maintained. Agreeing a single conversion policy is the outstanding decision.

VALIDATION
The parallel set matched the finance tool within 0.1 percent for three months, while the primary reports continued to differ as expected.

column1: Scheduled report subscriptions stop reaching some recipients
column2:
CONTEXT
Managers subscribe to scheduled reports that arrive each Monday morning.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Four managers stopped receiving their subscriptions while colleagues on the same schedule still receive them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every active subscriber should receive the report on each scheduled run.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The run completes and most recipients are served, but the four affected managers receive nothing and see no error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The subscriptions are present and active, and the affected managers can open the reports interactively. Their addresses are not on any suppression list and other platform messages reach them normally. Removing and recreating one subscription restored delivery for two weeks before it stopped again, which rules out a permanent configuration fault.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. Recreating subscriptions is a temporary recovery, not an explanation, and has not been applied to the remaining accounts.

VALIDATION
Two managers are still not receiving reports. The next step is comparing the scheduled run log with the message delivery log for a single run, and raising a support case if the messages are never generated.

column1: Case volume for one region drops sharply for a single historical month
column2:
CONTEXT
A three-year case volume trend supports capacity planning for each service region.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One region shows a drop of roughly 60 percent for a single month two years ago, distorting the seasonal model.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Historical volume should reflect the cases actually handled in that period.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The month sits far below its neighbours with no corresponding change in staffing or customer numbers.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Case records for the month exist and are internally consistent, so the trend reflects stored data rather than a reporting fault. Regional attribution depends on a field populated by an automation replaced in that period, so the volume may sit under another region, but the cross-region total for the month is also low. Archive exports from that period are no longer available.

RESOLUTION
No verified explanation exists. The month has not been adjusted, since altering historical figures without an established cause would be worse.

VALIDATION
The anomaly is unchanged and the seasonal model excludes that month with a documented note. The next step is checking whether the retired automation left a secondary attribution field that can be reconciled.

column1: Automated monitoring alerts create thousands of cases in the support queue
column2:
CONTEXT
Messages arriving at the support address create Cases so that customer requests are never missed.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The queue filled overnight with cases generated by an internal monitoring system.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only genuine customer correspondence should create Cases.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every monitoring alert creates its own Case, and one incident produced more than two thousand of them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The monitoring system had been pointed at the support address during an earlier project. Its messages carry a distinctive sender and a machine-generated subject pattern, and no filtering existed on the inbound path.

RESOLUTION
Inbound rules now divert messages from monitoring senders to an operations queue without creating Cases, alerts are grouped by incident reference, and the monitoring system was redirected to its own address.

VALIDATION
A replayed incident produced one operations entry instead of two thousand Cases, genuine customer messages continued to create Cases normally, and the backlog was closed in bulk.

column1: Colleague replies on a forwarded thread attach to the wrong case
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers sometimes forward a support thread to a colleague who then replies to the support team directly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Those replies appear on an unrelated Case belonging to a different customer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A reply should attach to the Case its thread belongs to, or create a new Case when the thread is unknown.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some forwarded replies attach to a Case that shares part of the quoted history from an earlier message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Matching relied on scanning the message body for a reference pattern, and forwarded messages can contain several. The handler took the first match found, which in the affected messages came from quoted text of an older thread rather than the current one.

RESOLUTION
Matching now uses the message header reference chain first and falls back to the most recent body reference only when no header is present, with unmatched messages creating a new Case linked to the sender.

VALIDATION
Forty forwarded and quoted messages attached to the correct Case, three messages with no reference created new Cases, and no cross-customer attachment occurred in the test set.

column1: Branded templates render as unreadable blocks on mobile clients
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer notifications use a branded template with a fixed-width layout and a header image.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers reading on phones report overlapping text and a layout wider than the screen.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Notifications should be readable on common desktop and mobile clients.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The fixed width forces horizontal scrolling, and the content column collapses behind the header image.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rendering tests across six clients showed failures on three mobile clients and correct display on all desktop clients. The template used a fixed pixel width with nested tables and no scaling instruction, which mobile clients do not adapt automatically.

RESOLUTION
The template was rebuilt with a fluid width, a scaling instruction, and a stacked layout below a threshold, keeping the same branding elements.

VALIDATION
Rendering tests passed on all six clients, a sample of 20 customers reported no further issues, and click rates on mobile returned to the level seen before the branding change.

column1: Agent attachments bounce because they exceed the recipient size limit
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents attach diagnostic reports to customer replies directly from the Case feed.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers say they never received the report, while the agent sees the reply as sent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A reply with an attachment should either be delivered or produce a visible failure for the agent.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages with attachments above the recipient limit are rejected by the receiving server, and the rejection is not shown on the Case.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rejection notices arrived at the sending mailbox rather than the Case, so agents never saw them. Of 220 sampled replies with attachments, 34 were rejected, all above ten megabytes and mostly diagnostic archives.

RESOLUTION
Attachments above a configured size are now replaced by an expiring download link generated from the file, and rejection notices are attached to the originating Case.

VALIDATION
All 34 previously rejected reports were delivered as links and downloaded by the customers, and a forced rejection appeared on the Case within minutes.

column1: Account timeline omits activities logged against contacts
column2:
CONTEXT
Account managers review a timeline that should show every interaction with anyone at the customer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The timeline shows far fewer interactions than the team recalls having.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Activities logged against a contact should appear on that contact's account timeline.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only activities whose related record is the account itself are shown, while contact-level activities are missing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Activities carry both a related record and a name reference, and the timeline query used the related record only. A count showed 78 percent of activities reference a contact by name with no account on the related field, which matches how agents log calls.

RESOLUTION
The timeline now includes activities whose name reference resolves to a contact on the account, presented alongside account-level activities with the contact shown for each entry.

VALIDATION
Timelines for 15 accounts matched a manual reconciliation of calls and messages, and activities logged against contacts of other accounts did not appear.

column1: Closure notifications go to the first contact rather than the requester
column2:
CONTEXT
When a Case is closed, an automated message summarizing the resolution is sent to the customer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers report that closure summaries reach a colleague who was never involved in the request.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The summary should reach the person who raised the request, with other participants optionally copied.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The message is addressed to whichever contact is listed first on the Case, which is often an earlier participant.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The automation selected the first related contact rather than the requester recorded at creation. In a sample of 90 closed Cases, 27 had more than one contact and 19 of those had notified the wrong person.

RESOLUTION
The automation now addresses the requester field, copies additional participants who have replied on the thread, and skips contacts marked as no longer at the organization.

VALIDATION
Ninety closures were replayed with the new logic and all addressed the recorded requester, participants were copied correctly, and departed contacts were excluded.

column1: Message classification works for English but not for the other supported languages
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound customer messages are classified by topic so they can be routed to the right specialist queue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Messages in Hebrew and French are routed to the general queue and wait longer for a first response.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Classification should work across every language the support team accepts.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Non-English messages fall below the confidence threshold and are sent to the general queue by default.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The classifier was trained on English messages only. Measured accuracy was 91 percent for English, 44 percent for French, and 38 percent for Hebrew, and the low-confidence fallback accounted for most non-English routing.

RESOLUTION
A language detection step now routes non-English messages to bilingual queues by language rather than topic. This is partial: topic-level routing still applies to English only, and a multilingual classifier requires labelled data the team has not yet collected.

VALIDATION
First response time for non-English messages improved by 38 percent over a month, while topic accuracy for those languages remains unmeasured.

column1: Keyword routing is configured for three of the seven service queues
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound messages are routed to specialist queues using keyword rules maintained by the service leads.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Four specialist areas receive their work only after a manual triage step each morning.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every specialist area should receive its messages directly through routing rules.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Rules exist for three areas, and messages for the remaining four land in a shared triage queue.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The three configured areas have distinctive vocabulary, while the remaining four overlap heavily in the terms customers use. A sample of 600 triaged messages showed that keyword rules drafted for those areas would have misrouted 22 percent.

RESOLUTION
Rules were added for the one remaining area with distinctive terms, bringing coverage to four of seven. This is partial: the last three areas share vocabulary, and routing them by keyword alone would misroute more messages than manual triage does.

VALIDATION
The new rules routed 94 percent of that area's messages correctly over three weeks, while the three overlapping areas remain in manual triage.

column1: Messages from shared customer mailboxes cannot be linked to a person
column2:
CONTEXT
Some customers correspond from a shared departmental mailbox rather than an individual address.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases raised from those addresses have no contact, so entitlement checks and reporting fail.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every Case should be associated with a contact that represents the requester.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No contact matches the shared address, so the Case is created with an empty contact and is excluded from entitlement processing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twelve customers use shared mailboxes, and the actual sender appears only in the message signature. Matching on the signature was tested and proved unreliable because signature formats vary between senders.

RESOLUTION
A placeholder contact representing the shared mailbox was created for each of the twelve customers. This is a workaround: reporting attributes all such correspondence to a single non-person contact, and the real sender must be identified manually. Encouraging individual addresses is the preferred direction.

VALIDATION
Entitlement checks now run for all twelve customers and their Cases appear in service reports, while person-level analysis excludes them by a documented flag.

column1: Some customers never receive messages the platform reports as delivered
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound customer messages are tracked with a delivery state recorded against the Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers occasionally insist a message never arrived although the platform records it as delivered.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A delivered state should mean the receiving server accepted the message for the intended recipient.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The state shows delivered, no bounce is recorded, and the customer finds nothing in their inbox or junk folder.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Delivery state reflects acceptance by the receiving server, not final placement, so onward filtering inside the customer's environment would not appear here. Affected recipients span several domains and no pattern by template or sender was found. Two customers checked their own mail logs and reported no record of the message arriving, which does not match acceptance being genuine.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. No change has been made to the sending configuration, since the evidence does not identify where the messages stop.

VALIDATION
Reports continue at a low rate. The next step is obtaining the platform message identifier for three recent cases and asking the customers' mail administrators to trace them in their own logs.

column1: Lead conversion fails on a validation rule the lead cannot satisfy
column2:
CONTEXT
Converting a qualified Lead creates an Account, Contact, and Opportunity in one action.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Conversions fail with an error naming a field that does not exist on the Lead.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Conversion should succeed for a qualified Lead, or explain what the user must complete first.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The conversion is rejected by a validation rule requiring an account segment that only exists on Account.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The segment rule was added for data quality and applies to every Account save, including the one created by conversion. Because the field is not mapped from the Lead, it is always empty at that moment. A test conversion with the rule deactivated completed normally.

RESOLUTION
The Lead now carries a segment field mapped to the Account field on conversion, and the validation rule was adjusted to allow the value to be set within the same transaction.

VALIDATION
Sixty conversions succeeded across all record types, the segment value carried through correctly, and Accounts edited manually without a segment were still blocked by the rule.

column1: Child cases are stranded when the parent case is closed
column2:
CONTEXT
Complex incidents are tracked as a parent Case with child Cases for each affected service.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Child Cases remain open indefinitely after the incident is resolved and the parent is closed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Closing a parent should close or explicitly reassign its children rather than leave them unattended.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Children keep their open status, disappear from incident reporting, and continue to age against service targets.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No automation linked the closure of a parent to its children, and reporting followed the parent only. A query found 380 open child Cases whose parent had been closed, the oldest more than a year earlier.

RESOLUTION
Closing a parent now closes children that are still in a waiting state with an inherited resolution, while children with their own active work are flagged for the owner to confirm rather than closed automatically.

VALIDATION
The 380 stranded Cases were reviewed and closed or reassigned, and ten test incidents closed their children correctly while leaving actively worked children open with a flag.

column1: Fields required on the page layout are left empty by integrations
column2:
CONTEXT
Several Case fields are marked required on the page layout so agents cannot save without them.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases created by integrations arrive without those fields, and reporting on them is incomplete.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Required business data should be present regardless of how the record was created.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Layout requirements apply to the user interface only, so integration records save without the fields.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three of the five fields were required on the layout alone. A completeness query showed those three empty on 34 percent of Cases, all created through the API, while the two fields required at field level were always populated.

RESOLUTION
The three fields are now enforced by validation rules that apply to all contexts, with a default applied by the integration mapping where the source can supply a value and a review queue for records that cannot.

VALIDATION
New integration Cases carried all five fields, the completeness gap fell to under one percent, and records with no source value appeared in the review queue as expected.

column1: Renaming a picklist value silently breaks the automation that references it
column2:
CONTEXT
An approval automation routes requests based on the request type picklist.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Requests of one type stopped being routed after the picklist values were tidied up.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Renaming a label should not change routing behaviour.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected type is never matched, and its requests wait unrouted until someone notices.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The tidy-up changed the stored value rather than the label alone, and the automation compared against the previous stored value. A dependency search found four automations and two validation rules referencing the old value, none of which were updated during the change.

RESOLUTION
The automations were updated to the current values, the routing comparison now uses a stable code field rather than the display value, and picklist changes require a dependency check before deployment.

VALIDATION
Requests of all six types routed correctly across 40 tests, and a rehearsal rename in a sandbox left routing unaffected because it no longer depends on the display value.

column1: Account team members are lost when the account changes owner
column2:
CONTEXT
Account teams give specialists such as solution engineers access to the accounts they support.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Specialists lose access to accounts after a routine ownership change and have to ask to be re-added.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Team membership should survive an ownership change unless it is deliberately removed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The previous owner's default team is replaced by the new owner's default team, and existing members are removed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Ownership changes apply the new owner's default team, which replaces rather than merges membership. A review of 40 recent transfers found specialists removed in 31 of them, and the affected users had no other access path to those accounts.

RESOLUTION
An automation now captures team membership before the transfer and restores members whose role is specialist, while sales roles continue to follow the new owner's default team.

VALIDATION
Twenty test transfers preserved specialist membership and applied the new sales team, and the 31 historical cases were repaired from the captured data.

column1: Recurring visit tasks flood the timeline for long-running accounts
column2:
CONTEXT
Field representatives schedule recurring visit tasks so that key accounts are contacted regularly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Account timelines are dominated by hundreds of future visit tasks, hiding real interactions.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Planned visits should be visible without overwhelming the record of what actually happened.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A weekly recurrence spanning three years creates more than 150 open tasks per account at once.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Recurrence generated the full series at creation with no horizon limit. Counting open tasks found 40 accounts with over 100 future tasks each, and completion history showed representatives rescheduled most of them anyway.

RESOLUTION
Recurring series are now limited to a rolling 90-day horizon extended by a scheduled job, and the timeline separates planned visits from completed interactions.

VALIDATION
Open future tasks per account fell from over 150 to at most 13, the rolling extension created the next period correctly for two cycles, and completed interactions were easy to find in a user review.

column1: Data quality scoring covers accounts but not the contacts beneath them
column2:
CONTEXT
A data quality score highlights records missing key attributes so stewards can prioritize cleanup.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Stewards cannot see which contacts need attention, so contact quality is not improving.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both accounts and contacts should carry a quality score with the same definition.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only accounts are scored, and contact quality is assessed manually during campaign preparation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scoring job evaluates one object, and the contact rules were never agreed because the required attributes differ by role. Marketing needs a valid address and role, while service needs a phone number and language preference.

RESOLUTION
Contact scoring now covers the four attributes both teams agree on and is published alongside the account score. This is partial: role-specific attributes are excluded until the two teams agree a single definition, so the contact score understates requirements for campaign use.

VALIDATION
Contact scores were produced for the full base and matched manual assessment for a 200 record sample, while marketing continued a separate check for role-specific attributes.

column1: Large duplicate clusters must be merged in repeated manual passes
column2:
CONTEXT
An acquisition introduced duplicate accounts, and some customers exist as clusters of five to nine records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Stewards spend hours merging large clusters and sometimes leave a cluster half merged.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A cluster should be consolidated into one surviving record in a single controlled operation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Merging is limited to three records at a time, so a cluster of nine requires four passes with a decision at each step.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The limit is a platform constraint rather than a configuration choice. A review found 210 clusters above three records, of which 18 had been left partially merged with related records split across survivors.

RESOLUTION
A guided job now orders each cluster by completeness and walks the steward through the passes, recording progress so a cluster cannot be abandoned midway. This is a workaround: the merges still happen three at a time and remain manual, and a cluster of nine still takes four passes.

VALIDATION
All 18 partially merged clusters were completed, and 40 further clusters were merged with no split relationships afterwards.

column1: Obsolete records cannot be deleted because other records reference them
column2:
CONTEXT
Product and pricing reference records accumulate over the years and clutter selection lists.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Administrators cannot remove obsolete reference records that no longer apply to any current offering.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records no longer in use should be removable, or clearly hidden from all selection contexts.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deletion is blocked because historical opportunities and contracts still reference the records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
References exist on closed records that must be retained for audit, so deletion would break historical reporting. Of 900 reference records, 340 have no current use but appear in 12,000 historical references.

RESOLUTION
Obsolete records are now marked retired and excluded from every selection list and search filter. This is a workaround: the records remain in the database and still appear in historical reports and in some list views built before the flag existed, which must be updated individually.

VALIDATION
Selection lists dropped from 900 to 560 entries, historical reports were unchanged, and three list views were found still showing retired records and corrected.

column1: Newly created records are missing from search results for several hours
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents find customer records through global search while speaking to the customer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records created earlier the same day cannot be found by search, although they open normally from a list view.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A new record should be findable by search within a short time of being created.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some records appear in search within minutes while others take several hours, with no visible difference between them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Affected records are complete and valid, and their fields are marked searchable. The delay does not correlate with record type, creating user, or field content, and it occurs for both interface and integration creations. Renaming an affected record made it findable immediately, which suggests records enter the index on a later change rather than at creation.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. Touching records to force indexing was rejected as a standing practice, since it would generate misleading audit history.

VALIDATION
The delay is reported several times a week. The next step is recording creation and first-findable timestamps for a controlled set of records and raising a support case with the distribution.

column1: Optional quote lines lose their discount when the quote becomes an order
column2:
CONTEXT
Approved quotes are converted into orders, carrying products, quantities, and negotiated discounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers are invoiced at list price for items that were quoted with a discount.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every quoted line should transfer with the discount that was approved.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Lines marked optional at quoting time transfer at list price when the customer later accepts them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The conversion copied discounts from lines flagged as included and treated optional lines as new additions priced from the catalogue. Comparing 50 converted orders found 11 with discount loss, all containing accepted optional lines, with an average overcharge of 9 percent on those lines.

RESOLUTION
Conversion now carries the approved discount for any accepted line regardless of its optional flag, and a validation blocks conversion when a line price differs from the approved quote without an approval reference.

VALIDATION
Fifty quotes with mixed included and optional lines converted at the approved prices, the 11 affected orders were corrected with credit notes, and the validation blocked a manually altered test line.

column1: Overlay specialists cause their accounts to be counted twice in quota rollups
column2:
CONTEXT
Quota attainment rolls up through the sales hierarchy, and overlay specialists support accounts they do not own.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Divisional attainment exceeds the sum of its regions, which makes the hierarchy figures unusable.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each closed deal should contribute once to any level of the hierarchy above it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deals supported by an overlay specialist contribute through both the owning region and the overlay structure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Overlay specialists sit in a parallel branch of the hierarchy, and the rollup summed all descendant nodes without distinguishing the two branches. Recomputing one quarter with the overlay branch excluded reconciled the divisional total to the sum of regions exactly.

RESOLUTION
The rollup now attributes revenue through the owning branch only, and overlay contribution is reported as a separate credit measure that is never added to hierarchy totals.

VALIDATION
Divisional totals matched the sum of regions for three quarters, the overlay credit measure matched the specialists' own records, and no deal appeared twice in the audit extract.

column1: Pipeline value includes tax and overstates expected bookings
column2:
CONTEXT
Opportunity amounts are populated from the quoting tool, which produces a customer-facing total.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Pipeline consistently exceeds the bookings that finance later recognizes, by a proportion that varies by country.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Pipeline should represent net revenue excluding indirect taxes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Amounts include tax at the local rate, so pipeline is inflated by between 0 and 25 percent depending on the country.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The quoting tool sends the gross customer total, and the mapping stored it directly. Comparing 300 closed deals with their invoices showed the difference matched the applicable tax rate in every case.

RESOLUTION
The quoting tool now sends net and tax components separately, the opportunity amount stores the net value, and the gross total is retained in a separate field for customer correspondence.

VALIDATION
Pipeline for four countries reconciled with finance bookings within 0.4 percent, historical opportunities were restated using the recorded tax rate, and both values remain visible on the record.

column1: Deals with a future close date are counted in the current period once won
column2:
CONTEXT
Bookings are reported by close date, and representatives sometimes mark a deal won before its scheduled close date.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Monthly bookings include deals whose close date falls in a later month.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A deal should be reported in the period matching its close date, which should reflect when the deal was actually won.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deals won early keep a future close date, and the extract assigns them to the current month by their won timestamp.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extract used the stage change timestamp while the reporting definition specified close date, and the two diverge whenever a deal is won ahead of schedule. In one month, 34 deals had a close date in a later period.

RESOLUTION
Winning a deal now sets the close date to the date of the win, the extract reports strictly by close date, and a validation prevents saving a won deal with a future close date.

VALIDATION
Three months were recalculated and matched the finance ledger, the 34 deals moved to their correct period, and the validation blocked a test deal won with a future date.

column1: Multi-year contracts are reported at their full contract value as annual revenue
column2:
CONTEXT
Annual and total contract values are both used, the first for recurring revenue and the second for deal size.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Annual recurring revenue jumped sharply in a quarter with several three-year deals, without a matching change in billing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Annual recurring revenue should reflect the yearly value, independent of contract length.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Multi-year deals contribute their full contract value, so a three-year deal counts three times its annual worth.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The opportunity amount holds total contract value, and the recurring revenue measure read that field directly with no division by term. Recomputing the quarter using term length reduced the reported figure by 22 percent and aligned it with billing.

RESOLUTION
Annual value is now derived from total contract value divided by the term in years, stored in its own field, and the recurring revenue measure reads that field. Both measures are labelled explicitly in reports.

VALIDATION
Four quarters were restated and matched billing within one percent, single-year deals were unaffected, and a three-year test deal produced the expected annual figure.

column1: Automated payment matching handles single invoices but not part payments
column2:
CONTEXT
Incoming payments are matched to invoices so that collections can focus on genuinely overdue accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Collections chase customers who have already paid part of an outstanding balance.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Payments should be matched to invoices including partial and combined settlements.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only payments equal to a single invoice total are matched, and everything else waits for manual allocation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The matching rule compared the payment amount with an invoice total for an exact match. Analysis of 4,000 payments found 61 percent matched exactly, 22 percent settled several invoices together, and 17 percent were partial.

RESOLUTION
Matching now also resolves payments that settle a combination of invoices for the same customer within a tolerance. This is partial: partial payments still require manual allocation because the customer remittance advice does not identify which invoice they relate to.

VALIDATION
Automatic matching rose from 61 to 83 percent over a month, incorrect matches stayed at zero in a 300 payment audit, and partial payments remain a manual queue.

column1: Pricing approval routing is automated for two of the five regions
column2:
CONTEXT
Discount approvals follow a matrix of thresholds that differ by region and product family.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Approvals in three regions are still requested by message, which slows deals and leaves no audit record.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every discount request should route automatically to the correct approver with a recorded decision.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two regions route automatically, while three rely on the representative contacting an approver directly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The automated regions have a documented threshold matrix, while the other three apply thresholds that vary by customer segment and are held informally by regional directors. Sampling 80 approvals in those regions found four different thresholds applied to comparable deals.

RESOLUTION
The two documented regions remain automated and a third was added after its director agreed a written matrix. This is partial: two regions still lack an agreed matrix, so their approvals stay informal and unaudited until the thresholds are defined.

VALIDATION
The third region routed 120 requests correctly with full audit history, while the remaining two regions continue without a recorded decision trail.

column1: Exchange rates are entered by hand each month because the feed was withdrawn
column2:
CONTEXT
Dated exchange rates convert deal values into the reporting currency for consolidated reporting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Rates were not updated for two months, so reported figures drifted from the finance position.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Rates should be loaded automatically at the start of each period from the agreed source.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The previous rate feed was withdrawn by the provider, and nobody was assigned to enter rates manually.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The feed had been decommissioned with the provider's older service, and no replacement was procured. The missing periods were identified by comparing dated rate records with the fiscal calendar, which showed two gaps.

RESOLUTION
A named owner now enters rates from the finance system on the first working day, with a reminder task and a monthly completeness check. This is a workaround: entry is manual and can be missed or mistyped, and rate history has no independent verification. A replacement feed is on the finance roadmap.

VALIDATION
Three periods were loaded on time and matched finance figures exactly, the missing months were backfilled, and the completeness check flagged a deliberately skipped period.

column1: Mid-quarter quota changes require attainment to be recalculated by hand
column2:
CONTEXT
Quotas are set per representative per quarter and drive attainment reporting and commission accrual.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Territory changes mid-quarter leave attainment figures that nobody trusts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A quota change during a period should produce a correct blended target automatically.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The quota record is overwritten, so attainment for the whole quarter is measured against the new value.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The model holds one quota row per representative per quarter with no effective dating. Eleven representatives changed territory last quarter, and each required a manual calculation that took about an hour.

RESOLUTION
A calculation sheet now produces a blended quota that operations enters as an adjustment, with the original values recorded in a note. This is a workaround: attainment is correct only after the manual step, intermediate reporting is wrong, and the history lives outside the model. Effective-dated quota records are the preferred solution.

VALIDATION
Eleven blended quotas were applied and matched the sheet, and the affected representatives confirmed their attainment figures, though reporting was wrong for the two weeks before the adjustment.

column1: A few contracts generate duplicate renewal opportunities each month
column2:
CONTEXT
A monthly job creates one renewal opportunity for each contract approaching its end date.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Between two and six contracts each month end up with two renewal opportunities.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each eligible contract should produce exactly one renewal per cycle.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Affected contracts have two renewals created within the same run, seconds apart, with identical values.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The job checks for an existing open renewal before creating one, and that check appears in the debug logs for the affected contracts. Job history shows one scheduled execution per month, so a repeated run is ruled out. The contracts share no product, term, or owner, and each pair is created in different batches of the same run.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. A unique constraint was considered and not applied, because it would fail the batch rather than explain why the duplicate is generated.

VALIDATION
Duplicates continue at a similar rate and are removed manually each month. The next step is logging the batch identifier and pre-check result for every contract in a full run, then comparing the batches that produced each pair.

column1: Numeric values sent as text are rejected by the upsert endpoint
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner system upserts inventory records into Salesforce through a REST endpoint.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A share of upserts fails with a field validation error naming the quantity field.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Valid numeric quantities should be accepted regardless of how the partner formats them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Quantities sent as quoted text with a thousands separator are rejected, while plain numbers succeed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner serializes quantities above 999 with a separator and quotes, which the platform cannot parse as a number. Every failing payload contained a value above 999, and the same record succeeded when resubmitted without formatting.

RESOLUTION
The partner now sends unformatted numeric values, and a middleware normalization step strips separators and converts numeric strings before the call, rejecting anything that is not a clean number with a clear error.

VALIDATION
A replay of 2,600 failed records succeeded, values above and below the threshold were accepted, and a deliberately malformed value produced the explicit error rather than a platform rejection.

column1: Consumer application fails when a new picklist value is introduced
column2:
CONTEXT
An external application reads Case records and maps the status field onto its own workflow states.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The application stopped processing Cases after a new status value was added.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A new value should be handled gracefully by consumers rather than stopping processing.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The consumer raises an unrecognized value exception and halts its queue rather than skipping the record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The consumer maps values through a fixed list with no default branch. Its queue stopped within minutes of the first Case carrying the new value, and the backlog grew until the value was temporarily withdrawn.

RESOLUTION
The consumer now maps unknown values to a review state and continues processing, an alert reports the first occurrence of any unknown value, and picklist additions are announced to consumers through the integration change process.

VALIDATION
Introducing a test value produced review-state records and one alert with no queue interruption, and the withdrawn value was reinstated without incident.

column1: Callout parsing fails when the provider omits an optional object
column2:
CONTEXT
Apex callouts retrieve customer risk profiles from an external service and store selected attributes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some qualification attempts fail with a parsing error instead of returning a profile.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A response missing optional sections should still produce the attributes that are present.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The parser raises an exception when the history section is absent, and the whole response is discarded.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The provider omits the history section entirely for customers with no trading history rather than sending an empty list. The parser dereferenced the section unconditionally. All 140 failures in the sample involved new customers, which matches the provider's documented behaviour.

RESOLUTION
Parsing now treats every optional section as absent by default, populates what is present, and records a partial-profile indicator when history is missing so the qualification logic can account for it.

VALIDATION
All 140 previously failing customers returned profiles with the partial indicator set, established customers were unchanged, and a malformed response still failed loudly rather than silently.

column1: A public Apex endpoint builds its query from unvalidated input
column2:
CONTEXT
An Apex REST endpoint lets an internal portal search accounts by name fragment.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security code review found the endpoint assembling its query by concatenating the caller's input.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Caller input must never alter the structure of the executed query.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Input containing query syntax changes the filter, and a crafted value returns records the caller should not receive.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The endpoint was disabled while the fix was prepared and the security team was informed. Testing confirmed that a crafted fragment widened the result set beyond the intended filter. Request logs for the previous 90 days were reviewed and showed no input containing query syntax, so no exploitation was evident.

RESOLUTION
The query now uses bound variables with the filter structure fixed in code, input is length-limited and character-restricted, and the class enforces sharing and field access in user mode.

VALIDATION
Crafted inputs from the review returned no additional records, legitimate searches were unaffected across 200 test terms, and a new test class asserts the endpoint rejects query syntax.

column1: Batch job exhausts connections by opening one per record
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly job enriches accounts by calling an external data provider for each record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The job fails part way through whenever the nightly volume exceeds a few thousand accounts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The job should process the full nightly volume within its window.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It stops with a connection error after roughly 4,000 records, and a rerun with fewer records succeeds.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client created a new connection per record and never released it, so the pool was exhausted rather than any platform limit being reached. Provider-side metrics showed thousands of short-lived connections from a single source, which matched the failure point.

RESOLUTION
The client now reuses a pooled connection, releases it explicitly after each call, and batches 50 accounts per request where the provider supports it.

VALIDATION
A run over 18,000 accounts completed in 22 minutes using six connections, the provider confirmed normal connection counts, and repeated runs showed no growth in open connections.

column1: Automatic retries are safe for reads but were not extended to writes
column2:
CONTEXT
Integration clients call Salesforce for both reads and record updates during business hours.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Transient failures on write operations require manual resubmission by the operations team.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Transient failures should be retried automatically without risking duplicate or conflicting changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Reads retry automatically, while writes fail to an error queue and wait for a person.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Writes were excluded from retry because the endpoints are not idempotent and a retry could apply a change twice. Of 900 write failures in a month, 780 were transient and would have succeeded on a second attempt, and the operations team spent about six hours a week resubmitting them.

RESOLUTION
Writes that carry a client-supplied request key are now retried, because the server rejects a repeated key. This is partial: two legacy endpoints cannot accept a request key, so their writes are still queued for manual resubmission.

VALIDATION
Retries recovered 640 of 780 transient write failures over a month with no duplicate changes detected, and the two legacy endpoints continued to require manual handling.

column1: Partner platform cannot accept bulk requests, so records are sent individually
column2:
CONTEXT
Order confirmations are sent to a logistics partner whose interface accepts one order per request.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Peak-day volumes take several hours to transmit, which delays warehouse picking.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A day's orders should reach the partner within minutes of confirmation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Each order requires its own request, and the partner's rate limit caps throughput at 120 orders per minute.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner has no bulk endpoint and confirmed none is planned this year. Measurement showed transmission was rate-limited rather than latency-bound, and parallel connections beyond four produced rejections.

RESOLUTION
Dispatch now runs four parallel workers within the agreed rate and prioritizes same-day delivery orders first. This is a workaround: throughput is still bounded by the per-record interface, and a peak day remains a two-hour transmission. A bulk interface is the requested long-term change.

VALIDATION
Same-day orders reached the partner within eight minutes on three peak days, total transmission time fell from five hours to two, and no rate-limit rejections were recorded.

column1: Consumers make a second call per record to retrieve a field the response omits
column2:
CONTEXT
A reporting consumer reads opportunity records and needs the owner's regional assignment for each one.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The consumer's nightly load takes far longer than the data volume suggests it should.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
One request per page should return every attribute the consumer needs.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Regional assignment is not on the opportunity, so the consumer calls the user endpoint once per record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Regional assignment lives on a related user record that the current query does not traverse. Call counts showed 21,000 additional requests per night, and the load spent 80 percent of its time on them.

RESOLUTION
The consumer now caches user regions for the duration of a run, cutting the additional calls to one per distinct owner. This is a workaround: the extra calls remain, the cache can go stale within a long run, and a formula field exposing the region on the opportunity is the preferred fix.

VALIDATION
Additional requests fell from 21,000 to 240 per night and load time dropped by 70 percent, with region values matching a direct query for all sampled records.

column1: Secure connections fail intermittently from one middleware node
column2:
CONTEXT
Three middleware nodes behind a load balancer call Salesforce with the same configuration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One node reports connection failures during the handshake several times an hour, while the other two do not.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All three nodes should establish connections with identical reliability.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected node fails to complete the secure handshake on a small share of attempts and succeeds on retry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Configuration, runtime version, and trust store contents are identical across the three nodes. The node was rebuilt from the same image and the failures returned within a day. Captures show the connection closing after the client hello with no alert message, and this node's outbound path traverses a different firewall pair.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. Traffic has not been moved away from the node, since that would remove the only environment where the failure can be observed.

VALIDATION
Failures continue at three to eight per hour on that node only. The next step is a joint capture with the network team on both firewall pairs during a failing window, comparing the discarded connections.

column1: Requests are throttled although usage stays far below the published limit
column2:
CONTEXT
Integration clients share the organization's request allowance, which is monitored daily.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Clients receive throttling responses in short bursts while daily usage sits at about 40 percent of the allowance.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Requests should be served unless a documented limit is genuinely reached.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Bursts of throttling responses last two to three minutes and then clear without any change by the clients.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Daily counters were checked against the allowance and are well within it, so the daily quota is not the constraint. Concurrent request counts during the bursts were sampled and stayed below the concurrency threshold as measured, though sampling every 30 seconds may miss a shorter spike. The bursts do not align with any scheduled job.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. Client request rates were left unchanged, because reducing them without understanding the trigger would only mask the pattern.

VALIDATION
Bursts continue two or three times a week. The next step is enabling per-second request metrics on the gateway and correlating a burst with the platform's own limit counters through a support case.

column1: Generated queries mix two business processes that share an object
column2:
CONTEXT
Complaints and service requests are both stored as Cases and separated by record type.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Answers about complaint volume are roughly three times higher than the compliance team's own figures.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question about complaints should count complaint records only.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query counts every Case, because no record type condition is applied.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schema description listed objects and fields but not record types, so the model had no way to express the distinction. Traces showed correct date and status filters with no record type condition in 15 of 15 complaint questions.

RESOLUTION
Record types are now described in the schema with their business meaning, the generator adds a record type filter when a question names a process that maps to one, and the answer states which process was used.

VALIDATION
Fifteen complaint questions matched the compliance figures exactly, service request questions were unaffected, and a question spanning both processes returned a combined total with both record types named.

column1: Assistant invents field names that do not exist in the schema
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant generates SOQL from a schema description and executes it against the organization.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions using uncommon business vocabulary produce an invalid field error rather than an answer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should use only fields that exist, or state that the requested attribute is unavailable.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Plausible but non-existent field names appear in the generated query, such as a satisfaction score the organization does not store.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nothing checked generated identifiers against the schema before execution, so invention surfaced as a platform error. A 50-question set produced eight invalid queries, all naming fields that sound reasonable for the domain but are absent.

RESOLUTION
Every object and field in a generated query is now validated against the schema before execution. Unknown identifiers trigger one regeneration attempt with the invalid names listed, and a persistent failure returns a message naming the unavailable attribute.

VALIDATION
The eight failing questions returned either a valid query or a clear unavailable-attribute message, and no invalid query reached execution across 200 subsequent runs.

column1: Amounts are reported without stating which currency they represent
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization trades in five currencies, and opportunity amounts are stored in the deal currency with a converted value alongside.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A manager compared two answers and found totals that could not both be right for the same period.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Monetary answers should be expressed in one stated currency, normally the corporate currency.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query sums the deal currency amount across records in different currencies and presents a meaningless total with no currency named.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schema exposed both the deal amount and the converted amount without explaining the difference, and the model chose the shorter field name. Reviewing 20 monetary answers found 14 summing mixed currencies.

RESOLUTION
The schema now marks the converted field as the reporting measure and the deal field as informational, aggregation is restricted to the converted field, and every monetary answer names its currency.

VALIDATION
Twenty monetary questions returned corporate currency totals matching the finance report, and a question explicitly asking for local amounts returned them grouped by currency.

column1: Filters built from translated labels return no results
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask questions in Hebrew, while picklist values are stored in English with translated labels.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions naming a status in Hebrew return an empty result with no explanation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A status named in the user's language should resolve to the stored value it represents.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The Hebrew label is placed into the filter directly, and no stored value matches it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schema carried English values only, so the model passed through the term from the question. Testing 30 Hebrew questions produced empty results for all 12 that filtered on a picklist, while numeric and date questions were unaffected.

RESOLUTION
The schema now carries the translated label alongside each stored value, and generation resolves any label in a supported language to its stored value before building the filter, rejecting labels it cannot resolve with a list of valid options.

VALIDATION
All 12 previously failing questions returned correct results, an unrecognized status term produced the valid options list, and English questions were unchanged.

column1: Aggregate answers return personal contact details that were never requested
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant answers questions about customer volumes and service performance for operational teams.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A privacy review found answers to counting questions listing names, phone numbers, and addresses.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An aggregate question should return aggregate values without personal detail.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query selects a broad field list and the answer displays the rows behind the count.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Field selection was not tied to the question's intent, so the model included descriptive fields by default. Reviewing 40 aggregate answers found 26 containing at least one personal attribute that the question had not asked for.

RESOLUTION
Aggregate intents now select grouped and aggregate expressions only, fields classified as personal are excluded unless the question explicitly requires them and the user is entitled to them, and any such answer is recorded in the access log.

VALIDATION
Forty aggregate questions returned no personal attributes, an explicit contact-detail request by an entitled user succeeded and was logged, and the same request by an unentitled user was refused.

column1: Assistant fabricates a join when the requested data is in another system
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant queries Salesforce only, while billing and consumption data live in a separate finance platform.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions that combine CRM and billing data return confident answers that finance cannot reconcile.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should answer within its data scope and say clearly when data lies outside it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query maps billing concepts onto loosely related CRM fields and presents the result as if it answered the question.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No scope boundary was defined, so every question was treated as answerable. Of 25 mixed questions, 19 produced a query using an unrelated CRM field, most often substituting opportunity amount for invoiced revenue.

RESOLUTION
A scope definition now lists the domains the assistant covers, questions naming out-of-scope concepts return a statement of what is unavailable and where it is held, and substitution of a related field requires an explicit user confirmation.

VALIDATION
All 25 mixed questions returned the scope statement instead of a query, in-scope questions were unaffected, and a confirmed substitution was labelled as such in the answer.

column1: Evaluation measures query correctness but not the wording of the answer
column2:
CONTEXT
A regression suite runs before each prompt change and compares generated queries with approved ones.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Changes that pass the suite still produce answers that users find misleading.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Evaluation should cover both the query and the explanation presented to the user.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only query structure is compared, so a correct query with a misleading summary passes unnoticed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The suite compares normalized query text against a reference. Reviewing 30 answers that passed found six whose wording implied a filter that was not applied, mostly around date ranges described loosely.

RESOLUTION
The suite now also asserts that the answer states the period, the record scope, and the row limit when one applies. This is partial: these are structural checks, so an answer can satisfy them and still read poorly, and no measure of clarity exists yet.

VALIDATION
The extended suite caught five of the six misleading answers when they were replayed, while the sixth passed every structural check and was found only in manual review.

column1: Mixed Hebrew and English questions produce incomplete filters
column2:
CONTEXT
Users write questions in Hebrew that include English product names and technical terms.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Mixed questions often return results ignoring one of the conditions the user stated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every condition should be applied regardless of the language it is written in.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Conditions expressed in the secondary language are sometimes dropped, and the answer does not mention the omission.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Parsing handles a single language per question and picks the dominant one. Of 40 mixed questions, 15 dropped a condition, and 12 of those had the condition written in the minority language, most often an English product name inside a Hebrew sentence.

RESOLUTION
Product and status terms are now matched against a bilingual dictionary regardless of the surrounding language, and every applied condition is restated in the answer. This is partial: free-text descriptive conditions in the minority language are still not parsed, so the answer restatement is the only signal that one was dropped.

VALIDATION
Twelve of the 15 failing questions now apply every condition, and the remaining three show a restatement that makes the omission visible to the user.

column1: The full schema does not fit in the prompt, so a curated subset is used
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization has more than 300 objects, while the assistant needs schema context within its prompt budget.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions about less common objects fail because those objects are not described to the model.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should reach any object the user is entitled to query.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only the curated subset is available, and questions outside it return an unavailable-object message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Describing all objects would exceed the prompt budget several times over. Usage analysis showed 22 objects cover 94 percent of questions, while the remaining traffic spreads thinly across 60 further objects.

RESOLUTION
A curated subset of 30 objects is maintained by hand and included in every prompt. This is a workaround: coverage is fixed regardless of the question, the list ages as the organization changes, and 6 percent of questions cannot be answered. Retrieving relevant schema per question is the preferred design.

VALIDATION
Questions within the subset succeeded at the previous rate over a month, and out-of-subset questions returned the unavailable message rather than a wrong answer.

column1: The same question produces different queries on different attempts
column2:
CONTEXT
Business users repeat questions during a review and expect consistent figures.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Asking an identical question twice sometimes returns different totals.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The same question against unchanged data should produce the same query and the same answer.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Generated queries differ between attempts, usually in the date boundary or in whether a status condition is included.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The prompt, schema version, and user context were captured for repeated attempts and are identical, so input variation is excluded. Sampling settings were reduced in a test configuration and the variation narrowed but did not disappear across 300 repeats. The variants are individually defensible readings of the question, which suggests genuine ambiguity rather than a defect in one specific rule.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. The test configuration was not promoted, since it changed answer quality on other question types without removing the inconsistency.

VALIDATION
Repeated questions still diverge in roughly one attempt in twelve. The next step is a controlled study of 50 questions repeated 20 times each, classifying every variant so that ambiguity and instability can be separated.

column1: Migrated picklist values are stored but invisible on record layouts
column2:
CONTEXT
Legacy service records carry a resolution category that maps onto a Salesforce picklist.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents see an empty resolution field on migrated records, while reports show a value.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Stored values should appear on the layout and be selectable when a record is edited.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Values not defined in the picklist are stored by the load but not rendered in the field on the record page.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The picklist is unrestricted, so the load accepted values outside the defined set. A distinct value query found 14 stored values, of which 5 are not defined in the field. Editing an affected record and saving cleared the value, which risked silent data loss.

RESOLUTION
The five legacy values were mapped to defined values in a controlled update, the picklist was set to restricted to prevent recurrence, and a load-time check rejects values outside the defined set.

VALIDATION
All migrated records display a resolution value, editing no longer clears it, and a test load containing an undefined value was rejected with a clear message.

column1: Migrated amounts default to the corporate currency for foreign contracts
column2:
CONTEXT
Contracts are migrated from a legacy system into a multi-currency Salesforce organization.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Contract values for international customers appear far larger than the amounts in the legacy system.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each contract should carry the currency it was agreed in, with amounts unchanged.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Amounts load numerically correct but are labelled in the corporate currency, so converted reporting overstates them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The load file omitted the currency code column, so records defaulted to the corporate currency. Of 9,400 contracts, 2,700 belong to foreign entities, and their converted values were inflated by the applicable exchange rate.

RESOLUTION
The currency code is now supplied from the legacy entity mapping, affected records were updated with their correct currency in a controlled batch, and the load template requires the column for any currency-bearing object.

VALIDATION
Converted totals for the 2,700 contracts matched the legacy figures within rounding, a sample of 100 records showed the correct currency, and a load without the column was rejected.

column1: Phone numbers lose their leading zeros during migration
column2:
CONTEXT
Contact phone numbers are migrated from a legacy database and used for outbound calling.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents report that many migrated numbers cannot be dialled.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Numbers should arrive exactly as stored in the source, including leading zeros and formatting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Domestic numbers lose their leading zero, so the dialler treats the remaining digits as an incomplete number.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extract was opened in a spreadsheet during preparation, which interpreted the column as numeric and dropped leading zeros. Comparing the raw extract with the prepared file showed the zeros present in the first and absent in the second, affecting 31,000 of 78,000 numbers.

RESOLUTION
The pipeline no longer passes through a spreadsheet, the phone column is typed as text end to end, and a validation compares digit counts against the country pattern before load.

VALIDATION
The 31,000 affected numbers were reloaded from the raw extract and matched the source exactly, dialling tests succeeded on a 200 number sample, and the digit-count validation rejected a seeded bad file.

column1: Migrated files are visible only to the account that loaded them
column2:
CONTEXT
Documents from the legacy system are migrated as files linked to their Case and Account records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents open a migrated Case and see no documents, although the migration reports them as loaded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A migrated file should be visible to everyone who can see the record it belongs to.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Files exist and are visible to the migration account only, and the related lists appear empty for everyone else.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Files were created without a share link to the parent record, so they defaulted to private ownership. A query found 62,000 files with no record link, all created by the migration account, while a small set loaded through a later revised process linked correctly.

RESOLUTION
The migration now creates the record link with viewer access in the same step as the upload, and the 62,000 existing files were linked by a one-time job using the stored legacy parent reference.

VALIDATION
Agents saw the expected documents on 40 sampled Cases across three record types, permission tests confirmed users without record access still cannot open the files, and no unlinked files remain.

column1: Legacy yes and no indicators load as unticked for every record
column2:
CONTEXT
Legacy customer records store consent and preference indicators as single-character flags.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every migrated record shows all preferences switched off, which contradicts the source.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each indicator should migrate to its equivalent checkbox state.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All checkboxes load unticked regardless of whether the source held a yes or a no.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Checkbox fields accept a defined set of representations, and the single characters used by the source are not among them, so unrecognized input became the default. Counting the source showed 41 percent of records held a yes for at least one indicator, none of which survived the load.

RESOLUTION
The transformation now maps the source characters explicitly to true and false, rejects any other value, and a post-load comparison counts ticked boxes against the source for every batch.

VALIDATION
Reloaded records matched the source count exactly for all four indicators, a batch seeded with an unexpected character was rejected, and the marketing team confirmed consent figures against the legacy report.

column1: Migration load triggers live customer notifications
column2:
CONTEXT
Historical Cases are migrated into an organization where automation notifies customers on Case creation and closure.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers received messages about Cases from several years ago during a migration wave.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Loading historical records must not generate customer-facing communication.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Creation and closure automation ran for every loaded record, and roughly 1,800 messages reached real customers before the load was stopped.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The load was halted within twelve minutes, remaining sends were suspended, and the affected customers received a correction notice agreed with the service leadership. Deactivation of the notification automation was in the runbook but had not been carried out, and nothing in the load process verified it.

RESOLUTION
A pre-load gate now checks that customer-facing automation is deactivated and refuses to start otherwise, and notification automation excludes records marked as migrated regardless of that gate.

VALIDATION
A rehearsal load of 5,000 Cases produced no outbound messages with the gate active, the gate blocked a load when automation was left enabled, and the remaining waves completed without customer contact.

column1: Only the most recent three years of custom history is migrated in full detail
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy platform holds eleven years of service history, and the migration scope covers the fields users need day to day.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Analysts asked for older history at the same level of detail as recent records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Historical analysis should be possible across the full eleven-year period.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records older than three years arrive with core fields only, so trend analysis breaks at the boundary.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Fourteen custom fields were added to the legacy platform four years ago and are sparsely populated before that. Volume analysis showed full-detail migration of eleven years would roughly triple the loaded record size and exceed the agreed storage allocation.

RESOLUTION
Three years are migrated in full, and years four to eleven are migrated with core fields plus a monthly summary per account. This is partial: detailed analysis before the boundary is not possible, and questions needing the older detail must go to the retained archive extract.

VALIDATION
Trend reports run continuously across eleven years at summary level, detailed reports were verified for the three-year window, and analysts confirmed the summary answers four of their six recurring questions.

column1: Calculated legacy values cannot be loaded into their formula equivalents
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy system stored calculated values such as account tenure and lifetime value as stored numbers.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Migrated records show different values from the legacy reports for those measures.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Historical measures should match the legacy figures that the business has been reporting for years.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The Salesforce equivalents are formula fields that recalculate from current data, so historical values cannot be written.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The formulas use current-date arithmetic and current related records, which differ from the legacy snapshot. Comparing 200 accounts showed differences on 178, in most cases because the legacy value was calculated at a past point in time.

RESOLUTION
The legacy values are loaded into companion number fields labelled as historical, alongside the live formula fields. This is a workaround: two similar measures now exist on the record, and users must know which to use for which period. Snapshotting the formula on a schedule would remove the ambiguity.

VALIDATION
Historical fields matched the legacy report for all 200 sampled accounts, live formulas continued to recalculate, and reports were relabelled to name the measure they use.

column1: Load throughput collapses from the third wave onward
column2:
CONTEXT
