Customer records are migrated in weekly waves of roughly 400,000 records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The third and fourth waves ran four times longer than the first two with identical configuration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Load duration should scale with record count and stay broadly consistent between waves.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Throughput fell from about 5,000 records per minute to 1,200 and stayed there for the rest of each run.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Batch size, parallelism, and file structure are identical across waves. Automation was disabled for the load user and duplicate rules were off, so the usual causes are excluded. Ownership is spread across 200 users, so owner concentration does not apply. Record counts on the target object grew from 0.8 to 2.1 million between the second and third waves, which is a candidate but unproven.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. No index or model change has been made, since the slowdown is unattributed.

VALIDATION
Both remaining waves ran at the reduced rate. The next step is a controlled test loading 50,000 records into an empty sandbox and into a copy holding two million, comparing throughput under identical conditions.

column1: Delta migration reloads records that were already migrated from one source partition
column2:
CONTEXT
After the initial load, a delta process migrates records changed in the source since the previous run.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Each delta run resubmits several thousand unchanged records, all from one source partition.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A delta run should select only records modified since the previous watermark.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records from one of six partitions are selected repeatedly, and their upserts overwrite target values with identical data.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The watermark is stored per partition and advances correctly for five of six. On the affected partition, modification timestamps for the resubmitted records sit slightly ahead of the watermark on every run, which explains the selection, but the source team reports no process touching those records. Two consecutive extracts showed identical field values with different modification timestamps.

RESOLUTION
No verified cause or fix exists. The watermark was not moved forward manually, because that would risk skipping genuine changes on the same partition.

VALIDATION
Reloads continue each run with no data difference detected. The next step is a source-side audit of what advances the modification timestamp on that partition, including maintenance jobs that touch rows without changing values.

column1: Automation stops matching records after deployment to production
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow applies premium handling rules to Cases of one record type.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The rules worked throughout sandbox testing and applied to nothing after release.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Behaviour should be identical in every environment after a straightforward deployment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No Case matches the entry criteria in production, and no interview is created.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The entry condition compared the record type identifier against a value copied from the sandbox. Identifiers are generated per environment, so the production value differs and the comparison never succeeds. A search of the metadata found the same pattern in two other automations that had not yet been noticed.

RESOLUTION
All three automations now resolve the record type by its developer name rather than its identifier, and a deployment check rejects metadata containing environment-specific identifiers.

VALIDATION
Premium Cases matched correctly in production within minutes of the change, the two other automations were confirmed working, and the deployment check blocked a test package containing a hard-coded identifier.

column1: Screen flow fails for agents who lack access to a field it updates
column2:
CONTEXT
A screen flow lets support agents log a service outcome, which updates a compliance field on the Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents on the standard support profile cannot complete the flow, while team leads can.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any agent permitted to run the flow should be able to complete it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The final update fails with an insufficient access error naming the compliance field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow runs in user context, and the compliance field is read-only for the support profile by design, since it must not be edited directly on the record. Team leads have edit access, which is why the defect appeared to affect only some users.

RESOLUTION
The update was moved into a subflow that runs in system context with sharing, so the field is written only through the controlled outcome path while remaining read-only on the layout.

VALIDATION
Twenty agents across three profiles completed the flow successfully, direct edits to the field remained blocked on the record page, and the field history shows the flow as the only writer.

column1: Reminder messages are sent immediately instead of before the due date
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled path sends a reminder three days before the commitment date recorded on a service agreement.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some customers receive their reminder within minutes of the agreement being created.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A reminder should be scheduled relative to a real commitment date, or not scheduled at all.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Agreements with no commitment date produce an interview that runs at the next available opportunity.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scheduled path uses the commitment date as its base, and an empty base resolves to a time already in the past, so the platform executes it immediately. Of 640 agreements, 58 had no commitment date at creation, and all 58 produced an early reminder.

RESOLUTION
The flow now requires a commitment date before scheduling, records with no date are routed to the owner for completion, and the reminder is scheduled when the date is later supplied.

VALIDATION
Agreements without a date produced no reminder and appeared on the owner list, dated agreements reminded exactly three days early, and a date added later scheduled correctly.

column1: Bulk case updates fail once a load exceeds two hundred records
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow updates related asset records whenever a Case reaches a closed state.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Closing Cases individually works, while bulk closures fail for the whole batch.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A batch closure should update every related asset without failing.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Batches above roughly 200 Cases fail with a limit error, and no asset in the batch is updated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The update element sits inside the loop, so each iteration issues its own statement and the transaction exceeds the permitted number. Debug logs for a 250 record batch showed the limit reached partway through, and the whole transaction rolled back.

RESOLUTION
The loop now collects assets into a collection variable and a single update runs after the loop, which issues one statement per transaction regardless of batch size.

VALIDATION
Batches of 200, 500, and 2,000 Cases completed successfully, every related asset was updated, and debug logs showed one statement per transaction.

column1: Notifications reach customers in a language they did not choose
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers select a correspondence language, and automated service notifications should follow it.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers who chose a language other than English receive English notifications.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each notification should use the template matching the recipient's language preference.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every notification uses the same template, and the preference field is never read.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The send action referenced one template directly. Translated templates existed but had been created for a different process and were never linked to this flow. A count showed 31 percent of active contacts have a non-English preference.

RESOLUTION
The flow now selects the template through a mapping from the language preference, falls back to English when no translation exists, and records the language used on the notification log.

VALIDATION
Test sends for four languages produced the correct template, a contact with an unsupported language received the English fallback with a log entry, and the service team reviewed each translation before release.

column1: Product selection screen offers items that can no longer be sold
column2:
CONTEXT
A screen flow lets service agents add a replacement product to a warranty claim.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents select products that the fulfilment team then rejects as unavailable.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The picker should offer only products that are active and available for the customer's region.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Discontinued and region-restricted products appear alongside valid ones with nothing to distinguish them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The lookup component had no filter, so it searched the whole product catalogue. Of 4,200 products, 1,100 are discontinued and a further 600 are restricted to regions other than the customer's, which matches the pattern of rejected claims.

RESOLUTION
The picker now filters on active status and the customer's region, and shows the product code alongside the name so agents can confirm their selection.

VALIDATION
Searches in three regions returned only permitted products, fulfilment rejections for unavailable items stopped over a four-week period, and a discontinued product could not be selected in testing.

column1: Error handling has been added to some automations but not all
column2:
CONTEXT
A review after a silent automation failure recommended fault handling on every record-triggered flow.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Failures in automations without fault paths remain invisible until a user notices missing data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every automation should record its failures where support can see them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Twelve of nineteen flows now log failures, while the remaining seven fail silently.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The twelve updated flows follow a shared error subflow. The remaining seven are older, contain elements that cannot connect to a fault path, and two are managed package flows that cannot be edited at all.

RESOLUTION
The shared error subflow was applied to every flow that supports it, covering twelve of nineteen. This is partial: five flows need restructuring before fault paths can be attached, and two managed flows can only be monitored indirectly through their output.

VALIDATION
Deliberate failures in the twelve covered flows produced log entries within a minute, while a failure in an uncovered flow was detected only by the output monitor.

column1: Releasing the automation requires a manual deactivation sequence
column2:
CONTEXT
Three flows call a shared subflow, and all four are deployed together during releases.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deployments fail partway through and leave the automations in an inconsistent state.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The set should deploy as one unit without manual steps.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The subflow cannot be replaced while the calling flows reference the current version, so the deployment stops with a dependency error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Active flows hold a reference to the exact subflow version they were saved against. Two of the last three releases failed at this step, each requiring about 40 minutes of manual recovery.

RESOLUTION
Releases now follow a documented sequence that deactivates the calling flows, deploys the subflow, then reactivates them. This is a workaround: the automations are inactive for two to three minutes during the release, records saved in that window are not processed, and the sequence depends on the operator following it exactly.

VALIDATION
Three releases completed without a dependency error, and a reconciliation job identified and reprocessed the 14 records saved during the inactive windows.

column1: Selecting an account in the intake screen is slow for large territories
column2:
CONTEXT
An intake screen flow asks agents to choose the customer account before capturing request details.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents wait several seconds for the account list to load and often abandon the screen.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Selecting an account should feel immediate regardless of how many accounts exist.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The picklist loads the agent's full territory, which can exceed 30,000 accounts, before the screen renders.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The choice set was built from a query with no limit, so the entire territory was retrieved on every render. Screen render time correlated directly with territory size across eight agents.

RESOLUTION
The picklist was replaced with a search field returning the 200 closest matches as the agent types. This is a workaround: an agent whose search term matches more than 200 accounts must refine it, and no total count is shown. A dedicated search component with paging is the preferred replacement.

VALIDATION
Screen render dropped from six seconds to under one for the largest territory, and agents found their account within two attempts in 95 of 100 observed intakes.

column1: Automation fails only when the record is saved from the mobile application
column2:
CONTEXT
Field engineers update job records from the mobile application, and a flow calculates travel allowance on save.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Allowance is calculated correctly from the browser and fails intermittently from mobile.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The calculation should behave identically regardless of the client used to save the record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Mobile saves occasionally complete without an allowance, and the engineer sees no error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow logic contains no client-specific branch, and the same records calculate correctly when re-saved from a browser. Failures cluster on engineers working in areas with poor connectivity, which suggests an interrupted or partial save, but the platform records the save as complete and the audit history shows only one save event.

RESOLUTION
The mechanism has not been identified, so nothing has been changed in the flow or the mobile configuration.

VALIDATION
Missing allowances continue at roughly two per week. The next step is adding a device and session marker to each save, then comparing the marked records against the engineers' connectivity logs for the same period.

column1: Cases are routed to the wrong business unit after a routing table change
column2:
CONTEXT
Middleware maps incoming service requests to business units using a routing table held in its configuration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Requests for a newly created business unit continued to reach the old owner after the table was updated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A routing change should take effect for messages processed after the update.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The middleware kept applying the previous mapping until it was restarted several days later.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The configuration is read once when the process starts and held for its lifetime, with no reload on change. Message traces showed the old mapping applied to 1,900 requests after the update, and correct routing resumed exactly at the restart.

RESOLUTION
The routing table is now read from a versioned source on each batch, the active version is written into every message log entry, and a mismatch between expected and active version raises an alert.

VALIDATION
A routing change took effect on the following batch without a restart, the 1,900 misrouted requests were reassigned, and a forced version mismatch raised the alert as designed.

column1: Records whose names contain an apostrophe fail to synchronize
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware component builds queries and payloads to reconcile customer records between two systems.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A consistent group of customers never synchronizes and always appears in the error report.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Customer names should synchronize regardless of the characters they contain.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Names containing an apostrophe produce a malformed statement error, and the record is skipped.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The component assembled its filter by concatenating the name into the statement text without escaping, so an apostrophe terminated the literal early. Every one of the 430 persistently failing records contained an apostrophe, and the same records succeeded when the character was removed manually.

RESOLUTION
The component now uses parameter binding for every value it passes, so no caller data alters the statement structure, and a test suite covers quotes, backslashes, and non-Latin characters.

VALIDATION
All 430 records synchronized on the next run, the character test suite passed for six scripts, and a review confirmed no remaining concatenated statements in the codebase.

column1: Records at the window boundary are transferred twice each night
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly extract selects records modified between the previous run time and the current run time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of records appear in two consecutive nightly files.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each modified record should appear in exactly one nightly extract.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records modified exactly at a boundary timestamp are included by both the run that ends there and the run that starts there.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both ends of the window used an inclusive comparison, so a record modified at the boundary satisfied both. Between 20 and 60 records fell exactly on a boundary each night, which is plausible given that batch jobs update many records at the same second.

RESOLUTION
The window is now inclusive at the start and exclusive at the end, and each run records the exact boundary it used so consecutive windows join without a gap or an overlap.

VALIDATION
Fourteen consecutive nights produced no repeated record, a controlled test placing records exactly on the boundary transferred each once, and total counts matched the source change log.

column1: Outbound messages stop being understood after a field label change
column2:
CONTEXT
Salesforce sends outbound notifications to a partner system whenever a service order changes state.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The partner began rejecting notifications after an internal change that renamed several field labels.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cosmetic label changes should have no effect on integration messages.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The partner's parser cannot find two elements it expects and rejects the entire message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Message elements use the field's programmatic name, which did not change, but the partner had built their parser against the human-readable labels supplied in an early specification document. Reviewing the message payload confirmed the programmatic names were unchanged throughout.

RESOLUTION
The partner corrected their parser to use the programmatic names, and the integration contract was documented with those names as the binding reference and the labels marked as informational.

VALIDATION
The rejected notifications were replayed and accepted, a deliberate label change in a sandbox produced no parser effect, and both parties signed the corrected contract.

column1: Integration writes approved status without passing through the approval process
column2:
CONTEXT
Discount requests require an approval before their status may be set to approved.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit found approved requests with no approval history and no approver recorded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A request should reach approved status only through the approval process.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The pricing integration writes the status field directly, bypassing the process entirely.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration was built to reflect decisions taken in the pricing system, and nothing prevented it from writing a controlled field. Of 3,100 approved requests, 240 had no approval history, all created by the integration user, and 12 exceeded the threshold that requires a second approver.

RESOLUTION
A validation rule now blocks direct writes to the status field, the integration submits requests to the approval process with the external decision recorded as the justification, and the 12 threshold breaches were reviewed by the approvers.

VALIDATION
New integration requests produced full approval history, direct status writes were rejected in testing, and the audit sample found no request approved outside the process.

column1: Change-based synchronization covers most objects but not all
column2:
CONTEXT
The data platform receives Salesforce changes through change events rather than nightly extracts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reports built on some objects are up to a day behind those built on others.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every replicated object should arrive through the same near real-time path.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Eight of eleven objects publish change events, and the remaining three still rely on the nightly extract.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Two of the three are objects for which change events are not available on the platform, and the third produces an event volume that exceeds the platform allowance during business hours.

RESOLUTION
Change events were enabled for the eight supported objects and the consumers were migrated. This is partial: two objects have no event support and remain nightly, and the high-volume object publishes only for records flagged as material, so its remaining changes still arrive overnight.

VALIDATION
The eight migrated objects arrived within two minutes over three weeks, event volume stayed within allowance, and the three remaining objects continued on the nightly schedule as documented.

column1: Alerting catches outright failures but not partially applied messages
column2:
CONTEXT
Integration monitoring raises alerts when a message fails so that support can intervene quickly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Data inconsistencies are still discovered by users days after the messages that caused them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any message that does not fully apply should raise an alert.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Alerts fire only when a message is rejected outright, while a message that applies some records and skips others is treated as successful.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Multi-record messages return a per-record result, and the handler examined only the overall response. A review of one week found 87 messages with at least one skipped record, none of which raised an alert.

RESOLUTION
The handler now inspects per-record results and alerts on any skipped record with its reason. This is partial: two legacy endpoints return a single aggregate response with no per-record detail, so partial application on those paths is still invisible.

VALIDATION
The 87 historical messages were reprocessed and their skipped records identified, and new partial results raised alerts within a minute except on the two legacy endpoints.

column1: Intra-day updates are emulated by polling because the feed is daily
column2:
CONTEXT
Credit limits are supplied by a finance platform that publishes a single file each morning.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users work with credit limits that are stale after a mid-day change, which blocks or wrongly permits orders.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A credit limit change should reach Salesforce within a short time of being approved.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Changes wait for the following morning's file, so a customer whose limit was raised cannot order that day.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The finance platform has no event capability, though it exposes a status endpoint that reports a customer's current limit on request. Analysis showed roughly 40 limit changes a day across 12,000 customers.

RESOLUTION
The daily file remains the baseline, and a poll checks the status endpoint for customers with recent order activity every 30 minutes. This is a workaround: customers with no recent activity still wait for the next file, and polling covers about 900 of 12,000 customers.

VALIDATION
Limit changes for actively trading customers appeared within 35 minutes over two weeks, and the daily file continued to reconcile the full base each morning.

column1: Some synchronized records arrive holding another customer's field values
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware process transforms customer records in parallel worker threads before writing them to Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Three records were found carrying contact details belonging to a different customer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each record must contain only the values supplied for that customer.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Affected records hold a correct identifier with two or three fields populated from another record in the same batch.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The affected records were corrected from source, the integration was reduced to a single worker as containment, and the incident was escalated to the data protection lead because customer data crossed records. Source payloads for the three cases were retrieved and are correct, so the values were combined after extraction. A replay of the same batch through the multi-threaded path did not reproduce the defect in twenty attempts.

RESOLUTION
The defect has not been located and no code change has been released. Running single-threaded is containment rather than a fix.

VALIDATION
No further crossed records have appeared, though throughput has halved. The next step is a code review of shared state in the transformation workers and a soak test with instrumented identifiers.

column1: The previous day's file is occasionally processed a second time
column2:
CONTEXT
A supplier drops a daily inventory file that the middleware collects, processes, and archives.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Roughly once a month the previous file is processed again, reverting a day of inventory changes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each file should be processed exactly once and then archived.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
An archived file is collected and applied a second time, and the log shows two runs for the same file name.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The collector moves each file to an archive folder outside the collection path, so simple reprocessing should not be possible. On the affected dates the supplier uploaded a corrected file under the same name, but the collector's recorded timestamps do not consistently support that explanation.

RESOLUTION
Nothing has been changed in the collector, because the sequence that leads to reprocessing is still unclear and a guard built on the wrong assumption could reject legitimate corrected files.

VALIDATION
The pattern has recurred twice since the investigation began. The next step is recording a content hash and the supplier's upload timestamp for every collected file, so a repeat can be classified as a correction or a collection fault.

column1: A departed employee's integration token continues to work after deactivation
column2:
CONTEXT
Staff authorize a mobile productivity application that stores a long-lived token for background access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A leaver review found that a deactivated user's application access was still returning data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All access must stop when a user account is deactivated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The stored authorization survived deactivation and continued to serve requests for that user's records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The authorization was revoked immediately and the security team was informed. Deactivation ends interactive sessions but does not automatically revoke every previously granted application authorization. A review of the connected application found 14 authorizations belonging to former staff, of which two had been used since the person left.

RESOLUTION
Offboarding now revokes application authorizations as an explicit step, a scheduled job reports authorizations held by inactive users, and the connected application policy was tightened to expire unused authorizations.

VALIDATION
All 14 stale authorizations were revoked, a test deactivation showed the authorization removed within the same hour, and the scheduled report has returned no rows for three weeks.

column1: A refreshed sandbox exposes live customer contact details to external developers
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner development team works in a full sandbox refreshed from production each quarter.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found real customer names, addresses, and phone numbers present in the partner sandbox.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Non-production environments accessible to external parties must not contain identifiable customer data.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The refresh copied production records unchanged, and the partner team had full read access to them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Partner access was suspended the same day and the data protection lead opened an incident. A full sandbox copies data by design, and the masking step existed in the runbook but ran only on request. Access logs showed browsing activity consistent with development work and no bulk extraction.

RESOLUTION
Masking now runs automatically as part of the refresh before access is restored, personal fields are replaced with generated values, and partner access is granted only after the masking job reports completion.

VALIDATION
The sandbox was re-masked and a sample of 500 records contained no identifiable values, the refresh pipeline blocked access until masking completed, and the partner team confirmed the masked data remained usable.

column1: Files shared through public links remain reachable without a login
column2:
CONTEXT
Users can generate shareable links for files so that customers can download documents without an account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit found active public links to internal pricing documents created more than a year earlier.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Public links should exist only for documents intended for external distribution and should expire.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Links never expire, remain valid after the file owner leaves, and can be created for any file the user can see.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The links were deactivated immediately and the security team was notified. A query found 1,430 active public links, of which 260 pointed at documents classified as internal. Access records showed no retrieval of the internal documents from outside the corporate network.

RESOLUTION
Public link creation is now restricted to a permission granted to customer-facing roles, links expire after 30 days, and a weekly report lists active links with their document classification.

VALIDATION
The 260 internal links were removed and confirmed unreachable, users without the permission could no longer create links, and a test link expired on schedule.

column1: A pilot permission left assigned to everyone allows validation rules to be bypassed
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom permission was created so that a pilot group could bypass validation rules during a data cleanup.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Data quality reports show records saved without mandatory fields long after the cleanup ended.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The bypass should have been limited to the pilot group and removed when the cleanup finished.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The permission is included in a permission set assigned to all internal users, so every user can save invalid records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The permission was added to a widely assigned permission set for convenience during the pilot and never removed. An assignment report showed 780 users holding it, and 2,300 records had been saved with fields the rules would otherwise require.

RESOLUTION
The permission was removed from the broad permission set and granted to a named data steward group, and a quarterly report now lists custom permissions with unusually wide assignment.

VALIDATION
Validation rules applied for all standard users in testing, stewards retained the bypass, and the 2,300 incomplete records were routed to their owners for correction.

column1: Audit history is retained for less time than the compliance policy requires
column2:
CONTEXT
Configuration changes and field history support an internal control requiring three years of evidence.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit request for evidence from 20 months ago returned nothing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Audit evidence should be retrievable for the full retention period stated in the policy.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Setup audit entries are retained for six months and field history for eighteen, after which they are no longer available.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retention periods are platform defaults and were never compared against the policy. Testing confirmed the oldest available setup entry was 181 days old, and the gap between platform retention and policy had existed since the org was created.

RESOLUTION
A scheduled job now exports setup audit entries and tracked field history to the corporate log store where retention is seven years, with an integrity check on each export.

VALIDATION
Exports have run daily for six weeks with matching record counts, a retrieval test returned evidence from the export for a date outside platform retention, and the control owner accepted the arrangement.

column1: Protected identifiers are written in clear text to an integration log field
column2:
CONTEXT
National identifiers on the customer object are protected so that only a small team can read them.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found the same identifiers readable in a custom integration log object visible to support staff.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Protected values must not be copied into records with weaker access controls.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration writes the full request payload into a log field, including the protected identifier.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Access to the log object was restricted the same day and the data protection lead was informed. The logging step captured the whole payload for troubleshooting with no field filtering. A query found identifiers in 46,000 log records spanning fourteen months.

RESOLUTION
The logger now writes an allowed field list only and masks anything classified as protected, the historical log records were purged after an evidence sample was retained under restricted access, and a scheduled scan checks log fields for identifier patterns.

VALIDATION
New log records contained no protected values across a 2,000 record sample, the scan flagged a deliberately seeded value, and support retained the diagnostic detail they need.

column1: Permission set consolidation is complete for support but not for sales
column2:
CONTEXT
A programme is replacing overlapping permission sets with a role-based model built from functional building blocks.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Access reviews remain difficult because two models exist side by side.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every user should receive access through the role-based model alone.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Support roles are fully migrated, while sales users hold a mixture of new blocks and legacy sets.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Support access was straightforward to decompose, whereas sales access varies by product line and includes territory-driven grants that the building blocks do not yet express. An analysis found 34 legacy sets remaining, 22 of them held by fewer than five users each.

RESOLUTION
Support is fully migrated and 12 of the sales legacy sets were retired. This is partial: 22 legacy sets remain because territory-driven access has no equivalent in the new model, and reviews for those users still require manual interpretation.

VALIDATION
Support access reviews completed from the model alone with no manual steps, and the retired sets were confirmed unassigned, while sales reviews still required manual work for 140 users.

column1: Monitoring covers login events but not data export activity
column2:
CONTEXT
Security monitoring ingests platform events to detect unusual behaviour.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An investigation into a suspected large export could not establish what was extracted.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both authentication and data access activity should be monitored and retained.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Login events are ingested and alerted on, while report exports and bulk queries are not collected at all.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The ingestion was built around authentication use cases. Testing showed export and bulk query events are produced by the platform but were never subscribed to, and the retained login data cannot answer questions about what was read.

RESOLUTION
Report export events are now ingested with alerting on volume thresholds. This is partial: bulk query events are not yet ingested because their volume exceeds the current licence allowance, so large programmatic reads remain unmonitored.

VALIDATION
A test export of 50,000 rows produced an alert within four minutes, and the retained events answered the questions the earlier investigation could not, while a scripted bulk query produced no event.

column1: Access to a sensitive object cannot be logged natively, so an automation records it
column2:
CONTEXT
A control requires a record of every read of the customer vulnerability object.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
No native mechanism records who has viewed an individual record of that object.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every read of a vulnerability record should be attributable to a user and a time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Read activity leaves no trace beyond aggregate login information.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Record-level read logging is not available for this object on the current licence. Testing showed that reads through the record page can be captured by an automation on the page, while reads through reports, list views, and the API cannot.

RESOLUTION
An automation on the record page writes an access entry for each view. This is a workaround: it covers the record page only, so a user who reads the same data through a report or the API leaves no entry, and the control is documented as partial coverage.

VALIDATION
Page views produced an entry for 200 test reads with the correct user and time, while a report listing the same records produced none, as expected and documented.

column1: Users briefly see another user's data after switching between applications
column2:
CONTEXT
Staff move between the internal application and the partner community in the same browser session.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two users saw a colleague's task list for a moment after switching applications.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every screen must render only data belonging to the authenticated user.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A previous user's list appears briefly before the screen refreshes correctly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both reports came from shared workstations where a colleague had used the browser earlier, and the security team was engaged because content crossed between users. Sessions were revoked and shared workstations now close the browser between users as containment. Session records show a clean logout in one case and a timeout in the other. The behaviour was not reproduced in 60 scripted attempts across three browsers.

RESOLUTION
The cause is unconfirmed, and no application change has been made because the conditions that produce the stale render are unknown.

VALIDATION
No further reports since the workstation change, though that also removes the conditions needed to observe it. The next step is a controlled test on an instrumented workstation with session tracing, and a vendor case citing both incidents.

column1: Filter logic returns far more rows than the stated criteria
column2:
CONTEXT
A compliance report lists high-value cases that are either overdue or escalated within a chosen region.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The report returns cases from every region, which makes the regional review meaningless.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The region condition should apply to both the overdue and the escalated branches.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Escalated cases from all regions appear, while overdue cases are correctly limited.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The custom filter logic combined the conditions without parentheses, so the region test bound to the first branch only. Reproducing the logic by hand on ten sample cases matched the report output exactly, which confirmed the grouping rather than the data.

RESOLUTION
The filter logic now groups the two branches explicitly before combining them with the region condition, and the report description states the intended logic in words.

VALIDATION
Row counts matched a manually written query for four regions, out-of-region escalations disappeared, and a reviewer reproduced the logic from the description without ambiguity.

column1: Weekly snapshot captures an incomplete week and understates volume
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled job stores a weekly snapshot of case volume per team for long-term trend reporting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every week in the trend sits below the figure the same period shows when queried directly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A weekly snapshot should cover the complete week it represents.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The snapshot runs on Friday evening and misses cases created over the weekend, which are then never counted.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schedule was set when the business did not operate at weekends, and weekend support was introduced two years ago. Comparing snapshots with direct queries for eight weeks showed a consistent shortfall matching weekend volume, averaging 11 percent.

RESOLUTION
The snapshot now runs early Monday for the week that has just closed, with the period boundaries written into each snapshot record so the covered range is explicit.

VALIDATION
Eight weeks were rebuilt from history and matched direct queries exactly, new snapshots reconciled for four consecutive weeks, and the stored boundaries were confirmed on each record.

column1: Growth percentages are unusable for products with no prior-period sales
column2:
CONTEXT
A product performance report shows period-on-period growth as a percentage change.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Newly launched products show blank or extreme growth figures that dominate the sorted view.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Products with no comparable prior period should be identified rather than assigned a percentage.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Division by a zero prior period produces an empty value, and near-zero prior periods produce percentages in the thousands.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The formula divided the difference by the prior period with no guard. Of 340 products, 28 had no prior-period sales and 14 had prior sales below a hundred units, which produced the extreme values that topped the sorted report.

RESOLUTION
The report now labels products with no prior period as new, suppresses the percentage for prior periods below a materiality threshold, and shows the absolute change alongside the percentage in every row.

VALIDATION
The sorted view was reviewed by the product team and no longer led with new products, the 28 new products were labelled correctly, and absolute changes reconciled with the sales ledger.

column1: Customer cohorts are built from orders that were later cancelled
column2:
CONTEXT
Retention analysis groups customers into cohorts by the month of their first order.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Retention curves show an implausible drop in the first month for several cohorts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A cohort should be defined by the first order the customer actually completed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Cancelled orders establish the cohort, so customers appear to join and immediately disappear.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The cohort query selected the earliest order regardless of status. Recomputing with cancelled orders excluded moved 1,900 of 24,000 customers to a later cohort, and the first-month drop disappeared from every affected curve.

RESOLUTION
Cohort assignment now uses the earliest order in a completed or fulfilled state, and the definition is recorded in the analytics dictionary alongside the query.

VALIDATION
Recomputed cohorts produced smooth retention curves for twelve months, the 1,900 reassigned customers were spot-checked against their order history, and the dictionary entry was reviewed by the analytics owner.

column1: Value bands overlap, so records are counted in two ranges
column2:
CONTEXT
A deal size report groups opportunities into value bands for the sales planning review.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Band totals sum to more than the overall pipeline figure.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each opportunity should fall into exactly one band, and the bands should sum to the total.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Opportunities at a band boundary appear in the band below and the band above.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The band definitions used inclusive limits at both ends, so a deal at a boundary satisfied two conditions. A query on boundary values found 210 opportunities counted twice, which matched the difference between the band sum and the pipeline total exactly.

RESOLUTION
Band definitions now use an inclusive lower bound and an exclusive upper bound, and a check compares the sum of the bands with the unbanded total whenever the report is refreshed.

VALIDATION
Band totals matched the pipeline figure for four quarters, the 210 boundary opportunities each appeared once, and the check flagged a deliberately overlapping test definition.

column1: Certified datasets exist for two teams while others build their own queries
column2:
CONTEXT
A programme publishes certified datasets so that teams stop building conflicting definitions of the same measure.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Leadership still receives different figures for the same measure from different teams.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every reporting team should build on certified datasets with agreed definitions.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two teams use certified datasets, while three continue to write their own queries against raw objects.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Certification requires an agreed owner for each measure, and the three remaining teams report on measures with no single business owner. Comparing eleven headline measures found four with two or more competing definitions in active use.

RESOLUTION
Certified datasets cover the seven measures with agreed owners and are used by two teams. This is partial: four measures remain uncertified because ownership is unresolved, and teams reporting on them continue to build independent queries.

VALIDATION
The seven certified measures returned identical values across both teams for three months, while the four uncertified measures still differed between teams in the same period.

column1: The data dictionary documents core objects but not custom ones
column2:
CONTEXT
A data dictionary explains what each field means so that analysts build reports on the right attributes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Analysts misuse custom fields whose names do not make their meaning obvious.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every field used in reporting should have a documented definition and owner.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Standard objects are documented, while custom objects and fields added by project teams are largely undocumented.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Documentation was produced during the original implementation and not maintained since. Of 1,100 fields used in active reports, 690 are documented, and the undocumented remainder is concentrated in fields added over the past three years.

RESOLUTION
Definitions were written for the 120 undocumented fields that appear in more than five reports, and new fields now require a definition at deployment. This is partial: about 290 rarely used fields remain undocumented, and their original authors have in many cases left.

VALIDATION
Analyst queries about field meaning fell by roughly half over two months, the deployment check rejected two undefined new fields, and the rarely used fields remain flagged as undocumented in the dictionary.

column1: A metric definition changed, so two versions run side by side
column2:
CONTEXT
The customer satisfaction measure was redefined to exclude survey responses from internal testers.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The redefinition changes historical figures that have already been reported to the board.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Reporting should move to the improved definition without invalidating previously published figures.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Applying the new definition retrospectively changes every published historical value by up to two points.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Internal test responses are identifiable from a flag added eighteen months ago, and earlier responses cannot be classified reliably. Recomputing the past two years showed changes of 0.4 to 2.1 points per quarter.

RESOLUTION
Both measures are published side by side with a documented switch date, and the old measure remains for periods before it. This is a workaround: two similar measures now appear in reporting, readers must know which applies to which period, and a single continuous series is not available.

VALIDATION
Both series were published for two quarters and reconciled with their definitions, and the board pack was reviewed to confirm the switch date is stated wherever the measure appears.

column1: Group reporting requires manual consolidation across two organizations
column2:
CONTEXT
An acquired business runs its own Salesforce organization, and group reporting must cover both.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Group figures take several days to assemble each month and are prone to error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Group reporting should draw from both organizations without manual assembly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Reports are exported separately and combined by hand, with product and region values mapped manually each time.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two organizations use different picklist values for products and regions, and no common customer key exists. A comparison found 40 product values in one organization mapping to 27 in the other, with six needing judgement.

RESOLUTION
A documented mapping sheet and a fixed export procedure reduced assembly from three days to about four hours. This is a workaround: consolidation is still manual and monthly, the six judgement cases are decided by one analyst, and no group figure exists between cycles.

VALIDATION
Three monthly cycles completed within the shorter window and reconciled with both source organizations, while the judgement cases required the same analyst each time.

column1: A scheduled report returns fewer rows than the same report run by hand
column2:
CONTEXT
A daily report of open escalations is delivered on a schedule and also opened manually by the duty manager.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The delivered version regularly contains fewer escalations than the manual run minutes later.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both runs should return the same rows when the underlying data has not changed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The scheduled version is missing between two and nine rows, and the missing rows differ each day.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report has no relative date filter that would shift between runs, and the missing escalations were created hours earlier, so a data change during the interval is unlikely. Scheduled reports run as their owner, whose access is broader than the duty manager's rather than narrower, which does not explain absent rows.

RESOLUTION
The discrepancy is not explained by anything found so far, so the schedule has been left unchanged rather than reconfigured on a guess.

VALIDATION
The gap recurs on most days. The next step is capturing the delivered file and a manual run within the same minute for a week, then comparing the missing record identifiers against their creation and sharing details.

column1: Customer replies go to an unmonitored mailbox and are never answered
column2:
CONTEXT
Automated service notifications are sent from a no-reply style address with a separate reply address configured.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers complained that replies to service notifications received no response for weeks.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A customer reply should reach the support team and create or update a Case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Replies arrive in a legacy mailbox that no longer forwards anywhere, and nothing is created in Salesforce.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The reply address pointed at a mailbox retired during a mail platform migration, and the forwarding rule was removed with it. Mailbox administrators recovered 2,100 unread messages spanning nine weeks, 340 of which needed a response.

RESOLUTION
The reply address now points at the monitored support routing address, the recovered messages were imported and triaged by priority, and a monthly check verifies that every configured reply address resolves to a monitored destination.

VALIDATION
Test replies created Cases within two minutes, the 340 messages needing action were answered within five working days, and the monthly check confirmed all seven configured addresses resolve correctly.

column1: Signature and disclaimer are missing from messages sent by quick action
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound customer messages must carry the team signature and a regulatory disclaimer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Compliance sampling found messages without the disclaimer, all sent from the Case page.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every outbound customer message should include the signature and disclaimer regardless of how it is composed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages composed through the standard action include both, while those sent through a custom quick action include neither.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The quick action was built with its own composition template that predates the disclaimer requirement. Sampling 400 sent messages found 96 without the disclaimer, all from the quick action, which accounts for about a quarter of outbound volume.

RESOLUTION
The quick action now uses the shared template that appends the signature and disclaimer, and a test asserts the disclaimer is present in messages sent through every available path.

VALIDATION
A sample of 200 messages across four sending paths all contained the disclaimer, the compliance team repeated their sampling with no exceptions, and the test failed as expected against the previous configuration.

column1: Internal working notes are included in the message sent to the customer
column2:
CONTEXT
A resolution message sends the customer a summary of how their case was resolved.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A customer quoted internal wording that should never have left the organization.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Customer messages should contain the customer-facing summary only.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The template merges the internal working notes field instead of the customer summary field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Sending was suspended and the affected messages were identified within the hour, and the service lead contacted the customers concerned. The two fields have similar labels, and the template was built against the wrong one. A review found 260 messages sent with internal notes over five weeks, 18 of which contained commercially sensitive wording.

RESOLUTION
The template now merges the customer summary field, the internal notes field was renamed to make its purpose unmistakable, and a pre-send check blocks templates that reference internal-only fields.

VALIDATION
Test sends contained the customer summary only, the pre-send check rejected a template referencing the notes field, and the 18 sensitive cases were handled individually by the service lead.

column1: Messages to a departmental address create cases in a queue with no members
column2:
CONTEXT
Each product line has its own inbound address that creates Cases in a dedicated queue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases for one product line went unanswered for four days.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every routing queue should have members who receive and work its Cases.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The queue exists and receives Cases, but its only member left the company and was never replaced.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Queue membership is maintained manually and was not part of the offboarding process. A review of all 14 queues found two with no active members and three more with a single member, and the affected queue had accumulated 47 unworked Cases.

RESOLUTION
The queues were populated from the current team structure, membership is now granted through a public group tied to team roles, and a daily check reports queues with fewer than two active members or Cases untouched for 24 hours.

VALIDATION
The 47 Cases were assigned and worked within two days, the daily check reported no empty queues over three weeks, and a test deactivation triggered the alert as designed.

column1: Attachment names in Hebrew and Arabic arrive as unreadable characters
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents attach documents to customer messages, and filenames often use Hebrew or Arabic script.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive attachments whose names are unreadable sequences of characters.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Filenames should display correctly in common mail clients regardless of script.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Names in non-Latin scripts arrive garbled, while the document content opens correctly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The sending component wrote the filename into the message without applying the encoding that non-ASCII header values require. Message headers for affected sends showed raw characters where an encoded value was expected, and clients each rendered them differently.

RESOLUTION
Filenames are now encoded according to the standard for non-ASCII header values before sending, with a fallback transliterated name for clients that cannot interpret the encoded form.

VALIDATION
Attachments with Hebrew, Arabic, and accented Latin names displayed correctly in six mail clients, and the fallback name appeared only in the one legacy client that required it.

column1: Messages sent from the mobile app are logged but replies are not
column2:
CONTEXT
Account managers send and receive customer messages from the mobile application while travelling.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Colleagues cannot see the customer's response on the record and duplicate the outreach.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both sides of a mobile conversation should appear on the customer record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Outbound messages are logged, while customer replies remain only in the manager's personal mailbox.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Logging is triggered by the send action in the application, and replies arrive in the mail platform with no equivalent trigger. Sampling 60 mobile conversations found the reply missing from the record in 54.

RESOLUTION
Replies to logged outbound messages are now captured by matching the conversation reference in the mail platform. This is partial: replies to messages the manager sent from a personal mail client without logging cannot be matched and remain invisible.

VALIDATION
Replies appeared on the record for 52 of 60 sampled conversations after the change, and the eight remaining gaps were traced to messages sent outside the application.

column1: Team messages are sent from a generic address because sending as the team is not permitted
column2:
CONTEXT
A specialist team wants customer messages to appear from their team address rather than a generic service address.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers reply to the generic address, and the specialist team loses the thread.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Messages should be sent from the team address so that replies return to the team.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The team address cannot be used as a sender because the mail platform will not grant send permission for it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mail administrators declined the permission because the address is a distribution list rather than a mailbox, and converting it would break internal routing. A test confirmed sends from that address are rejected.

RESOLUTION
Messages are sent from the generic address with the team named in the signature and a reply reference that routes responses to the team queue. This is a workaround: the visible sender is still generic, replies to very old messages reach the generic queue, and routing depends on the reference surviving the customer's mail client.

VALIDATION
Replies reached the specialist queue for 88 of 100 monitored conversations, with the rest arriving at the generic queue and needing manual routing.

column1: The archiving platform cannot ingest messages sent from the CRM
column2:
CONTEXT
Regulatory retention requires all customer correspondence to be held in the corporate archiving platform.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Messages sent from Salesforce are absent from the archive, which leaves a retention gap.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every customer message should reach the archive regardless of the system that sent it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The archiving platform ingests only from the corporate mail platform, which these messages bypass.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Salesforce sends directly through its own delivery service, so the messages never traverse the mail platform the archiver monitors. Routing them through the mail platform was tested and caused deliverability failures because of sender alignment.

RESOLUTION
A nightly export writes sent messages and their metadata to a restricted store the archiving team can reach. This is a workaround: the export lags by a day, the messages are held outside the archiving platform's search interface, and legal hold cannot be applied from the archive tool.

VALIDATION
Fourteen nightly exports completed with counts matching the sent log, and a retrieval test located five sampled messages, though the archiving team performed the search manually.

column1: A share of inbound messages arrives hours after it was sent
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer messages create Cases, and response times are measured from the moment the message arrives.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers report waiting far longer than the recorded response time suggests.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An inbound message should reach the platform within minutes of the customer sending it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some messages arrive three to six hours late, and the Case is created at the late arrival time.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Headers show the delay occurring before the message reaches the corporate mail platform, so neither the platform nor Case creation adds it. The affected messages come from several sender domains with no shared mail provider. Two customers supplied their own sent timestamps, which matched the header origin times and confirmed the delay is real rather than a clock difference.

RESOLUTION
The point at which the delay is introduced has not been identified, and no change has been made to inbound processing.

VALIDATION
Late arrivals continue at roughly 2 percent of inbound volume. The next step is a joint trace with the mail platform provider using full headers from ten affected messages to establish which hop holds them.

column1: Customers occasionally receive a copy of an old message weeks later
column2:
CONTEXT
Service notifications are sent once when a Case changes state and are recorded against the Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several customers received a message about a Case that had been closed weeks earlier.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A notification should be delivered once and never re-sent without a new triggering event.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
An identical copy of an earlier message arrives long afterwards, and the Case shows no new activity.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The Case activity history records one send for each affected notification, so the platform does not appear to have sent a second copy. The re-delivered messages carry their original identifier and timestamp, which is consistent with a re-delivery in transit rather than a new send. All reported instances involve recipients at two customer organizations that share a mail provider.

RESOLUTION
Nothing has been changed in the sending configuration, since the evidence points outside the platform and no internal trigger has been found.

VALIDATION
Reports arrive every few weeks. The next step is asking the two customers' mail administrators to trace one message identifier, and reviewing delivery logs for any retry against the same identifier.

column1: Converted leads are still counted in campaign performance
column2:
CONTEXT
Campaign performance counts responses and resulting pipeline from the leads a campaign generated.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Marketing reports show more prospects than exist, and totals disagree with the sales view.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A converted lead should be counted once, through the account and opportunity it became.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The converted lead record remains and is counted alongside the opportunity it produced.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Converted leads are retained by design but are not excluded from the campaign reports. A count found 12,400 converted leads in the reporting period, of which 3,100 also had an opportunity counted separately, which matched the discrepancy between the two views.

RESOLUTION
Campaign reports now exclude converted leads from prospect counts and attribute their pipeline through the resulting opportunity, with conversion shown as its own measure.

VALIDATION
Marketing and sales views reconciled for four campaigns, the conversion measure matched the conversion log, and no prospect was counted twice in a manual audit of one campaign.

column1: Cases cloned from a closed case start life already closed
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents clone a previous Case when a customer reports the same problem again.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Repeat issues are missing from open workload reports and breach their response targets unnoticed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A cloned Case should begin in a new state with fresh response timers.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The clone copies the closed status and resolution from the source, so it never enters a queue and no timer starts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Cloning copies all writable fields including status. A query found 480 Cases created as clones in a closed state, of which 140 had customer correspondence after creation and were genuinely open work.

RESOLUTION
A before-save automation now resets status, resolution, and closure fields on any cloned Case, and the clone action was relabelled so agents understand what carries over.

VALIDATION
Twenty clones across three record types opened in a new state with timers running, the 140 genuinely open Cases were reopened and assigned, and workload reports matched the queue counts.

column1: Enabling standardized country and state values breaks existing addresses
column2:
CONTEXT
Standardized country and state picklists were enabled to improve address quality and reporting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users cannot save records whose existing state value is not in the standard list.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Standardization should apply to new entries without blocking edits to historical records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Any save on an affected record is rejected until the state value is corrected, including edits to unrelated fields.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Existing free-text values were not migrated before the picklists were enabled. A scan found 8,700 records with a state value outside the standard list, mostly abbreviations and local-language spellings across four countries.

RESOLUTION
A mapping was built for the 60 most common variants and applied in a controlled update, records that could not be mapped were assigned a review flag with the original value preserved in a text field, and the remaining 240 were corrected by regional teams.

VALIDATION
Records saved normally after the update across all four countries, the review flag list fell to zero within three weeks, and address reporting grouped correctly by standardized values.

column1: Case comments are lost when one case is merged into another
column2:
CONTEXT
Duplicate Cases raised through different channels are merged so that one record holds the history.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents find the merged Case missing the diagnostic notes recorded on the duplicate.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A merge should preserve the correspondence and notes from both Cases on the surviving record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages transfer to the surviving Case while comments recorded on the losing Case are deleted with it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Comments are not among the child records the merge carries across. Comparing 30 merges showed comments present before and absent afterwards in every case, with an average of four comments lost per merge.

RESOLUTION
A pre-merge step now copies comments from the losing Case onto the surviving Case with their original author and timestamp preserved in the text, and the merge action was wrapped so it cannot run without that step.

VALIDATION
Fifteen rehearsal merges preserved every comment with attribution, the wrapped action refused to merge when the copy step failed, and agents confirmed the history was complete.

column1: Agents cannot add notes while a record is locked for approval
column2:
CONTEXT
Contract records are locked while an approval is in progress so that terms cannot change mid-review.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents cannot record customer conversations during the approval period and keep the information in personal notes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Commercial terms should be protected while communication about the record continues normally.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The lock prevents any related activity from being added, including notes and logged calls.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The lock applies to the record and its child activities. Approvals take an average of three days, and a review found agents recording conversations outside the system for 40 percent of contracts under approval.

RESOLUTION
Locking was narrowed to the contract fields through a validation rule keyed on approval state, so terms remain protected while activities, notes, and files can still be added.

VALIDATION
Twenty contracts under approval accepted notes and logged calls while rejecting edits to commercial terms, and a follow-up review found conversations recorded in the system for all sampled contracts.

column1: Contacts from a parent organization cannot be selected on a subsidiary's case
column2:
CONTEXT
Cases are raised against subsidiary accounts, and a lookup filter restricts the contact to that account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents cannot select the group procurement contacts who raise most requests for corporate customers.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Contacts from the account or its parent organization should be selectable on a subsidiary's Case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The lookup returns contacts of the exact account only, so agents create duplicate contact records to proceed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The filter compares the contact's account with the Case account directly. A count found 380 duplicate contacts created in six months, each matching an existing contact at a parent organization.

RESOLUTION
The filter now permits contacts whose account is the Case account or its parent, and the duplicate contacts were merged into the original records at the parent.

VALIDATION
Agents selected parent organization contacts on subsidiary Cases in testing, duplicate creation stopped over the following month, and the 380 duplicates were merged with their activities preserved.

column1: Merge history is available for accounts but not for contacts
column2:
CONTEXT
Records are merged regularly as part of data quality work, and stewards must be able to explain any merge.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions about why a contact disappeared cannot be answered after the fact.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every merge should leave a record of the losing record, the survivor, the operator, and the time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Account merges are recorded by an automation, while contact merges leave nothing behind.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The automation was built for accounts during an earlier cleanup and never extended. A review found 2,600 contact merges in the past year with no retrievable detail beyond the surviving record.

RESOLUTION
The merge log now captures contact merges performed through the standard interface, recording both records and the operator. This is partial: merges performed through the data loader bypass the automation entirely, and about a third of contact merges are done that way during bulk cleanups.

VALIDATION
Interface merges produced a complete log entry across 50 tests, while a loader-based merge produced none, as documented.

column1: Record type changes must be applied in small batches with manual checks
column2:
CONTEXT
A service redesign requires 40,000 existing Cases to move to a new record type with a different picklist set.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Bulk record type changes leave records with picklist values that are invalid for the new type.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Changing record type should reassign dependent picklist values according to a defined mapping.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The record type changes while the stored picklist values remain, so records display blank fields until they are edited.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Record type changes do not remap dependent values automatically. Testing 500 records found 310 holding at least one value not defined for the new type, spread across three fields.

RESOLUTION
Changes are applied in batches of 2,000 with a mapping update in the same operation and a verification query after each batch. This is a workaround: the process is manual, each batch takes about 40 minutes of operator attention, and a batch that fails verification must be corrected by hand before continuing.

VALIDATION
Twenty batches completed with the verification query returning no invalid values, and a deliberately unmapped test value was caught by the check before the batch was accepted.

column1: A few records carry a last-modified timestamp in the future
column2:
CONTEXT
Records carry a system-maintained last-modified timestamp used by extracts and by conflict detection.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of records show a modification time several hours ahead of the current time.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
System timestamps should never be later than the moment they are read.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Affected records are skipped by delta extracts, because their timestamp is always ahead of the extract window.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The timestamp is maintained by the platform and cannot be set directly, which makes a data load unlikely. All 23 affected records were last touched by the same integration user, though that user handles most updates. Re-saving a record corrects the timestamp, so the condition does not survive a later write.

RESOLUTION
Nothing has been altered, since the mechanism that produces a future timestamp has not been identified and re-saving records would destroy the evidence.

VALIDATION
The affected records remain excluded from delta extracts and are being loaded by a separate list. The next step is capturing the full request context for the integration user's next writes and raising a support case with the 23 record identifiers and their timestamps.

column1: A field reverts to its previous value moments after being saved
column2:
CONTEXT
Account managers maintain a service tier field that drives entitlement and routing.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Managers report changing the tier, seeing it saved, and finding the old value again a few seconds later.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A saved value should persist until someone or something deliberately changes it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field returns to its previous value shortly after the save, and the history shows two changes seconds apart.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Field history records the manager's change followed by a second change attributed to the integration user, so something writes the old value back. The nightly enrichment job is the obvious candidate but runs only at night, while reversions occur during the day. The reverted values match what that job last wrote, suggesting a queued or replayed message rather than a live calculation.

RESOLUTION
No confirmed explanation has been established, and the enrichment job has been left running because disabling it would remove the only evidence trail.

VALIDATION
Reversions continue several times a week. The next step is correlating the reversion timestamps with the middleware message log to establish whether a delayed or replayed message carries the old value.

column1: Approved quotes can be edited afterwards without a new approval
column2:
CONTEXT
Quotes above a discount threshold require approval before they are sent to the customer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit found quotes sent at discounts higher than the level that was actually approved.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Changing commercial terms after approval should invalidate it and require a new decision.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The approved flag remains set when the discount is increased, so the quote can be sent without further review.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nothing reset the approval state on subsequent edits. Comparing approved discount values with sent values found 46 quotes where the sent discount was higher, 9 of them by more than ten points.

RESOLUTION
Any change to discount, term, or total now clears the approval state and returns the quote to draft, with the previous decision retained in the history for comparison.

VALIDATION
Editing an approved test quote returned it to draft in every scenario, sending was blocked until re-approval, and the 46 historical quotes were reviewed with 9 escalated to the deal desk.

column1: Pipeline coverage includes deals whose close date has already passed
column2:
CONTEXT
Pipeline coverage compares open opportunity value against the quota for the coming quarter.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Coverage looks healthy while the sales leadership sees the quarter falling short.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Coverage should count open deals that can still close within the target quarter.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Open deals with close dates in past quarters are included, which inflates coverage by a growing margin.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The measure filtered on open stage without any date condition. A count found 1,700 open opportunities with a close date before the current quarter, worth 22 percent of the reported coverage figure, some more than a year overdue.

RESOLUTION
Coverage now counts open deals with a close date inside the target quarter, overdue deals are reported separately as a hygiene measure, and a reminder asks owners to re-date or close them.

VALIDATION
Recalculated coverage matched a manual review for three regions, the hygiene report drove closure or re-dating of 1,200 stale deals in six weeks, and coverage tracked the eventual quarter result far more closely.

column1: Bundle revenue is counted at both the bundle and the component level
column2:
CONTEXT
Product bundles are sold as a single line that expands into component lines for fulfilment.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Product revenue reports total more than the company's booked revenue.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Bundle revenue should be counted once, either at bundle level or across its components.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The bundle line carries the full price and the component lines carry allocated prices, and reports sum both.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Component lines were introduced for fulfilment without a reporting rule to exclude them. Reconciling one quarter showed an overstatement of 18 percent, entirely attributable to bundles, while non-bundled products reconciled exactly.

RESOLUTION
Component lines are now flagged as fulfilment-only and excluded from revenue reporting, while a separate product-level view uses the component allocation and excludes the bundle header.

VALIDATION
Both views reconciled with booked revenue for four quarters, the product view attributed bundle revenue to components without double counting, and finance signed off both definitions.

column1: Churn excludes customers who downgraded rather than left
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer churn is reported monthly as the proportion of customers whose subscription ended.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reported churn stayed flat while recurring revenue fell for three consecutive months.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The churn measure should reflect revenue lost, including partial losses from downgrades.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
