Only full cancellations count, so a customer who moves from a large plan to the smallest is treated as retained.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The measure counted customers rather than revenue. Analysis of the three months showed 340 downgrades representing more revenue loss than the 90 full cancellations counted as churn.

RESOLUTION
Revenue churn is now reported alongside customer churn, calculated from the change in recurring revenue per customer, with downgrades and cancellations shown separately.

VALIDATION
Revenue churn tracked the observed recurring revenue decline for six months, the two measures reconciled with the subscription ledger, and the leadership review adopted the revenue measure as primary.

column1: Approval turnaround is measured from submission rather than from a complete request
column2:
CONTEXT
The deal desk reports how long approvals take, measured against an agreed service target.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reported turnaround consistently misses the target while approvers say they respond quickly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The measure should reflect time the deal desk controls, separating waiting time caused by incomplete submissions.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The clock starts at submission and keeps running while the desk waits for missing information from the requester.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Requests are returned for missing information in 38 percent of cases, and that waiting time averages 1.4 days. Recomputing turnaround excluding those periods brought the average within the agreed target.

RESOLUTION
The measure now pauses while a request sits with the requester, records both elapsed and desk-controlled time, and reports the returned-for-information rate as its own measure.

VALIDATION
Recalculated turnaround for two quarters matched a manual reconstruction of 60 requests, and the information rate gave the desk a concrete target for improving the submission form.

column1: Contracts renewed ahead of schedule miss the annual price increase
column2:
CONTEXT
Renewals carry an annual price uplift applied from the anniversary of the original contract.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance found renewals priced at the previous year's rates.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every renewal should apply the uplift due for the period it covers.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Contracts renewed before the anniversary keep the current rate for the whole new term.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The uplift was applied by comparing today's date with the anniversary rather than the renewal term start. Of 620 renewals in the period, 140 were signed early and none carried the uplift, representing a measurable shortfall against plan.

RESOLUTION
The calculation now applies the uplift due for the renewal term start date regardless of when the renewal is signed, and a validation blocks activation of a renewal whose rate does not match the pricing schedule.

VALIDATION
Early, on-time, and late renewals all applied the correct rate across 40 test cases, the validation blocked a manually altered rate, and the 140 affected renewals were repriced with customer agreement.

column1: Automated collections cover late invoices but not the earlier reminder stages
column2:
CONTEXT
Overdue invoices are chased through a sequence of reminders escalating to the collections team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Early-stage reminders are sent inconsistently, so invoices reach the collections team later than they should.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every reminder stage should be triggered automatically from the invoice due date.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Reminders beyond 30 days overdue are automated, while the courtesy reminder and the first notice are sent manually when someone has time.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The automation was built for the escalation stages first. A review found the courtesy reminder sent for 44 percent of eligible invoices, and invoices that received one were settled on average nine days sooner.

RESOLUTION
The first notice at 15 days is now automated alongside the existing stages. This is partial: the courtesy reminder before the due date remains manual, because it requires a relationship judgement the account teams are not willing to automate yet.

VALIDATION
The 15-day notice was issued for every eligible invoice over two months and average days outstanding fell by four, while courtesy reminder coverage remained unchanged.

column1: Quote documents are standardized for some product lines only
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer-facing quote documents are generated from templates maintained by revenue operations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive quotes with inconsistent terms wording depending on which team prepared them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every quote should use an approved template with current legal wording.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Three product lines use the approved template, while the others use documents assembled by hand from older files.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The three standardized lines share a simple commercial structure. The remaining lines include usage tiers and professional services terms that the current template cannot express. A review of 40 manual quotes found six different versions of the liability clause.

RESOLUTION
The approved template now covers three of six product lines and includes the current legal wording. This is partial: usage-based and services quotes still use manual documents, and their clause wording is verified by a checklist rather than by the template.

VALIDATION
All quotes for the three covered lines used current wording over two months, while the checklist caught two outdated clauses in manually prepared quotes.

column1: Finance receives a monthly bridge file because the CRM cannot express their measure
column2:
CONTEXT
Finance reports revenue on a recognition basis that differs from the booking basis held in the CRM.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reconciling the two views takes several days each month and produces recurring disputes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both bases should be derivable from a single agreed dataset.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The CRM holds bookings only, and the adjustments finance needs live in spreadsheets held by two analysts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Recognition requires delivery milestones and deferral rules that the CRM does not model. An analysis showed 12 adjustment categories, of which 5 could be derived from CRM data and 7 could not without new objects.

RESOLUTION
A structured bridge file with the 12 categories is produced monthly from the CRM extract plus the analysts' inputs. This is a workaround: seven categories remain manual, the file is a point-in-time artefact with no history, and errors are found only during the next reconciliation.

VALIDATION
Three months reconciled within a day rather than several, and the disputed items fell from about fifteen per month to three, all in the manual categories.

column1: Opportunities disappear from one manager's forecast each cycle
column2:
CONTEXT
Forecast figures roll up through the management hierarchy for each submission cycle.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One regional manager finds a small number of opportunities missing from their forecast view each cycle.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every open opportunity owned within a manager's hierarchy should appear in their forecast.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Between three and eight opportunities are absent, and they appear correctly in the owner's own view and in reports.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The missing opportunities have valid stages, close dates within the period, and forecast categories that should be included. Their owners sit in the manager's hierarchy, and no territory assignment differs from their peers. Reassigning one to another owner in the same team made it appear, and it vanished again when reassigned back.

RESOLUTION
The pattern has not been explained, and no hierarchy or territory change has been made, since altering the structure would remove the reproducible test case.

VALIDATION
The behaviour recurs each cycle with a different set of records. The next step is a support case including the role hierarchy export, the affected record identifiers, and the reassignment test that reproduces the disappearance.

column1: Client fails on records whose text fields contain line breaks
column2:
CONTEXT
A reporting client requests case data in a delimited format and loads it into a local database.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Loads fail with a column count error for certain days and succeed for others.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Text content should load correctly regardless of the characters it contains.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records whose description contains a line break are split across two rows, which breaks the column alignment for the remainder of the file.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client split the response on line endings without honouring quoted fields. Every failing file contained at least one description with an embedded line break, and the failure position always matched the first such record.

RESOLUTION
The client now uses a parser that respects quoting and escaping, and a structural check verifies the column count of every row before the load begins.

VALIDATION
Files that previously failed loaded correctly, including records with line breaks, quotes, and delimiters in the text, and the structural check rejected a deliberately corrupted file.

column1: Large extraction jobs fail before returning any results
column2:
CONTEXT
A quarterly extract pulls several million historical records through the bulk interface.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The job fails during the query phase and produces no output at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The extract should complete, taking longer for larger volumes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The job aborts while assembling results, and retrying with the same parameters fails identically.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The query selects a very large record set in one operation, which exceeds the time the platform allows for assembling results. Reducing the date range to a single month completed successfully, which pointed at result size rather than query structure.

RESOLUTION
The job now uses primary key chunking so the platform divides the record set into manageable ranges, with chunk size tuned to complete each range well inside the limit.

VALIDATION
A full extract of 6.2 million records completed in 90 minutes across 62 chunks, record counts matched a direct count query, and two subsequent quarterly runs completed without failure.

column1: Webhook deliveries lose their body when the endpoint redirects
column2:
CONTEXT
Salesforce posts event notifications to a partner endpoint that recently moved to a new path.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The partner reports receiving notifications with no content since their migration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The full notification body should reach the endpoint that ultimately handles the request.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The partner's server issues a redirect, and the follow-up request arrives with an empty body.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client followed the redirect but did not resend the body, which is the standard behaviour for the redirect status the partner returned. A trace showed the first request carrying the payload and the second arriving empty, and the partner confirmed both requests in their access log.

RESOLUTION
The endpoint configuration now points directly at the new path so no redirect occurs, and the client treats an unexpected redirect as a delivery failure that raises an alert rather than following it silently.

VALIDATION
Notifications arrived complete for 500 test events, the partner confirmed full payloads, and a deliberately configured redirect produced an alert instead of an empty delivery.

column1: Integration breaks after a platform release removed an undocumented field
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware component reads Case data and depends on the structure of the response.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The component began failing immediately after a scheduled platform release.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Integrations should depend only on documented, versioned parts of the response.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The component reads an attribute that was never part of the documented response and is now absent.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The attribute appeared in responses from an older version and was used as a convenient shortcut for a value that is available through a documented field. A review of the codebase found two further places relying on undocumented attributes.

RESOLUTION
All three usages were replaced with documented fields, the component was pinned to a supported version, and a pre-release check runs the integration test suite against the next platform version in a preview environment.

VALIDATION
The component processed the backlog successfully, the test suite passed against the preview version before the following release, and no further undocumented dependencies were found in a repeat review.

column1: Signed requests are rejected because the client's clock has drifted
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner signs each request with a timestamp, and the receiving service accepts signatures within a short window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Requests from one partner node are rejected as invalid while identical requests from other nodes succeed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Correctly signed requests should be accepted from every node.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Requests from the affected node are refused with a signature validation error that does not explain the cause.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Comparing the timestamp inside the signed payload with the receiving service's time showed the node running four minutes ahead, outside the permitted window. The node's time synchronization service had been disabled during a maintenance change, which the partner confirmed. No signing material was exposed during the investigation.

RESOLUTION
Time synchronization was restored and monitored on the partner side, and the receiving service now returns a specific error for a timestamp outside the window rather than a generic validation failure.

VALIDATION
Requests from the affected node were accepted immediately after synchronization, a deliberately skewed test request produced the specific error, and the partner added a clock check to their deployment procedure.

column1: Error responses are standardized for some integrations but not others
column2:
CONTEXT
Several inbound integrations call custom endpoints, and support staff triage their failures.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Diagnosing a failure requires knowing which integration produced it, because the error formats differ.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every endpoint should return a consistent error structure with a stable code and a readable message.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two integrations return a structured error, while the others return free-text messages or an empty body with a status code.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The endpoints were built by different teams over four years with no shared contract. A review of 300 support tickets found triage taking twice as long for the unstandardized endpoints.

RESOLUTION
A shared error structure was implemented on two of four integrations along with a documented code list. This is partial: the remaining two are consumed by partner systems that parse the current free-text format, so changing them requires coordinated partner releases scheduled for next quarter.

VALIDATION
Triage time for the two updated integrations fell by roughly half over six weeks, and the code list covered every error encountered, while the other two remain unchanged.

column1: Partner access depends on a single proxy node with no failover
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner accepts traffic only from a registered network address, so outbound calls route through a dedicated proxy.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A proxy restart during maintenance stopped all partner traffic for 40 minutes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Partner integration should survive the loss of any single component.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All traffic depends on one proxy node, because the partner registers one address and their change process takes weeks.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner's registration process allows additional addresses but requires a security review per address. Testing confirmed calls from any unregistered address are refused at their edge.

RESOLUTION
Requests are now queued and replayed when the proxy is unavailable, so traffic is delayed rather than lost. This is a workaround: the single point of failure remains, queued requests age, and a long outage would exceed the partner's acceptance window. A second registered address is in their review queue.

VALIDATION
A simulated 30-minute proxy outage queued 1,400 requests and replayed them successfully, while a four-hour simulation produced 60 requests the partner rejected as too old.

column1: A deprecated endpoint stays online for a single remaining consumer
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom endpoint was replaced by a version with better validation, and consumers were asked to migrate.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The old endpoint cannot be retired, which leaves two implementations of the same logic to maintain.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All consumers should use the current endpoint so the old one can be removed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One consumer runs on a vendor platform with no development capacity until their next major release.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Traffic analysis showed the old endpoint receiving 4 percent of calls from that single consumer. The two implementations had already diverged, with a validation added to the new endpoint and never applied to the old one.

RESOLUTION
The old endpoint now delegates to the same internal logic as the new one, so behaviour cannot diverge further. This is a workaround: the deprecated surface remains published, its weaker input contract still applies, and retirement waits on a third party.

VALIDATION
Both endpoints produced identical results for 300 replayed requests, the previously missing validation now applies on both, and the consumer reported no change in behaviour.

column1: A consumer occasionally receives records outside its permitted scope
column2:
CONTEXT
Several partner consumers read case data through one endpoint that filters records to each partner's accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One partner reported two cases in their response belonging to a different partner.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A consumer must receive only records within its permitted scope.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two out-of-scope records appeared in one response, and identical repeat requests returned the correct set.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The endpoint was disabled for all partners within the hour, the partner confirmed deleting the received data, and the data protection lead opened an incident. The filter derives scope from the authenticated consumer per request, and a code review found no path omitting it. Request logs show the affected response served by the same node as the other partner's request milliseconds earlier.

RESOLUTION
The defect has not been isolated. The endpoint remains disabled as containment, and no code change has been released because the mechanism is unproven.

VALIDATION
No further out-of-scope records have been observed, though the endpoint is offline. The next step is a review of request-scoped state in the handler and a concurrency test interleaving requests from two consumers against an instrumented build.

column1: Bulk job results occasionally omit rows the job reports as processed
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly bulk job updates records and writes a results file the operations team reconciles against the input.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The results file sometimes contains fewer rows than the job's own processed count.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The results file should contain one row for every submitted record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Between five and forty rows are missing from the file, while the job reports the full count as processed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Spot checks confirm the missing records were updated correctly, so processing succeeded and only the result rows are absent. The gap does not align with batch boundaries, and rerunning the same input produces a complete file. Results are retrieved in pages, and the missing rows have not been traced to a particular page.

RESOLUTION
Nothing has been changed in the job, because it is not yet established whether the rows are missing from the platform's results or lost while the client retrieves them.

VALIDATION
The discrepancy appears in roughly one run a week. The next step is capturing each retrieved page separately with its record count and comparing the assembled total against the job's reported figures.

column1: Counts include records the business considers archived
column2:
CONTEXT
Operational records are marked archived rather than deleted once they pass their retention point.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Volume answers are consistently higher than the operational dashboards show.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Questions about current operations should exclude archived records unless the user asks for them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Generated queries include archived records, because nothing in the schema indicates that the archive flag matters.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flag is one boolean field among many and carries no special meaning in the schema description. Comparing twelve answers with the dashboards showed differences of 8 to 30 percent, matching the archived proportion for each object.

RESOLUTION
The archive flag is now described as a lifecycle filter that is applied by default, questions asking for historical or archived data lift it explicitly, and every answer states whether archived records were included.

VALIDATION
Twelve answers matched the dashboards exactly, an explicitly historical question returned the larger figure, and the inclusion statement appeared in each response.

column1: Severity rankings are returned in alphabetical order
column2:
CONTEXT
Case severity is a picklist whose values carry a business order from critical down to low.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions asking for the most severe open cases return an arbitrary selection.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Ordering by severity should follow the business ranking rather than the text of the values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query sorts the picklist alphabetically, so low sorts above medium and critical lands in the middle.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Picklist values sort as text unless an explicit order is supplied. Traces showed correct filters with an alphabetical sort in every severity question, and the top result was almost never the most severe case.

RESOLUTION
The schema now carries a numeric rank for each value of ordered picklists, generation sorts on the rank, and answers name the ordering that was applied.

VALIDATION
Ten severity questions returned correctly ordered results matching a manual ranking, other picklists were unaffected, and a question asking for alphabetical order still produced a text sort.

column1: Questions asking for figures per person per month return a single total
column2:
CONTEXT
Team leads ask for productivity figures broken down by person and by month.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Answers return one number for the whole period instead of the requested breakdown.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question naming two dimensions should produce a result grouped by both.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query aggregates without grouping, so the breakdown is lost and the answer looks plausible but useless.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Intent classification recognized the aggregation but captured only one dimension, and the second was dropped without comment. Of 25 two-dimension questions, 21 returned a single total and four grouped by one dimension only.

RESOLUTION
Dimension extraction now collects every grouping term in the question, the query groups by all of them, and the answer lists the dimensions used so a missed one is visible to the reader.

VALIDATION
All 25 questions returned the requested breakdown matching manually written queries, and a three-dimension question grouped correctly or stated which dimension it could not apply.

column1: Questions about the user's own records return everyone's data
column2:
CONTEXT
Sales users ask the assistant about their own accounts, opportunities, and activities.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Answers to questions phrased in the first person cover the whole organization.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question about the user's own records should filter to records they own.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Terms such as my and mine are ignored, and the query returns every record the user is permitted to see.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nothing bound first-person terms to the session identity, so they carried no meaning in generation. Of 30 first-person questions, 27 produced an unfiltered query, and users only noticed because the totals were implausibly large.

RESOLUTION
First-person terms now resolve to an owner filter on the requesting user, team phrasing resolves to the user's role hierarchy, and the answer restates whose records were included.

VALIDATION
Thirty first-person questions returned correctly scoped results, team questions matched the hierarchy, and the restatement let two users catch a question they had phrased ambiguously.

column1: Common status words do not match any stored value
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask about open, pending, or closed work using everyday vocabulary.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions using those words return empty results or unexpected counts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Everyday status vocabulary should map to the set of stored values it represents.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The word open is placed into the filter directly, and no stored value is called open, since the object uses five working statuses.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schema listed the individual values without any grouping. Testing 20 status questions produced empty results for 13 and partial results for 4, where the term happened to match one value out of several.

RESOLUTION
Status groups were defined in the schema so that open, pending, and closed each expand to their member values, and the answer names the values used in the filter.

VALIDATION
All 20 questions returned counts matching manually written queries, the named values let the service owner confirm the groupings, and questions naming a specific status were unaffected.

column1: Answers show the query but not what the fields mean
column2:
CONTEXT
Each answer includes the generated query so that users can check how the figure was produced.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users cannot judge whether a field is the right one, because the query shows names without meanings.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An answer should explain the fields it used in business language.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query is shown as written, and users ask an analyst what the fields represent.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Field definitions exist for core objects in the data dictionary but are not connected to the assistant. Sampling 40 sessions found 11 follow-up questions asking what a field meant, mostly about similarly named amount fields.

RESOLUTION
Answers now include a short definition for each field used, drawn from the dictionary. This is partial: only documented fields carry a definition, so roughly a third of fields still appear as a bare name, and undefined fields are marked as undocumented.

VALIDATION
Follow-up questions about field meaning fell from 11 to 3 across a comparable sample, and the remaining three concerned fields with no dictionary entry.

column1: Negative feedback is captured without a reason that can be acted on
column2:
CONTEXT
Users can mark an answer as unhelpful, and the product team reviews the feedback weekly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The team cannot tell whether unhelpful answers were wrong, incomplete, or simply hard to read.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Feedback should identify what was wrong so that improvements can be prioritized.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only a rating is stored, so every review begins by re-running the question and guessing what the user objected to.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Of 140 unhelpful ratings in a month, the team could classify 46 by re-running them, and the rest were ambiguous. Two users said they had rated an answer unhelpful because it was correct but too slow.

RESOLUTION
The feedback control now offers four reasons and an optional comment, stored with the question and the generated query. This is partial: the reasons cover accuracy and completeness but not presentation, and historical feedback cannot be reclassified.

VALIDATION
Of 90 ratings received since the change, 78 carried a reason and the team prioritized two fixes directly from them, while the historical backlog remains unclassified.

column1: Questions are queued at peak times because of provider rate limits
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant calls a hosted language model whose plan permits a fixed number of requests per minute.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During the Monday reporting peak, users receive errors instead of answers.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every question should be answered, with a longer wait if the service is busy.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Requests beyond the limit are refused outright, and the user sees a failure with no indication to retry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Peak demand reaches roughly three times the permitted rate for about twenty minutes. Measurement showed 210 refusals in one Monday window, concentrated between two reporting deadlines.

RESOLUTION
Requests are now queued with a visible position and answered as capacity allows. This is a workaround: peak questions wait up to four minutes, the queue is not prioritized, and the underlying capacity is unchanged pending a plan review.

VALIDATION
Refusals fell to zero across three Mondays, the longest observed wait was three minutes forty seconds, and no user abandoned a queued question according to the session logs.

column1: Long questions are cut off at the prompt limit without warning
column2:
CONTEXT
Analysts sometimes paste long, detailed questions containing several conditions and background context.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Very long questions produce answers that ignore the later conditions.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should use the whole question or state clearly that it cannot.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Input beyond the prompt budget is truncated silently, so conditions at the end of the question are never seen.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The prompt assembles schema, instructions, and the question, and the question is truncated last when the budget is exceeded. Of 60 questions above the threshold, 52 had at least one condition dropped.

RESOLUTION
Questions above the threshold are now rejected with a message asking the user to split them, and the truncation point is shown. This is a workaround: long questions still cannot be answered as asked, and splitting loses the relationship between the parts. Summarizing the question before generation is the preferred approach.

VALIDATION
No silently truncated question was recorded over three weeks, users split 31 long questions successfully, and 6 were abandoned because splitting changed the meaning.

column1: Some valid questions return an empty answer with no error
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant returns a figure, a short explanation, and the query it generated.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Occasionally a question produces a blank answer with no figure, explanation, or error message.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every question should return an answer or a clear failure the user can act on.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The response arrives empty, and repeating the same question moments later usually works.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Session logs show a generated query and a successful execution with rows returned for several affected requests, so the data reached the formatting step. The affected questions span different objects and users with no shared pattern in length or complexity. Response times for blank answers sit slightly below the median, which does not fit a timeout during formatting.

RESOLUTION
The point at which the content is lost has not been established, and no change has been made to the formatting layer.

VALIDATION
Blank answers occur in roughly one request in 200. The next step is logging the intermediate result between execution and formatting for a full week, so it can be established whether the content exists at that boundary.

column1: Migrated dates are wrong for every day before the thirteenth of a month
column2:
CONTEXT
Service records are migrated from a legacy system that exports dates in day-first format.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reported service history does not match the legacy system for a large share of records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migrated dates should match the source exactly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Dates where the day is twelve or lower are transposed, so the fifth of March becomes the third of May, while later days load correctly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The loader interpreted the file as month-first, which fails silently whenever both parts are valid month numbers and errors only when the day exceeds twelve. Comparing 500 records against the source showed 39 percent transposed, all with a day of twelve or lower.

RESOLUTION
The extract now writes dates in an unambiguous international format, the loader is configured for that format explicitly, and a post-load check compares a sample of dates against the source before the batch is accepted.

VALIDATION
The affected 41,000 records were reloaded and matched the source exactly, the check rejected a deliberately ambiguous test file, and service history reports reconciled with the legacy reports.

column1: Manager hierarchy import creates loops that break rollup reporting
column2:
CONTEXT
Employee records carry a manager reference to themselves, forming the reporting hierarchy.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Hierarchy reports fail or run indefinitely after the employee migration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The hierarchy should form a tree in which every path terminates at a top-level record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some records reference each other as manager in a cycle, so traversal never reaches a root.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The legacy system permitted temporary cycles during reorganizations and had no validation. A traversal of the loaded data found 14 cycles involving 33 records, most created during an acquisition when two managers were recorded as reporting to each other.

RESOLUTION
A cycle check now runs before load and rejects the file with the offending records listed, the 14 cycles were resolved with the human resources team, and a validation rule prevents a record from being placed under its own subordinate.

VALIDATION
Hierarchy reports completed in seconds for the full population, the cycle check rejected a seeded test cycle, and the validation blocked a manual attempt to recreate one.

column1: Records with several addresses in one email field fail to load
column2:
CONTEXT
Legacy contact records store a single free-text field that sometimes contains more than one address separated by a semicolon.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A consistent group of contacts fails to load with an invalid format error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every contact should load, retaining each address in a usable form.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records containing more than one address are rejected, because the field accepts a single valid address only.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Of 60,000 contacts, 2,900 hold more than one address and 40 hold three or more. Reviewing a sample showed the first address is the primary contact point in almost every case, with the others belonging to assistants or shared mailboxes.

RESOLUTION
The transformation now splits the field, loads the first address as primary, creates the remainder as secondary contact points linked to the record, and rejects any part that is not a valid address into a review list.

VALIDATION
All 2,900 records loaded with their primary address, 3,100 secondary contact points were created and spot-checked against the source, and 18 malformed entries appeared on the review list.

column1: Duplicate rules block a large share of the migration load
column2:
CONTEXT
Duplicate rules protect data quality by blocking records that match existing accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A migration wave loaded only 88 percent of its records, and the failures were not investigated before the next wave began.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migration should load its full record set, with genuine duplicates identified deliberately rather than blocked silently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Active duplicate rules rejected 12 percent of records, and the loader recorded them as errors that nobody reviewed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rules were left active because deactivating them was not in the runbook. Reviewing the rejected records showed most were legitimate branches of existing customers, and about 400 were genuine duplicates that should be merged rather than loaded.

RESOLUTION
The runbook now suspends duplicate rules for the migration user through a permission-based bypass, rejected records are reported per wave, and the 400 genuine duplicates were routed to the stewardship queue rather than loaded.

VALIDATION
The following wave loaded 100 percent of its intended records, the bypass applied only to the migration user, and the stewardship queue received the expected duplicates for review.

column1: Migrated contacts arrive with no marketing preference recorded
column2:
CONTEXT
Contacts are migrated ahead of a campaign, and marketing preference governs whether they may be contacted.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A pre-campaign check found empty preference fields, which the campaign tool treats as permission to send.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated contact should carry the preference recorded in the source system.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The preference field is empty for all 34,000 migrated contacts, because the source holds it in a separate consent table that was out of scope.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The campaign was held before any send and the marketing lead was informed, since contacting someone who had opted out would breach policy. The consent table exists in the source and holds a state for 31,000 of the 34,000 contacts.

RESOLUTION
The consent table was added to the migration scope and loaded, contacts with no source consent record default to no contact, and a validation prevents the campaign tool from treating an empty preference as permission.

VALIDATION
Preferences matched the source for a 500 record sample, the 3,000 contacts with no record were excluded from the campaign, and a test send confirmed opted-out contacts were skipped.

column1: Only the latest version of each migrated document is available
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy document store keeps every version of a contract document, and users refer to superseded versions during disputes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users find only one version of each document after migration and cannot retrieve earlier drafts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Version history should migrate so that earlier versions remain retrievable with their dates.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The migration extracted the current version only, and the version count in Salesforce is one for every document.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extract query selected the latest version per document, which matched an early scope decision that was later reversed without updating the extract. The legacy store holds 210,000 versions across 78,000 documents, and 40 percent of contract documents have more than one.

RESOLUTION
The extract now retrieves every version and loads them as version history under the same document, preserving the original version dates and authors where a matching user exists.

VALIDATION
Version counts matched the legacy store for a 300 document sample, users retrieved superseded versions with correct dates in a review session, and document totals reconciled after the reload.

column1: Cutover rehearsal has been completed for most object groups but not all
column2:
CONTEXT
A full cutover rehearsal validates load order, duration, and reconciliation before the production migration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The programme cannot yet confirm that the cutover fits inside the agreed weekend window.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every object group should be rehearsed end to end with a measured duration.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Four of six groups have been rehearsed, while the two largest have been tested only with sample volumes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two untested groups depend on a source extract the legacy team can produce only during their own quiet period. Extrapolating from sample volumes suggests they will take between five and nine hours, and the remaining window after the rehearsed groups is seven hours.

RESOLUTION
Four groups are rehearsed with measured durations totalling 11 hours and a working reconciliation. This is partial: the two largest groups have no measured full-volume duration, so the total cutover time remains an estimate with a four-hour spread.

VALIDATION
The four rehearsed groups completed within 10 percent of their estimates on two runs, while the remaining estimate stays unverified until the legacy team can supply a full extract.

column1: Legacy identifiers are stored in a plain text field because the key field is taken
column2:
CONTEXT
Records need to carry their legacy identifier so that historical documents and tickets can be traced.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The external identifier field is already used by the finance integration and cannot hold a second key.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The legacy identifier should be indexed and unique so lookups are fast and reliable.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only one external identifier field is available per object on the current configuration, and it is in use.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The finance key is written on every synchronization and cannot be repurposed. A second field was created as plain text, and testing showed lookups on it take several seconds on the full record set.

RESOLUTION
The legacy identifier is stored in a plain text field with a documented naming convention. This is a workaround: the value is neither indexed nor enforced as unique, so lookups are slow and duplicates are possible. A custom index request has been raised with support.

VALIDATION
Traceability queries returned correct results for 200 sampled records, taking four to six seconds each, and a duplicate check found no repeated values at load time.

column1: Loads fail with a storage error while the organization is below its limit
column2:
CONTEXT
Migration batches load into an organization whose data storage usage is monitored before each wave.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Batches intermittently fail with a storage-related error although reported usage sits at 62 percent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Loads should succeed while the organization is within its storage allocation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Roughly one batch in fifteen fails immediately with a storage error, and the same batch usually succeeds when resubmitted.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Storage usage was checked immediately before and after failing batches and did not change materially. File storage is at 34 percent, so the error does not obviously match either allocation. The failures do not cluster by object, batch size, or time of day, and no other operation was running during two of the observed failures.

RESOLUTION
The reported figures do not account for the error, so nothing has been changed in the load configuration or the storage arrangement.

VALIDATION
Failures continue at a similar rate and are handled by resubmission. The next step is a support case with the batch identifiers, the error responses, and the storage readings taken either side of three failures.

column1: Some migrated records cannot be opened by any user
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated service records should be visible to the teams that own them under the standard sharing model.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small set of records returns an insufficient access error for every user, including administrators.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Administrators should be able to open any record, and owning teams should see their own.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Around 90 records appear in report results but cannot be opened from any profile.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The affected records were excluded from go-live scope and flagged so no process depends on them. Owner, record type, and sharing entries look identical to records that open normally. They loaded in the same batch as working records, and a query returns their field values without error, so the data is intact and readable programmatically.

RESOLUTION
The reason the detail page refuses access has not been determined, and the records have been left untouched to preserve them for diagnosis.

VALIDATION
The 90 records remain inaccessible through the interface. The next step is a vendor support case with the record identifiers, the sharing entries, and the access error, since creating a new record does not reproduce the condition.

column1: Values passed to a subflow arrive empty at every call
column2:
CONTEXT
A shared subflow calculates a service credit and is called from three parent automations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The subflow always returns a zero credit regardless of the values the parent supplies.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The subflow should receive the contract value and tier from its caller and calculate accordingly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Both input variables are empty inside the subflow, so the calculation runs against defaults.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The subflow variables were created without being marked as available for input, so the parent assignments were accepted at design time but discarded at runtime. Debug logs from the subflow showed both variables empty on entry while the parent logs showed correct values immediately before the call.

RESOLUTION
Both variables were marked available for input, the subflow now fails explicitly when a required input is empty rather than falling back to a default, and the three parents were retested end to end.

VALIDATION
Credits calculated correctly for 30 contracts across all three callers, an empty input produced an explicit failure instead of a silent zero, and 74 historical records were recalculated.

column1: Completing the intake screen returns the agent to the home page
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents launch a screen flow from a Case to capture diagnostic details, which are saved back to that Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents lose their place after finishing the flow and must search for the Case again.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Finishing the flow should return the agent to the record they started from.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow ends on the application home page, and agents reopen the Case from their recent items.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow's finish behaviour was left at its default, which navigates to the start of a new interview rather than back to the originating record. Timing 20 intakes showed an average of 25 seconds lost per intake finding the Case again.

RESOLUTION
The finish behaviour now navigates to the record the flow was launched from, using the record identifier passed in at launch, and the flow closes its modal when launched from a quick action.

VALIDATION
Twenty intakes returned to the correct Case with the new details visible, launches from the list view and the record page both behaved correctly, and agents confirmed the lost time was recovered.

column1: Assigning a record to a queue fails at runtime for one object
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow routes both Cases and custom inspection records to shared regional queues.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Inspection records fail to route while Cases in the same run route correctly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both record types should reach their regional queue through the same routing logic.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Setting the owner to a queue is rejected for inspections with an invalid owner error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A queue accepts records only for objects listed as supported in its configuration, and the inspection object was never added when it was introduced. Reviewing all 12 queues showed inspections missing from 9 of them, which matched the failing regions exactly.

RESOLUTION
The inspection object was added to the affected queues, and the flow now checks that the target queue supports the object before assigning, routing to a fallback queue with an alert when it does not.

VALIDATION
Inspections routed correctly across all 12 regions, the fallback path handled a deliberately unsupported queue, and the 310 stuck inspections were reassigned.

column1: Formatted message body arrives as a single unbroken paragraph
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow assembles a customer message from a text template containing a list of outstanding items.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive the list as one continuous run of text that is difficult to read.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each outstanding item should appear on its own line as it does in the template preview.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Line breaks are present in the preview but absent in the delivered message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template was set to plain text while the send action delivered a rich text body, so the line breaks were not converted into markup and collapsed on rendering. A test sending the same template as plain text preserved the breaks, which isolated the mismatch.

RESOLUTION
The template was switched to rich text with explicit paragraph markup, and the send action now states the body format so the two cannot diverge again.

VALIDATION
Messages rendered with correct line breaks in six mail clients, plain text recipients received a readable fallback, and the service team reviewed a sample of 20 live messages.

column1: Automation fails whenever a record has no related items
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow summarizes related shipment records onto the parent order and stores the earliest delivery date.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Orders with no shipments cannot be saved, and users see an unhandled error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An order with no shipments should save normally with an empty summary.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow reads the first element of the shipment collection without checking whether the collection is empty.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Every failing order had zero related shipments, while orders with one or more succeeded. The collection is populated before the first element is read, and no decision guarded the empty case, so the read failed and the transaction rolled back.

RESOLUTION
The flow now tests the collection size before reading it, clears the summary fields when it is empty, and a fault path records any remaining failure to the error log.

VALIDATION
Orders with zero, one, and forty shipments all saved correctly, the summary cleared when the last shipment was deleted, and the previously blocked orders were saved without further changes.

column1: Legacy rules have been rebuilt as flows for some objects only
column2:
CONTEXT
A programme is replacing retiring workflow rules and field updates with record-triggered flows.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The organization cannot complete the migration before the platform retires the older tooling.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every legacy rule should be rebuilt as a flow with equivalent behaviour and test evidence.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Three of five objects are migrated, while two retain a mixture of legacy rules and flows.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The migrated objects had straightforward field updates. The two remaining objects carry 34 rules with interdependent conditions and time-based actions whose ordering is not documented anywhere.

RESOLUTION
Three objects are fully migrated with behaviour tests, covering 61 of 95 legacy rules. This is partial: 34 rules remain on the two complex objects, and their time-based actions must be drained before they can be rebuilt, which takes a further two months.

VALIDATION
The migrated objects produced identical outcomes to the legacy rules across 120 test scenarios, and the remaining rules continue to run with a documented retirement date.

column1: Guided selling covers new business but not renewals
column2:
CONTEXT
A guided flow walks sales users through qualification questions and recommends a product configuration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Renewal deals are configured manually, which produces inconsistent products and pricing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Guided selling should support renewals as well as new business.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Starting the flow on a renewal produces recommendations that ignore what the customer already owns.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The recommendation logic reads qualification answers only and has no view of the existing entitlement. Reviewing 60 renewals found 22 configured with products the customer already held and 9 missing a product they were using.

RESOLUTION
The flow now loads current entitlements and excludes products the customer already owns for straightforward like-for-like renewals. This is partial: renewals involving an upgrade or a product migration still fall back to manual configuration, which is about 30 percent of renewal volume.

VALIDATION
Like-for-like renewals produced correct configurations in 45 of 47 test cases, while upgrade scenarios were correctly routed to manual configuration rather than given a wrong recommendation.

column1: Real-time credit checks are replaced by a scheduled batch
column2:
CONTEXT
An order flow should confirm a customer's credit standing with an external service before submission.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users submit orders that are rejected hours later for credit reasons, after the customer has been told the order is placed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The credit position should be confirmed while the user is still on the order screen.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow cannot call the credit service, because the provider requires a signed request the flow cannot construct.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The service demands a request signature and a certificate exchange that flow callouts do not support. Building an intermediate service was estimated at six weeks, which the programme could not fund this quarter.

RESOLUTION
A batch job checks credit every 15 minutes and flags orders that fail. This is a workaround: users are still told the order is placed before the check runs, the delay averages eight minutes, and a failed check requires the account team to contact the customer.

VALIDATION
Orders were flagged within 15 minutes across a two-week measurement, and the customer contact rate fell from about 20 a week to 6, all still after the fact.

column1: Automation succeeds in the sandbox and fails for the same records in production
column2:
CONTEXT
An order validation flow was released after passing every scenario in a sandbox refreshed the same week.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The flow fails in production for about one order in forty, and the same orders pass when replayed in the sandbox.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Identical records and configuration should produce identical results in both environments.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Production interviews fail at a lookup element with no matching record, while the sandbox finds it and continues.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The reference data the lookup depends on was compared row by row and matches, and the flow version, entry criteria, and running user permissions are identical. Failures cluster in the first hour after the nightly reference load, which suggests interaction with that job, though the load reports completion before they begin.

RESOLUTION
The difference between the two environments has not been pinned down, and the flow has been left as released rather than changed on an assumption.

VALIDATION
Failures continue and are reprocessed manually each morning. The next step is instrumenting the lookup to record its filter values and result count, then comparing failing interviews against the reference load's completion record.

column1: Automation errors rise sharply for two hours after every release
column2:
CONTEXT
Releases are deployed on Thursday evenings and include metadata across several objects.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Flow error volume rises to roughly ten times its baseline for about two hours after each release, then returns to normal.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Error rates should be unchanged by a release that does not alter the affected automations.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Errors appear in flows that were not part of the release, and they stop without intervention.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The last three releases contained no changes to the failing flows, which was confirmed against the deployment manifests. The errors name several different elements rather than one consistent point. Restarting nothing and simply waiting resolves the spike, and one release deployed to a sandbox produced no equivalent spike under light load.

RESOLUTION
Nothing in the release content accounts for the pattern, so no change has been made to the deployment process.

VALIDATION
The spike recurred at the last three releases and is absorbed by retries. The next step is capturing the full error payloads for one release window and comparing them against platform maintenance events for the same period.

column1: Fractional quantities are silently rounded down on arrival
column2:
CONTEXT
Consumption records for metered services are imported from the billing platform and drive usage reporting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reported consumption is consistently lower than the billing platform shows.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Quantities should arrive with the precision the source records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Fractional quantities lose their decimal part, so 0.4 hours of usage becomes zero.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The target field was defined with zero decimal places, so values were truncated on save without an error. Comparing 2,000 records showed 38 percent had a fractional component, and the aggregate shortfall matched the reporting gap almost exactly.

RESOLUTION
The field was redefined with three decimal places, the affected period was reloaded from source, and a load-time check compares the sum of incoming quantities with the sum stored after the load.

VALIDATION
Reloaded consumption matched the billing platform to three decimal places for two months, the sum check passed on every subsequent load, and usage reporting reconciled with invoices.

column1: Picklist writes fail for the integration user but succeed for staff
column2:
CONTEXT
Middleware sets a service category picklist on records it creates, using the value defined in the mapping.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every record created by the integration fails with an invalid picklist value, while staff can select the same value.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should be able to set any value defined for the field.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The write is rejected although the value in the payload matches what appears in the interface.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration user's language was set to a translated locale during an earlier test, so the interface showed translated labels while the stored values remained in the base language. The mapping had been built by copying labels from that user's screen, so it carried translations rather than stored values.

RESOLUTION
The mapping was rebuilt from the field definition using stored values, and the integration user's language was set to the base language with a note explaining why it must not be changed.

VALIDATION
The 1,240 queued records were created successfully, a translated label supplied deliberately was rejected with a clear error, and staff selections were unaffected.

column1: Two systems overwrite each other's value on the same field
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer risk rating is written by a compliance platform and by a credit platform, both through middleware.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The rating on some accounts changes several times a day between two different values.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
One system should own the field, or the two inputs should be combined by an agreed rule.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Each platform writes its own rating whenever it recalculates, so the stored value reflects whichever wrote last.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both integrations were built independently and mapped to the same field. Field history on 40 affected accounts showed alternating writes from the two integration users, up to nine changes in a day, with no rule reconciling them.

RESOLUTION
Each platform now writes to its own field, and a documented rule derives the overall rating as the more conservative of the two, recalculated whenever either input changes.

VALIDATION
The derived rating changed only when an input genuinely changed across a two-week observation, the conservative rule was confirmed against 50 combinations, and compliance accepted the derivation.

column1: Transferred documents cannot be opened by the applications that need them
column2:
CONTEXT
Signed documents are transferred from the contract system into Salesforce files linked to the agreement record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users download migrated documents and find their applications refuse to open them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A transferred document should open in the application associated with its format.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Files download with a generic type and no extension, so the operating system cannot choose an application.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The transfer set a single default content type for every document and dropped the file extension from the name. The bytes themselves were intact, and renaming a downloaded file by hand opened it correctly, which confirmed only the metadata was wrong.

RESOLUTION
The transfer now maps the source content type onto the file and preserves the original extension, and files with an unrecognized type are rejected to a review list rather than defaulted.

VALIDATION
The 8,900 affected documents were corrected in place and opened directly in six sampled formats, and a document with an unknown type appeared on the review list.

column1: Only the last of several source rows survives for each customer
column2:
CONTEXT
The source system holds one row per customer per service location, and the integration maps them into Salesforce accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Service details for customers with several locations are wrong, showing one location's data for the whole customer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each service location should be represented so that its details remain distinguishable.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every source row updates the same account, so each row overwrites the previous one and only the last survives.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping assumed one row per customer, which holds for 70 percent of the base. Counting source rows found 3,400 customers with two or more locations, and their account records changed with every load in a pattern matching the source ordering.

RESOLUTION
Service locations are now loaded into a child object linked to the account, with account-level fields deriving from the primary location, and the load rejects a row that would overwrite a different location.

VALIDATION
The 3,400 multi-location customers loaded with complete location records, account-level values matched their primary location, and repeat loads produced no field changes.

column1: Failed writes are acknowledged to the sender as successful
column2:
CONTEXT
The middleware acknowledges each message to the source system once it has been handed to Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The source system believes updates are applied that never reached Salesforce, and the two drift apart.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An acknowledgement should mean the change is committed and visible.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The acknowledgement is sent when the request is dispatched, before the response confirms the outcome.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dispatch and acknowledgement were in the same step, with the response handled asynchronously and only logged. A reconciliation found 2,100 acknowledged messages over three months whose changes are absent from Salesforce, most rejected by validation rules.

RESOLUTION
The acknowledgement now waits for the response and reports success only on a committed write, failures are returned to the source with their reason, and a daily reconciliation compares acknowledged messages against stored records.

VALIDATION
The 2,100 divergent records were resubmitted and applied or explicitly rejected, a forced validation failure produced a negative acknowledgement, and the daily reconciliation has reported no drift for three weeks.

column1: Reference data is synchronized for currencies but not for units
column2:
CONTEXT
Shared reference data must stay aligned between the ERP and Salesforce for pricing and fulfilment to match.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Orders are rejected by the ERP because they carry a unit of measure it does not recognize.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Reference data should be maintained in one place and distributed automatically.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Currency codes synchronize nightly, while units of measure are maintained by hand in both systems and drift apart.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The currency feed was built first because the list is short and stable. Units of measure are extended by product teams several times a month, and a comparison found 14 units present in Salesforce that the ERP does not hold.

RESOLUTION
Units of measure now synchronize on the same nightly schedule as currencies, with the ERP as the source. This is partial: units created in Salesforce are removed by the next sync rather than promoted to the ERP.

VALIDATION
The 14 mismatched units were reconciled and order rejections for unit errors stopped over three weeks, while two units created in Salesforce were removed by the sync as documented.

column1: Recovering from a failed run means reloading everything
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly integration applies thousands of updates, and a failure partway through leaves the load incomplete.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Recovery from a partial failure takes most of the following day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A failed run should be resumable from the point of failure, or the failed subset should be replayable.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The middleware does not retain processed messages, so the only reliable recovery is a full reload from the source.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Messages are discarded once dispatched, and the run log records counts rather than identifiers. Two failures in the last quarter each required a full reload taking six hours and blocking the following night's run.

RESOLUTION
Each run now writes the record identifiers it processed to a run manifest, so recovery reloads only the remainder. This is a workaround: the manifest reconstructs scope rather than replaying the original messages, so any transformation applied in flight has to be recomputed from current source data.

VALIDATION
A simulated mid-run failure was recovered in 40 minutes rather than six hours, and the manifest matched the source change set for the affected window.

column1: Most of the partner feed is received and discarded
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner publishes a daily catalogue feed covering their whole product range, of which only one division is relevant.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Processing time and storage costs are driven by records the organization never uses.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The feed should contain only the division the organization subscribes to.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All 400,000 records arrive daily and roughly 80 percent are discarded after being parsed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner publishes one feed for all subscribers and confirmed they cannot filter per recipient before their platform replacement next year. Processing the full feed takes 70 minutes, of which about 55 is spent on irrelevant records.

RESOLUTION
Filtering now happens as the file streams, before parsing and storage. This is a workaround: the full file is still transferred and read, so network and read time are unchanged, and a partner change to the division field would silently discard relevant records.

VALIDATION
Processing time fell from 70 to 22 minutes and stored volume by 78 percent, while transfer time was unchanged and a division field check now alerts if the discarded proportion moves by more than five points.

column1: Queue depth grows without a matching rise in source activity
column2:
CONTEXT
A message queue carries account updates from the source system to Salesforce and is monitored for depth.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Depth rises to several times its normal level for an hour or two, roughly twice a week.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Queue depth should track the volume of genuine changes in the source system.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Depth grows while the source change log shows normal activity, and the surplus messages carry values identical to what Salesforce already holds.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The additional messages are well formed and reference real accounts, so they are being published rather than generated in transit. The source team confirmed no batch job runs in those windows, and their change log does not record the corresponding updates. Comparing message contents with stored records showed no field difference in 300 sampled messages.

RESOLUTION
The origin of the additional messages is unidentified, and no filtering has been introduced because discarding them could suppress genuine updates.

VALIDATION
The pattern recurs and is absorbed without data harm. The next step is enabling publisher-side tracing on the source platform for a full week to attribute the surplus messages to a process.

column1: A shared team login makes activity impossible to attribute
column2:
CONTEXT
A back-office team of six used a single shared account to process adjustments.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit could not determine who had made a set of disputed adjustments.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every action should be attributable to an individual.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All six people work under one identity, so record history names the shared account for every change.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The shared account predated the team's growth and had been kept for licence reasons. Login history showed concurrent sessions from six locations, and the disputed adjustments could not be attributed to a person even with full history.

RESOLUTION
Six named accounts were provisioned with the same permission set, the shared account was deactivated and its credential retired, and a control now reports accounts with concurrent sessions from multiple addresses.

VALIDATION
Adjustments made after the change were attributable in every sampled case, the shared account showed no further logins, and the concurrency control raised no findings over four weeks.

column1: Staff keep old access after moving to a new role
column2:
CONTEXT
Internal moves are common, and access is granted through permission sets assigned per role.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An access review found people holding permissions from two or three previous roles.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Access appropriate to a previous role should be removed when someone changes role.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
New permission sets are added on the move, while the previous ones stay assigned indefinitely.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The joiner and leaver processes were automated, but the mover case was never built. A review found 210 users holding permission sets outside their current role definition, 40 of them with access to financial adjustment functions they no longer needed.

RESOLUTION
Role changes now trigger a reconciliation that removes permission sets not in the new role's definition, with exceptions requiring a documented approval and an expiry date.

VALIDATION
The 210 users were reconciled with 18 documented exceptions, a test role change removed the previous access within an hour, and the next quarterly review found no unexplained assignments.

column1: Community accounts are held to a weaker password standard than staff
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers authenticate to the support community with a username and password issued at registration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the community policy far weaker than the internal standard.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
External accounts should meet a password standard proportionate to the data they can reach.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Community passwords have a short minimum length, no complexity requirement, and never expire.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The policy was left at its default when the community launched. Testing confirmed a five-character password was accepted, and the community exposes case history and contact details for the customer's organization.

RESOLUTION
The community profile now enforces a longer minimum length, complexity, lockout after repeated failures, and a check against a list of commonly used passwords, with existing users prompted to reset at next login.

VALIDATION
New and reset passwords were rejected below the standard in testing, lockout triggered as configured, and 82 percent of active community users had reset within three weeks with support handling the remainder.

column1: Support staff use user impersonation without a recorded reason
column2:
CONTEXT
Administrators can log in as another user to reproduce problems reported by staff.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found frequent impersonation with no record of why it was needed or whether the user agreed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every impersonation should have a recorded reason linked to a support request.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The platform records that impersonation occurred but not the justification, and no internal process required one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Login history showed 340 impersonation events in a quarter by nine administrators. Sampling 30 events against support tickets found 22 with a plausible matching ticket and 8 with none.

RESOLUTION
Impersonation now requires an open support ticket recorded in a request log before access is granted, the permission was narrowed to four administrators, and a weekly report reconciles impersonation events against tickets.

VALIDATION
Every impersonation in the following month carried a matching ticket, the report flagged two events for follow-up that proved legitimate, and the eight historical events were reviewed with the users concerned.

column1: Signing certificates are readable by every administrator
column2:
CONTEXT
Certificates used to sign integration requests are stored in the platform's certificate store.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found that all fourteen administrators could manage the signing certificates.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Custody of signing material should be limited to a small named group with recorded changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Certificate management is granted by a broad administrative permission held by everyone in the administrator profile.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Access was reduced the same day and the security team was informed. The permission is bundled with general setup rights, so it had been granted implicitly rather than deliberately. Setup history showed no unexpected certificate changes in the retained period.

RESOLUTION
Certificate management was separated into a dedicated permission held by three named custodians, changes now require a second approver, and any certificate change raises an alert to the security team.

VALIDATION
Administrators outside the custodian group could no longer view or replace certificates, a test replacement produced the alert and required the second approval, and the integration continued without interruption.

column1: Download monitoring covers managed devices only
column2:
CONTEXT
Controls aim to detect large volumes of customer data leaving the platform onto personal storage.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The organization cannot demonstrate coverage of data leaving through unmanaged devices.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Bulk downloads should be detected regardless of the device used.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Managed laptops report download activity to the monitoring agent, while personal devices used by contractors report nothing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Detection relies on an endpoint agent that cannot be installed on unmanaged devices. Access records showed 40 contractors working from unmanaged devices, accounting for roughly 12 percent of report exports.

RESOLUTION
Platform-side export events are now monitored for all users regardless of device, which covers report exports and file downloads. This is partial: activity after the data leaves the platform is still invisible on unmanaged devices, so onward copying cannot be detected.

VALIDATION
Exports by contractors on unmanaged devices produced platform-side alerts in testing, while a file copied onward from an unmanaged device produced no signal, as expected.

column1: A risky permission cannot be removed because a report depends on it
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission allowing users to view all records of one object was granted so that a shared report would work.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The permission grants far wider visibility than the report requires and was raised as an access risk.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Users should see only the records their role requires, and reporting should work within that boundary.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Removing the permission empties the report, because it aggregates records across teams the users cannot see.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report needs aggregate figures rather than record access, and the platform applies the running user's access to the underlying rows. Rebuilding it against a pre-aggregated summary object was estimated at three weeks and not yet scheduled.

RESOLUTION
The permission remains, with compensating controls: access is time-limited and reviewed monthly, the group was reduced from 60 users to 18, and their access to the object is monitored with alerts on bulk retrieval.

VALIDATION
The user group was reduced and confirmed by an access report, monthly reviews have run twice, and a scripted bulk retrieval by a member of the group raised the expected alert.

column1: Shift workers cannot use the shorter session timeout
column2:
CONTEXT
A shorter inactivity timeout was introduced to reduce the risk of unattended sessions on shared devices.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Warehouse shift workers are logged out repeatedly during tasks that keep them away from the screen.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Unattended sessions should end quickly without disrupting legitimate work patterns.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Workers are logged out mid-task several times per shift and lose entered data.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Their work involves ten to twenty minute periods away from the terminal, which the shorter timeout cannot accommodate. Measuring one shift showed 14 forced logouts across six workers and about 40 minutes of lost time.

RESOLUTION
The warehouse profile keeps the longer timeout, with device-level screen locking after three minutes and physical access controls in the area. This is a workaround: the platform session remains open longer than policy prefers, and protection depends on the screen lock rather than the platform.

VALIDATION
Forced logouts fell to zero over two shifts, screen lock was confirmed active on all twelve terminals, and the risk acceptance was recorded with a review date.

column1: An account briefly held permissions nobody granted
column2:
CONTEXT
Permission set assignments are made through an approved request process and reviewed quarterly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Monitoring detected an account holding an administrative permission set for about 40 minutes overnight.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Permissions should change only through the approved process, with an approver recorded.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assignment appeared and was removed with no corresponding request and no approver named.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The account's sessions were revoked, its permissions were reset to the role baseline, and the security team opened an incident. Setup history records the assignment and its removal but attributes both to an automated process rather than a person. The deployment pipeline ran that night, though its manifest contains no permission set changes. No activity was recorded on the account during the 40 minutes.

RESOLUTION
The escalation path taken remains unexplained, and the pipeline has not been altered because the link to it is unproven.

VALIDATION
