No recurrence in three weeks of heightened monitoring. The next step is enabling verbose pipeline logging and correlating the next deployment with permission assignment events at second-level granularity.

column1: Configuration changes are recorded during a window with no administrator activity
column2:
CONTEXT
Configuration changes are expected during business hours and are reviewed weekly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The weekly review found eleven field-level changes recorded at a time when no administrator was logged in.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every configuration change should correspond to an authenticated session and a known activity.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The audit entries name an administrator whose login history shows no session in that period.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The account's credential was rotated and its permissions reduced pending investigation, and the security team was engaged. The changes are consistent with a metadata deployment, and one did run that evening under a different service account. Whether the audit trail attributes deployed changes to the named administrator has not been confirmed with the vendor.

RESOLUTION
How the changes came to be recorded under that account is not established, and no conclusion has been drawn about whether the activity was legitimate.

VALIDATION
The eleven changes were reviewed and match the release content, which is reassuring but not conclusive. The next step is a vendor case asking how deployed changes are attributed, and a controlled deployment to observe which account the trail names.

column1: Subtotals in the service report do not add up to the grand total
column2:
CONTEXT
A service report groups cases by region and then by team, with a custom formula showing resolution rate.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Regional resolution rates are inconsistent with the team rates beneath them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each grouping level should show the rate calculated from its own records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The regional row repeats the value from the first team rather than recalculating across the region.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The custom summary formula was configured to display at the lowest grouping only, so higher levels inherited a value rather than computing one. Calculating three regions by hand confirmed the correct rates differ from those displayed by up to eleven points.

RESOLUTION
The formula now displays at all grouping levels and computes from summarized values at each level, and the report help text explains how the rate is derived.

VALIDATION
Regional and team rates matched hand calculations for four regions, the grand total matched an independent query, and a reviewer reproduced the figures from the help text.

column1: Blocks in the combined report show blank values for shared columns
column2:
CONTEXT
A combined report shows opportunities and support cases side by side for each account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The case block shows blanks in the account column, so the two blocks cannot be read together.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both blocks should align on the account so that each row set belongs to the same customer.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The opportunity block populates the account while the case block leaves it empty.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A combined report aligns blocks only on a field common to every block, and the grouping had been set on a field that exists on opportunities alone. Grouping by the shared account field in a test copy populated both blocks correctly.

RESOLUTION
The report now groups on the common account field, with block-specific fields moved into their own columns and a note explaining which measures belong to which block.

VALIDATION
Both blocks aligned for 200 sampled accounts, totals in each block matched their standalone reports, and the account team confirmed the report was usable for their review.

column1: The volume trend has been flat since the snapshot job stopped
column2:
CONTEXT
A trend report reads a snapshot object populated weekly by a scheduled job.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The trend shows an unchanging figure for the last eleven weeks, which nobody questioned until a review.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each week should add a new snapshot row, and a missing run should be visible.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The job stopped after its scheduled user was deactivated, and the report simply repeated the last stored value.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Scheduled jobs run as the user who scheduled them and stop when that user is deactivated. The job's last successful run matched the leaver's departure date, and no alert existed because the report continued to render.

RESOLUTION
The job was rescheduled under a service account not tied to an individual, the eleven missing weeks were rebuilt from history where possible, and a check reports any snapshot object with no new rows in its expected interval.

VALIDATION
New snapshots have been written for four consecutive weeks, nine of the eleven missing weeks were reconstructed and two documented as unavailable, and the freshness check flagged a deliberately paused test job.

column1: The category chart hides most of the volume behind a single slice
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard chart shows case volume by product category for the weekly operations meeting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Attendees make decisions from the chart that do not match the underlying report.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The chart should represent the distribution faithfully or state clearly what it omits.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The chart shows the top five categories and silently groups the remaining 40 into an unlabelled slice that is larger than any named one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The component was configured with a display limit and the remainder grouping left unlabelled. The grouped remainder accounted for 46 percent of volume and contained three categories individually larger than the fifth named one.

RESOLUTION
The chart now shows the top ten categories with the remainder labelled explicitly and its category count stated, and a linked report gives the full breakdown.

VALIDATION
The named categories covered 81 percent of volume, the remainder was labelled with its count, and the meeting reviewed the full breakdown for two consecutive weeks.

column1: Activity reporting excludes tasks marked as private
column2:
CONTEXT
Managers review customer contact volume per representative from an activity report.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several representatives appear to make far fewer customer contacts than their calendars suggest.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Business activities should be counted for reporting regardless of individual display preferences.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Tasks flagged as private are excluded from the report for everyone except their owner.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Some representatives had set private as their default when logging activities, mostly to hide entries from a shared calendar view. Counting activities per representative found four with more than half their tasks marked private, which matched the apparent shortfall.

RESOLUTION
Guidance and a default change removed private as the standard setting for customer activities, existing customer-related private tasks were unflagged after confirming with each owner, and the report now shows a count of excluded private activities.

VALIDATION
Contact volumes for the four representatives rose to match their calendars, the excluded count fell to near zero, and personal activities kept the private flag where owners intended it.

column1: A needed dimension is unavailable in the custom report type
column2:
CONTEXT
Analysts report on service cases using a custom report type built for the support team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases cannot be analyzed by the customer's industry, so segment analysis is done by exporting to a spreadsheet.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Account attributes should be available as dimensions on case reporting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type includes the case object and its contact but not the account, so account fields cannot be selected.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report type was created before account attributes were needed and includes two objects only. Testing a copy with the account added confirmed every requested dimension became available with no change to row counts.

RESOLUTION
A new report type including the account was published alongside the original, the four affected reports were migrated to it, and the original was marked for retirement once no reports depend on it.

VALIDATION
Segment analysis ran inside the platform for two months with results matching the previous spreadsheet method, and row counts matched the original report type exactly.

column1: Grouping into ranges is unavailable for calculated fields
column2:
CONTEXT
Analysts group records into ranges to summarize distributions without editing the data model.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Ranges cannot be defined on the calculated fields that carry the most useful measures.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Range grouping should be available for any numeric field an analyst can report on.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Range grouping is offered for stored fields and not for formula fields, so analysts export and band the data elsewhere.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The limitation is inherent to the reporting tool rather than a configuration choice. Of the nine measures analysts band regularly, five are stored fields and four are formulas, all four derived from stored values available on the same record.

RESOLUTION
Two of the four formulas were replaced with stored fields maintained by automation, which restored range grouping for them. This is partial: the remaining two depend on values from related records that cannot be stored without a design change, so they are still banded outside the platform.

VALIDATION
Range grouping worked for seven of nine measures with values matching the formulas they replaced, and the two remaining measures continue to be exported.

column1: Report rationalization is complete for two functions only
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization holds several thousand reports accumulated over years, many of them near duplicates.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users cannot tell which report is authoritative and often pick one that is out of date.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each business question should have one clearly identified authoritative report.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Service and sales have a curated set, while three other functions still hold hundreds of uncurated reports.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Usage analysis found 3,400 reports of which 900 had been run in the past year and 210 accounted for 80 percent of runs. The two rationalized functions had engaged owners, while the remaining three have no nominated report owner.

RESOLUTION
Service and sales now have curated folders with named owners, covering about 40 percent of report runs. This is partial: the other three functions are unchanged, and unused reports elsewhere have been left in place rather than deleted without an owner's agreement.

VALIDATION
Users in the two curated functions found the authoritative report first in a usability test, while the same test in a third function produced three different reports for one question.

column1: Report access is managed by naming convention rather than permissions
column2:
CONTEXT
Reports containing sensitive commercial measures should be reachable only by the teams entitled to them.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sensitive reports sit in shared folders because the team structure does not map onto the folder model.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Folder access should reflect entitlement, so a user cannot open a report they should not see.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Several teams need overlapping subsets, which would require more folders than the team is able to maintain.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Mapping entitlements onto folders produced 34 folders for 11 teams, which the analytics team judged unmaintainable. Report-level access is not available separately from folder access, so practice relies on prefixing report names with their audience.

RESOLUTION
Sensitive reports were moved into four restricted folders covering the clearest boundaries, and the naming convention marks audience within them. This is a workaround: names guide behaviour rather than enforce it, and a user with folder access can still open every report in that folder.

VALIDATION
The four restricted folders were confirmed inaccessible to users outside their groups, while an audit showed reports whose audience prefix does not match every viewer entitled to the folder.

column1: A dashboard component fails to render for some viewers
column2:
CONTEXT
An operations dashboard is opened each morning by around forty users across three regions.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One component shows an error tile for a handful of users while the rest of the dashboard renders.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every component should render for any user entitled to the dashboard.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected users see a generic error in one tile, and refreshing sometimes clears it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The underlying report opens normally for the same users when run directly, which rules out access to the report itself. The affected users share no profile, role, or region, and the set changes between mornings. The component uses a filter that references a user attribute, though replicating that filter in a direct run reproduces nothing.

RESOLUTION
The render failure has not been reproduced under controlled conditions, so the component has been left in place rather than rebuilt speculatively.

VALIDATION
Reports continue at two or three users a day. The next step is collecting the browser console output and the request identifier from an affected user at the moment of failure, then raising a vendor case with those details.

column1: Messages with no subject line are rejected instead of creating a case
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer messages arriving at the support address create Cases with the subject as the Case title.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some customer messages never appear in the queue, and the customers receive no acknowledgement.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A message should create a Case whether or not it carries a subject.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages with an empty subject fail because the Case title is required and no default is supplied.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Processing logs showed 90 failures in a month, all with an empty subject, most sent from mobile clients where the customer typed only a body. The failures were logged but produced no alert or bounce, so the messages were lost silently.

RESOLUTION
An empty subject now produces a generated title from the sender and date, the body is preserved unchanged, and any inbound processing failure raises an alert.

VALIDATION
Test messages with no subject created Cases with a readable generated title, the 90 lost messages were recovered from the mail platform and processed, and a forced failure raised the alert.

column1: Customers cannot open the case link included in their notification
column2:
CONTEXT
Service notifications include a link so that customers can view their case in the support community.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers report an access error when following the link from their notification.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The link should open the case for customers entitled to the community, and be omitted for those who are not.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every notification carries the link, including messages to customers with no community account, who reach a login page they cannot pass.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template included the link unconditionally. A count showed 38 percent of contacts receiving notifications have no community account, which matched the volume of confused replies to the support queue.

RESOLUTION
The template now includes the link only when the recipient has an active community account, and other recipients receive the case reference with instructions to reply to the message instead.

VALIDATION
Notifications to enabled and non-enabled contacts rendered correctly in testing, replies asking about access stopped over a four-week period, and the community login page saw no further failed arrivals from notifications.

column1: Writing to two support addresses at once creates two cases
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization publishes a general support address and several product-specific addresses.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers who address a message to two of them get two Cases and two different agents replying.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
One customer message should produce one Case regardless of how many of the addresses it reaches.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Each address processes the message independently, so two Cases are created seconds apart with the same content.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Inbound handling runs per address with no shared view of what has already been processed. A month's data showed 210 duplicate pairs, all with the same message identifier, which provides a reliable way to recognize them.

RESOLUTION
Inbound processing now records the message identifier and attaches a repeat arrival to the existing Case as an additional recipient rather than creating a second one.

VALIDATION
Test messages sent to two and three addresses produced one Case each, the 210 historical pairs were merged, and duplicate agent replies stopped being reported.

column1: The resolution summary is cut short in the customer's message
column2:
CONTEXT
Closure messages include the agent's resolution summary taken from the Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive summaries that stop mid-sentence, and some ask what the rest said.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The full resolution summary should appear in the message.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The text stops at 255 characters, which is shorter than most summaries agents write.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template merged a short text field that mirrors the beginning of the full summary, created years earlier for list views. Of 400 closures sampled, 280 had summaries longer than the mirrored field.

RESOLUTION
The template now merges the full summary field, the mirrored field was removed from the layout to prevent further confusion, and closure messages are previewed by the agent before sending.

VALIDATION
Full summaries appeared in 50 test messages including one of 1,800 characters, agents confirmed the preview matched what was sent, and customer queries about truncated text stopped.

column1: Compliance copies are missing for messages sent by automation
column2:
CONTEXT
A compliance requirement copies every outbound customer message to a supervised mailbox.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A control test found automated messages absent from the supervised mailbox.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every outbound customer message should be copied regardless of whether a person or a process sent it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages sent by agents are copied, while messages sent by automation are not.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The copy is applied by a user-level setting that automation does not inherit. Comparing sent volume with mailbox volume for one month showed 14,000 sent and 5,200 copied, and the gap matched automated volume precisely.

RESOLUTION
The compliance copy is now applied at the organization level so it covers every sending path, and a monthly reconciliation compares sent volume against copies received.

VALIDATION
Sent and copied volumes matched within 0.2 percent for two months, automated messages appeared in the supervised mailbox in testing, and the compliance owner accepted the reconciliation as evidence.

column1: Templates can merge case fields but not the related asset
column2:
CONTEXT
Service messages should name the specific equipment a case relates to, which is held on a related asset record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents paste equipment details by hand into every message, which is slow and inconsistent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Templates should merge asset details automatically alongside case fields.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Merge fields resolve for the case and its contact, while asset fields render empty.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Templates traverse one relationship level from the base record, and the asset sits behind a lookup that the template cannot follow. Reviewing 120 messages found equipment details pasted manually in 96, with three formatting variants and two transcription errors.

RESOLUTION
Three asset attributes are now copied onto the case by automation when the asset is linked, and templates merge those copies. This is partial: attributes changed on the asset after the case is created do not refresh, and other asset fields remain unavailable.

VALIDATION
Equipment details appeared correctly in 40 test messages, manual pasting fell to near zero, and a deliberate asset change after case creation was correctly identified as not refreshing.

column1: Out-of-hours acknowledgements are suppressed except on public holidays
column2:
CONTEXT
Automatic acknowledgements tell customers when to expect a response, with different wording outside working hours.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers writing on public holidays receive a message promising a response the same day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Acknowledgement wording should reflect actual availability, including holidays.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Evening and weekend messages get the correct wording, while public holidays are treated as ordinary working days.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The logic evaluates the time of day and the day of the week without consulting the holiday calendar. Holiday records exist and are maintained for entitlement processing, covering the two largest regions but not the other three.

RESOLUTION
The acknowledgement now consults the holiday calendar for the two maintained regions. This is partial: the other three regions have no maintained holiday data, so their customers still receive working-day wording on local holidays.

VALIDATION
Messages sent on two public holidays in the covered regions carried the correct wording, and a holiday in an uncovered region reproduced the original behaviour as documented.

column1: Content sent in error cannot be withdrawn from the customer's mailbox
column2:
CONTEXT
Occasionally an agent sends a message containing the wrong attachment or an internal note.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
There is no way to withdraw the content once it has left, and each incident is handled improvised.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An incorrect send should follow a defined remediation path with a recorded outcome.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Recall is not possible for messages already delivered to external recipients, and the record still shows the sent content.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Delivery to an external mail system cannot be reversed by the sender. Reviewing seven incidents from the past year showed each handled differently, with two never reported to the data protection lead as policy requires.

RESOLUTION
A documented procedure now covers notification to the recipient, a correction message, an internal record marked with the remediation, and escalation criteria. This is a workaround: the original content remains in the recipient's mailbox, and remediation depends on their cooperation.

VALIDATION
Two incidents since the change followed the procedure with recorded outcomes and timely escalation, and a walkthrough with the data protection lead confirmed the criteria were clear.

column1: Inbound sorting rules are maintained outside the platform
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound messages are sorted into service streams before they reach Case creation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Support administrators cannot change the sorting rules and must raise a request with the mail team.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Service owners should maintain their own routing rules where they can see the effect.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rules require conditions on message headers that the platform's routing cannot express, so they live in the mail platform.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nine of fourteen rules test header values the routing configuration cannot read. Change requests took an average of six working days last quarter, and two rules were implemented incorrectly at the first attempt.

RESOLUTION
The five rules expressible in the platform were moved there, and the remaining nine stay in the mail platform with a documented request path and a shared rule register. This is a workaround: routing logic lives in two places, and the register is maintained by hand.

VALIDATION
The five migrated rules were confirmed working, turnaround for the rest fell to two days with the register giving clearer specifications, and no rule was implemented incorrectly in the following quarter.

column1: Messages from one customer arrive with an empty body
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound customer messages create Cases whose description is taken from the message body.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases from one corporate customer are created with an empty description, and agents must ask the customer to resend.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The message body should be captured for every inbound message.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The Case is created with the correct sender and subject and no description, although the customer's message clearly contained text.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Retained copies of two affected messages show a multipart structure with both plain and formatted parts present, so the content did arrive. The same customer's messages sent from a phone are captured correctly, while those from their desktop client are not. Forwarding an affected message from an internal account reproduces nothing.

RESOLUTION
Where the body is lost between arrival and Case creation has not been determined, and no change has been made to inbound processing.

VALIDATION
The problem persists for that customer and has not appeared for others. The next step is capturing the raw message as received for the next occurrence and comparing its structure against a successfully processed message from the same sender.

column1: The previous owner remains named on reassigned records
column2:
CONTEXT
Accounts carry both a system owner and a custom relationship manager field used in customer correspondence.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive letters naming a manager who left the company months ago.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both fields should reflect the person currently responsible for the account.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Reassignment updates the system owner while the relationship manager field keeps its previous value.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The custom field was introduced for correspondence and is maintained manually. Comparing the two fields across the base found 1,600 accounts where they disagreed, and 210 named a deactivated user.

RESOLUTION
The relationship manager field is now maintained by automation from the system owner unless an explicit override flag is set, and overrides referencing an inactive user are reported weekly.

VALIDATION
The two fields agreed across the base after the correction except for 40 approved overrides, correspondence named the current manager in sampled letters, and the weekly report returned no inactive overrides.

column1: Dependent picklist values become unavailable after the controlling field changes
column2:
CONTEXT
The case subcategory picklist depends on the category, with a defined set of valid combinations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents cannot select any subcategory for two categories introduced last month.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every category should offer its intended subcategories.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The subcategory list is empty for the new categories, and agents leave the field blank.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Adding a controlling value does not create dependency mappings, which must be defined explicitly. The dependency matrix showed no entries for the two new categories, and 1,900 cases had been created with an empty subcategory since they were introduced.

RESOLUTION
The dependency mappings were defined for both categories, a deployment check verifies that every controlling value has at least one dependent value, and the 1,900 cases were routed to their owners for classification.

VALIDATION
Subcategories were selectable for all categories in testing, the deployment check rejected a test category with no mappings, and the unclassified backlog cleared within three weeks.

column1: The escalation flag is never cleared once a case is de-escalated
column2:
CONTEXT
Cases carry an escalation flag that drives management reporting and a daily review list.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The escalation list grows every week and now includes cases resolved long ago.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flag should be cleared when a case is de-escalated or closed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Escalation sets the flag while nothing clears it, so the list only ever grows.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
De-escalation exists as a manual step with no automation attached, and closure does not touch the flag. The review list held 640 cases of which 580 were closed, which is why managers had stopped using it.

RESOLUTION
Closure and de-escalation now clear the flag and stamp the reason and time, historical closed cases were cleared in a controlled update, and the review list filters on open cases as a further safeguard.

VALIDATION
The review list fell to 44 genuinely escalated open cases, clearing behaved correctly across 30 test transitions, and managers resumed the daily review.

column1: Child records can be created without the parent they belong to
column2:
CONTEXT
Inspection records belong to a site and should never exist independently.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Inspections appear in reports with no site, and their findings cannot be attributed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every inspection should reference the site it was carried out at.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The site lookup is optional, so records created through the mobile app and the API save without it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The lookup was left optional when the object was created to simplify an early import. A count found 2,300 orphan inspections, of which 1,850 could be matched to a site through the inspector's assignment for that day.

RESOLUTION
The lookup is now required at field level so it applies in every context, the 1,850 matchable records were linked, and the remainder were flagged for the regional teams to resolve.

VALIDATION
New inspections could not be saved without a site in any client, orphan creation stopped, and the flagged backlog fell from 450 to 60 within a month.

column1: The related list shows the oldest entries and hides recent activity
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents review recent interactions from a related list on the account page.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents believe accounts have had no recent contact and duplicate outreach that colleagues have already made.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The most recent interactions should appear first.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The list sorts oldest first and shows five rows, so recent contact is hidden behind years of history.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The related list kept its default ordering, which is ascending by creation. On accounts with long histories, the visible five rows averaged four years old, and agents rarely expanded the full list.

RESOLUTION
The related list now sorts by interaction date descending, shows ten rows, and displays the interaction type so agents can scan it quickly.

VALIDATION
The visible rows covered the most recent interactions on 50 sampled accounts, duplicate outreach reports fell over the following month, and agents confirmed the list was usable without expanding it.

column1: Retention deletion covers cases but not their attachments
column2:
CONTEXT
A retention policy requires customer service records to be deleted after a defined period.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit found documents still present for cases that had been deleted under the policy.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deleting a record under retention should remove its associated content.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Case records are deleted on schedule while their files remain, since files can be linked to more than one record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Files survive deletion of one linked record if other links remain or if the file is owned separately. A scan found 96,000 files whose only related case had been deleted, some containing customer identity documents.

RESOLUTION
The retention job now deletes files whose remaining links are all to deleted records. This is partial: files linked to a surviving record are retained by design, so a document shared between two cases outlives the deleted one, and that behaviour needs a policy decision.

VALIDATION
The 96,000 orphan files were removed after a review sample confirmed none were needed, and the shared-file case was documented and referred to the retention policy owner.

column1: Records placed under the wrong parent cannot be moved
column2:
CONTEXT
Service agreements belong to a customer account through a relationship configured when the object was designed.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agreements created under the wrong account cannot be corrected, and users create duplicates instead.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An agreement placed under the wrong account should be movable with its related records intact.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The relationship was configured to disallow reparenting, so the account cannot be changed after creation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Changing the setting would allow reparenting but also recalculate sharing for every existing agreement, which the platform team would not approve without a maintenance window. Roughly 15 corrections are needed per month.

RESOLUTION
A documented procedure recreates the agreement under the correct account, moves its related records, and marks the original as superseded with a reference. This is a workaround: the original record identifier changes, external references to it break, and history stays on the superseded record.

VALIDATION
Twelve corrections were completed with related records intact and cross-references in place, while two required manual follow-up because an external system held the old identifier.

column1: A bad bulk update can only be reversed from a manual extract
column2:
CONTEXT
Data stewards apply bulk updates to correct data quality issues across thousands of records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An incorrect update overwrote a field on 12,000 records with no straightforward way to reverse it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A bulk update should be reversible to its prior state without reconstructing values by hand.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Field history holds prior values for tracked fields only, and the affected field was not tracked.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Only 40 of 180 fields on the object are history tracked, and the platform limits how many can be. Recovery took two days and relied on a weekly export that happened to predate the update.

RESOLUTION
Stewards must now take a targeted extract of the affected records and fields immediately before any bulk update, retained for 30 days. This is a workaround: reversal is a manual reload, the extract depends on the operator taking it, and changes made by others between update and reversal would be overwritten.

VALIDATION
Three bulk updates ran with a pre-extract in place, a rehearsal reversal restored 5,000 records correctly, and the procedure was added to the steward checklist.

column1: One team intermittently cannot save records with a generic error
column2:
CONTEXT
A claims team of twelve people edits claim records throughout the day.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Members of that team see an unexpected error on save several times a day, while other teams are unaffected.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A valid edit should save without error for any user permitted to make it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The save is rejected with a generic message, and retrying the same edit usually succeeds within a minute.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The error text carries no field or rule name, and no validation rule or automation logs a matching failure. The team's records are larger than average, though other teams edit comparable records without incident. Debug logs captured for two users over three days recorded no failing transaction, which suggests the save is rejected before automation runs.

RESOLUTION
The save failure has not been traced to a rule, automation, or data condition, and no configuration has been changed.

VALIDATION
Failures continue at roughly ten a day across the team. The next step is capturing the request identifier shown with the error and raising a vendor case, since platform-side logs may hold detail the org's logs do not.

column1: Records vanish from a queue view while still owned by the queue
column2:
CONTEXT
Work is distributed through queues, and members pick records from a queue list view.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records disappear from the queue view although nobody has taken ownership of them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record owned by a queue should remain visible in that queue's view until someone accepts it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Affected records still show the queue as owner when opened directly, but are absent from the list view.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The list view filter matches the queue and the open status, and the missing records satisfy both when checked individually. Sharing recalculation completed normally. Re-saving a missing record returns it to the view, which points at list view indexing rather than ownership.

RESOLUTION
Why the records leave the view is unexplained, and re-saving has not been adopted as a routine measure because it would obscure how often this happens.

VALIDATION
Roughly five records a week are found through a daily comparison of queue membership against the view. The next step is recording when a record leaves the view and raising a vendor case about list view indexing.

column1: Zero-quantity lines appear on the document sent to the customer
column2:
CONTEXT
Sales users add optional products to a quote with a quantity of zero while negotiating scope.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers receive quote documents listing items they did not ask for, priced at zero.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only lines the customer is being asked to buy should appear on the document.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every line on the quote is rendered, including zero-quantity placeholders kept for internal reference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The document generator iterated all lines with no filter. Reviewing 60 sent quotes found 41 containing at least one zero-quantity line, and two customers had queried what the items were.

RESOLUTION
The generator now excludes lines with zero quantity unless they are explicitly marked as an optional offer, in which case they appear in a clearly separated optional section.

VALIDATION
Sixty quotes were regenerated and matched the intended scope, marked optional items appeared in their own section, and the sales team confirmed the internal view still shows every line.

column1: Conversion rates ignore deals that moved backwards through the stages
column2:
CONTEXT
Stage conversion rates measure how many opportunities move from each stage to the next.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reported conversion is far higher than the sales leadership recognizes from experience.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Conversion should reflect genuine forward progress through the pipeline.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A deal that advances, falls back, and advances again is counted as converting twice, so rates exceed reality.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The measure counted stage entries rather than distinct opportunities reaching a stage. Analysis of one quarter showed 22 percent of opportunities regressed at least once, and recomputing on distinct opportunities lowered reported conversion by 9 to 14 points per stage.

RESOLUTION
Conversion now counts distinct opportunities that reach each stage, with regression reported separately as its own measure so the coaching signal is not lost.

VALIDATION
Recomputed rates for four quarters matched a manual reconstruction from stage history, and the regression measure identified two stages where deals commonly slip back.

column1: Discount is recorded as a percentage in one place and an amount in another
column2:
CONTEXT
Discounts are captured on the quote line as a percentage and stored on the order line as an amount.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Order values do not always match the approved quote, and the difference is not consistent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The discount agreed on the quote should carry through to the order without reinterpretation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The conversion treats the percentage as an amount for lines where the percentage exceeds one, which produces a small fixed reduction instead of a proportional one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two fields share a similar label and the mapping assumed a common unit. Comparing 200 converted orders found 63 mismatches, all on lines with a discount above one percent, with differences up to 18 percent of line value.

RESOLUTION
The order line now stores both the percentage and the computed amount, the conversion derives the amount from the percentage and the list price, and a validation blocks an order line whose amount does not match its percentage.

VALIDATION
Two hundred conversions produced matching values, the 63 affected orders were corrected with finance, and a deliberately inconsistent line was rejected by the validation.

column1: Revenue is credited to two territories when an account moves mid-quarter
column2:
CONTEXT
Territory reporting credits closed revenue to the territory that owns the account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Territory totals sum to more than company revenue in quarters with territory changes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each closed deal should be credited to exactly one territory.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A deal closed before an account moves is credited to the old territory historically and the new one currently, so both include it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report resolves territory from the account's current assignment while historical snapshots hold the previous one, and both feed the same total. In the last quarter, 240 accounts moved and 380 closed deals were counted twice.

RESOLUTION
Territory is now stamped onto the opportunity at close and reporting uses that stamped value, so a later account move does not change historical credit.

VALIDATION
Territory totals matched company revenue for three quarters, the 380 double-counted deals resolved to a single territory each, and a test account move left prior-quarter figures unchanged.

column1: Referral fees are missed when a partner-sourced deal is closed by direct sales
column2:
CONTEXT
Partners register opportunities they source, and an accrual is calculated when those deals close.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Partners raised disputes about deals they had registered and been paid nothing for.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A registered deal should accrue a referral fee regardless of who closes it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The accrual triggers only when the closing owner is a partner user, so deals transferred to direct sales accrue nothing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The accrual logic keyed on the owner at close rather than on the registration record. A review found 74 registered deals closed by direct sales in a year, of which 31 were within the referral window and should have accrued.

RESOLUTION
The accrual now keys on an active registration within its validity window, independent of the closing owner, and the registration is stamped onto the opportunity so it survives a transfer.

VALIDATION
The 31 disputed deals were recalculated and settled with the partners, new transfers retained the registration in testing, and partner disputes stopped over the following two quarters.

column1: The commit forecast includes deals that have already been lost
column2:
CONTEXT
Each opportunity stage maps to a forecast category that determines whether it counts towards commit.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The commit figure did not fall when several large deals were marked lost.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Moving a deal to a closed lost stage should move it out of every forecast category that counts.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The stage changes while the forecast category retains its previous value, so lost deals remain in commit.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The category had been overridden manually on those opportunities, and a manual override suppresses the mapping from stage. A query found 96 closed lost opportunities still in a counting category, worth a substantial share of the reported commit.

RESOLUTION
Closing an opportunity now clears any manual override and applies the mapped category, and overrides on open deals expire at the end of the quarter in which they were set.

VALIDATION
Commit fell by the expected amount once the 96 opportunities were corrected, closing a test deal with an override applied the mapped category, and the quarter-end expiry ran as designed.

column1: Profitability is calculated for products but not for services
column2:
CONTEXT
Deal profitability compares revenue with cost so that the deal desk can advise on pricing.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deals combining products and services show a profitability figure that overstates the margin.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Profitability should include the cost of delivering services as well as product cost.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Product cost comes from the catalogue while service cost is absent, so service revenue appears to carry no cost.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Service cost depends on the effort estimate, which lives in a planning tool with no link to the opportunity. Of 300 deals reviewed, 140 included services averaging 30 percent of deal value.

RESOLUTION
A standard cost rate per service role is now applied to the estimated effort recorded on the opportunity. This is partial: the rate is an average rather than the actual delivery cost, and deals without a recorded effort estimate still show product cost only.

VALIDATION
Profitability for 90 deals with recorded estimates came within eight percent of the delivery team's own figures, while 50 deals without an estimate remain flagged as product-only.

column1: Contract amendments are recorded as new contracts, hiding the true term
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers frequently amend contracts mid-term to add products or extend coverage.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Nobody can state a customer's current commitment without manually reading several contract records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An amendment should update the customer's single active agreement with its full history.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Each amendment creates a separate contract, so a long-standing customer has six or seven overlapping records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The contract object does not support versioning, and adding it was estimated at a quarter of development. Reviewing 40 customers found an average of 4.2 contract records each, with three cases where the active commitment had been misquoted to the customer.

RESOLUTION
Amendments now link to the original contract through a parent reference, and a rolled-up view presents the combined position. This is a workaround: the underlying records remain separate, reporting must always traverse the chain, and a broken link produces an incomplete picture.

VALIDATION
The rolled-up view matched a manual reconstruction for 40 customers, the three misquoted commitments were corrected, and a deliberately broken link was caught by an integrity check.

column1: Approval requests occasionally reach an approver outside the hierarchy
column2:
CONTEXT
Discount approvals route to the requester's manager and then upwards according to the amount.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A few requests each month reach a manager in a different division who has no relationship to the deal.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Requests should route only through the requester's own management chain.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Affected requests skip the expected approver and appear in the queue of an unrelated manager, who usually rejects them.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The routing reads the manager field on the user record, and the affected requesters have correct values before and after the event. Approval history names the unexpected approver from the first step, so the request did not escalate there. The requesters share no division, and two were recently reassigned between teams.

RESOLUTION
The routing decision cannot be accounted for from the data available, and the approval configuration has been left unchanged.

VALIDATION
Between two and five requests a month are rerouted manually. The next step is capturing the user record's manager value at the exact moment of submission through a trigger-level log, so the routing input can be compared with the outcome.

column1: Some closed deals never produce a downstream order
column2:
CONTEXT
Closing an opportunity as won triggers creation of an order in the fulfilment system through middleware.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance found closed deals from the last quarter with no corresponding order and no invoice.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every won deal should produce exactly one order, or a visible failure.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Fourteen deals closed with no order created and no error recorded in the middleware or on the opportunity.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The affected opportunities are complete, carry products, and satisfy the trigger criteria, and re-triggering one manually created its order correctly. Middleware logs for the relevant windows contain no request for those deals, which suggests the message was never published rather than lost downstream. All fourteen closed within minutes of a bulk stage update run by sales operations.

RESOLUTION
Why no message was published for these deals has not been established, and the bulk update process continues while the link to it is unconfirmed.

VALIDATION
The fourteen orders were created manually and invoiced. The next step is repeating a controlled bulk stage update in a sandbox with publishing instrumented, to establish whether bulk context suppresses the message.

column1: Large batches are rejected because requests are sent uncompressed
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner submits batches of order updates through a REST endpoint several times an hour.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Batches above a few hundred records are rejected, forcing the partner to split them manually.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Reasonable batch sizes should be accepted without manual splitting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Requests above the maximum size are refused, and the partner's records average four kilobytes each.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client sent uncompressed payloads and included several fields the endpoint ignores. Measuring a 500 record batch showed 2.1 megabytes uncompressed and 190 kilobytes compressed, well within the limit.

RESOLUTION
The client now compresses requests and sends only the fields the endpoint consumes, and the endpoint returns a specific error naming the size limit when a request is still too large.

VALIDATION
Batches of 500 and 1,000 records were accepted, the partner stopped splitting files, and an oversized test request produced the explicit error rather than a generic rejection.

column1: Validation failures are returned with a success status
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom endpoint accepts customer updates from a portal and applies them to Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The portal shows updates as saved that never reached the customer record.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A request that does not apply should return an error status the caller can detect.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Validation failures return a success status with a message in the body, which the portal does not inspect.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The endpoint caught validation exceptions and returned them in a body field while keeping the status unchanged. Comparing portal submissions with stored records found 1,100 silently discarded updates over two months, mostly failing a postcode format rule.

RESOLUTION
The endpoint now returns a client error status with a structured body naming the field and rule, and the portal surfaces the message to the user for correction.

VALIDATION
Invalid submissions produced an error status and a readable message in testing, the portal displayed it correctly, and the 1,100 affected customers were contacted to confirm their details.

column1: Nightly jobs fail when too many sessions are opened at once
column2:
CONTEXT
Several scheduled integrations authenticate to Salesforce before their nightly work.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two integrations fail with an authentication error on nights when all of them run.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every scheduled integration should authenticate successfully regardless of how many run together.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The organization reaches its concurrent session limit, and further logins are refused until sessions expire.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Each integration opened a new session per batch and never closed it, leaving sessions to expire on their own. Session counts peaked at 24 against a limit of 20, and the two failing integrations were simply the last to start.

RESOLUTION
The clients now reuse a single session for the duration of a run and release it explicitly at the end, and a monitor reports session counts approaching the limit.

VALIDATION
Peak session count fell to seven across two weeks with no authentication failures, released sessions were confirmed closed, and the monitor raised no threshold alerts.

column1: Paged extraction skips records when the sort field repeats
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer extracts records in pages ordered by their last modified time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The consumer's copy is missing records that exist in Salesforce, with no failure reported.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Paged extraction should return every matching record exactly once.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records sharing a modified time with the record at a page boundary are skipped or repeated depending on how the page splits.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Ordering on a non-unique field leaves the position of tied rows undefined between pages. Bulk updates produce thousands of records with an identical timestamp, and every observed gap fell on a boundary within such a group.

RESOLUTION
Extraction now orders by modified time and record identifier together, so the ordering is total, and each page continues from the last identifier seen rather than an offset.

VALIDATION
A run across 400,000 records including a bulk-updated block returned every record exactly once, counts matched a direct query, and repeated runs produced identical result sets.

column1: Only the first error in a failed request is recorded
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware component submits records and logs any errors returned so support can correct them.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Correcting a rejected record often reveals a second problem, so records take several attempts to fix.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every error on a rejected record should be visible from the first attempt.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The response carries a list of errors while the component logs only the first entry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The logger read the first element of the error array. Sampling 200 rejections showed 78 carried more than one error, averaging 2.4 each, which matched the observed pattern of repeated correction rounds.

RESOLUTION
The component now logs every error with its field and code, and the correction report groups records by the full set of errors so similar records can be fixed together.

VALIDATION
Rejected records were corrected in one round for 92 percent of a 300 record sample, against 41 percent previously, and the grouped report let support fix 60 similar records in one action.

column1: Retries cover server errors but not dropped connections
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound callouts to a logistics provider retry automatically on transient failures.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some shipments are never dispatched, and the failures are found only during the daily reconciliation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Transient network failures should be retried in the same way as transient server errors.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Server error responses are retried, while a connection reset raises an exception that ends the attempt.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retry logic examined the response status, so a failure with no response was not covered. Of 340 failures in a month, 210 were connection resets, and none had been retried.

RESOLUTION
Retry now covers connection failures and timeouts as well as server error statuses, with a bounded number of attempts and increasing intervals, while client errors are still not retried.

VALIDATION
Injected connection resets were retried and succeeded in 96 percent of cases, client errors were not retried, and the daily reconciliation found no undispatched shipments over three weeks.

column1: Repeat protection covers creates and updates but not deletions
column2:
CONTEXT
Consumers supply a request key so that a retried write is not applied twice.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A retried deletion produced an error that the consumer treated as a genuine failure, leading to manual investigation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every operation should be safe to retry with the same request key.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Creates and updates recognize a repeated key and return the original outcome, while deletions return a not-found error on the second attempt.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The key store was implemented in the write path only. Of 90 retried operations in a month, 12 were deletions, each generating an investigation that concluded no action was needed.

RESOLUTION
Deletions now record their request key and return the original outcome on a repeat. This is partial: the key store retains entries for 24 hours, so a retry after that window still returns not found, and one legacy consumer does not send keys at all.

VALIDATION
Repeated deletions inside the window returned the original outcome across 40 tests, investigations stopped for those cases, and a retry after 25 hours reproduced the not-found result as documented.

column1: Interface documentation exists for some endpoints only
column2:
CONTEXT
Five custom endpoints serve partner and internal consumers with differing conventions.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
New consumers rely on example payloads passed around informally, and their first integration attempts usually fail.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every endpoint should have a published specification describing its fields, types, and errors.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two endpoints have a maintained specification, while three are described only by examples in old messages.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The documented endpoints were built most recently under a standard that came in afterwards. Onboarding a partner to an undocumented endpoint took an average of three weeks against four days for a documented one.

RESOLUTION
Specifications were published for the two documented endpoints plus a third reverse-engineered from its implementation and confirmed by its consumer. This is partial: two endpoints remain undocumented because their behaviour depends on undocumented downstream systems that need review first.

VALIDATION
A new consumer integrated against the third endpoint in five days using the specification alone, while an onboarding onto an undocumented endpoint again took three weeks.

column1: Responses are capped because the consumer cannot page
column2:
CONTEXT
A reporting consumer built on an older platform requests record sets that can run to tens of thousands of rows.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Large requests time out and the consumer receives nothing at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The consumer should retrieve complete result sets reliably.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The consumer cannot follow a continuation reference, so it must receive everything in one response or fail.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The consumer's platform has no support for paged retrieval and cannot be extended before its replacement next year. Measurement showed requests above 8,000 rows failing consistently.

RESOLUTION
The endpoint now caps responses at 5,000 rows, returns the total count and a documented indicator that the set was truncated, and the consumer narrows its date range when it sees the indicator. This is a workaround: full retrieval needs several narrower requests driven by the consumer's own logic, and a period with more than 5,000 rows in a single day cannot be split further.

VALIDATION
Daily retrieval completed reliably for three weeks with the indicator observed twice, and both cases were resolved by narrowing the range.

column1: Requests intermittently fail with no matching entry in the platform logs
column2:
CONTEXT
Middleware calls Salesforce continuously during business hours and records every request and response.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of calls return a server error, and support cannot find them in the platform's own logs.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every request reaching the platform should appear in its request logs whether it succeeds or fails.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The client records a server error with a request identifier that does not exist on the platform side.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The failures carry response headers consistent with a platform response rather than a proxy error page, which argues against the request being stopped in transit. Client logs show the full request written to the connection. Failure timing aligns with neither maintenance windows nor load peaks.

RESOLUTION
The failure has no corresponding platform record, and the cause is unknown, so no client change has been made beyond continuing to record the identifiers.

VALIDATION
Failures run at roughly one in 40,000 calls and are absorbed by retries. The next step is a vendor case supplying twenty request identifiers with timestamps and response headers, since only the platform can explain why they are unlogged.

column1: Comparison questions return figures for one period only
column2:
CONTEXT
Managers ask the assistant to compare a measure across two periods, such as this quarter against the same quarter last year.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Comparison questions come back with a single figure and no comparison at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A comparison question should return both periods together with the difference between them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query filters on whichever period was mentioned last, and the answer presents that figure as though it addressed the question.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Intent classification captured the measure and one date range, and the second range was discarded during generation without comment. Of 22 comparison questions, all returned a single period, and three managers had quoted the figure as a year-on-year change in a review meeting.

RESOLUTION
Comparison intent is now detected explicitly, two scoped aggregates are generated and executed, and the answer states both periods with the absolute and percentage difference between them.

VALIDATION
Twenty-two comparison questions returned both periods matching manually written queries, the differences reconciled with the published trend report, and single-period questions were unaffected.

column1: Totals count related rows rather than the customers behind them
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask how many customers had a particular kind of interaction in a period.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Answers are far larger than the customer base, which makes them obviously wrong to the reader.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question about customers should count customers, not the interactions belonging to them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query counts interaction rows, so a customer with twelve interactions contributes twelve to the total.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Generation selected the object holding the filter and counted its rows, without recognizing that the question's subject was the parent. Of 20 such questions, 17 counted the child object, and the error was largest for the most active customers.

RESOLUTION
Intent classification now identifies the subject of the question separately from the object carrying the filter, and counts distinct parents when the two differ, naming both in the answer.

VALIDATION
Twenty questions returned counts matching manually written queries, answers named the subject and the filter object, and questions genuinely about interaction volume still counted rows.

column1: Generated statements use syntax the platform does not support
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant generates queries in the platform's own query language, which resembles but differs from standard SQL.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions requiring joins or filtered aggregates fail with a syntax error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Generated statements should use only constructs the platform supports, or explain that the question cannot be expressed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The model produces explicit joins and aggregate filters that the platform rejects outright.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The prompt described the schema but never stated the dialect's restrictions. Of 40 failing questions, 26 used an explicit join and 11 used an aggregate filter clause, both of which have accepted alternatives in this dialect.

RESOLUTION
The prompt now states the supported constructs with worked alternatives for joins and aggregate filters, generated statements are parsed before execution, and unsupported constructs trigger one regeneration attempt before the assistant explains the limitation.

VALIDATION
Thirty-four of the 40 questions returned valid statements matching manual equivalents, six returned a clear explanation, and no unsupported statement reached execution across 200 later runs.

column1: Explanatory questions are answered with a query instead of a caveat
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask both factual questions and explanatory ones, such as why a measure moved last month.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Explanatory questions receive a confident figure that does not answer what was asked.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should answer questions data can answer and say plainly when a question calls for analysis it cannot perform.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A why question produces a query for the measure itself, and the answer reads as though it explains the cause.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Every question was routed to query generation, since no classification distinguished factual from explanatory intent. Reviewing 25 explanatory questions found all 25 answered with a figure, and two users had repeated a figure as an explanation in a meeting.

RESOLUTION
Questions are now classified as factual or explanatory, explanatory ones return the relevant figures with an explicit statement that the cause is not determined, and suggested follow-up breakdowns are offered.

VALIDATION
All 25 explanatory questions returned the caveat with supporting figures, factual questions were unaffected, and a review with the two users confirmed the wording prevented the earlier misreading.

column1: Filtering by a related record's name matches more records than intended
column2:
CONTEXT
Users name a customer or product in their question, and the assistant filters on the related record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Answers include records for customers whose name merely contains the one asked about.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Naming a customer should restrict results to that customer, or ask which one is meant when the name is ambiguous.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The filter uses a partial text match on the related name, so a question about one customer includes its subsidiaries and unrelated similar names.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Partial matching was chosen so that abbreviated names would resolve. Of 30 questions naming a customer, 11 returned extra records, and in three cases the extra records belonged to a different corporate group entirely.

RESOLUTION
Named entities now resolve to a record identifier before generation, an exact reference is used in the filter, and an ambiguous name returns the candidate matches for the user to choose between.

VALIDATION
Thirty questions returned only the intended customer's records, ambiguous names produced a choice of candidates, and abbreviations still resolved correctly through the candidate list.

column1: Failed generations are retried with the identical query
column2:
CONTEXT
When a generated query fails to execute, the assistant retries before returning an error to the user.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Retries add several seconds and almost never produce a different outcome.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A retry should give the model the failure detail so it can correct the statement.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The same prompt is submitted again, so the same statement is generated and fails identically.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retry re-sent the original prompt without the error. Of 180 retried failures, 168 produced an identical statement, and the 12 that differed did so only because of sampling variation.

RESOLUTION
The retry now includes the platform's error message and the failing statement. This is partial: it works well for syntax and unknown field errors, while errors about non-filterable fields or unsupported operations usually recur, because the correction requires schema knowledge the message does not carry.

VALIDATION
Retry success rose from 7 to 61 percent across a 200 failure sample, with the residual failures concentrated in the two categories described.

column1: Schema changes reach the assistant only when someone refreshes it by hand
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant works from an exported description of objects, fields, and relationships.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions about recently added fields fail until an engineer regenerates the description.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should reflect the current schema without manual intervention.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The description is exported by hand, and the interval between a metadata change and the refresh has been as long as three weeks.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The export requires review because business descriptions are edited by hand after generation, so it cannot simply run unattended. Metadata changes reach production most weeks, and 14 questions in a month failed on fields that existed but were not described.

RESOLUTION
A weekly scheduled export produces a draft that an owner reviews and publishes, with an alert when metadata changes since the last publication. This is a workaround: the description can still be up to a week stale, and publication depends on the owner acting on the alert.

VALIDATION
Staleness fell from as much as three weeks to at most seven days over two months, the alert fired correctly for four metadata changes, and failures on undescribed fields fell to two.

column1: A model upgrade changed the answer format and broke downstream parsing
column2:
CONTEXT
A reporting workflow consumes the assistant's answers programmatically and extracts the figure and the query.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The workflow began failing after the hosted model was upgraded by its provider.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Downstream consumers should not break when the underlying model changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The upgraded model returns the same content with different section labels and ordering, which the workflow's parser does not recognize.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The workflow parsed the free-text answer directly, since no structured output existed. The provider gave no advance notice of the formatting change, and 340 scheduled extractions failed over two days before anyone noticed.

RESOLUTION
A compatibility layer now recognizes both formats and normalizes them for the consumer. This is a workaround: parsing free text remains fragile, and a further formatting change would break it again. Returning a structured result alongside the readable answer is the intended fix.

VALIDATION
The 340 failed extractions were reprocessed successfully, both formats parsed correctly in testing, and a deliberately altered third format failed as expected, confirming the fragility that remains.

column1: The confidence indicator does not track whether the answer is right
column2:
CONTEXT
Each answer carries a confidence indicator intended to help users judge how much to rely on it.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users report high confidence on answers that prove wrong and low confidence on answers that prove correct.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The indicator should correlate with the likelihood that the answer is correct.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Across a reviewed sample the indicator shows no useful relationship to correctness.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of 120 scored answers found high-confidence answers correct 71 percent of the time and low-confidence answers 64 percent, a difference too small to guide a user. The indicator derives from the model's own reported certainty, which appears to reflect fluency rather than correctness. Removing it was rejected, since users want a reliability signal.

RESOLUTION
Why the indicator behaves this way has not been established, and it remains displayed with a note that it is under review rather than being silently withdrawn.

VALIDATION
The weak correlation persists in a second sample of 80 answers. The next step is testing a query-derived signal built from schema coverage and filter specificity, scored against the same labelled set.

column1: Some questions take far longer to answer with no pattern in their complexity
column2:
CONTEXT
Answers normally return within four to six seconds, which users consider acceptable.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small share of questions take 30 seconds or more, and users abandon them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Response time should relate to the work involved, so similar questions should behave similarly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The same question can return in five seconds on one attempt and 35 on another, with identical results.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Timing was instrumented at each stage for 500 requests. Query execution took under a second in every slow case, so the platform is not the constraint. Generation carried the whole difference, and slow cases share no pattern in prompt length, object count, or user. Provider metrics available to the team show no matching spikes.

RESOLUTION
The latency has not been attributed to a stage under the team's control, and no timeout or fallback has been introduced yet.

VALIDATION
Slow responses run at about 3 percent of requests. The next step is recording the provider's own request identifier for every call so slow cases can be raised with them directly, with a client-side timeout considered once the cause is understood.

column1: Delta loads create duplicates because keys carry trailing spaces
column2:
CONTEXT
Delta loads match records on a legacy identifier held in an external key field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A share of records is inserted again on each delta run instead of being updated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record already loaded should be matched by its key and updated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Keys with a trailing space do not match the stored value, so the load inserts a new record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The source pads keys to a fixed width for some record types, and the initial load trimmed them while the delta extract did not. Of 4,800 duplicates, every key had trailing whitespace, and trimming reproduced the correct match in a test.

RESOLUTION
Both extracts now trim and normalize keys before comparison, the 4,800 duplicates were merged into their originals, and a load-time check rejects a file whose keys differ from stored values only by whitespace.

VALIDATION
Three delta runs produced no inserts for existing records, the merged duplicates retained their related records, and a seeded padded key was caught by the check.

column1: Migrated opportunities sit in stages that no longer exist
column2:
CONTEXT
Historical opportunities were migrated with the stage values used by the legacy sales process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users cannot edit migrated opportunities, and pipeline reports show stages nobody recognizes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migrated records should use the current sales process stages so they behave like any other record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records hold stages outside the active process, so saving requires choosing a new stage and reports show orphan groupings.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The legacy process had nine stages against the current six, and the mapping was not applied for closed records because they were considered read-only. A count found 26,000 opportunities across three retired stages, all closed.

RESOLUTION
A mapping assigned each retired stage to its current equivalent, the original value was retained in a legacy stage field for historical analysis, and the records were updated in a controlled batch.

VALIDATION
Pipeline reports grouped into the six current stages with totals unchanged, migrated records saved without forcing a stage change, and the legacy field preserved the original values for a sampled 500 records.

column1: Historical amounts convert at the wrong rate because no rate existed for those dates
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated deals in foreign currencies are converted for reporting using dated exchange rates.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Converted historical values disagree with the legacy system's reported figures.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each historical deal should convert at the rate applicable on its close date.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deals closed before the earliest dated rate convert at the oldest available rate, which overstates older periods.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Dated rates had been loaded for the previous two years while the migration covered seven. Comparing 300 deals showed differences up to 22 percent for the oldest, and every affected deal closed before the earliest rate date.

RESOLUTION
Historical rates for the full seven years were loaded from the finance system, the affected records were reconverted, and the load procedure now verifies rate coverage for the full date range before a currency-bearing batch runs.

VALIDATION
Converted values matched the legacy figures within rounding for all seven years, the coverage check blocked a test batch with a gap, and finance signed off the restated history.

column1: Migrated records are owned by users who cannot access the platform
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated records are assigned to the legacy owner where a matching user exists in Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records assigned to some owners cannot be worked, and their queues appear empty to the teams responsible.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated record should be owned by a user able to log in and work it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some records are owned by users created for identity purposes only, who hold no licence and never log in.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The user mapping matched on name and email without checking licence or active status. A query found 7,400 records owned by 23 such users, and the affected teams had assumed the work had not been migrated.

RESOLUTION
Ownership was reassigned to the current team lead for each affected group, the mapping now validates licence and active status before assigning an owner, and unmatched owners route to a team queue.

VALIDATION
The 7,400 records appeared in the correct team queues, a test mapping to an unlicensed user was rejected and routed to the queue, and the teams confirmed their backlog was complete.

column1: Product bundles migrate as unrelated individual items
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy catalogue holds bundles composed of component products with a defined structure.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users cannot add bundles and must select each component individually, often missing one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Bundle structure should migrate so that selecting a bundle brings its components.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All products migrated as a flat list, and the parent and component relationships were dropped.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extract selected the product table without the composition table that defines membership. The composition data exists in the source and covers 240 bundles containing 1,900 component entries.

RESOLUTION
The composition table was added to the migration scope and loaded as bundle relationships, with quantity per component preserved and a validation preventing a bundle from containing itself.

VALIDATION
All 240 bundles resolved to their components with correct quantities against the source, adding a bundle to a quote brought its components in testing, and the self-reference validation rejected a seeded cycle.
