column1: Child records attach to the wrong kind of parent record
column2:
CONTEXT
Notes migrate with a reference that can point at several object types depending on what they were attached to.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Notes appear on unrelated records, and some records show notes belonging to another customer's case.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each note should attach to the same record it was attached to in the legacy system.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Notes attach by identifier alone, and where two object types share an identifier value the note lands on whichever record the loader resolved first.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Legacy identifiers are unique per type but not across types, and the mapping carried the identifier without the type. Of 61,000 notes, 3,200 attached to the wrong object type, and 190 were visible to users who should not see them.

RESOLUTION
The mapping now carries the source object type alongside the identifier and resolves the pair, the 3,200 misattached notes were relinked, and the 190 exposures were reported to the data protection lead.

VALIDATION
A full comparison against the source matched every note to its intended parent, spot checks confirmed the relinked notes, and a repeat visibility review found no remaining cross-customer content.

column1: Data cleanup is complete for major accounts only
column2:
CONTEXT
Source data is remediated before migration so that quality problems are not carried into the new platform.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The programme cannot confirm that migrated data will meet the agreed quality threshold.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every record in scope should meet the quality rules before it is migrated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The top 2,000 accounts are remediated, while the long tail of 40,000 smaller accounts is untouched.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Remediation of the top accounts was done by the account teams who knew the customers. The long tail has no owner able to verify details, and profiling showed 31 percent failing at least one rule, mostly missing industry and incomplete addresses.

RESOLUTION
The top 2,000 accounts meet every rule and carry a verified flag, and automated normalization fixed address formatting across the long tail. This is partial: missing attributes cannot be filled without an owner, so those accounts migrate with a data quality flag.

VALIDATION
The top accounts passed the full rule set in a rehearsal, long-tail address formatting improved from 61 to 94 percent compliant, and 12,400 accounts remain flagged for missing attributes.

column1: Rollback is proven for single objects but not for dependent ones
column2:
CONTEXT
The cutover plan requires a tested way to reverse a migration wave if verification fails.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The programme cannot demonstrate that a failed wave can be reversed within the cutover window.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any wave should be reversible to its pre-migration state within a defined time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Single-object rollback is rehearsed and timed, while reversing a wave spanning parents and children has never been tested end to end.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Object-level rollback deletes loaded records by their batch marker, which is straightforward. Dependent objects must be removed in reverse order, and records touched by automation after loading no longer carry a clean marker, which affects an estimated 8 percent of a typical wave.

RESOLUTION
Rollback is proven and timed for four single-object waves at 25 minutes each. This is partial: the two dependent-object waves have no tested procedure, and records altered post-load need a documented decision on whether to delete or retain them.

VALIDATION
Four single-object rollbacks completed within the measured time in two rehearsals, while a dependent-object rehearsal was stopped when child records without markers were encountered.

column1: The legacy system stays available because some data cannot be migrated
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy platform was due to be decommissioned once its data had been migrated.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several data categories have no target in Salesforce and would be lost on decommissioning.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All data required for operations and compliance should be available in the new platform.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Structured records migrated successfully, while scanned correspondence images and a bespoke audit log have no equivalent model.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The images total 4.2 terabytes, which exceeds the storage allocation, and the audit log's structure does not map onto any standard object. Both are needed for regulatory queries that arrive a few times a month.

RESOLUTION
The legacy platform remains available in read-only mode for the two categories, with access limited to a small team and a documented request route. This is a workaround: a second system must be maintained and licensed, its data is not searchable alongside migrated records, and decommissioning is deferred indefinitely.

VALIDATION
Eleven regulatory queries were answered from the read-only system over two months, access was confirmed limited to the nine named users, and the retained scope was agreed with the compliance owner.

column1: Migrated records raise duplicate alerts against themselves
column2:
CONTEXT
Duplicate rules alert users when a record they are editing resembles an existing one.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users editing certain migrated accounts see a duplicate alert naming the record they already have open.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record should never be reported as a duplicate of itself.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The alert appears on save, names the same record, and clears if the record is saved a second time without changes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The matching rule excludes the record being edited, and the behaviour never occurs for records created directly in the platform. All affected records came from one wave, and querying them reveals no second copy under any matching field. That wave was loaded twice after a failed attempt, though the failed load reported no records committed.

RESOLUTION
The alert's trigger has not been identified, and the duplicate rule has been left active because suppressing it would hide genuine duplicates.

VALIDATION
Roughly 20 alerts a week are dismissed by users. The next step is exporting the matching engine's own match records for a sampled account, which will show what the rule believes it matched against.

column1: A record-triggered flow hits the SOQL query limit during bulk data loads
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow on the shipment object queries a related pricing table once per triggering record to determine a surcharge.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Loads of more than 150 shipments at once fail with a limit exception, while smaller loads succeed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should process any batch size the platform's bulk load tooling submits.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The transaction exceeds the per-transaction query limit and every shipment in the batch rolls back, including ones that would have succeeded alone.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The query ran inside a loop once per record rather than once per batch, so a 200 record load issued 200 separate queries against a limit of 100. Reviewing failed loads over a month showed every failure exceeded 100 records exactly at this step.

RESOLUTION
The pricing lookup now runs once outside the loop against the full set of shipment identifiers, with results matched back to each record in memory.

VALIDATION
A load of 5,000 shipments completed in a single transaction chain without a limit exception, surcharges matched a manual calculation for 40 sampled records, and existing single-record saves were unaffected.

column1: Case owners receive two identical assignment notifications for one change
column2:
CONTEXT
A case object has two record-triggered flows, one built by the support team and one added later by the escalations team, both watching the owner field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents receive two identical assignment emails whenever a case owner changes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A single owner change should generate a single notification.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Both flows fire on the same update and each sends its own copy of the same message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The escalations flow was built without checking whether existing automation already covered the same trigger condition, since the two teams work in separate change processes. Entry criteria on both flows matched identically for every owner change, confirmed against 60 sampled transitions.

RESOLUTION
The escalations flow was retired and its one additional condition, notifying a supervisor for high priority cases, was added to the original support flow, leaving one flow responsible for owner notifications.

VALIDATION
Sixty owner changes produced exactly one notification each, the supervisor alert fired only for high priority cases in ten test transitions, and agents confirmed the duplicate messages stopped.

column1: New opportunities receive the wrong record type after a sandbox refresh
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow sets the record type on new opportunities created through a lead conversion process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every opportunity created since the last sandbox refresh carries the default record type instead of the intended one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Converted opportunities should always receive the record type configured for their business unit.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow silently falls back to the default record type for every conversion.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow referenced the record type by its stored identifier rather than by developer name, and identifiers differ between environments. The reference had been copied from production during testing and never updated when the flow was deployed back, so it pointed at a record type that does not exist in this org.

RESOLUTION
The flow now resolves the record type by developer name at runtime, and a deployment check flags any hardcoded identifier found in flow metadata before release.

VALIDATION
Conversions across all four business units produced the correct record type in testing, the 90 affected opportunities were corrected in a batch update, and the deployment check rejected a test flow containing a hardcoded identifier.

column1: Displayed totals are off by rounding for one currency only
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow calculates a displayed order total from several currency fields and stores it for the confirmation screen.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Totals for orders placed in one currency are consistently a fraction off the sum of their lines.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The displayed total should equal the sum of its lines to the currency's own decimal precision.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula rounds to two decimal places regardless of the currency, which is wrong for a currency defined with zero decimal places.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rounding precision was fixed in the formula rather than read from the currency's configuration. Comparing 80 orders in the affected currency against their line sums showed a consistent fractional discrepancy matching the two-decimal rounding.

RESOLUTION
The formula now rounds to the decimal precision configured for the order's currency, read at calculation time rather than assumed.

VALIDATION
Eighty reprocessed orders matched their line sums exactly, three other currencies with non-standard precision were checked and passed, and standard two-decimal currencies were unaffected.

column1: An approval step is skipped after a status label was renamed
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow decision element compares a case status field against a specific picklist value to route high-risk cases into an approval step.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
High-risk cases stopped requiring approval after a routine label update.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The routing decision should keep working when a picklist label is edited.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The decision element compares against the old label text, which no longer matches any value in the field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
An administrator renamed the status label for clarity without checking flow dependencies, since the platform does not warn that a flow references the value by label text. Fourteen high-risk cases had skipped approval since the change, discovered when one reached a customer uncorrected.

RESOLUTION
The decision element was rebuilt to compare against the picklist's stored API value rather than its label, and the fourteen cases were routed through approval retroactively.

VALIDATION
A further label rename left the routing unaffected in testing, the fourteen historical cases completed approval with recorded outcomes, and five other flows referencing the same field were audited and found unaffected.

column1: Automated retries recover callout failures but not save conflicts
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow that processes inventory adjustments includes a fault path intended to retry the operation once before escalating to a person.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Adjustments still fail permanently on the first attempt for a class of errors the retry does not catch.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any transient failure should be retried automatically before an adjustment is escalated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retry only triggers after a callout failure; a record lock conflict during save ends the interview with no retry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The fault path was built while the flow's only external dependency was a callout, and the save conflict case was added later without extending the fault handling. Of 60 failed adjustments in a month, 22 were lock conflicts that a simple retry would likely have resolved.

RESOLUTION
The retry now also covers save conflicts, waiting briefly before reattempting once. This is partial: a second consecutive lock conflict still escalates without a further retry.

VALIDATION
Simulated lock conflicts recovered on retry in 34 of 40 tests, escalation still occurred correctly after two failures, and peak-hour tuning remains an open item.

column1: Expense approvals route correctly for staff but not for contractors
column2:
CONTEXT
An approval flow for expense claims resolves the approver from the submitter's manager field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Contractor claims stall unassigned because contractors have no manager field populated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every submitter type should resolve to a valid approver without manual intervention.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Staff claims route correctly, while contractor claims wait indefinitely with no approver assigned.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Contractors are represented as a separate user type without the standard manager hierarchy, which the flow assumed existed for everyone. Of 40 stalled claims found, all belonged to contractors, and each required a manual assignment by an administrator.

RESOLUTION
Contractor claims now resolve to their sponsoring department's approval queue, added as a second lookup path. This is partial: claims from contractors without a recorded sponsoring department still stall, which affects a small residual group awaiting a data cleanup.

VALIDATION
Thirty-eight of forty stalled claims resolved automatically once the sponsor path was added, the remaining two matched the known data gap, and staff routing was unaffected in regression testing.

column1: A second verification callout was replaced with a nightly batch check
column2:
CONTEXT
An onboarding flow already calls an identity verification service and needed to add a second check against a sanctions list provider.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Adding the second callout in the same flow interview exceeds the per-transaction callout limit when both services are invoked from nested flows.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both checks should complete before onboarding is marked verified.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Attempting the second callout inside the same transaction throws a limit exception intermittently, depending on how many nested elements already ran.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Restructuring the flow to remove nested elements was estimated at several weeks given how many processes depend on the current structure. A batch job running every 15 minutes was assessed as achievable within days.

RESOLUTION
The sanctions check now runs from a scheduled batch shortly after onboarding, updating a verification field it reads. This is a workaround: onboarding is briefly visible as complete before the second check runs.

VALIDATION
The batch checked 300 new onboardings within 15 minutes of creation across two weeks, no callout limit exceptions recurred, and the brief visibility gap was accepted by the compliance owner.

column1: A handful of flow interviews each week never finish and leave no error
column2:
CONTEXT
A multi-step screen flow guides agents through a refund request, saving progress at each screen.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of interviews stop partway through with the agent still on the final screen, and no refund record is created.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every completed interview should either create a refund record or show the agent an explicit error.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The screen appears to accept the final input, but nothing is written and no fault path runs.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Debug logs for two captured cases show the interview simply absent from the log for that time window, as though it was never resumed after the last screen. The agents involved share no browser, location, or role, and the affected requests are not unusually large.

RESOLUTION
No mechanism has been identified for the interview disappearing, and the flow has not been changed pending more evidence.

VALIDATION
Roughly six incidents a week are currently handled by agents re-entering the request. The next step is adding a client-side heartbeat that logs screen transitions independently of the flow's own logging, to see whether the interview reaches the server at all.

column1: A daily cutoff calculation gives different answers depending on the user's time zone
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow determines whether a request was submitted before a daily cutoff to decide same-day or next-day processing.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Requests submitted at similar moments are sometimes classified differently depending on which user submitted them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The cutoff decision should depend only on the actual submission time, not on the submitting user.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Two requests logged within a minute of each other by users in different regions occasionally land on opposite sides of the cutoff incorrectly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow converts the submission timestamp using a formula that should apply the organization's processing time zone uniformly, and testing with a fixed timestamp under different users reproduced the split three times in twenty attempts. The affected users show no pattern in their time zone setting.

RESOLUTION
The intermittent nature has prevented isolating which layer applies the wrong conversion, and the cutoff logic remains unchanged.

VALIDATION
The split recurs roughly three times in twenty comparable submissions. The next step is logging both the raw timestamp and the converted value at each step of the flow for a full week to localize where the divergence enters.

column1: A middleware maps a boolean field to text and breaks downstream filters
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration writes a fulfillment status flag from the warehouse system into a checkbox field on the order object.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
List views and reports filtering on the checkbox return no results even though the warehouse confirms fulfillment.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The checkbox should reflect true or false exactly as the source system reports.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field receives the text values Y and N instead of a boolean, which Salesforce stores as unchecked for both.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping was built against a test payload that happened to use true and false, while the production feed uses single-letter codes. Comparing 500 orders showed every one stored as unchecked regardless of actual fulfillment status.

RESOLUTION
The mapping now translates the letter codes to boolean values explicitly, and a validation on the integration user rejects any unrecognized value rather than defaulting it.

VALIDATION
The 500 affected orders were recalculated and matched the warehouse system exactly, a deliberately malformed code was rejected by the validation, and downstream reports returned correct counts.

column1: A nightly sync silently drops records above a message size limit
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer profile updates are sent from the loyalty platform to Salesforce as individual messages during a nightly window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers with long purchase history notes never receive their profile updates, though smaller profiles sync normally.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A profile update should be delivered regardless of the length of its notes field.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages above a size threshold are dropped by the queue without an error reaching either system.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The queue enforces a maximum message size that neither integration team had documented against the field's actual length limit. Of 900 missing updates over a month, every one carried a notes field longer than 32 kilobytes, matching the threshold precisely.

RESOLUTION
Long notes are now compressed before sending and decompressed on arrival, keeping messages under the threshold, and a length check on the source flags any record still too large for review.

VALIDATION
The 900 backlog updates were resent and applied, the compression round trip preserved notes content exactly in 50 samples, and no drops occurred over three subsequent weeks.

column1: Related contact records are created twice when an account syncs before its contacts
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration receives accounts and their contacts as separate message types from the same source system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some contacts appear twice on the same account after a sync.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each source contact should map to exactly one Salesforce contact regardless of message arrival order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
When a contact message arrives before its account has been created, the integration creates a placeholder account and, separately, a duplicate contact once the real account message arrives.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The contact handler had no mechanism to wait for a missing parent, so it created what it could and moved on. Message timestamps for 140 duplicate pairs showed the contact message preceding its account message in every case, typically by a few seconds.

RESOLUTION
Contact messages that reference a missing account are now held in a short retry queue instead of creating a placeholder, and the 140 duplicate pairs were merged.

VALIDATION
A deliberately reordered test batch produced no duplicates, the retry queue cleared within its window in all observed cases, and the merged contacts retained their full activity history.

column1: A time zone offset error shifts appointment times by one hour for half the year
column2:
CONTEXT
Field service appointments are pushed from Salesforce to a scheduling partner as UTC timestamps with a fixed offset applied on their side.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Appointments booked during daylight saving months show up an hour early on the partner's schedule.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The displayed appointment time should match what was booked regardless of the time of year.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The partner's fixed offset does not account for the seasonal daylight saving shift observed locally.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration was configured with a static offset agreed at launch, during standard time, and never revisited for daylight saving. Comparing 200 appointments across both periods showed the one-hour discrepancy present only in daylight saving months.

RESOLUTION
The integration now sends the offset alongside the timestamp so the partner applies the correct seasonal adjustment rather than a fixed value, matching a field their platform already supported but the mapping had ignored.

VALIDATION
Appointments in both standard and daylight saving periods displayed correctly for four weeks spanning the transition, and 60 previously affected appointments were confirmed corrected with the partner.

column1: An integration retries a failed callout with a growing payload each time
column2:
CONTEXT
An order integration retries a failed callout by resubmitting the original request together with any newer changes queued since.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A callout that keeps failing accumulates an ever-larger payload until it exceeds the size the receiving system accepts, compounding the original failure.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A retry should resend the original request unchanged, with new changes queued separately.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Each retry attempt merges in subsequent changes before resending, so the payload grows with every failed attempt.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retry logic reused the same queue read used for new sends, rather than snapshotting the original payload at first failure. One order's payload was traced growing from 4 kilobytes to 210 kilobytes across nine retries before exceeding the limit.

RESOLUTION
The retry now resends a snapshot taken at the first failure, with subsequent changes queued as their own separate send once the retry succeeds or exhausts its attempts.

VALIDATION
A forced failure followed by nine retries kept the payload constant across all attempts, subsequent changes were sent correctly afterward, and the nine historical stuck orders were resent successfully.

column1: Case comments sync one-way, so agent replies never reach the partner portal
column2:
CONTEXT
Partner-submitted cases are mirrored into Salesforce, and both sides should see the full comment thread.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Partners see their own comments but never see replies typed by internal agents.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Comments added on either side should appear on both.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only the initial inbound comment set was ever built; agent replies inside Salesforce have no outbound path.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration was scoped for inbound case creation only, and the comment sync was assumed to be part of that scope but never implemented. Twenty-two partner cases were reviewed, all missing agent replies on the partner side, with partners re-asking questions already answered.

RESOLUTION
A new outbound path publishes agent-authored comments to the partner portal within a few minutes of posting, tagged so partner-authored comments are not sent back to themselves.

VALIDATION
Twenty-two backlog cases had their agent replies published, a new two-way comment exchange completed correctly in testing across five cases, and partners confirmed replies now arrive without needing to ask again.

column1: Product data syncs for standard items but not for configured bundles
column2:
CONTEXT
Pricing and availability sync nightly from the ERP for products sold through Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users see accurate figures for standard products but stale or missing figures for made-to-order configured items.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every sellable product, standard or configured, should carry current pricing and availability.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The sync reads the standard product table only, which does not include configured item variants generated at order time in the ERP.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Configured items are generated dynamically and have no stable identifier to sync against ahead of an order, which the original integration scope did not anticipate. They represent 18 percent of order volume.

RESOLUTION
A base price and lead time now sync for the configuration templates, giving sales an estimate before ordering. This is partial: the final price still depends on the specific configuration chosen at order time and is confirmed only after submission.

VALIDATION
Template-level estimates matched ERP figures for 30 sampled configurations within an agreed tolerance, and final order pricing continued to reconcile correctly after submission as before.

column1: A field-level encryption requirement blocks the standard sync tool, replaced with a custom step
column2:
CONTEXT
A national identifier field was moved to platform encryption to meet a new data protection requirement.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The standard integration tool cannot read or write the encrypted field, breaking the nightly customer sync for that attribute.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The identifier should continue to sync between systems under the new encryption.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The sync tool's connector does not support encrypted fields, and the vendor's roadmap for support is unconfirmed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Encrypted fields require a different access path than the tool's bulk connector uses, which the vendor confirmed is not currently planned. Delaying the encryption requirement was not an option given the compliance deadline.

RESOLUTION
A custom script using the supported encrypted-field API now handles this one field on its own schedule, alongside the unchanged standard sync for everything else. This is a workaround: two separate sync mechanisms must now be maintained and monitored for this one integration.

VALIDATION
The identifier synced correctly for 4,000 customers across two weeks, the encryption requirement passed its compliance review, and the two sync mechanisms were confirmed to run without interfering with each other.

column1: A rate limit on the partner API forces batching where real-time was intended
column2:
CONTEXT
Stock availability was intended to update in Salesforce within seconds of a change in the fulfillment system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The fulfillment system's API allows far fewer calls per minute than the volume of individual stock changes requires.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Salesforce should reflect current stock levels closely enough for sales users to trust them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Sending each change as it occurs exceeds the rate limit within minutes during busy periods, and calls beyond the limit are rejected.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner confirmed the limit is fixed for this tier of access, and an upgraded tier was not budgeted this year. Peak periods generate roughly four times the allowed call rate.

RESOLUTION
Changes now accumulate for two minutes and send as a single batched update per product, staying within the rate limit. This is a workaround: stock figures can lag actual availability by up to two minutes, occasionally allowing overselling on fast-moving items.

VALIDATION
Call volume stayed within the rate limit across three peak periods, the two-minute lag was confirmed in testing, and overselling incidents were tracked at two per week, accepted by the sales operations owner.

column1: A subset of accounts fail to sync with an error naming a field that does not exist
column2:
CONTEXT
Account updates sync from the ERP to Salesforce through a mapping covering forty fields.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
About fifteen accounts a week fail with an error citing a field name that is not present anywhere in the current mapping.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every account update should either apply successfully or fail with an error referencing an actual mapped field.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The named field does not exist in the mapping configuration, the target object, or the source extract for the affected records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping's version history shows a similarly named field was removed eight months ago, though the connector has restarted twice since, which should have cleared any cache. Retrying the identical payload later usually succeeds.

RESOLUTION
The stale reference has not been traced to its source, and the mapping has not been altered since no current field matches the error.

VALIDATION
Roughly fifteen accounts a week fail and succeed on manual retry. The next step is capturing the connector's configuration snapshot at the moment of failure, since the cached version may differ from what is published.

column1: A permission set grants delete access nobody intended for a shared object
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission set built for read-only reporting access was cloned to create a second set for a related team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found the cloned set granting delete rights on customer records, which the reporting team should never have had either.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Permission sets should grant only the access documented for their purpose.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Both the original and cloned sets carry delete rights alongside the intended read access.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The original set was built by cloning an administrative template and removing edit access, but delete was left unchecked by oversight. Object history showed no deletions traceable to either set's assigned users, so the exposure had not been exploited.

RESOLUTION
Delete access was removed from both sets, a documented build checklist now requires listing every permission explicitly rather than cloning and subtracting, and the two sets were rebuilt from that checklist.

VALIDATION
Assigned users could no longer delete records in testing, read access remained intact for reporting, and the rebuilt sets matched their documented permission lists exactly in a peer review.

column1: Login IP restrictions do not apply to the API-only integration user
column2:
CONTEXT
Login access is restricted to a defined range of office and VPN addresses for all users.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review found the integration user able to authenticate successfully from an address outside the defined range during testing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every user, including integration accounts, should authenticate only from an approved address range.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The restriction is applied through a profile-level login IP range that the integration user's profile does not carry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration user was placed on a separate profile created before the IP restriction policy existed, and it was never revisited when the policy was introduced for other profiles. Login history showed successful authentications from the hosting provider's address range, outside any defined office or VPN range.

RESOLUTION
The integration user's profile was updated with the hosting provider's fixed address range as its sole permitted range, and a quarterly review now checks every profile against the current policy.

VALIDATION
A login attempt from an unlisted address was rejected in testing, scheduled integration jobs continued running without interruption, and the quarterly review found no other unrestricted profiles.

column1: A deactivated user's approved delegated administrator rights remained active
column2:
CONTEXT
Delegated administration lets specific users manage a defined group of other users without full administrator rights.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A leaver's account was deactivated on their last day, but a review found their delegated administrator rights still listed as active against their deactivated profile.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deactivation should remove every privilege the account held, including delegated administration.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deactivating a user disables their login but leaves delegated administrator group assignments in place, which the offboarding checklist did not cover.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The setting has no effect while the account cannot log in, but reactivation would restore it silently. Checking eleven leavers from the past year found four with a stale delegated administrator assignment.

RESOLUTION
The offboarding checklist now includes removing delegated administrator group membership, the four historical stale assignments were removed, and a monthly report lists any deactivated user still assigned.

VALIDATION
The four assignments were confirmed removed, a test offboarding followed the updated checklist correctly, and the monthly report has returned no findings for six weeks.

column1: Two-factor authentication can be bypassed through one legacy login endpoint
column2:
CONTEXT
Two-factor authentication is enforced for all interactive logins to protect against credential compromise.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security assessment found a legacy mobile login path that completes authentication without prompting for the second factor.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every interactive login path should enforce the same two-factor requirement.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The legacy path, retained for an older mobile client version, authenticates on password alone.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two-factor policy was applied when it was introduced to the current login flow but not to the legacy path, which very few users still rely on but which remained technically reachable. Login history showed nine successful authentications through that path in the past quarter.

RESOLUTION
The legacy path was disabled entirely, the nine users still using it were migrated to the current mobile client, and a scan now checks periodically for any authentication path not enforcing the policy.

VALIDATION
The legacy path rejected all login attempts after being disabled, the nine migrated users authenticated successfully with two-factor in the current client, and the periodic scan found no further gaps.

column1: A sharing rule intended for one region silently applied company-wide
column2:
CONTEXT
A sharing rule was created to give a regional support team visibility into accounts owned by their own region's sales team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An access review found the regional support team could see accounts belonging to every region, not just their own.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The rule should extend visibility only within the intended region.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rule's criteria group evaluated to true for any account regardless of region, granting company-wide visibility.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rule's region condition referenced a field that is blank on about 60 percent of accounts due to inconsistent data entry, and the rule's logic treated a blank match as satisfying the condition rather than excluding it. Testing confirmed accounts with a different region's value visible to the support team.

RESOLUTION
The rule was rebuilt with explicit region matching that excludes blank values, and the underlying data gap was flagged separately for cleanup.

VALIDATION
Visibility testing after the change showed the support team could see only their own region's accounts, and a full access audit found no other rule with the same logic pattern.

column1: Field-level encryption now covers new records but not historical ones
column2:
CONTEXT
A programme is encrypting sensitive customer identifier fields at rest to meet a new data protection standard.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The organization cannot yet confirm the standard is met, because encryption applies only going forward.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every stored value in the covered fields should be encrypted, regardless of when it was written.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
New and edited records are encrypted correctly, while records untouched since the change remain in plain storage.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Enabling encryption does not retroactively encrypt existing values, which requires each record to be re-saved. A count found 340,000 records that have not been touched since the change and remain unencrypted.

RESOLUTION
A batch process is re-saving untouched records in controlled runs outside business hours, with 90,000 completed so far. This is partial: the remaining 250,000 records are scheduled over the coming weeks, and any record not re-saved by the compliance deadline needs an accepted exception.

VALIDATION
The 90,000 re-saved records were confirmed encrypted by a storage-level check, batch runs have caused no measurable performance impact, and the remaining volume is tracked against the deadline weekly.

column1: A vendor integration requires a broad permission the platform cannot scope narrower
column2:
CONTEXT
A field service scheduling vendor's integration user needs to read and write appointment data across every territory.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The only permission that grants the required object access also grants visibility into unrelated financial records on the same profile tier.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration user should hold only the access its function requires.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Narrowing the permission set breaks the integration, because the vendor's connector checks for the broader permission during authentication regardless of what it actually uses.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The vendor confirmed the broad check is a known limitation of their current connector version. Removing the permission was tested and confirmed to break scheduling entirely.

RESOLUTION
The integration user keeps the broader permission, with compensating controls: the user cannot log in interactively, its activity is monitored for access outside appointment data, and a field-level restriction blocks it from the financial records it does not need. This is a workaround: full removal of the exposure depends on the vendor's roadmap.

VALIDATION
No financial record access by the integration user appeared in three months of monitoring, and the field-level restriction was confirmed effective in testing.

column1: Session-based access restrictions cannot distinguish two office networks that share one address
column2:
CONTEXT
One access policy grants a trusted session to users connecting from the corporate network, identified by its public address.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A contracted facility sharing the same public address as the corporate network gives its own staff, who should not be trusted, the same elevated session.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Trusted session status should apply only to genuine corporate network users.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Anyone on the shared facility's network receives the same trust as a corporate user, because the platform cannot see past the shared address.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The facility's network provider confirmed a dedicated address was not available under the current contract. The facility's staff have no legitimate need for the platform.

RESOLUTION
Session trust from that address now requires a secondary device certificate issued only to corporate laptops, checked in addition to the address. This is a workaround: it depends on certificate issuance staying current, and the shared address exposure remains until the contract is renegotiated.

VALIDATION
A test device without the certificate received standard rather than trusted session behaviour despite matching the address, and all 140 corporate laptops presented valid certificates.

column1: A permission set license disappears from one user overnight with no recorded change
column2:
CONTEXT
Permission set licenses grant access to a premium feature and are assigned individually to named users.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A user lost access to the feature overnight, and setup history shows no removal event for their license.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A license assignment should persist until explicitly removed, with the removal recorded.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assignment is simply absent the next morning, with no corresponding entry in setup audit history.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The user's other permissions were unaffected, and reassigning the license restored access immediately with no side effects. License consumption counts for the organization show one fewer assignment than expected for that day. No deployment or scheduled job touched permission set licenses that night.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been identified, and the license was simply reassigned rather than any configuration being changed.

VALIDATION
No recurrence for this user in three weeks, and no other user has reported the same issue. The next step is opening a vendor case with the exact timestamp, since license assignment changes made outside the visible audit trail would need to be confirmed on the platform side.

column1: A locked-out account shows a successful login in the same minute as the lockout
column2:
CONTEXT
Accounts lock after five consecutive failed password attempts within a short window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Login history for one account shows a successful login recorded one minute after five failed attempts triggered a lockout, which should not be possible.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A locked account should be unable to authenticate until the lockout is cleared by an administrator or its timer expires.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The successful login is recorded from the same address as the failed attempts, inside the lockout window, with an eleven-minute session following.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The account's password was reset and the user re-verified, and monitoring was increased for related accounts. The failed attempts and successful login carry consistent request identifiers, ruling out a logging artifact. No related lockout has recurred in a quarterly review.

RESOLUTION
How a session was established during an active lockout is unresolved, and no configuration change has been made.

VALIDATION
Heightened monitoring has shown no recurrence in three weeks. The next step is a vendor case with the full request trace, since lockout internals are not visible from the org's logs.

column1: A cross-filter excludes records instead of including them
column2:
CONTEXT
A report uses a cross filter to find accounts with no open opportunities for a re-engagement campaign list.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The report returns accounts that do have open opportunities, the opposite of what was intended.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The cross filter set to exclude a related record should return only accounts without a matching related record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The filter was configured to include rather than exclude the related object, inverting the intended population.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The include and exclude options sit adjacent in the filter builder and the wrong one was selected when the report was first built, a year before the error was noticed. Every one of 40 sampled records on the report had at least one open opportunity.

RESOLUTION
The cross filter was corrected to exclude, and the report was renamed to state its logic explicitly in the description to reduce the chance of a repeat mistake.

VALIDATION
The corrected report returned only accounts with zero open opportunities across a full check of 600 accounts, and the campaign list built from it was reviewed and approved by the marketing team.

column1: A dashboard filter applies to only one of its two source reports
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard filter lets viewers narrow all its components to a single sales region at once.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Selecting a region narrows most components correctly, but one chart continues showing company-wide figures.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every component on the dashboard should respect the selected filter.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The one chart's source report has no field matching the filter's criteria, so the platform silently leaves it unfiltered rather than flagging the mismatch.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The chart was added later from a report built on a different object without a region field, and no warning surfaced when it was added to the filtered dashboard. Comparing filtered and unfiltered totals for that chart confirmed they were identical regardless of the selected region.

RESOLUTION
A region field was added to the underlying report so the filter applies correctly, and dashboard documentation now notes which fields a component must carry to respect the shared filter.

VALIDATION
Selecting each of four regions produced correctly scoped figures on all components including the previously unaffected chart, verified against direct queries for each region.

column1: An aggregate report double-counts opportunities linked to two campaigns
column2:
CONTEXT
A campaign influence report sums opportunity value across campaigns that contributed to each deal.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The total influenced value across all campaigns exceeds total closed revenue for the period, which is not possible.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Opportunities linked to more than one campaign should still sum to no more than their own value across the total.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
An opportunity linked to three campaigns contributes its full value to each campaign's total rather than a shared or split amount.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report aggregates at the influence junction level, which is correct for a per-campaign view but was being summed again into a grand total without deduplicating the underlying opportunities. Of 300 influenced opportunities, 80 carried more than one campaign, accounting for the entire overstatement.

RESOLUTION
The grand total now derives from a distinct opportunity count and sum rather than summing the junction rows, while individual campaign figures remain unchanged.

VALIDATION
The corrected grand total matched actual closed revenue for the period exactly, and individual campaign figures were confirmed unchanged against the previous report.

column1: A scheduled report email arrives with the previous run's data attached
column2:
CONTEXT
A weekly report is emailed to regional managers early Monday morning ahead of their team meeting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Managers occasionally notice figures from the email do not match the report when they open it directly minutes later.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The emailed snapshot should reflect data current at the time the schedule runs.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The email periodically carries figures matching the previous week's run rather than the current one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scheduled job occasionally ran before an overnight data load had finished writing the week's closing figures, capturing a stale cache. Comparing five weeks of email timestamps against the load's completion log showed two overlaps exactly matching the reported discrepancies.

RESOLUTION
The report schedule was moved to run after a check confirms the overnight load has completed, with a fallback delay if the load is still running.

VALIDATION
Five subsequent scheduled runs all occurred after load completion with matching figures, a deliberately delayed load correctly postponed the email, and managers confirmed no further mismatches.

column1: A funnel report treats reopened cases as new entries into the funnel
column2:
CONTEXT
A support funnel report tracks cases through triage, investigation, and resolution stages for a weekly quality review.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Funnel volumes at the triage stage are inflated well beyond the number of genuinely new cases each week.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The funnel should count a case once when it first enters, even if it is later reopened.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A reopened case re-enters the triage stage count as though it were new, since the report keys on the current stage rather than first entry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Reopening had not been considered when the funnel was designed, and 15 percent of cases in a typical week are reopens rather than new. Recomputing one week by hand using first-entry timestamps showed triage volume 15 percent lower than reported.

RESOLUTION
The report now counts triage entries using each case's first arrival timestamp, with reopens tracked as a separate labelled measure rather than folded into new volume.

VALIDATION
Four weeks of recomputed figures matched a manual first-entry reconstruction, and the separate reopen measure was reviewed and adopted by the quality team as a useful signal in its own right.

column1: A currency-aware report shows the wrong total when the corporate currency changes
column2:
CONTEXT
A global revenue report converts every opportunity into the corporate currency for a single combined total.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The combined total shifted noticeably overnight with no change in underlying deals.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The combined total should change only when underlying revenue or exchange rates genuinely change.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report converted using the corporate currency as configured at report open time rather than a fixed reporting-period rate.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Finance had updated a dated exchange rate the same night for an unrelated reason, and the report recalculates dynamically against the latest dated rate available rather than the rate in effect at period close. The shift matched the rate change exactly.

RESOLUTION
The report now converts using the exchange rate dated to the reporting period's close rather than the latest available, so a later rate update does not retroactively change historical totals.

VALIDATION
Historical totals for three closed periods remained stable after a further rate update, and the change was confirmed against finance's own period-end reporting.

column1: Row-level security is enforced in reports but not in the dashboard's export
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard summarizes account data with row-level access controlling which underlying records each viewer can see.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A viewer exporting a dashboard component as an image or PDF can see aggregate figures reflecting records they have no direct access to.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Exports should respect the same row-level access as the interactive view.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Chart images render from a cached aggregate computed under a broader running context, exposing totals wider than the viewer's own access.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The caching mechanism was designed for performance and computes once under the dashboard owner's access rather than per viewer, a limitation the vendor confirmed but has not scheduled to fix. Nine dashboards were found using this pattern with sensitive data.

RESOLUTION
The nine dashboards were rebuilt without result caching, restoring per-viewer accuracy at some cost to load time. This is partial: other dashboards using the same caching pattern have not yet been identified, and a full audit is pending.

VALIDATION
The nine rebuilt dashboards showed correctly scoped figures per viewer in testing, load time increased by roughly two seconds, and the remaining audit is tracked as open.

column1: Historical trend data exists for cases but not yet for the newer inquiry object
column2:
CONTEXT
A snapshot process captures nightly volumes for trend reporting, originally built for the case object alone.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A newer inquiry object introduced last year has no historical trend, so analysts cannot compare its growth against cases.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both objects should have comparable trend history available for the same reporting periods.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Case trends go back three years, while inquiry trends only exist from the day the snapshot job was extended to cover it, four months ago.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The inquiry object's daily counts before the snapshot job was extended cannot be reconstructed exactly, because status changes on inquiries are not tracked with the same field history depth as cases. Available creation dates give an approximate lower bound only.

RESOLUTION
Going-forward inquiry trends are now captured identically to cases. This is partial: history before the extension is approximated from creation dates alone and flagged as such wherever it appears in reports.

VALIDATION
Four months of matched trend data confirmed the two objects now track identically, and the approximated historical section was reviewed and accepted by analysts with its limitation documented.

column1: A required statistical function is unavailable, replicated with a formula field
column2:
CONTEXT
Analysts wanted a median resolution time alongside the average already shown on the service dashboard.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The reporting tool offers no median function, only sum, average, minimum, and maximum.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A median figure should be available alongside the other summary statistics.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No built-in option produces a median, and analysts had been estimating it by eye from a distribution chart.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The limitation is inherent to the platform's report builder. A formula-based approximation using percentile buckets was tested and found to track the true median closely for the case volumes involved.

RESOLUTION
A bucketed formula field now approximates the median within a small margin, displayed alongside a note that it is an approximation rather than an exact calculation. This is a workaround: exactness is traded for availability, and the approximation would degrade for a much smaller sample.

VALIDATION
The formula's output matched a manually calculated exact median within two percent across eight weeks of data, and analysts confirmed the approximation was accurate enough for trend discussion.

column1: The same report returns different row counts on consecutive runs with no data change
column2:
CONTEXT
A weekly compliance report counts records meeting a fixed set of criteria, run twice for cross-checking.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Running the identical report twice within a minute occasionally returns a different row count, with no records created or changed between runs.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An identical query against unchanged data should return the identical result every time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The count varies by one or two rows on roughly one run in twenty, with no pattern in which records appear or disappear.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Field history for the object shows no changes in the affected windows, and the report's filters depend on no date-relative or user-relative value that could shift between runs. Comparing two result sets from one instance showed one record present in only one run, unchanged in every field.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been identified, and the report has not been rebuilt since nothing about its configuration appears wrong.

VALIDATION
The instability recurs at roughly the same rate. The next step is exporting full result sets from paired runs and comparing them field by field, then raising a vendor case with a reproducible pair if confirmed.

column1: Autoresponder fires on internal test messages and confuses the support queue
column2:
CONTEXT
An autoresponder confirms receipt for every inbound message reaching the support address.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Internal test messages sent by the engineering team to verify the mail pipeline trigger the same customer-facing autoresponse.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Internal test traffic should not receive a customer-facing acknowledgement.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The autoresponder treats every inbound sender identically, including a recognizable internal test address.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No exclusion existed for internal senders because the autoresponder predates the current testing practice. Fourteen test messages in the past month triggered acknowledgements, two of which confused an on-call engineer into treating a test as a real customer report.

RESOLUTION
The autoresponder now excludes a maintained list of internal test addresses, and the testing team's messages carry a marker subject prefix as a second safeguard.

VALIDATION
Ten subsequent test messages produced no autoresponse, a genuine customer message from a similar-looking domain still triggered the response correctly, and no further confusion was reported.

column1: Attachment size limits reject legitimate diagnostic files without explanation
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers sometimes attach diagnostic logs to support messages to help agents reproduce a problem.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Messages with larger diagnostic files disappear entirely, and customers receive no indication their attachment was the problem.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An oversized attachment should still create a Case, with the customer told why the attachment did not come through.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The entire message is discarded silently when its total size exceeds the inbound limit, taking the message body with it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The size check applied to the whole message rather than being able to separate the body from the attachment. Twenty-six messages in a month were discarded entirely, all carrying an attachment over ten megabytes.

RESOLUTION
Oversized messages now create a Case from the body alone, with the attachment dropped and a note added directing the customer to a secure upload link instead.

VALIDATION
Ten test messages with oversized attachments created Cases with the body preserved and the note attached, and the twenty-six historical senders were followed up for their diagnostic files.

column1: Case merge does not consolidate the two cases' email threads
column2:
CONTEXT
Agents merge duplicate Cases when a customer's issue was logged twice, keeping one surviving record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a merge, only the surviving Case's own email thread is visible, and the merged Case's earlier messages appear lost.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Merging should preserve the full combined correspondence history under the surviving Case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Email message records remain linked to the Case that no longer exists as a standalone record, making them effectively unreachable from the merged view.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The merge operation relinks most related records automatically but does not include the email message object, which was added to the platform after the merge behaviour was last reviewed. Eighteen merges in the past quarter left correspondence orphaned this way.

RESOLUTION
A post-merge step now relinks email messages to the surviving Case, and the eighteen historical merges were corrected by rerunning that step against their retained identifiers.

VALIDATION
Ten test merges preserved the full combined thread under the surviving Case, the eighteen historical corrections were spot-checked and confirmed complete, and agents reported no further missing correspondence.

column1: Reply-to address routes customer replies away from the case ever reaching Salesforce
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound Case messages are sent from a no-reply address with a separate reply-to address intended to route responses back into the Case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customer replies to closed and reopened Cases stopped appearing as new Case activity for one message type.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any reply to an outbound Case message should be captured and attached to that Case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Messages sent through one newer template carry a reply-to address pointing at a general mailbox rather than the Case-specific routing address.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template was built by copying an older one and the reply-to field was left blank, which the sending platform then defaulted to a general fallback mailbox rather than erroring. Sixty replies over three weeks landed in that mailbox unprocessed.

RESOLUTION
The template's reply-to field was corrected to the Case-specific routing address, and inbound processing now alerts if any outbound template is found with a missing or incorrect reply-to configuration.

VALIDATION
The sixty stranded replies were manually attached to their Cases, five test replies routed correctly afterward, and the new alert flagged a deliberately misconfigured test template.

column1: A signature block includes an outdated phone number for every agent
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound messages include a signature block populated from each agent's user record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers calling the number in agent signatures reach a disconnected line.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The signature should show the organization's current support number.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every signature shows a number that changed when the support line was consolidated eight months ago.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The number was hardcoded into the signature template rather than pulled from a maintained setting, so the consolidation was never reflected in outbound messages. No process existed to review template content when contact details change.

RESOLUTION
The signature template now references a custom setting maintained by the operations team, updated once for the current number, and a checklist item for future number changes was added to the operations runbook.

VALIDATION
New outbound messages showed the correct number in testing, the operations team confirmed the setting matched the current line, and a test change to the setting propagated to new signatures immediately.

column1: Sentiment flagging works for English messages but not for other supported languages
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound messages are scored for sentiment to help prioritize agent response, supporting five customer-facing languages.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Messages in three of the five supported languages receive no sentiment score at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Sentiment scoring should function for every language the support channel accepts.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
English and one other language score correctly, while the remaining three return a blank score silently.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scoring service's language detection model was trained on a narrower set than the channel actually supports, and requests in unsupported languages return an empty result rather than an error the integration would surface. This affected 22 percent of inbound volume.

RESOLUTION
A translation step now converts unsupported-language messages to English before scoring, restoring a score for those messages. This is partial: translation quality varies for informal or technical phrasing, so scores for the three languages carry a lower confidence flag pending a language-native model the vendor has not yet released.

VALIDATION
Scored coverage rose from 78 to 100 percent of inbound volume, spot-checked translated scores were plausible against a bilingual reviewer's judgment, and the confidence flag correctly distinguished native from translated scoring.

column1: Escalation emails reach the primary approver but not their designated backup
column2:
CONTEXT
High-value case escalations email the assigned approver and should fall back to a designated backup if unanswered within two hours.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Escalations sit unanswered well past two hours because the backup is never notified.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An unanswered escalation should notify the backup automatically at the two-hour mark.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The scheduled check that should trigger the backup notification exists for only two of the five approval regions.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The backup mechanism was built region by region and the rollout stalled after the first two, with no tracking to show the remaining three were incomplete. Nine escalations in the affected regions went unanswered for four hours or more before someone happened to notice.

RESOLUTION
Backup notification is now live for four of the five regions. This is partial: the fifth region's approval structure has two backups rather than one, which the current mechanism cannot express and needs a small design change.

VALIDATION
The four completed regions showed backup notifications firing correctly at the two-hour mark in nine test escalations, and the fifth region's design change is scheduled with an interim manual check in place.

column1: A regulator-mandated retention period exceeds the mailbox archive's supported range
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer correspondence for one product line must be retained for ten years under a regulatory requirement.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The email archiving tool in use only guarantees retrieval for seven years.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All correspondence within the regulated retention period should remain retrievable on request.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The archiving vendor's platform is contractually limited to seven years, and extending it was quoted at a cost the programme could not approve.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The seven-year limit is a product tier restriction rather than a technical one, confirmed with the vendor, and a higher tier would close the gap. The affected product line represents a small share of total correspondence volume.

RESOLUTION
Correspondence for the regulated product line is now also exported to a separate long-term storage system covering the full ten years. This is a workaround: two storage locations must now be searched for retrieval, and the export adds a manual step each quarter.

VALIDATION
A test retrieval of nine-year-old correspondence succeeded from the separate storage, two quarterly exports completed with volume matching the source, and the procedure was documented for the compliance team.

column1: Case creation from email cannot recognize forwarded chains, so context is stripped by hand
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers occasionally forward an internal email chain to support, expecting the conversation to inform their request.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Case creation treats the forwarded chain as a single opaque body, and agents cannot easily tell which part is the customer's request.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A forwarded chain should be parseable into its individual messages so agents can read it in order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The inbound processor has no chain-parsing capability and was not designed to separate quoted history from new content.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Building chain parsing was estimated at several weeks given the variety of email client quoting formats, and was not prioritized against other work this quarter. Roughly thirty such messages arrive a month.

RESOLUTION
A macro now lets agents flag a Case as containing a forwarded chain, adding a prompt reminding them to summarize the relevant portion into the Case description by hand. This is a workaround: parsing still depends on the agent's reading, and no structure is captured for reporting.

VALIDATION
Fifteen flagged Cases over three weeks showed agents summarizing consistently, and a team lead review found the summaries adequate for handling the request.

column1: Outbound delivery confirmation is missing for a specific but unidentified subset of messages
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound Case messages should each receive a delivery confirmation from the sending platform within a few minutes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of messages each day never receive a confirmation, though there is no evidence the customer failed to receive them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every sent message should produce either a delivery confirmation or a bounce notification.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected messages simply have no confirmation record, and customers in several confirmed cases replied normally, indicating the message did arrive.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The sending platform's own delivery logs, checked for six sampled messages, show a confirmation sent that never reached the org's inbound endpoint. The affected messages share no common domain, template, or agent, and represent roughly half a percent of volume.

RESOLUTION
Whether the confirmation is lost in transit or not sent at all has not been established, and no change has been made pending clearer evidence.

VALIDATION
The gap persists at roughly the same low rate. The next step is a joint session with the vendor comparing their delivery log against the org's inbound log for a shared window, to localize where the confirmation goes missing.

column1: A validation rule blocks legitimate edits made by an integration user
column2:
CONTEXT
A validation rule requires a reason code whenever a case's priority is downgraded, intended for agent-initiated changes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The integration that closes resolved cases in bulk fails every time a downgrade happens as part of that process.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Automated closures should not be blocked by a rule meant to govern manual agent decisions.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The validation rule applies uniformly regardless of who or what is making the change.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rule was written without excluding the integration user, since the integration did not exist when the rule was created. Failed integration runs over two weeks totaled 340 cases stuck unresolved in the source system as well.

RESOLUTION
The rule now excludes changes made by the integration user, whose downgrades are governed by the source system's own controls instead, documented in the rule's description for future reviewers.

VALIDATION
The 340 stuck cases processed successfully after the fix, agent-initiated downgrades still required a reason code in testing, and the integration's error rate returned to zero.

column1: Merging two accounts drops a custom field that had no merge behavior defined
column2:
CONTEXT
Duplicate accounts are merged periodically by data stewards, keeping one survivor and combining related records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A custom field tracking a customer's preferred contact method is blank on merged accounts even when one of the two originals had it set.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A merge should retain a populated value from either record when the survivor's own value is blank.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Standard merge behavior favors the survivor's existing value regardless of whether it is populated, so a blank survivor field stays blank even if the loser had one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This field-level behavior is a platform default stewards did not know applied to custom fields the same way as standard ones. Reviewing 90 recent merges found 34 with a blank preferred contact method despite one side having a value.

RESOLUTION
Stewards now review a short list of fields with this behavior before confirming a merge, prompted by a pre-merge comparison screen built as a screen flow.

VALIDATION
The 34 affected accounts were corrected by hand, ten subsequent test merges using the comparison screen retained the correct values, and stewards confirmed the extra step added negligible time.

column1: A rollup summary undercounts because it excludes a status added after the field was built
column2:
CONTEXT
A rollup summary field counts active contracts on an account for a renewal dashboard.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Accounts with contracts in a status introduced last year are undercounted on the dashboard.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The rollup should count every contract status considered active by the business.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rollup's filter lists specific statuses explicitly, and the newer status was never added to that list.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The status was introduced for a new contract type without revisiting existing rollups that filtered on status. A count found 2,100 contracts in the missing status across 900 accounts, all undercounted by exactly one on the dashboard.

RESOLUTION
The rollup filter was updated to include the missing status, and a note was added to the status field's description warning that adding a new active status requires reviewing dependent rollups.

VALIDATION
The 900 affected accounts recalculated to the correct count, a test contract created in the newer status incremented the rollup correctly, and the dashboard total reconciled with a direct query.

column1: A related list action creates a child record without the required parent lookup populated
column2:
CONTEXT
A quick action on the account page lets users log a new service request without leaving the account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Service requests created through this action save without a link back to the account, though users see no error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A service request created from the account's related list should always be linked to that account.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The account lookup on the new record is left blank, requiring a separate manual step to link it afterward.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The quick action's layout did not include the account field with automatic prepopulation configured, an option available but not applied when the action was built. Of 60 sampled requests created this way, all 60 required a manual relink noticed only when someone checked the account's related list.

RESOLUTION
The quick action was reconfigured to prepopulate the account field from the page context, and the 60 historical requests were relinked.

VALIDATION
Ten new service requests created through the action showed the account correctly populated without manual intervention, and the related list showed complete history afterward.

column1: A required field bypass through data loader created thousands of incomplete records
column2:
CONTEXT
A field marked required at the page layout level is meant to ensure every service ticket carries a category.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An analysis found thousands of tickets with no category, despite the field appearing mandatory to users.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every ticket, however created, should carry a category.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Page-layout-level requirement does not apply to records created through the bulk data loading tool, which bypassed it entirely during a historical import.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Only a field-level required setting is enforced regardless of creation path, and this field had only the weaker layout-level setting. The import that created the gap ran two years ago and inserted 18,000 tickets with no category.

RESOLUTION
The field was changed to field-level required with a documented default for automated processes that genuinely have no category at creation time, and the 18,000 historical tickets were categorized using pattern matching against their descriptions where possible.

VALIDATION
A repeat bulk load without a category was rejected in testing, 15,200 of the 18,000 historical tickets were categorized with confidence and the remainder flagged for manual review.

column1: Duplicate detection covers person accounts but not business accounts with similar names
column2:
CONTEXT
A duplicate management rule warns users when a new account resembles an existing one closely enough to likely be the same customer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Business account duplicates keep being created at a steady rate despite the rule being active.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The rule should catch likely duplicates across both account types the organization uses.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The matching rule was built and tuned against person account name patterns, and performs poorly on business names, which vary more in formatting.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing the rule against 200 known business duplicate pairs caught only 40 percent, largely missing pairs differing by legal suffix or abbreviation. Person account matching performed well, catching 91 percent.

RESOLUTION
The business account matching rule was retuned with suffix and abbreviation normalization, raising the catch rate. This is partial: 68 percent are now caught, short of the 90 percent target, and further tuning is scheduled.

VALIDATION
The retuned rule caught 136 of the 200 known pairs in a rerun, a false positive check on 100 distinct accounts found five incorrectly flagged, and further tuning continues against an expanded test set.

column1: A record type cannot be retired because thousands of records still reference it
column2:
CONTEXT
An old record type for a discontinued product line was meant to be retired once its data was no longer needed.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The record type cannot be deactivated while 40,000 historical records carry it, and reassigning them all was judged too costly for records nobody actively works.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Discontinued record types should be removable from active use without losing historical data.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deactivating the record type would prevent it rendering correctly on existing records, since the platform still needs it for their layout.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Migrating 40,000 records to a current record type was estimated at several weeks of validation, against a low ongoing cost of simply hiding the record type from creation.

RESOLUTION
The record type remains active but was removed from every profile's assignable list, so it cannot be selected for new records while historical ones render normally. This is a workaround: the record type still appears in metadata and administrative lists as active.

VALIDATION
No new records could be created with the retired type in testing, historical records displayed correctly, and administrators confirmed the reduced clutter in day-to-day selection.
