column1: A field cannot be deleted because a managed package still references it
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom field used only during an early rollout is no longer needed and was flagged for cleanup.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deleting the field is blocked because a managed package installed for an unrelated purpose references it internally.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An unused field should be removable once the organization no longer needs it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The platform refuses deletion while any dependency exists, including one inside a package the organization does not control the internals of.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The package vendor confirmed the reference is part of an optional feature the organization does not use, but removing it requires a version update not yet scheduled. The field itself holds no current data of value.

RESOLUTION
The field was cleared of its historical data, renamed to indicate it is retired, and hidden from every page layout and report type. This is a workaround: it remains in the schema and cannot be fully removed until the vendor's package update ships.

VALIDATION
The renamed field no longer appeared on any layout or in report field selection during a check across all profiles, and the vendor's planned update was logged for follow-up.

column1: A specific record type combination occasionally saves with two owners recorded
column2:
CONTEXT
Every record has a single owner field, enforced by the platform's data model.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A data quality scan found eleven records where the current owner and the owner in a related history entry disagree, as though two owners were briefly recorded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record should have exactly one owner at any time, consistently reflected everywhere.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The record's owner field and its history entry for the most recent ownership change name different users.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
All eleven records were touched by two automated processes within the same few seconds, a flow reassignment and an API update, and both appear in the audit trail claiming the change.

RESOLUTION
Which process's value is authoritative has not been determined, and no fix has been applied since guessing could make ownership less reliable.

VALIDATION
Ownership on the eleven records was manually corrected, and no new instance has appeared in three weeks of monitoring. The next step is a preemptive lock so the two processes cannot update the same record within the same second.

column1: A small number of records revert a recent edit without any subsequent user or process touching them
column2:
CONTEXT
Field history tracks every change to a monitored set of fields on the customer contract object.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of contracts each month show a field reverting to its previous value hours after being correctly updated, with no new history entry for the reversion.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A field's value should only change as the result of a recorded update.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The value is simply different when next viewed, with the field history log showing only the original correct update and nothing after it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The reverted value always matches the value immediately before the update, ruling out a random change. No scheduled job, flow, or integration writes to this field on a delay. The affected contracts share no owner or record type pattern.

RESOLUTION
No writing process has been identified for the reversion, and the field remains as is pending further evidence.

VALIDATION
Roughly four contracts a month are affected and corrected once noticed. The next step is a database-level trigger to capture every write to the field outside the normal audit path, since the reversion appears to bypass field history entirely.

column1: A quote's total ignores a line-level tax exemption flag
column2:
CONTEXT
Certain product lines can be flagged tax-exempt on a quote for qualifying nonprofit customers.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Exempt lines still have tax calculated and included in the quote total.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A line flagged exempt should contribute zero tax to the total.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The tax calculation reads the customer's overall exemption status but ignores the line-level flag meant for partial exemptions.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The line-level flag was added for customers exempt on some products but not others, a scenario the original tax logic had not been built to handle. Twenty-two quotes reviewed all showed tax applied on lines explicitly flagged exempt.

RESOLUTION
The tax calculation now checks the line-level flag first, falling back to the customer-level status only when the line is unflagged, and the twenty-two quotes were recalculated.

VALIDATION
The twenty-two quotes reflected correct exemption after recalculation, ten new test quotes with mixed exempt and taxable lines calculated correctly, and finance confirmed the logic against their own tax rules.

column1: Pipeline coverage ratio is calculated against last quarter's target instead of the current one
column2:
CONTEXT
A pipeline coverage dashboard divides open pipeline value by the quarter's sales target to give a coverage ratio.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The ratio jumped sharply at the start of the new quarter before any pipeline activity had occurred.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The ratio should always divide by the current quarter's target.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The underlying formula referenced a target field that updates a few days into the new quarter rather than at its start.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The target field is populated by a finance process that runs a week after quarter start, so the dashboard divided current pipeline by the prior quarter's now-stale target during that week. This has happened at the start of every quarter for the past year.

RESOLUTION
The dashboard now reads a separately maintained target field that finance updates before quarter start specifically for this purpose, decoupling it from their internal process timing.

VALIDATION
The ratio at the start of the following quarter reflected the correct target from day one, and finance confirmed their internal process could continue on its own unchanged schedule.

column1: A renewal opportunity is created for cancelled contracts as well as active ones
column2:
CONTEXT
An automation creates a renewal opportunity ninety days before a contract's end date.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cancelled contracts still generate renewal opportunities, which sales then has to identify and close as invalid.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only contracts still active as their end date approaches should generate a renewal opportunity.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The trigger checks the end date alone and does not check whether the contract has since been cancelled.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Cancellation was introduced as a status after the renewal automation was built, and the condition was never revisited. Forty invalid renewal opportunities were found over two quarters, each requiring a sales rep to notice and close it.

RESOLUTION
The trigger now checks contract status is active at the time it would fire, and the forty existing invalid opportunities were closed with an explanatory note.

VALIDATION
A test cancellation before the renewal window correctly suppressed opportunity creation, five genuine active renewals still generated correctly, and sales confirmed no further invalid renewals appeared over the following month.

column1: Commission calculations use list price instead of the negotiated price on discounted deals
column2:
CONTEXT
Sales commission is calculated as a percentage of the final negotiated deal value once a deal closes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reps on heavily discounted deals are paid commission based on a higher figure than what the customer actually agreed to pay.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Commission should be calculated from the actual closed deal value, discount included.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The calculation references the opportunity's list price total rather than its net amount after discount.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The field used was correct for deals without discounting, which was the common case when the formula was first built, and became wrong as discounting became more frequent. Fifty closed deals in the last quarter showed overpaid commission, averaging 14 percent above the correct figure.

RESOLUTION
The calculation now references the net amount field, and finance reconciled and adjusted the fifty affected commission payments going forward per the compensation policy.

VALIDATION
Fifty deals were recalculated and matched finance's independent figures, ten new closed deals with discounts calculated correctly, and finance confirmed the compensation policy was followed for the adjustment.

column1: A price book activation leaves inactive an older book still referenced by open quotes
column2:
CONTEXT
An annual price update activates a new price book and deactivates the previous year's.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users with open quotes built against the previous price book find those quotes unable to be edited or added to once it deactivates.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Open quotes should remain fully usable on their original price book until closed, even after a newer one is activated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Adding a new line to a quote requires its price book to be active, so deactivation blocks any further edits to in-flight quotes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The activation process assumed quotes complete within the same pricing period, which held until deal cycles lengthened. Sixty open quotes were affected by the most recent activation.

RESOLUTION
The previous price book now stays active for a defined grace period after the new one is introduced, with new quotes defaulting to the new book while open ones remain usable until closed.

VALIDATION
The sixty affected quotes were edited successfully once the grace period took effect, new quotes created during the grace period defaulted to the current book, and the following year's activation caused no equivalent disruption.

column1: A rounding difference between two currency fields causes invoices to be rejected by finance
column2:
CONTEXT
An order total is stored on both the order and a summary field on the account, calculated independently for different purposes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance's invoicing process rejects a small share of orders where the two totals differ by a cent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both totals should agree exactly for the same order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One total sums individually rounded line amounts while the other rounds the sum once at the end, occasionally producing a one cent difference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two calculations were built independently by different teams without a shared rounding convention. Reviewing 500 orders found 31 with a one cent mismatch, all on orders with an odd number of fractional-cent lines.

RESOLUTION
Both calculations now round individual lines first and sum the rounded values, matching finance's own convention, eliminating the source of divergence.

VALIDATION
The 31 mismatched orders recalculated to agree exactly, five hundred further orders processed with no mismatches, and finance confirmed invoicing rejections for this reason stopped.

column1: Automated deal desk review covers standard terms but not custom legal language
column2:
CONTEXT
An automated check flags deals with non-standard discount, payment term, or duration combinations for deal desk review.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deals with custom legal language inserted into the contract still pass automated review even when the language conflicts with standard terms.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any deal carrying custom legal language should route to deal desk regardless of whether its commercial terms look standard.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The check reads structured fields only and has no visibility into free-text contract language attached as a document.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Detecting meaningful conflicts in free-text legal language reliably was assessed as requiring a specialized review capability not currently available, while a simpler presence check was achievable quickly. Twelve deals with problematic custom language had passed undetected in the past two quarters.

RESOLUTION
Any attached document flagged by the rep as containing custom legal language now routes to deal desk automatically. This is partial: the flag depends on the rep applying it correctly, and unflagged language would still be missed.

VALIDATION
Ten test deals with the flag applied routed to deal desk correctly, and the twelve historical deals were reviewed with two requiring contract amendments.

column1: A currency the finance system does not support forces manual conversion before entry
column2:
CONTEXT
A new regional office began quoting customers in a local currency not configured in the finance system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deals in that currency cannot be entered directly, since the finance integration rejects any code it does not recognize.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deals in any currency the sales team quotes should flow through to finance without manual work.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Adding support for a new currency requires a configuration change controlled by a different team, with a queue several months long.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The finance team confirmed the currency will be added in a future release but could not prioritize it sooner given other regulatory work. Deal volume in it is modest but growing.

RESOLUTION
Deals in the unsupported currency are converted to the regional group currency at close using a documented rate before entering finance. This is a workaround: the local amount is not preserved in finance's records, and the rate applied may differ slightly from the rate in effect at invoicing.

VALIDATION
Eight deals were processed through the conversion procedure with finance confirming the entries were accepted, and the rate discrepancy was measured at under one percent.

column1: A subset of closed-won deals disappear from the revenue dashboard for a few hours after close
column2:
CONTEXT
Closed deals should appear on the revenue dashboard within minutes, since leadership checks it throughout the day.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of deals each week are visibly closed on the opportunity record but absent from the dashboard for hours before appearing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A closed deal should be reflected on the dashboard promptly and consistently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The deal is queryable directly and satisfies every dashboard filter, yet does not appear in the dashboard's own report until much later.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report was rerun manually and immediately showed the missing deal, ruling out a genuine filter mismatch. The delay is not consistent, ranging from twenty minutes to six hours, and does not correlate with deal size, owner, or time of day.

RESOLUTION
The mechanism causing the delayed appearance has not been identified, and no scheduled refresh change has been made without understanding the cause.

VALIDATION
The pattern continues at roughly the same low rate. The next step is comparing the report's cache metadata against the deal's close timestamp for the next occurrence, to see whether a caching layer rather than the report itself is responsible.

column1: A specific renewal cohort shows conflicting churn status across two reports
column2:
CONTEXT
Two reports independently classify customers as retained or churned at renewal, one for sales and one for finance.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
For a cohort of about thirty accounts, the two reports disagree on churn status even though both read from the same contract data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both reports should agree on churn classification for any account, since they describe the same fact.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The sales report classifies the cohort as retained through a downsell, while the finance report classifies the same accounts as churned.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both reports' logic was reviewed and each is internally consistent with its own definition, but the definitions diverge for a downsell scenario neither owner had considered. Neither is clearly wrong on its own terms.

RESOLUTION
No technical fix has been applied, since the disagreement is a definitional question rather than a data error, and it has been escalated to the sales and finance leads to agree a single definition.

VALIDATION
The thirty affected accounts remain classified differently between the two reports pending that decision. Once agreed, the next step is aligning both reports' logic and confirming agreement across a full rerun.

column1: A composite API request partially applies changes despite an all-or-nothing expectation
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner submits related record changes as a single composite request, expecting either all or none to apply.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some composite requests leave a subset of records changed when a later step in the same request fails.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A composite request configured for all-or-nothing behavior should never leave a partial result.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The partner's client was not sending the all-or-nothing flag, defaulting to independent processing of each step.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flag exists and is documented, but the partner's integration was built from an older example that predated its introduction. Twelve partial-application incidents in the past month all traced to requests missing the flag.

RESOLUTION
The partner's client was updated to include the flag, and the endpoint now rejects composite requests explicitly opting out of it with a warning encouraging its use, rather than silently defaulting.

VALIDATION
A deliberately failing step inside a flagged request rolled back every change in the request, the twelve historical partial incidents were manually reconciled, and the partner confirmed no recurrence over two weeks.

column1: Field-level security silently strips a field from the API response instead of erroring
column2:
CONTEXT
A reporting consumer requests a fixed set of fields from an endpoint, expecting all of them back.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One field is consistently absent from the response, and the consumer's parser fails when a mapped field is missing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A field the requesting user cannot see should either be excluded with a clear indication or the request should fail explicitly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field is silently omitted from the response body with no error or notice, which the consumer interpreted as a malformed response.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration user's profile lacked field-level access to that field, added after the integration was first built, and the platform's default is to omit rather than error. The consumer had no visibility into why fields could vary.

RESOLUTION
Field-level access was granted to the integration user, and the consumer's parser was updated to treat a missing expected field as an explicit error rather than failing unpredictably.

VALIDATION
The field appeared consistently in responses after the access grant, a deliberately restricted field produced a clear parser error rather than a silent failure, and the consumer's failure rate returned to zero.

column1: An API version pinned in client code stops receiving a bug fix already released
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner's client pins a specific API version for stability, upgrading deliberately on their own schedule.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A known bug affecting the pinned version was already fixed in a later version, but the partner cannot benefit without an upgrade they had not planned.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Partners should be informed when a fix relevant to their pinned version becomes available in a newer one.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No notification mechanism existed, so the partner continued encountering the bug for months after the fix shipped.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Version support communications went to a general partner mailing list that this partner's engineering contact was not subscribed to. Their integration had been running against the affected version for eleven months past the fix release.

RESOLUTION
Partner-specific version tracking now flags known fixes relevant to a partner's pinned version, sent directly to their registered technical contact rather than relying on a general list.

VALIDATION
The affected partner was notified and upgraded within two weeks, confirming the bug no longer occurred, and two other partners on older pinned versions received equivalent notifications in the same rollout.

column1: A webhook retries indefinitely against an endpoint that will never succeed
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound webhooks notify a partner's endpoint of case updates, retrying on failure with increasing delay.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A partner endpoint that had been permanently decommissioned continued receiving retry attempts for weeks, consuming resources for no benefit.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Retries should stop after a reasonable bounded number of attempts rather than continuing indefinitely.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retry logic had no maximum attempt count, so failures against a permanently dead endpoint retried forever at the maximum interval.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retry mechanism was designed for transient outages and never given an upper bound, since sustained permanent failure had not been anticipated. The dead endpoint had accumulated over four thousand retry attempts before being noticed.

RESOLUTION
Retries now stop after a defined maximum count, moving the event to a dead letter queue for manual review, and an alert fires when any endpoint's failure streak crosses a threshold well before the maximum.

VALIDATION
A simulated permanently failing endpoint stopped retrying at the configured maximum and landed correctly in the dead letter queue, and the alert fired at the expected threshold in testing.

column1: Query results omit records recently restored from the recycle bin
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer periodically queries for records modified since its last successful run to stay synchronized.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records deleted and then restored from the recycle bin never reappear in the consumer's data even though they exist again in Salesforce.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A restored record should be picked up by the next incremental query like any other change.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The restore operation does not update the modified timestamp the query filters on, so a restored record with an old timestamp is skipped by queries scoped to recent changes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a platform behavior rather than a configuration choice, confirmed against documentation once identified. Six restored records over two months were found missing from the consumer, each traced to this exact scenario.

RESOLUTION
The consumer now also queries the deletion and restoration audit log on each run, catching restores the modified-timestamp query would miss, and merging any found restorations into its sync.

VALIDATION
A test delete-and-restore cycle was picked up correctly on the next sync run, and the six historical missing records were backfilled and confirmed present.

column1: Bulk API job status reports complete before all result files are actually available
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly integration submits a bulk job and downloads result files once the job reports as complete.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Occasionally the download step fails because a result file is not yet available, despite the job status showing complete.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A complete job status should mean every result file is ready to download.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
There is a brief window after the status changes to complete during which the last result file is still being finalized.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The vendor confirmed status and file availability are updated by separate internal processes with a small unsynchronized gap between them, occurring in roughly one job in five hundred. The integration had no tolerance for this gap.

RESOLUTION
The download step now retries with a short backoff if a result file is briefly unavailable immediately after job completion, rather than treating it as a hard failure.

VALIDATION
The retry handled fifteen occurrences of the gap over a month without a failed run, and jobs unaffected by the gap were unaffected by the added retry logic.

column1: Rate limit headers are honored by the newer client but not the legacy one
column2:
CONTEXT
Two client versions call the same API, an older one used by a legacy tool and a current one used elsewhere.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The legacy tool occasionally gets throttled with repeated errors instead of pacing requests, while the current client backs off smoothly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both clients should respect the API's rate limit information.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The legacy client does not read the rate limit headers and simply retries immediately on a throttling error, worsening the condition it caused.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The legacy tool has no active maintainer, and a full rewrite was not judged worthwhile given its planned retirement next year. A lightweight wrapper was assessed as a faster interim fix.

RESOLUTION
A thin proxy now sits in front of the legacy tool's calls, reading rate limit headers and pacing requests on its behalf without touching the tool's code. This is partial: the proxy handles pacing but not smarter batching, so the tool still makes more individual calls than necessary.

VALIDATION
Throttling errors from the legacy tool fell to zero over two weeks with the proxy in place, and the current client's behavior stayed unaffected.

column1: Change data capture events are reliable for standard objects but lag for custom ones under load
column2:
CONTEXT
A downstream analytics platform subscribes to change events to keep a near-real-time copy of key records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Custom object events sometimes arrive many minutes late during high update volume, while standard object events stay prompt.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Change events for any subscribed object should arrive within a consistent, short delay.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Custom object event delivery degrades noticeably under load in a way standard object delivery does not.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The vendor indicated custom object event publishing shares a different internal queue with different capacity characteristics than standard objects, a distinction not previously documented. Peak load periods showed custom object delivery lagging by up to eighteen minutes against a target of under one.

RESOLUTION
High-volume custom object updates were split into smaller batches to reduce peak queue pressure, improving typical lag. This is partial: lag during the highest load periods still exceeds target, and the vendor has not committed to a capacity change.

VALIDATION
Typical lag fell from minutes to under ninety seconds outside peak periods, while the highest load periods still showed lag up to six minutes, tracked against the vendor's open capacity question.

column1: A consumer needs a stable identifier across environments, which record IDs cannot provide
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner correlates records across a sandbox environment and production using the record identifier returned by the API.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Record identifiers differ between environments for what the partner considers the same logical record, breaking their correlation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The partner needs a way to recognize the same logical record across environments.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Record identifiers are generated per environment and have no relationship to each other even for records created by the same test data set.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is an inherent property of how records are created independently per environment, not a configurable behavior. The partner's testing process depended on an assumption the platform never guaranteed.

RESOLUTION
A dedicated external identifier field, populated identically by the partner's test data generation in both environments, is now used for correlation instead of the platform's record identifier. This is a workaround: it depends on the partner populating the field consistently, and any record created outside their process has no correlation value.

VALIDATION
Fifty test records correlated correctly across both environments using the new field, and the partner updated their test data documentation to require it consistently.

column1: A specific consumer's requests occasionally receive a response for a different consumer's request
column2:
CONTEXT
Multiple consumers call the same API concurrently, each expecting a response matched to its own request.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One consumer reported receiving data in a response matching nothing it had requested, matching instead what a different consumer had asked for around the same moment.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A response should always correspond to the request that produced it, regardless of concurrent traffic.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mismatched response carried a request identifier tracing to the other consumer's call, captured in logs from both sides during the incident.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both consumers' logs were preserved for the window, and their requests differ in every parameter yet the response body matches the other consumer's expected result precisely. No shared caching layer between the two consumers has been identified in current architecture documentation.

RESOLUTION
The mechanism has not been identified, and this has been escalated as a priority security concern given the potential for cross-consumer data exposure.

VALIDATION
No further occurrence has been confirmed in two weeks of heightened logging. The next step is a vendor engagement providing both request identifiers and timestamps for platform-side investigation.

column1: A question about the current week resolves to the wrong week after a Sunday
column2:
CONTEXT
Users frequently ask questions scoped to the current week, which the assistant translates into a date range.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions asked on a Sunday return figures for the week that just ended rather than the week beginning that day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question scoped to the current week should consistently resolve according to the organization's defined week start, every day of the week including Sunday.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The date resolution logic treated Sunday as the last day of the previous week rather than the first day of the new one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The organization's fiscal week starts on Sunday, but the resolution logic used a common convention treating Monday as the start. Of 40 Sunday questions sampled over two months, all 40 resolved to the prior week.

RESOLUTION
The resolution logic now reads the organization's configured week start rather than assuming a default, tested explicitly against every day of the week.

VALIDATION
Questions asked on each day of the week, including Sunday, resolved to the correct range in 70 test cases, and the 40 historical Sunday questions were confirmed to have shown incorrect figures at the time.

column1: Negated conditions in a question are dropped from the generated query
column2:
CONTEXT
Users sometimes ask questions phrased as exclusions, such as accounts without a recent order.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions with a negated condition return the same results as the equivalent question without the negation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A negated condition should exclude matching records rather than being ignored.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query includes only the positive conditions extracted from the question, silently dropping any exclusion clause introduced by a word such as without or not.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Intent extraction identified entities and positive filters well but had no handling for negation words, treating them as noise. Of 25 negated questions tested, all 25 returned results identical to their non-negated counterparts.

RESOLUTION
Negation words are now recognized during extraction and translated into an explicit exclusion condition in the generated query, with the negated condition also restated in the answer for clarity.

VALIDATION
Twenty-five negated questions returned correctly excluded results matching manually written queries, and the restated condition in the answer was confirmed accurate for all twenty-five.

column1: Currency figures in answers are shown without their currency code
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization operates in several currencies, and monetary questions can be scoped to any of them.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users receiving a monetary answer cannot tell which currency the figure is in, and some have assumed the wrong one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every monetary figure in an answer should state its currency explicitly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The answer states the number alone, formatted with a thousands separator but no currency indicator.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The answer generation step formatted numeric results generically without distinguishing currency fields from plain numbers. A review of 30 monetary answers found none included a currency code, and two users had reported a figure to colleagues in the wrong currency as a result.

RESOLUTION
Monetary fields are now tagged during query generation so the answer step can attach the correct currency code to every figure, including converted totals when a query spans multiple currencies.

VALIDATION
Thirty monetary answers, including five spanning multiple currencies, correctly stated their currency in testing, and the two users who had previously misreported a figure confirmed the new format resolved their concern.

column1: A question naming a deactivated user returns no results with no explanation
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask questions naming a colleague, such as how many cases a particular person is handling.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions naming someone who has since left the organization return an empty result with no indication why.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should explain when a named person cannot be found or is no longer active, rather than returning a silent empty answer.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Entity resolution only matches active users, so a deactivated user's name resolves to nothing and the query simply returns zero records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The active-only filter on user lookup was applied for a different reason, to avoid suggesting departed staff for new assignment, but it was reused unintentionally for this lookup too. Eight questions in a month named a since-departed user and returned an unexplained zero.

RESOLUTION
Entity resolution now includes deactivated users for lookup purposes, and the answer states clearly when a named person is no longer active, alongside whatever historical figures the query can still return.

VALIDATION
Eight retested questions about departed users returned historical figures with a clear note on their status, and active user questions were unaffected.

column1: A smallest-customer question ignores customers with zero recorded transactions
column2:
CONTEXT
Superlative questions ask for the largest, smallest, or most active record matching some criteria.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question about the smallest customer by order count returned a customer with one order rather than the several customers with none.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A smallest-by-count question should recognize zero as smaller than one.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query ordered by count ascending after joining to the order object, which drops customers with no matching order entirely rather than counting them as zero.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The join-based aggregation naturally excludes non-matching parents, a standard behavior the generation step had not accounted for when the question implies zero is a valid value. Of 15 minimum-count questions tested, 9 exhibited this exclusion.

RESOLUTION
Minimum-count questions on a joined count now use an outer join so zero-count parents are included and correctly identified as the minimum where applicable.

VALIDATION
The nine affected question types returned correct zero-inclusive results in retesting, and maximum-count questions, which are unaffected by the same issue, remained correct throughout.

column1: Multi-object questions work for two related objects but not three
column2:
CONTEXT
Some questions require joining across three related objects, such as products within orders within accounts of a given type.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two-object questions generate correctly, while three-object questions frequently produce an invalid or incomplete query.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should handle a reasonable chain of relationships needed to answer a legitimate business question.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Three-object questions succeed roughly half the time, often generating a query missing one required join.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The generation prompt's schema examples covered two-object relationships extensively but included only one three-object example, giving the model too little pattern to generalize from. Of 30 three-object questions tested, 16 failed to generate a valid query on the first attempt.

RESOLUTION
Additional three-object worked examples were added to the prompt covering the most common relationship chains. This is partial: success rose to 24 of 30, with the remaining failures concentrated in chains involving a polymorphic relationship the added examples did not cover.

VALIDATION
Twenty-four of thirty three-object questions generated valid queries matching manual equivalents, and two-object question accuracy was confirmed unaffected by the added examples.

column1: A required aggregation is unsupported in the query dialect, computed client-side instead
column2:
CONTEXT
Some questions ask for a weighted average that the query dialect has no direct function for.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Weighted average questions consistently fail to generate a valid query, since no combination of supported functions expresses the calculation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should still be able to answer a weighted average question where the underlying data supports it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Generation attempts repeatedly produce invalid statements approximating the calculation, none of which the dialect accepts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dialect genuinely lacks a weighted average function or an equivalent combination of supported constructs, confirmed against its documentation. These questions represent a small but recurring share of requests, mostly from the pricing team.

RESOLUTION
For this question pattern, the assistant now retrieves the raw component values with a simpler query and computes the weighted average in the application layer before answering. This is a workaround: it applies only to this recognized pattern, and a similarly unsupported calculation phrased differently would not benefit from the same handling.

VALIDATION
Twelve weighted average questions returned correct results matching manual spreadsheet calculations, and the fallback was confirmed not to trigger for unrelated questions.

column1: Long-running questions against a large object are capped with a documented sampling note
column2:
CONTEXT
Questions against the largest transactional object occasionally require scanning volumes the query engine cannot complete within timeout.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
These questions fail outright with a timeout error and no partial answer, especially for broad date ranges.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Users should get a useful answer even when a fully precise calculation is not feasible in time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query times out and the user receives an error with no figure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Restructuring the object for faster aggregation was out of scope for the assistant team and would require a data platform change with no near-term timeline. Roughly 4 percent of questions against this object timed out.

RESOLUTION
Detected broad questions against this object now query a recent sample and extrapolate, with the answer stating clearly it is an estimate rather than an exact count. This is a workaround: estimated figures carry a margin of error exact answers elsewhere do not.

VALIDATION
Twenty sampled estimates were compared against overnight exact batch calculations and stayed within an agreed margin in all twenty cases, and the estimate disclosure was confirmed visible in every affected answer.

column1: The assistant occasionally answers a completely different question than the one asked
column2:
CONTEXT
Each question is classified for intent before a query is generated against the matched intent.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of times a week, the answer clearly addresses a different question than the one typed, with no apparent relationship between the two.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The generated answer should always correspond to the question asked.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Logged cases show the correct question text captured, but the answer and its underlying query match an unrelated question pattern.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mismatched answers do not correspond to anything the same user asked previously in their session, ruling out session state carrying over. Comparing five captured incidents against the full question log found no other user asking the mismatched question in the same narrow window.

RESOLUTION
No mechanism has been identified for how the wrong intent gets attached to a question, and no change has been made without a working theory.

VALIDATION
Incidents occur roughly four times a week and are reported by users as clearly wrong. The next step is logging the full model request and response payload for the classification step, since currently only the final answer is retained.

column1: Identical questions asked back to back sometimes produce different generated queries
column2:
CONTEXT
The same question is sometimes asked twice in quick succession by a user checking a figure.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A minority of repeated questions produce a differently structured query the second time, sometimes with a different answer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An identical question against unchanged data should produce the same query and answer every time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The second query is logically similar but structured differently, and sometimes evaluates a slightly different scope, producing a different figure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Generation is expected to carry some variability by design, but the team had assumed this would not affect the numeric answer. Testing 50 identical repeated questions found 6 producing a different query structure, and 2 of those a materially different figure.

RESOLUTION
Reducing variability further has not been attempted, since it may trade off the flexibility that lets the assistant handle varied phrasing well, and the team has not agreed how much determinism to require.

VALIDATION
The 2-in-50 materially different figure rate persists. The next step is testing a lower variability setting against a broader question set to measure whether it removes discrepancies without harming answer quality on varied phrasing.

column1: Migrated phone numbers lose their country code for one source region
column2:
CONTEXT
Contact phone numbers migrated from four regional legacy systems into a single Salesforce phone field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Numbers from one region cannot be dialed correctly because the country code was dropped during migration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated number should retain enough information to be dialed correctly regardless of source region.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Numbers from the affected region were stored in the legacy system without a country code, relying on an implicit regional default that did not carry over.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The other three regions' legacy systems stored the country code explicitly, so the migration mapping had never needed to add one, and the gap was missed until dialing tests were performed post-migration. All 60,000 numbers from the affected region lacked a code.

RESOLUTION
The migration was rerun for that region with the country code prefixed based on the known source system, and a validation now checks every migrated phone number can be parsed as a complete international number.

VALIDATION
A sample of 300 corrected numbers dialed successfully in testing, the validation caught a deliberately malformed test number, and the remaining regions were confirmed unaffected by the correction.

column1: Migrated task records point at contacts through a field the object no longer uses
column2:
CONTEXT
Legacy activity history was migrated into standard task records linked to contacts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Migrated tasks do not appear on the contact's activity timeline even though the task record references the correct contact.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A task linked to a contact should appear in that contact's activity history.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The migration populated a generic relationship field rather than the specific field the activity timeline component reads from.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The task object offers more than one way to reference a related contact, and the timeline component only reads one of them. The migration mapping used the more generic field because it appeared first in the object's field list during mapping design. All 210,000 migrated tasks used the wrong field.

RESOLUTION
The 210,000 tasks were updated in a batch to populate the field the timeline reads from, keeping the original field populated as well for any other consumer relying on it.

VALIDATION
A sample of 500 contacts showed their migrated tasks now appearing correctly on the activity timeline, and the batch update completed with no errors across the full volume.

column1: Migrated case comments are attributed to the migration user instead of the original author
column2:
CONTEXT
Historical case comments were migrated as new comment records created by the migration process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every migrated comment shows the migration service account as its author, losing the record of which agent actually wrote it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A migrated comment should show its original author for accountability and audit purposes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The comment object records the creating user automatically, which during migration was always the service account performing the load.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The comment object does not allow the created-by field to be set explicitly during a standard load, a platform constraint discovered during migration design but not resolved before go-live. The original author existed in the source data for all 1.4 million migrated comments.

RESOLUTION
The original author's name was preserved in a dedicated text field displayed alongside each comment, and a data load technique using a temporary elevated permission restored the correct created-by value for the comments where the platform allowed it.

VALIDATION
A sample of 800 comments showed correct original authorship displayed, and the technique's coverage was confirmed against source records with no comment left unattributed.

column1: Migrated opportunities carry a stage history that does not match their current stage
column2:
CONTEXT
Opportunity stage history was migrated separately from the opportunity records themselves, sourced from a different legacy table.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some migrated opportunities show a stage history that never reaches their current stage as the final entry.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An opportunity's stage history should end with an entry matching its current stage.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The two source tables were extracted at different times during the migration window, so a small number of opportunities changed stage in the source system between the two extracts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extract timing gap was eleven hours, during which normal source system activity continued. Comparing extracted opportunities found 340 with a mismatch, all involving a stage change during that specific window.

RESOLUTION
The 340 opportunities had their stage history reconciled against the source system's live data, and future extracts for related migrations are now required to run from a single consistent snapshot rather than separate windows.

VALIDATION
The 340 opportunities showed consistent stage history ending at their current stage after reconciliation, and a full comparison across all migrated opportunities found no further mismatches.

column1: Migrated file attachments lose their original creation date, showing the migration date instead
column2:
CONTEXT
Documents attached to legacy records were migrated as Salesforce files linked to their corresponding records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users sorting a record's files by date see every migrated file dated the day of migration, rather than when it was originally uploaded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A migrated file should show its original upload date to preserve a meaningful chronological order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The file's creation date is set automatically to the moment the file is loaded, and standard loading does not allow overriding it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The original date existed in the source system's metadata for all 340,000 migrated files but had not been mapped anywhere in the target, since the team had not realized the creation date could not be overridden.

RESOLUTION
The original date was preserved in a custom field on the file's related record, and a related list sorted by that field gives users the chronological view they need, alongside the platform's own creation date for reference.

VALIDATION
A sample of 200 records showed files correctly ordered by original date using the new list, and users confirmed the chronological view met their needs for document review.

column1: A currency conversion rounding rule differs between the legacy and target systems for zero-decimal currencies
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated deal values in currencies without a fractional unit were converted using the target system's currency configuration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of migrated deal totals differ from the legacy system's own recorded figure by one unit.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migrated totals should match the legacy system's figures exactly for currencies already at zero decimal places.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The migration rounded using a general half-up rule while the legacy system used banker's rounding, occasionally producing a one unit difference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two rounding conventions only disagree on values exactly at the midpoint between two whole units, which is rare but not negligible at scale. Of 90,000 zero-decimal currency deals, 340 showed a one unit discrepancy, all at an exact midpoint value.

RESOLUTION
The migration's rounding was changed to match the legacy system's banker's rounding convention for this currency class, and the 340 discrepant records were corrected.

VALIDATION
The 340 corrected records matched the legacy figures exactly, a reprocessed sample of 5,000 zero-decimal deals showed no further discrepancies, and finance confirmed the totals reconciled.

column1: Historical email correspondence migrated for cases but not for the related opportunities
column2:
CONTEXT
Historical customer correspondence exists in the legacy system attached to both service cases and sales opportunities.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales users cannot see historical correspondence on migrated opportunities, though service agents see it correctly on cases.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Correspondence should be available on whichever record type it was originally associated with.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only the case-linked correspondence was included in the migration's original scope, since initial requirement gathering focused on the service team.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The opportunity-linked correspondence exists in the same source format as the case-linked correspondence already migrated successfully, so the same extraction approach applies. It was not identified as in scope until sales raised the gap after go-live, covering an estimated 90,000 messages.

RESOLUTION
A second migration wave using the proven case-linked approach is loading this correspondence, with 40,000 of the estimated 90,000 messages completed. This is partial: the remaining volume is scheduled, and messages linked to since-deleted opportunities are logged rather than migrated.

VALIDATION
The 40,000 completed messages matched source content and threading in a 200-message sample, and the remaining volume is tracked weekly against the source count.

column1: Data type conversion succeeds for numeric fields but not for one legacy multi-select field
column2:
CONTEXT
A legacy field storing several selected options as a delimited text string needed to migrate into a multi-select picklist.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Most records converted correctly, but a subset show garbled or partial values in the new field.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every combination of selected options in the source should convert to the equivalent set of target values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records whose source string used an unexpected delimiter or a value not in the target picklist's defined set converted incorrectly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The source field had accumulated several delimiter conventions over years of manual entry, and free-text values never formally added as picklist options. Of 22,000 records, 1,800 showed a conversion problem, split between delimiter inconsistency and unmapped values.

RESOLUTION
Delimiter handling was broadened to cover the additional conventions found, correcting most affected records. This is partial: 260 records contain values with no defined equivalent in the target picklist, flagged for a business decision on whether to add new options or discard them.

VALIDATION
1,540 of the 1,800 affected records converted correctly after the fix, verified against source strings, and the remaining 260 are logged for the pending decision.

column1: A legacy numbering scheme cannot be replicated, so a cross-reference table bridges old and new identifiers
column2:
CONTEXT
Customers and partners are used to referencing accounts by a legacy sequential number printed on years of paperwork.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Salesforce record identifiers bear no resemblance to the legacy numbers, and staff struggle to locate accounts when a customer quotes theirs.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Staff should be able to locate a migrated account using the number a customer knows.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Searching by the legacy number returns nothing, since it was not carried into a searchable field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Replicating the legacy scheme as the platform's primary identifier is not supported, and generating new numbers in that sequence would conflict with the legacy system, still in limited use elsewhere. The legacy number exists for all 210,000 migrated accounts.

RESOLUTION
The legacy number was added as a searchable custom field, populated for all 210,000 records, with new accounts left blank since they never had one. This is a workaround: two identifier schemes coexist, and staff must know to search the custom field.

VALIDATION
A sample of 100 legacy numbers returned the correct account through the new field, and a support survey confirmed lookup time for legacy-numbered accounts improved substantially.

column1: A small number of migrated records show a modification timestamp earlier than their creation timestamp
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated records carry both a creation and a last modified timestamp set from source values during the load.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An audit found around 200 records across several objects where the last modified timestamp predates the creation timestamp, which should not be possible.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record's last modified timestamp should never precede its creation timestamp.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Both timestamps were set from source fields during the same load, and for these records those two source values are themselves in the wrong order.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Checking the source system for ten sampled records found the same inverted order at the source, ruling out an error introduced during migration. The source team could not explain how their fields came to be inverted, some dating back over a decade.

RESOLUTION
Since the anomaly originates in the source data rather than migration, no migration-side fix has been applied, and the question has been referred to the source team.

VALIDATION
The 200 affected records remain as migrated, faithfully reflecting the source. The next step is awaiting the source team's investigation, before deciding whether a corrective data patch in Salesforce is appropriate.

column1: Two overlapping entry conditions cause a scheduled path to fire twice for the same case
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow on the case object has two scheduled paths, one for a 24-hour reminder and one for a 48-hour escalation, both built from the same base entry criteria.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some cases receive the 24-hour reminder twice, a day apart, instead of once.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each scheduled path should fire exactly once per qualifying record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A case that is edited after the reminder's scheduled time re-enters the same scheduled path a second time.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scheduled path re-evaluates its entry criteria on every record update rather than only at creation, so any edit within the window re-queues the reminder. Twenty-six cases in a month received the reminder twice, all edited by an agent between the two sends.

RESOLUTION
The scheduled path now checks a reminder-sent flag before queuing, set once the first reminder fires, so a later edit cannot re-queue it.

VALIDATION
Editing a case after its reminder fired no longer queued a second send in twenty test cases, and the twenty-six historical duplicates were confirmed as the only affected records.

column1: A flow reads a roll-up total before it has finished recalculating in the same transaction
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow on the opportunity object reads a roll-up summary field counting related line items immediately after a line item is added by the same transaction.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The flow occasionally acts on a count that is one lower than the actual number of lines just added.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should see the roll-up value fully recalculated before evaluating it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The roll-up has not yet recalculated when the flow reads it, since roll-up recalculation happens after the triggering DML in the same transaction completes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow ran on the same object as the line item insert rather than the parent, evaluating the roll-up before the platform's recalculation step. Twelve orders in a month were flagged as under-threshold when they should have qualified.

RESOLUTION
The flow was moved to a separate after-save context on the parent object, running once the roll-up has recalculated, and the twelve affected orders were reprocessed.

VALIDATION
Fifty test orders showed the flow reading the correct recalculated total in every case, and the twelve historical orders reprocessed correctly.

column1: A flow assignment overwrites a field an agent edited seconds earlier
column2:
CONTEXT
A background flow recalculates a customer tier field every time certain account fields change, running asynchronously after save.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An agent's manual correction to the tier field is sometimes overwritten moments later with no visible cause.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A manual edit should not be silently reverted by an unrelated automated recalculation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow queued by an earlier save runs after the agent's edit and writes its own calculated value over it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The flow was queued by a save that happened just before the agent's manual edit, and asynchronous processing meant it executed after the edit rather than before it. Field history on nine affected accounts showed the pattern precisely: agent edit, followed within a minute by the flow's overwrite.

RESOLUTION
The flow now checks whether the tier field changed since it was queued and skips the write if a newer edit exists, logging the skip for review.

VALIDATION
A simulated race between a manual edit and a queued flow run left the manual edit intact in ten tests, and the nine historical accounts were corrected and confirmed stable.

column1: A decision element treats a blank discount the same as a zero discount
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow on the quote line object applies a bulk-order price break only when the discount field is exactly zero, meaning no discount has been manually applied yet.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Lines where the discount field was never populated are treated as ineligible, the same as lines explicitly set to a nonzero value.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An untouched, blank discount field should be treated as eligible for the price break, distinct from a field explicitly set to a nonzero value.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The decision element's equals-zero comparison evaluates false for a blank field, so blank and nonzero are both excluded.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Numeric comparisons in the flow do not treat blank as zero, a distinction the flow's author had not accounted for. Reviewing 300 quote lines found 84 blank lines incorrectly excluded from the price break.

RESOLUTION
The condition now explicitly checks for blank or zero, and the 84 affected lines were recalculated with the price break applied.

VALIDATION
Blank, zero, and nonzero discount lines all routed correctly in 30 test cases, and the 84 corrected lines matched a manual recalculation.

column1: A broadly granted bypass permission stops automation firing for an entire team
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom permission lets a small data operations team bypass certain flows during bulk corrections, assigned through a dedicated permission set.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An entire regional sales team stopped triggering lead assignment automation, with new leads left unrouted.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only the data operations team should bypass the automation; everyone else should trigger it normally.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The bypass permission set was included in a bundled permission set group assigned to the regional team during an unrelated access update.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The bundling was done to simplify a separate access request and nobody reviewed which individual permission sets it pulled in. Forty regional users held the bypass permission, and 210 leads over a week went unrouted.

RESOLUTION
The bypass permission was removed from the bundle, a dedicated permission set now exists solely for that purpose, and the 210 unrouted leads were reassigned.

VALIDATION
The forty regional users triggered lead assignment correctly in testing after the change, and the 210 backlog leads were confirmed routed to the right owners.

column1: A flow's decimal formatting works for period-based locales but not comma-based ones
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow builds a formatted price string for a customer-facing quote message, inserting a numeric value into a text template.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Quotes sent to customers in comma-decimal locales show a price with the wrong decimal placement.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The formatted price should respect the recipient's locale decimal convention.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow always formats using a period as the decimal separator regardless of the account's locale.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The formatting was hardcoded when the flow was built for a single-locale pilot and never generalized. Of five supported locales, two use a comma decimal separator, affecting roughly 18 percent of quotes sent.

RESOLUTION
The flow now selects a formatting pattern based on the account's locale field. This is partial: two of the five locales are covered so far, with the remaining three scheduled once their exact formatting conventions are confirmed with the regional teams.

VALIDATION
The two corrected locales produced correctly formatted quotes in 20 test cases each, and the three pending locales continue to use the interim period-based format with a known limitation.

column1: Delegated approvers can view a request but the flow won't let them act on it
column2:
CONTEXT
An approval flow lets a delegated approver stand in for someone on leave, using the platform's built-in delegation feature.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Delegated approvers can open a pending request but the approve and reject buttons do nothing when they click them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A delegated approver should be able to approve or reject exactly as the original approver could.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow's action checks the running user against the named approver field directly, which does not recognize a delegate acting on someone else's behalf.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The approval logic was written before delegation was adopted by the business and never updated to check delegate relationships. Six requests over a month sat unresolved because the delegate could not act and the primary approver was unavailable.

RESOLUTION
The check now also accepts a currently active delegate for the named approver. This is partial: it covers person-level delegation only, not the queue-based delegation used by two smaller teams, which still requires a workaround.

VALIDATION
A delegate successfully approved a test request in five scenarios, and the six historical stuck requests were resolved manually pending the queue-based fix.

column1: A flow-based merge tool loses related activity history, so merges now go through a manual queue
column2:
CONTEXT
A screen flow lets data stewards merge duplicate contacts, moving related activities and cases to the surviving record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some merges completed through the flow left activities and cases still attached to the record that was deleted, orphaning them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every related record should move to the survivor before the loser is deleted.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow's relinking step and the deletion step are not transactional, so a mid-process failure can delete the loser before all relinking finishes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform does not support wrapping a multi-object relink and delete in a single guaranteed transaction within a screen flow. Four merges in two months lost related records this way, recovered from backup.

RESOLUTION
Merges above a threshold of related records now route to a manual queue reviewed by a steward before deletion, rather than running unattended. This is a workaround: larger merges are slower and depend on steward availability.

VALIDATION
Twelve queued merges completed with no orphaned records over a month, and the four historical losses were recovered and reattached.

column1: A flow occasionally pauses indefinitely waiting for a platform event that never arrives
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow uses a wait element to pause until a platform event confirms an external system has processed a request.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of paused interviews never resume, even though the external system's own records show the request was processed successfully.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The wait element should resume as soon as the matching platform event is published.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The interview stays paused indefinitely, with no error and no resumption, while the platform event appears to have been published based on external logs.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Platform event delivery to a paused interview cannot be traced from standard debug logs, and the six affected interviews show no correlation in size, timing, or the external system involved. Manually resuming a stuck interview with the same conditions completes normally.

RESOLUTION
No cause for the missed resumption has been identified, and the wait configuration has not been changed pending clearer evidence.

VALIDATION
Roughly two interviews a month are found stuck and resumed manually. The next step is enabling platform event delivery tracing for a stuck interview's exact identifier and comparing it against the publishing system's send log.

column1: Flow execution time creeps upward through the day with no clear driver
column2:
CONTEXT
A frequently run flow processes incoming service requests and is monitored for execution time as part of a performance dashboard.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Average execution time roughly doubles between the start and end of the business day, then resets overnight.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Execution time for a comparable request should stay roughly constant throughout the day.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Identical test requests submitted at different times of day show a steady increase in execution time as the day progresses.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Record volume in the queried objects does increase through the day but not enough to account for the doubling alone. Org-wide API and automation activity also rises through the day, though no specific contention point has been isolated.

RESOLUTION
No single contributing factor has been confirmed, so no change has been made to the flow itself.

VALIDATION
The daily doubling pattern has recurred for three consecutive weeks. The next step is capturing per-element timing within the flow at three points in the day to localize the slowdown.

column1: Multi-currency amounts sync without their currency code, distorting reported totals
column2:
CONTEXT
Order amounts are synced from a billing platform that operates in several currencies into a single amount field in Salesforce.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Orders placed in a foreign currency display and total as though they were in the org's default currency.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A synced amount should carry its original currency so it converts and totals correctly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration writes the numeric amount only, leaving the currency field at its default value.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping was built before the org enabled multiple currencies and was never revisited. Comparing 400 foreign-currency orders against the source showed every one stored under the default currency, overstating some totals by a wide margin.

RESOLUTION
The mapping now writes the source currency code alongside the amount, and the 400 affected orders were corrected using their original source values.

VALIDATION
The 400 corrected orders matched the source currency and amount exactly, and 50 new orders across four currencies synced correctly in testing.

column1: A retried create request produces a duplicate because its idempotency key changed on retry
column2:
CONTEXT
Middleware creates service tickets from a partner queue, using a key derived from the message to prevent duplicate creation on retry.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A retried message occasionally creates a second ticket instead of being recognized as a repeat.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A retried message should always resolve to its original ticket, never a new one.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The key included a processing timestamp that differs between the original attempt and the retry, so the two attempts are treated as distinct.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The key was intended to use only stable fields from the source message, but a timestamp field was included by mistake during an earlier revision. Eighteen duplicate tickets over a month all traced to a retried message with a differing timestamp in its derived key.

RESOLUTION
The key now derives from stable source fields only, excluding any processing-time value, and the eighteen duplicates were merged.

VALIDATION
A forced retry of the same message resolved to the original ticket in twenty tests, and the eighteen historical duplicates were confirmed merged with no data loss.

column1: Integration writes overwrite good values with blanks whenever the source omits a field
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration updates customer contact details from a partner system that sends only the fields that changed on their side.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Fields not present in a given update are cleared in Salesforce instead of being left untouched.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An update should only change the fields the source actually included.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration maps every target field regardless of whether the source payload included a value, so omitted fields are set to blank.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping was built assuming a full-record payload every time, which held during initial testing but not once the partner switched to a changed-fields-only format. Auditing 200 recent updates found 61 that blanked at least one previously populated field.

RESOLUTION
The mapping now writes only fields present in the incoming payload, leaving others unchanged, and the 61 affected records were restored from a retained history snapshot.

VALIDATION
A partial payload updating only one field left all other fields intact in ten tests, and the 61 restored records matched their pre-incident values.

column1: A new source picklist value breaks the integration mapping silently
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration maps a shipment status code from the logistics platform to a Salesforce picklist using a fixed lookup table.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Shipments arriving with a newly introduced status code fail to update, and the failure was not noticed for several weeks.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A new source status should either map cleanly or trigger a visible alert, not fail silently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping table has no entry for the new code, so the record update is rejected and logged only in a file nobody was monitoring.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The logistics platform added the new status without notifying the integration team, and error logging existed but had no active alerting attached. 640 shipments accumulated with a failed status update before discovery.

RESOLUTION
The new status was added to the mapping table, the 640 shipments were reprocessed, and mapping failures now trigger an alert to the integration team the same day.

VALIDATION
The 640 shipments updated correctly after reprocessing, and a deliberately unmapped test code produced the expected same-day alert.

column1: Unchanged files are re-uploaded on every sync run, creating growing duplicate attachments
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly integration attaches product specification documents from a supplier catalogue to their corresponding Salesforce product records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Product records accumulate several copies of the same unchanged document over time.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A document should be uploaded once and only replaced when its content actually changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration uploads every document on every run regardless of whether it has changed since the previous sync.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No check compared the incoming file against what was already attached, since the original scope assumed infrequent catalogue updates. Products reviewed after six months showed an average of 34 duplicate copies of the same specification document.

RESOLUTION
The integration now compares a content hash of the incoming file against the most recent attachment and skips the upload when they match, and duplicate copies were cleaned up in a batch pass.

VALIDATION
Ten consecutive nightly runs against unchanged documents produced no new duplicates, and a deliberately modified document was correctly re-uploaded and replaced.

column1: A cached authentication token keeps using rotated-out credentials until it expires
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration authenticates using a token cached for its full validity period to avoid requesting a new one on every call.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a scheduled credential rotation, some calls kept failing intermittently for almost an hour before stabilizing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Calls should authenticate successfully immediately after a credential rotation completes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration continued presenting a token issued under the old credential until its cached copy naturally expired.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rotation process revoked the old credential immediately but gave the integration no signal to refresh its cache early, so any cached token issued shortly before rotation remained in use until its normal expiry. Three scheduled rotations in the past quarter each produced a similar window of intermittent failures.

RESOLUTION
The integration now discards its cached token and requests a fresh one whenever it receives an authentication failure, rather than waiting for the cache to expire naturally.

VALIDATION
A test rotation produced authentication failures for under a minute before the integration recovered on its own, compared to nearly an hour previously.

column1: A tax ID field truncates longer identifiers from countries outside the original design
column2:
CONTEXT
A national tax identifier field syncs from the billing platform, sized originally for the format used in the home market.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Tax identifiers from several other countries are cut off partway through, since their format is longer than the field allows.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every supported country's tax identifier format should fit without truncation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field's maximum length matches the home market's format and silently truncates anything longer on save.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The field was sized during initial build for a single-market rollout, and no validation was added to catch an oversized value from a later market. Of six markets now live, three use a longer format and 190 accounts show a truncated identifier.

RESOLUTION
The field length was extended to accommodate the longest known format. This is partial: the 190 already-truncated identifiers cannot be reconstructed from Salesforce alone and require a re-pull from the source system, which is scheduled but not complete.

VALIDATION
New syncs for all six markets stored complete identifiers in testing, and 70 of the 190 truncated records have been corrected from source so far.

column1: Multi-currency refunds cannot be represented in the integration, handled through a manual adjustment
column2:
CONTEXT
Cancelled orders trigger a refund record synced to the finance system, calculated in the order's original currency.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Refunds for orders whose currency has since been retired from the finance system's active list fail to sync.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A refund should sync successfully regardless of whether its original currency remains active in finance.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The finance system rejects any refund referencing a currency it no longer accepts new transactions in.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Finance retires a currency from active use periodically for regulatory reasons, but historical orders remain in that currency indefinitely. Nine refunds in the past year hit this rejection, all for orders more than two years old.

RESOLUTION
Affected refunds are now converted to the group reporting currency at the rate in effect on the refund date and entered manually by finance. This is a workaround: the customer's original currency is not preserved in the finance record, only in Salesforce.

VALIDATION
The nine historical refunds were processed manually and reconciled, and the conversion procedure was documented for finance's ongoing use.

column1: A bulk cleanup filter matched more records than intended, contained by routing deletes through review
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled integration removes stale trial accounts from Salesforce based on a filter matching inactivity criteria from the source system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One run deleted 140 accounts that had recent activity, because the source system's inactivity flag had a data quality issue for a subset of accounts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only genuinely stale accounts should ever be deleted by the automated cleanup.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The filter trusted the source flag without a secondary check, and a source data error flagged active accounts as inactive.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
