Queries against the object from that specific external tool fail with a syntax error referencing the reserved word.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The object should be queryable from any connected external tool without a naming conflict.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The tool's parser treats the object's API name as its own reserved keyword rather than an object reference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Renaming the object's API name was assessed as high risk given how many existing integrations and reports reference it by that name. The external tool's vendor confirmed the reserved word is fixed and cannot be changed on their side.

RESOLUTION
Queries from that tool now wrap the object name in the tool's own escape syntax, documented for anyone building a report against it. This is a workaround: every new report built with that tool against this object must remember to apply the escape manually.

VALIDATION
Ten test queries using the escape syntax ran successfully, and the documentation was added to the team's integration reference guide.

column1: A small share of API calls show elevated latency with no identifiable correlation
column2:
CONTEXT
Most API calls from the primary integration platform complete within 300 milliseconds, monitored continuously as part of standard operations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Roughly one call in a thousand takes over five seconds to complete, with no apparent pattern connecting the affected calls.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Call latency should stay consistently low regardless of which endpoint, object, or time of day is involved.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The slow calls span different endpoints, different objects, and different times of day, with payload size showing no correlation either.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Network-level tracing on the calling side shows the request leaving promptly and the response simply arriving late, pointing toward the receiving platform rather than the network path. The platform's own published status has shown no incidents coinciding with the observed spikes.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been identified from the calling side's available diagnostics, and no timeout or retry behavior has been changed pending more information.

VALIDATION
The roughly one-in-a-thousand rate has held steady over a month. The next step is opening a vendor case with specific request identifiers and timestamps, since only the platform's own internal telemetry could show where the delay occurs.

column1: A question naming the status field resolves to the wrong object when two objects share that field name
column2:
CONTEXT
Both the case object and the order object have a field called status, and users ask status questions about either one by context alone.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question about order status sometimes generates a query against the case object's status field instead.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should resolve which object's status field is meant from the surrounding context of the question.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Field resolution matched on field name alone when the question's subject object was ambiguous, defaulting to whichever object appeared first in its internal schema list.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The case object happened to precede the order object in the schema list, so the case field won by default whenever the question's own wording did not clearly disambiguate. Of 30 order status questions tested, 11 resolved against the wrong object.

RESOLUTION
Field resolution now weighs the question's other mentioned entities and recent conversation context to disambiguate, rather than falling back on schema list order.

VALIDATION
The eleven previously misresolved questions returned correct order status results after the change, and case status questions remained correctly resolved throughout.

column1: A percentage-of-total question divides by the wrong denominator once a filter is applied
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask what percentage of cases in a category fall into a specific status, expecting the percentage scoped to that category.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When the question also specifies a region filter, the percentage is calculated against the company-wide total rather than the filtered regional total.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The denominator should reflect the same filtered scope as the numerator, whatever filters the question specifies.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The denominator query was generated without carrying forward the region filter applied to the numerator query.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two queries, numerator and denominator, are generated somewhat independently, and the filter-carrying logic had only been tested for the unfiltered case. Of 20 filtered percentage questions, all 20 showed a denominator missing the filter.

RESOLUTION
The denominator query generation now explicitly inherits every filter present on the numerator query, keeping the two consistently scoped.

VALIDATION
Twenty filtered percentage questions returned correctly scoped results matching manual calculations, and unfiltered percentage questions remained correct as before.

column1: A question about last quarter resolves incorrectly near the fiscal year boundary
column2:
CONTEXT
The organization's fiscal year starts in April, and quarter-relative questions should resolve according to that fiscal calendar.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions about last quarter asked during the first weeks of a new fiscal year returned figures for the wrong quarter.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Last quarter should always resolve to the fiscal quarter immediately preceding the current one, calendar year notwithstanding.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The resolution logic correctly used the fiscal calendar within a fiscal year but mishandled the wraparound at the fiscal year boundary, resolving to the wrong calendar year's quarter.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The wraparound case was not included in the original test scenarios, since it only manifests during a narrow window each year. All 15 questions asked during the first three weeks of the new fiscal year in the affected window resolved incorrectly.

RESOLUTION
The resolution logic was corrected to handle the fiscal year wraparound explicitly, tested specifically against the boundary window.

VALIDATION
Fifteen boundary-window questions resolved correctly after the fix, and quarter resolution elsewhere in the fiscal year was confirmed unaffected.

column1: A follow-up question in the same conversation loses the filter from the question before it
column2:
CONTEXT
Users often ask a filtered question and then a natural follow-up that implicitly assumes the same filter still applies.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Follow-up questions sometimes return company-wide figures instead of continuing to respect the filter from the prior question in the same conversation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A follow-up question that does not explicitly change or remove the filter should inherit it from the preceding question.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Filter inheritance worked reliably for a direct one-step follow-up but was lost after two or more follow-ups in the same conversation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Filter context was carried forward from only the immediately preceding turn rather than the full conversation state, so it silently dropped after the second follow-up. Of 25 multi-step conversations tested, 9 lost the filter by the third question.

RESOLUTION
Filter context is now maintained across the full conversation state rather than a single prior turn, persisting until the user explicitly changes or clears it.

VALIDATION
The nine previously affected conversations retained the correct filter through a third and fourth follow-up question in retesting.

column1: A short customer name in a question matches unrelated records due to overly loose fuzzy matching
column2:
CONTEXT
Named entity resolution uses fuzzy matching to tolerate minor misspellings when a user types a customer name in their question.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Questions naming a short customer name return records for several unrelated customers whose names happen to be similarly short.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A short, exact customer name should resolve precisely, with fuzzy tolerance reserved for genuinely close misspellings.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The fuzzy matching threshold applies uniformly regardless of name length, so a three-letter name has a wide field of coincidentally similar matches.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The threshold was tuned against typical longer customer names, where the same tolerance rarely produces false matches, without separately validating short names. Of 20 short-name questions tested, 13 returned at least one unrelated match.

RESOLUTION
The fuzzy matching threshold now scales with name length, tightening for shorter names so an exact short name resolves precisely while still tolerating minor typos.

VALIDATION
The thirteen previously affected short-name questions resolved to only the intended customer after the change, and longer-name fuzzy matching was confirmed unaffected.
column6: Fuzzy Match Threshold For Short Names

column1: Percentage figures display as a raw decimal instead of a formatted percent for one object
column2:
CONTEXT
Answers involving a percentage should format the figure with a percent sign and appropriate rounding, applied consistently across objects.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Percentage answers about the newer partner performance object display as a raw decimal like 0.42 instead of 42 percent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every percentage-type field, regardless of which object it belongs to, should format consistently as a percent in the answer.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formatting step recognizes percentage fields by a naming convention that the newer object's fields do not follow.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The naming convention check was written against the original object set and never updated when the partner performance object was added with a different field naming pattern. Six fields on the new object were affected.

RESOLUTION
Percentage field recognition now also checks the field's declared type rather than relying on naming convention alone, correctly catching the six affected fields. This is partial: two related rollup fields still rely on the older naming check and remain unformatted, pending a small rework.

VALIDATION
The six corrected fields displayed as properly formatted percentages in testing, and the two remaining fields are tracked for the pending rework.

column1: A ranking question needing window functions is answered through a documented multi-step pattern instead
column2:
CONTEXT
Users occasionally ask for a ranking within groups, such as the top deal per region, which naturally maps to a window function in standard SQL.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The query dialect has no window function support, so these questions consistently failed to generate a valid query.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should still answer a within-group ranking question using constructs the dialect actually supports.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Generation attempts produced statements using window function syntax that the dialect rejects outright every time.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dialect's documentation confirmed window functions are not supported and are not planned. A two-step pattern, retrieving per-group maximums separately and then joining back to identify the matching record, was tested and found to answer the same question correctly.

RESOLUTION
Within-group ranking questions now trigger the two-step pattern automatically rather than attempting a single unsupported query. This is a workaround: the pattern is limited to top-one-per-group questions and does not generalize to arbitrary rank cutoffs like top three per group.

VALIDATION
Fifteen top-one-per-group questions returned correct results matching manual queries, and a top-three variant was correctly identified as still unsupported with an explanation given.

column1: A grouping combined with a having-style filter isn't directly expressible, answered with a two-step query
column2:
CONTEXT
Users ask questions like which regions have more than five open escalations, combining a grouping with a filter on the aggregated result.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The query dialect's aggregate filter support does not cover this exact combination, so these questions failed to generate a valid query.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should still answer a grouped-and-filtered aggregate question through some valid combination of supported constructs.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Single-query generation attempts consistently produced syntax the dialect does not accept for this specific combination.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dialect supports aggregate filtering only in a narrower form than this pattern requires, confirmed against documentation. A two-step approach, computing the full grouped aggregate first and filtering results in the application layer, answered the same questions correctly.

RESOLUTION
This question pattern now automatically triggers the two-step approach rather than a single failing query attempt. This is a workaround: it adds a small latency cost compared to a single-query answer and is limited to patterns the team has explicitly recognized.

VALIDATION
Ten grouped-and-filtered questions returned correct results matching manual calculations, and an unrecognized variant of the pattern was correctly identified as still unsupported.

column1: The assistant occasionally returns a correct query result with a narrative explanation that doesn't match it
column2:
CONTEXT
Each answer pairs the queried figures with a short narrative sentence summarizing what was found, generated from the same data.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of answers each week show a figure that is verifiably correct alongside a narrative describing something different from that figure.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The narrative should always accurately describe the figure it accompanies.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The figure and its query are correct in every reviewed case, but the narrative text references a different number, trend, or comparison than what was queried.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The narrative generation step receives the same query result as input, ruling out a data-passing error, and the mismatched narratives follow no obvious pattern in question type or complexity. Six captured examples show no shared characteristic beyond the mismatch itself.

RESOLUTION
No cause for the narrative diverging from its input data has been identified, and the generation prompt has not been changed without a working theory.

VALIDATION
The mismatch continues at roughly six times a week. The next step is comparing model input and output for a captured mismatch side by side, since currently only the final rendered answer is retained.

column1: A rare session handling issue showed one user's prior question context to a different user
column2:
CONTEXT
Each user's conversation history is meant to be isolated to their own authenticated session for privacy and answer accuracy.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One user reported seeing a reference to a question they had never asked, matching one a different user had asked minutes earlier on a shared kiosk browser.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Conversation context should never be visible to or influence a different authenticated user's session.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected session showed the assistant referencing the other user's prior question as part of the same conversation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both sessions were terminated immediately and the security team was engaged given the potential data exposure. Session identifiers for the two users were confirmed distinct in server logs, which does not explain how context crossed between them. No further occurrence has been reproduced under deliberate testing.

RESOLUTION
The mechanism for the crossing has not been identified, and the security team's review remains open pending reproduction.

VALIDATION
No recurrence has been observed in two weeks. The next step is instrumenting session-to-context binding with logging to catch the next occurrence in detail, since current logs did not capture enough to explain this one.

column1: Migrated category names were silently truncated by a picklist value length limit
column2:
CONTEXT
Product category names were migrated from a legacy catalogue that allowed longer free-text category values than a standard picklist supports.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some migrated categories appear cut off mid-word, with no error raised during the load.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated category should either fit the picklist value limit intact or be flagged for review rather than silently truncated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The load truncated any category name exceeding the picklist's character limit and inserted the shortened value without complaint.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The source categories were not checked against the target picklist's length limit before the load, since the limit had not been reviewed against the actual source data range. Of 1,100 migrated categories, 47 exceeded the limit and were truncated.

RESOLUTION
The 47 truncated categories were corrected using an abbreviated but complete naming convention agreed with the catalogue owners, and the load procedure now flags any value exceeding the target limit before committing it.

VALIDATION
The 47 corrected categories displayed completely and accurately, and a deliberately oversized test value was flagged rather than silently truncated.

column1: A migrated lookup pointed at the wrong record because a legacy identifier had been reused
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrated case records link to their originating contact using the legacy system's contact identifier, mapped to the corresponding migrated contact.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A number of migrated cases link to a contact that has nothing to do with the original case.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated case should link to the same contact it was associated with in the legacy system.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Some legacy identifiers had been reused for a different contact after the original was deleted years earlier in the source system, and the mapping matched on the identifier alone.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The legacy system reused deleted identifiers after a retention period, a behavior not documented anywhere the migration team had reviewed. Cross-checking mapped links against a secondary field, the contact's original creation date, found 210 cases linked to a reused identifier's newer contact.

RESOLUTION
The 210 affected cases were relinked using an archived legacy export that preserved the original contact association before the identifier was reused.

VALIDATION
The 210 relinked cases were confirmed against the archived export, and a spot check of 500 unaffected cases found no other reused-identifier mismatches.

column1: Migrated email addresses failed validation due to a source export formatting quirk missed in testing
column2:
CONTEXT
Contact email addresses were exported from the legacy system as part of the standard migration extract, validated on load against Salesforce's email format check.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of otherwise valid email addresses failed the load's validation and were rejected rather than migrated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Genuinely valid email addresses from the source should pass validation and migrate successfully.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The source export wrapped every email address in a pair of invisible formatting characters used internally by the legacy export tool, which the test data set used for migration rehearsal happened not to contain.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rehearsal data was pulled through a different export path than the full production extract, which is why the formatting quirk was not caught earlier. The full extract showed 1,900 addresses carrying the invisible characters.

RESOLUTION
The load procedure now strips the specific invisible characters before validation, and the 1,900 affected addresses were reprocessed and migrated successfully.

VALIDATION
The 1,900 reprocessed addresses passed validation and matched their source values once the invisible characters were stripped, confirmed against a visual diff of a sample.

column1: A batch job's resume logic skipped a range of records after an interrupted run
column2:
CONTEXT
A large migration batch job processes records in ordered chunks, recording a checkpoint after each chunk so an interrupted run can resume rather than restart.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One interrupted run resumed successfully but skipped roughly 900 records never processed by either the original run or the resume.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A resumed run should process every record not confirmed complete by the last checkpoint, no gap.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The checkpoint recorded the chunk as started rather than completed, and the resume logic treated a started chunk as already done, skipping it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The checkpoint was written at the start of chunk processing rather than after successful completion, a timing choice that worked as long as interruptions stayed rare enough not to be noticed until this run. The gap was found by comparing processed count against expected total.

RESOLUTION
The checkpoint now records completion rather than start, and the 900 skipped records were identified by comparison against source and processed in a follow-up run.

VALIDATION
The follow-up run processed all 900 records successfully, and a deliberately interrupted test run resumed with no gap using the corrected logic.

column1: Migrated records lost their locale flag, causing later automation to apply the wrong formatting
column2:
CONTEXT
Customer records carry a locale flag that downstream automation uses to format dates and currency correctly in outbound communications.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Migrated customers received communications formatted in the default locale rather than their own, regardless of their original locale setting.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated customer should retain their original locale so downstream formatting applies correctly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The locale field was present in the source data but was not included in the migration's field mapping, leaving it at the target system's default for every migrated record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The locale field was overlooked during mapping design because it was not considered business-critical data at the time, with its downstream formatting impact only surfacing once customer communications went out. All 60,000 migrated customers carried the default locale rather than their own.

RESOLUTION
The locale field was backfilled from the retained source export for all 60,000 customers, and the mapping gap was closed for any future incremental migration from the same source.

VALIDATION
A sample of 300 backfilled records showed correct locale-specific formatting in test communications, and the full backfill was confirmed complete against the source count.

column1: Only the latest file version carried over, losing prior version history from the source
column2:
CONTEXT
Documents with multiple revisions in the legacy system were migrated as Salesforce files, expected to preserve their version history.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users reviewing a migrated document's version history see only the single latest version, with earlier revisions missing entirely.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every prior version of a migrated document should be available in its version history, not just the latest.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The migration extracted and loaded only the current version of each document, since the source export was configured to pull latest versions by default.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Version history was assumed out of scope during initial planning because most documents had only one version, but 3,100 documents in the source had two or more revisions that mattered for audit purposes. The earlier versions still exist in a source archive not yet decommissioned.

RESOLUTION
The 3,100 multi-version documents are being re-extracted from the source archive with their full version history and reloaded using the platform's version upload capability.

VALIDATION
A sample of 200 re-loaded documents showed complete version history matching the source archive, with version order and content confirmed correct.

column1: Migration for one object stalled at roughly 80 percent due to unexpectedly deep related record volume
column2:
CONTEXT
Migrating service agreements includes loading related usage history, estimated during planning based on a sample of typical accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The migration for this object stalled around 80 percent, with the remaining agreements timing out during load.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All service agreements, regardless of related record volume, should complete migration within the load window.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The remaining 20 percent belong to a small number of long-standing enterprise accounts whose usage history volume is an order of magnitude larger than typical.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The original sample used to estimate load time and batch sizing did not include these long-standing accounts, since they were a small fraction of the account count despite carrying a large fraction of the total data volume.

RESOLUTION
A separate, smaller-batch load process is being built for the high-volume accounts, distinct from the standard process used for the completed 80 percent. This is partial: the new process is in testing against one pilot account before wider rollout.

VALIDATION
The pilot account's usage history loaded successfully using the new process within an extended but acceptable window, and remaining accounts are scheduled once stable.

column1: The planned cutover freeze window is too short for the full data volume, addressed with a phased batch strategy
column2:
CONTEXT
The cutover plan allows a single weekend freeze window during which no source changes occur while the final migration batch runs.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A revised estimate shows the full final batch would not complete within the freeze window, risking an incomplete migration or an extended freeze beyond what the business can tolerate.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The full data volume should migrate within a freeze window the business accepts.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The original freeze window was sized against an earlier, lower estimate that has since grown as more data was profiled.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Profiling the full source system rather than a sample revealed roughly 40 percent more volume than estimated, mostly historical records not previously counted. Running the full batch at current speed would exceed the window by several hours.

RESOLUTION
A phased strategy now migrates lower-priority historical data ahead of the freeze window, leaving only current records for the freeze. This is partial: the approach is being rehearsed, one rehearsal done and a second scheduled.

VALIDATION
The first rehearsal completed the freeze-window batch within the allotted time using the phased approach, and a second rehearsal will confirm consistency.

column1: A required uniqueness constraint conflicts with legacy duplicate data, resolved through a manual dedup queue
column2:
CONTEXT
The target object enforces a uniqueness constraint on a customer reference number, unenforced in the legacy system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of legacy records share a reference number that should have been unique, and the migration load rejects every record after the first with that number.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All genuine legacy records should migrate, with any true duplicates resolved deliberately rather than silently dropped by a rejected load.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The load simply fails each conflicting record, requiring someone to determine which of the colliding records is genuine before it can load.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Legacy data quality issues over many years produced 380 reference numbers each shared by two or more records, with no automatic way to determine which is authoritative without human judgment.

RESOLUTION
Conflicting records now route to a manual dedup queue where a steward assigns a corrected unique reference before the record loads. This is a workaround: it depends on steward throughput, and the queue currently processes roughly 40 records a day.

VALIDATION
The first 200 queued records were resolved and loaded successfully with steward-assigned references, and no data was lost in the process.

column1: Record counts match after migration but a content hash mismatch appears for an unexplained subset
column2:
CONTEXT
Post-migration validation compares a content hash of each migrated record against a hash computed from the source, alongside a record count check.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Record counts match exactly, but roughly 600 records show a content hash mismatch, meaning some field value differs from source despite the record existing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated record's content hash should match its source hash when no legitimate transformation was intended for that field.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Manually comparing several mismatched records field by field against source has not revealed a visible difference in any field checked.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mismatched records share no common object, batch, or load time, and field comparison for ten sampled records found every visible field identical to source, suggesting the difference is in encoding or whitespace not visible on screen.

RESOLUTION
No specific field or cause has been identified, and records have not been altered without knowing what to correct.

VALIDATION
The 600-record mismatch count has remained stable across two reruns. The next step is a byte-level comparison of raw field values for a sampled record, to catch a non-visible difference like encoding or trailing whitespace.

column1: A flow-triggered email alert fires before a validation rule blocks the same save, sending notifications for edits that never actually commit
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow on the case object sends an email alert to the assigned agent whenever the status field changes, running in a before-save context ahead of a validation rule that can still block the same update.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents receive status-change emails for edits that a validation rule subsequently rejects, so the case's status never actually changes despite the notification.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Notifications should only be sent for updates that successfully save.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow evaluates and sends its alert before the validation rule runs, so a rejected save still triggers a misleading email.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The alert flow was built to run before the record saves for performance reasons, without accounting for the validation rule on the same field. Review of a week's mail log found forty emails referencing status changes that were never applied.

RESOLUTION
The alert flow was rebuilt to run in an after-save context, so a blocked update can no longer queue a notification.

VALIDATION
Ten edits designed to trigger the validation rule produced zero alert emails, while ten valid edits produced exactly one alert each.

column1: A flow's fault path retries the same failed DML operation instead of logging and stopping, causing a runaway loop under one error condition
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow updates a related billing record and includes a fault path meant to log any DML failure for manual follow-up.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When the billing update fails due to a locked record, the fault path re-attempts the same update instead of logging the failure once.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A failed DML operation should be logged a single time and the flow interview should end.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The fault path called the same subflow that performed the original update, so a lock error repeated the update attempt until the transaction timed out.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The fault path had been copied from a retry pattern used elsewhere without removing the update call, turning error handling into an unintended retry loop. Five transactions in one week timed out this way, each generating dozens of failed attempts.

RESOLUTION
The fault path was replaced with a simple log-and-stop action, and the retry logic was moved to a separate scheduled job that waits before reattempting.

VALIDATION
Simulating a locked record produced exactly one log entry and no repeated update attempts across five test runs.

column1: A record-triggered flow built for a single record type fires for all record types after a UI cleanup removed the record-type filter
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow on the opportunity object was originally scoped to a single record type through an entry condition, applying a discount validation specific to that business line.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Opportunities of unrelated record types began receiving the same discount validation after a recent flow edit.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should only evaluate opportunities of the intended record type.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The record-type entry condition was missing, so the flow ran against every opportunity regardless of its record type.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A maintenance change intended to simplify the entry conditions had removed the record-type check along with an unrelated condition it was grouped with. Around fifteen opportunities from other business lines were incorrectly blocked from saving before the issue was caught.

RESOLUTION
The record-type condition was restored as its own standalone entry criterion, and the fifteen affected opportunities were manually re-validated and saved.

VALIDATION
Test opportunities across four record types confirmed the discount validation now applies only to the intended one.

column1: Two flows triggered on the same object save race to update the same field, and whichever finishes last silently wins
column2:
CONTEXT
Two independently built record-triggered flows on the account object both write to the same account-tier field, one based on revenue and one based on support history.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When both flows fire on the same save, the field's final value depends on unpredictable execution order rather than either flow's intended logic.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The account-tier field should reflect a single, deterministic set of business rules.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Whichever flow happens to execute second overwrites the other's result with no error or indication that a conflict occurred.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform does not guarantee ordering between separately built flows on the same object and event, and no explicit order had ever been set. A sample of updated accounts showed the tier value alternating between the two flows' outputs on repeated saves.

RESOLUTION
As an interim measure, one flow was given explicit priority ordering so it always evaluates last, while the two logic sets are merged into a single flow.

VALIDATION
Twenty repeated saves after the ordering change consistently produced the higher-priority flow's result, though the underlying merge work remains open.

column1: A flow's screen component saves a null value when a user leaves an optional field untouched, overwriting a value previously set by another process
column2:
CONTEXT
A guided screen flow lets agents update a subset of contact fields, including an optional preferred-language field that is often already populated by a prior automated process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Submitting the screen without touching the preferred-language field clears it instead of leaving the existing value in place.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A field the agent never interacts with should retain its existing value on submission.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The screen component initialized the field to blank rather than the record's current value, so an untouched field always saved as null.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The screen's default value was left unset when the component was built, relying on an assumption that blank inputs would be ignored on save, which is not how the update element behaves. Roughly sixty contacts lost their preferred-language value over two weeks.

RESOLUTION
The screen component's default value was set to the record's current preferred language, and the sixty affected contacts were restored from a backup extract.

VALIDATION
Ten test submissions leaving the field untouched all preserved the original value after the fix.

column1: A scheduled flow meant to run hourly is found running twice within the same hour after a maintenance window
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled flow processes overdue tasks every hour and reassigns them to a follow-up queue based on age.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Following a recent platform maintenance window, the flow was observed running twice within the same hour on three separate days.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should execute exactly once per scheduled hour.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A second, near-duplicate execution occurred a few minutes after the first, reprocessing the same batch of overdue tasks.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The extra runs correlate with maintenance windows, suggesting a scheduling job was re-queued after being interrupted, though the platform's scheduled job history does not show a clear duplicate entry to confirm the mechanism.

RESOLUTION
A record-level flag was added so the second run recognizes tasks already reassigned in the same hour and skips them, preventing duplicate processing while the root scheduling behavior is investigated further.

VALIDATION
The flag prevented reprocessing during two subsequent maintenance windows, though the underlying double-trigger cause has not yet been confirmed with the platform vendor.

column1: A flow calling an invocable Apex action treats a partial success as a full failure and rolls back records that had actually succeeded
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow processes a batch of related records through an invocable Apex action that can partially succeed, updating some records while skipping others that fail validation inside the action.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When the Apex action reports any failures within the batch, the flow rolls back the entire transaction, including records the action had successfully updated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records the Apex action successfully processed should be saved even if other records in the same batch failed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow checked only a single aggregate success flag rather than the action's per-record results, treating any failure as total failure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The invocable action's per-record result list was available but unused by the flow's fault-handling logic. Three affected batches lost updates to a combined ninety records that had actually succeeded inside the action.

RESOLUTION
The flow was updated to loop over the action's per-record results and commit only the failed subset for retry, and the ninety lost updates were reapplied.

VALIDATION
A test batch with a deliberate mix of passing and failing records confirmed passing records now save while failures alone are retried.

column1: A flow's loop over a large collection times out only when the collection crosses a specific size threshold
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow loops over a collection of related line items to apply a rounding adjustment, normally handling collections of a few hundred records without issue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Orders with more than roughly two thousand line items cause the flow interview to exceed its processing time limit and fail.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should complete regardless of the line item count on a given order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The loop's per-iteration element calls became measurably slower as the collection size grew, compounding into a timeout only past the threshold.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Each loop iteration performed a lookup that scaled poorly with collection size, a cost that stayed hidden at typical order sizes and only became visible on the small number of unusually large orders.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, orders above the threshold are routed to a nightly batch Apex job instead of the real-time flow, while a more scalable loop design is planned.

VALIDATION
Five previously failing large orders completed successfully overnight through the batch job, though the flow itself has not yet been redesigned for these volumes.

column1: A cloned flow version retained a hardcoded record ID from the sandbox it was built in, causing failures once deployed to production
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow was built and tested in a sandbox, where one decision element referenced a specific queue record by its record ID to route escalations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After deployment, the flow failed every time it reached the escalation routing step because the referenced ID did not exist in production.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should resolve the escalation queue dynamically rather than through an environment-specific identifier.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The decision element's hardcoded ID caused an unhandled fault whenever a case reached the escalation branch, silently failing the routing step.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The queue reference had been selected through a picker that stored the underlying ID rather than a portable reference, a detail missed during deployment review. Eighteen cases failed to escalate before the pattern was noticed.

RESOLUTION
The decision element was rebuilt to look up the queue by its developer name instead of a hardcoded ID, and the eighteen cases were manually escalated.

VALIDATION
A deployment to a second sandbox confirmed the flow resolves the correct queue without any environment-specific reference.

column1: A flow triggered from a platform event occasionally processes events out of the order they were published
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow subscribes to a platform event stream that publishes inventory adjustments, applying each adjustment in sequence to a running balance field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of balance fields have shown values inconsistent with the adjustment history, suggesting events were applied out of publish order.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Adjustments should apply to the running balance in the same order they were published.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
For a handful of records, the resulting balance matches a different application order than the platform event log shows as published.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform event log confirms publish order, but the flow's subscription processing does not currently log the order in which it consumed each event, so no cause for the discrepancy has been established.

RESOLUTION
No root cause has been identified and no fix has been applied; the flow continues to process events without a confirmed ordering guarantee.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to add sequence-number logging at the point the flow consumes each event, allowing consumption order to be compared directly against publish order for the next occurrence.

column1: A middleware transformation step drops custom fields it doesn't recognize instead of passing them through unchanged
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware platform maps fields between the CRM and a finance system using a transformation step that processes each field individually before forwarding the record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A custom field added to support a new product line never appeared in the finance system despite being populated correctly on the CRM side.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any field present on the source record, including newly added custom fields, should pass through unless explicitly excluded.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The transformation step silently discarded any field not already present in its static mapping table, with no error raised.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mapping table required a manual entry for every field and had not been updated when the new custom field was created, a gap that produced no warning anywhere in the sync pipeline. Two months of records were missing the field.

RESOLUTION
The mapping table was updated to include the new field, and a nightly check was added that flags any source field absent from the mapping table.

VALIDATION
The two months of missing records were backfilled from the CRM source, and the new mapping check has since flagged one other unrelated gap before it caused data loss.

column1: A sync job processes records in parallel threads, and two threads occasionally update the same record with conflicting values
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly sync job was recently changed to process records across multiple parallel threads to reduce total run time for a growing record volume.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of records each night show a field value that matches neither thread's expected input, suggesting a write conflict between threads.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each record should only ever be processed by one thread at a time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Occasionally two threads pick up related records from the same account in the same run, and their updates interleave on a shared parent field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The job's record partitioning does not currently guard against related records landing in different threads, though the exact interleaving mechanism causing the conflicting writes has not been fully isolated.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, partitioning was changed to group records by account so related records always process on the same thread, reducing but not fully eliminating the conflict window.

VALIDATION
Conflicting writes dropped from roughly a dozen per night to two over the following week, and the remaining cases are still under investigation.

column1: An integration re-authenticates on every single call instead of reusing a session, exhausting the login rate limit during peak hours
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration client calls several CRM endpoints throughout the day to keep an external scheduling tool synchronized with case data.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During peak hours the integration began failing with login rate limit errors, blocking all subsequent sync activity for the rest of the day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should authenticate once and reuse the resulting session for subsequent calls within its validity window.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The client had been built to request a fresh session token before every single API call rather than caching and reusing one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A code review of the integration client confirmed no session caching logic existed at all, so call volume during busy periods multiplied login attempts well past the platform's allowed rate. The pattern had gone unnoticed at lower volumes.

RESOLUTION
The client was updated to cache its session token and only re-authenticate when the token expires or a call fails with an authorization error.

VALIDATION
Login attempts during a peak-hour test dropped from several hundred to a handful, with no further rate limit errors observed over one week.

column1: A field mapped as a lookup relationship fails silently when the referenced record doesn't exist yet, dropping the relationship instead of erroring
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration creates order records that reference an existing account through a lookup field, relying on the account having already synced in an earlier step.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Some orders arrive with the account lookup left blank even though the corresponding account record exists in the CRM at the time of the order sync.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should either populate the lookup correctly or raise a visible error when it cannot.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
When the account lookup resolution briefly failed due to a timing gap, the integration proceeded to create the order with the field left empty instead of retrying or failing loudly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The lookup resolution step used a try-and-continue pattern that swallowed resolution failures rather than surfacing them, a design intended for optional fields but mistakenly applied here. Around thirty orders over a month were affected.

RESOLUTION
The lookup step was changed to retry briefly and then fail the record into an error queue rather than saving it with a blank relationship, and the thirty orphaned orders were manually relinked.

VALIDATION
A simulated timing gap during testing now produces a queued retry and a visible error rather than a silently blank lookup.

column1: A partner's sandbox test data was accidentally synced into the production integration queue after an environment URL was left unchanged
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner integration was reconfigured to point at a new sandbox for a joint testing exercise, requiring an endpoint URL change on the partner's side.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several dozen clearly fictitious test records appeared in the production sync queue shortly after the partner's testing exercise began.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Sandbox test traffic should never reach the production integration endpoint.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The partner's testing tool had been left pointed at the production endpoint URL from before the reconfiguration, sending real test payloads into live processing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner's own configuration change had not been completed on schedule, and no environment check existed on the receiving side to reject obviously mismatched test payloads. All affected records were traced to the same partner session.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate containment step, the affected test records were identified by their partner session identifier and removed from production, and inbound payloads are now checked against an expected environment tag before processing.

VALIDATION
A follow-up test submission using a mismatched environment tag was rejected at the queue boundary rather than reaching production records.

column1: A nightly reconciliation job compares record counts but not field values, so silent data drift goes undetected until a customer complaint
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly reconciliation job compares the number of synchronized records between the CRM and a partner billing system as its sole integrity check.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A customer reported a billing discrepancy that traced back to a field value that had drifted out of sync weeks earlier without the reconciliation job ever flagging it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Reconciliation should be able to detect meaningful field-level drift between the two systems, not only missing or extra records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The job only compares total record counts each night, which stayed matched throughout the period the field value was silently incorrect.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No field-level comparison currently exists in the reconciliation pipeline, and it is not yet known how many other records may carry similar undetected drift or what caused this specific value to diverge.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; the reconciliation job still performs count-only comparisons while a broader field-level check is scoped.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to run a one-time full field-level comparison across a sample of high-value records to estimate the scope of undetected drift before designing the ongoing check.

column1: An integration's error queue retries failed records in the original submission order, so one persistently bad record blocks all records behind it
column2:
CONTEXT
Failed integration records are placed in an error queue and retried in the same order they originally failed, processed one at a time by a scheduled job.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A single record with a permanently invalid value was blocking dozens of otherwise valid records from ever being retried behind it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A persistently failing record should not prevent other queued records from being retried.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retry job stopped processing the queue entirely on the first failure of each run, leaving every record behind the bad one untouched.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The retry job's error handling had been written to halt on the first failure as a safety measure, an approach that worked when failures were rare but created a blocking bottleneck once one record failed persistently. Fifty-four records were stuck behind the one bad record.

RESOLUTION
The retry job was changed to log a failure and continue to the next queued record rather than halting, and the bad record was routed to a manual-review queue.

VALIDATION
A test run with one deliberately invalid record confirmed the remaining fifty-three queued records all processed successfully afterward.

column1: A currency field syncs correctly for direct updates but not when the change comes from a workflow-triggered recalculation
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration listens for changes to an opportunity's currency amount field and forwards updates to a downstream reporting system in near real time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Amount changes made directly by a user sync correctly, but changes produced by an internal workflow recalculation are not reaching the downstream system.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should sync the field change regardless of what process updated it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Updates from the workflow recalculation do not consistently trigger the same change event the integration listens for.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The integration's listener responds to a specific update context that the workflow's recalculation does not always generate, though the precise conditions under which the event is or isn't emitted have not been fully mapped yet.

RESOLUTION
A scheduled reconciliation pass was added to catch amount discrepancies the real-time listener misses, while the underlying event-emission gap is investigated further with the platform vendor.

VALIDATION
The scheduled pass caught and corrected eleven missed updates in its first week, though real-time sync for workflow-triggered changes is not yet reliable.

column1: A middleware certificate rotation was not coordinated with the partner, causing an unannounced outage in the sync channel
column2:
CONTEXT
The middleware platform connecting the CRM to a partner system uses a client certificate for authentication, renewed periodically as part of routine maintenance.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A scheduled certificate renewal caused the partner's connection to fail for several hours because the partner had not been given the new certificate in advance.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Certificate rotations affecting an external partner connection should be coordinated with the partner before the change takes effect.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rotation proceeded on its automated schedule without a corresponding notification step to the partner, so their system continued trusting only the old certificate.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The rotation process had a notification step for internal consumers but none for external partners, an oversight from when the partner connection was first configured. The channel was down for roughly five hours before the partner reported it.

RESOLUTION
The certificate was reissued with the partner notified in advance, and the rotation process now includes a mandatory partner notification step with a confirmation window before old certificates are retired.

VALIDATION
The next scheduled rotation completed with the partner confirming receipt three days ahead of time and no connection interruption.

column1: A sync mapping references a field by label instead of API name, breaking after a label was translated for a new locale
column2:
CONTEXT
An older integration mapping configuration references several CRM fields by their display label rather than their underlying API name.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a recent localization project translated a subset of field labels for a new supported language, the integration stopped populating those fields for records in that locale.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should sync fields correctly regardless of which display language a record's users see.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping configuration can no longer find the fields it references because the translated labels no longer match the strings stored in the mapping.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
It has not yet been determined how many other fields or mappings in the same integration rely on label-based references, or whether other locales are similarly affected.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; affected fields remain unsynced for the new locale while the scope of label-based references across the integration is assessed.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to export the full mapping configuration and cross-check every referenced field name against the API name registry to identify all label-based references before remediation.

column1: A newly created permission set was cloned from an admin template and granted modify-all-data before anyone reviewed the assignment
column2:
CONTEXT
A new permission set was created for a reporting team by cloning an existing administrator template as a starting point, intended to be trimmed down before assignment.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The permission set was assigned to the reporting team before the modify-all-data privilege inherited from the template was removed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cloned permission sets should be reviewed and reduced to only the intended privileges before any assignment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Six reporting team members had modify-all-data access for approximately two weeks before a routine access review caught the discrepancy.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No activity indicating misuse of the excess privilege was found in the audit trail for the affected users during the exposure window. The gap traced back to a missing review step between cloning and assignment.

RESOLUTION
The excess privilege was removed immediately upon discovery, the permission set was rebuilt with only the intended reporting-object access, and a mandatory review checkpoint was added between cloning and assignment for future permission sets.

VALIDATION
The rebuilt permission set was tested to confirm reporting access remains intact with no elevated data-modification privilege, and the review checkpoint has since caught one other over-scoped clone before assignment.

column1: A former contractor's SSO federation was deprovisioned in the identity provider but the corresponding Salesforce user was left active
column2:
CONTEXT
Contractor offboarding deprovisions single sign-on federation in the identity provider as its primary step, with the expectation that the corresponding platform user is deactivated in the same process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A routine access audit found a contractor's Salesforce user still marked active more than a month after their federation was removed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deprovisioning federation should trigger deactivation of the corresponding platform user in the same offboarding step.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The user record remained active, though since federated login was removed the account could no longer actually authenticate through single sign-on.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Login history confirmed no successful access occurred after federation was removed, but a direct username-password login path independent of single sign-on remained technically available on the account the entire time.

RESOLUTION
The user was deactivated immediately upon discovery, the direct login path was disabled platform-wide for standard users, and the offboarding checklist was updated to require explicit platform deactivation as its own tracked step.

VALIDATION
A review of all other recently offboarded contractors confirmed no other account had a similar active-but-unfederated state.

column1: A named credential storing an integration password was visible in plaintext to any user with view-setup access
column2:
CONTEXT
A legacy named credential configured before the platform's masked-credential option was available stored an integration account's password in a field visible to setup viewers.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A configuration review found the password rendered in plaintext to any user granted view-setup-and-configuration access, far broader than intended.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Integration credentials should never be visible in plaintext to users outside the small group who manage the integration.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The legacy credential type does not support masking, so the password field displayed its actual value to anyone with the broad setup-viewing permission.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No evidence in the audit trail suggested the exposed password had been used improperly, but the number of users holding view-setup access made the exposure window difficult to fully rule out.

RESOLUTION
The integration account's password was rotated immediately as a precaution, and the named credential is being migrated to the newer masked-credential type; until migration completes, view-setup access has been restricted to a smaller named group.

VALIDATION
The rotated credential was confirmed functional for the integration, and the access restriction was verified to block plaintext visibility for all but the approved reviewers.

column1: A public-facing form's reCAPTCHA was disabled during a deployment and not re-enabled, exposing the endpoint to automated submissions for several days
column2:
CONTEXT
A public web-to-case form uses a captcha challenge to limit automated submissions, temporarily disabled during a deployment to simplify testing of an unrelated form field change.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A spike in low-quality case submissions was traced back to the captcha having been left disabled after the deployment concluded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The captcha should be re-enabled automatically or checked as part of deployment sign-off before a change is considered complete.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The captcha setting had no automated restoration step and was overlooked in the post-deployment checklist, leaving the form exposed for four days.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly three hundred automated submissions were received during the exposure window, none containing sensitive data, consistent with generic bot traffic rather than a targeted attempt against the organization.

RESOLUTION
The captcha was re-enabled immediately upon discovery, the low-quality submissions were bulk-removed, and the deployment checklist now includes an explicit captcha-status verification step.

VALIDATION
A follow-up deployment using the updated checklist confirmed the captcha status was checked and recorded before sign-off.

column1: An OAuth connected app was granted a refresh token scope broader than the integration actually required
column2:
CONTEXT
A connected app supporting a mobile field-service integration was configured with a broad set of OAuth scopes when it was first set up, before the integration's actual data needs were fully defined.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the app's refresh token scope includes full data access, though the integration only reads and writes work-order records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Connected app scopes should be limited to the minimum access the integration actually uses.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The broad scope has remained in place since initial setup, and narrowing it requires coordinating a token reissue with the mobile app's release cycle to avoid breaking active sessions.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of the app's actual API call history over the past quarter confirmed it has only ever accessed work-order and related asset records, supporting a narrower scope.

RESOLUTION
A narrowed scope has been defined and is scheduled for rollout alongside the mobile app's next release so existing sessions transition without disruption.

VALIDATION
The narrowed scope was validated in a test environment against the full range of the mobile app's known API calls with no functional loss; production rollout is pending the coordinated release.

column1: A password reset flow allowed an account takeover attempt to be retried without any lockout after repeated failures
column2:
CONTEXT
The self-service password reset flow verifies a set of security questions before allowing a new password to be set, without a configured limit on failed attempts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Monitoring flagged an account that received dozens of failed security-question attempts within a short window, consistent with an automated guessing attempt.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Repeated failed reset attempts against the same account should trigger a temporary lockout.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The reset flow allowed unlimited consecutive attempts with no delay or lockout threshold configured.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The account's actual password was never changed and no successful login followed the attempts, indicating the guessing attempt did not succeed before it was noticed and blocked at the network level.

RESOLUTION
The account was placed under a temporary lockout immediately upon discovery and its password was proactively rotated, and a failed-attempt lockout threshold was configured platform-wide for the reset flow.

VALIDATION
A test account confirmed that five consecutive failed attempts now triggers a lockout requiring administrator intervention to clear.

column1: A sharing rule exception intended for a temporary project was never removed after the project ended, leaving records exposed
column2:
CONTEXT
A sharing rule exception was created to give a cross-functional project team temporary visibility into a restricted set of account records for the duration of a joint initiative.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An access review nearly a year after the project concluded found the exception still active, granting visibility no longer needed by most of the original team.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Temporary sharing exceptions should have a defined expiration and be removed once their purpose ends.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The exception had no expiration mechanism and was not tracked anywhere for follow-up removal after the project's close-out.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No misuse of the extended visibility was found in the audit trail, but roughly a dozen users retained access well beyond any legitimate need.

RESOLUTION
The exception was removed for users no longer on an active related engagement as an interim step, while a broader periodic sharing-rule review process is established to catch similar cases going forward.

VALIDATION
Access confirmation with the two remaining legitimate users verified their continued need, and the removed users were confirmed to have lost visibility in a follow-up spot check.

column1: An audit trail showed a permission change made under a service account credential that no team claims ownership of
column2:
CONTEXT
The setup audit trail logged a permission set assignment change made under a service account credential used for automated administrative tasks.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
No team has been able to confirm the change was part of any planned or approved activity, and the service account's ownership itself is unclear.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every administrative change should be traceable to an identified, approved activity and an accountable owner.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The change appears in the audit trail with the service account as the actor, but no corresponding change ticket, deployment, or scheduled job references it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team has been engaged and is treating this as an open investigation; the credential has not yet been traced to a specific system or team, so its normal usage pattern is not yet established.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and the credential has not been rotated pending the investigation, since rotating it could interfere with a legitimate process that may still depend on it.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to correlate the account's full call history for the week against every team's deployment and integration logs to identify its actual owner before deciding on containment action.

column1: A mobile app cached authentication tokens locally with no expiration, so a lost device retained access well past its last use
column2:
CONTEXT
A field team's mobile app caches an authentication token locally after login to allow continued offline access to case data during site visits.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An employee reported a lost device roughly three months after their last confirmed use of the app, and the cached token was found to still be technically valid.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cached authentication tokens should expire well before a three-month window regardless of device activity.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The token had been issued with an unusually long validity period intended for extended offline field work, with no shorter-lived renewal requirement layered on top.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No access attempts were logged from the lost device after the report was filed, indicating the device was not used maliciously before access was cut off.

RESOLUTION
The token was revoked immediately upon the report, and the mobile app's token policy was changed to a shorter validity period paired with a periodic silent renewal that requires the device to check in.

VALIDATION
A test device left offline past the new expiration window was confirmed unable to authenticate until brought back online for renewal.

column1: Field history tracking was disabled on a sensitive object during a data load and never re-enabled afterward
column2:
CONTEXT
Field history tracking on a sensitive compliance-related object is normally enabled to support audit requirements, temporarily disabled during a large data load to improve load performance.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A compliance review found the tracking still disabled several months after the data load concluded, leaving a gap with no field-level change history for that period.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Field history tracking should be re-enabled immediately once a performance-driven data load completes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Tracking remains disabled, and it is not yet known whether changes made during the gap were otherwise logged through a different mechanism.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The compliance team has been notified and is assessing whether the gap is reportable; the full extent of changes made during the disabled window has not yet been reconstructed.

RESOLUTION
Tracking has not yet been re-enabled while the assessment is underway, since re-enabling it does not retroactively restore the missing history and the assessment may inform what documentation is still needed.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to cross-reference other system logs, such as integration and workflow audit records, to reconstruct as much of the missing change history as possible.

column1: A report type built on an indirect lookup relationship silently omits records where the intermediate object is missing
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom report type joins cases to a billing account through an intermediate contract object, following two lookup hops to reach the account.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases without a related contract record disappear from the report entirely, even though they otherwise meet every filter criterion.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cases missing the intermediate contract should still appear in the report with the account-level columns left blank.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type's join behaves as an implicit inner join across both lookup hops, excluding any case where either hop is unpopulated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly two hundred cases lacked a related contract, mostly from an earlier period before contract linking became mandatory, and all were silently absent from every report built on this report type.

RESOLUTION
A parallel report type was built using the platform's outer-join style relationship for the same two hops, restoring visibility into cases missing a contract.

VALIDATION
The new report type was confirmed to include all two hundred previously hidden cases alongside the fully linked ones, with account columns blank as expected.

column1: Two report filters combined with an OR condition are evaluated as AND due to filter logic syntax entered incorrectly during setup
column2:
CONTEXT
A report intended to surface cases matching either of two priority criteria was configured with custom filter logic combining two filter lines.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The report returns far fewer records than expected, matching only cases that satisfy both criteria simultaneously.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The report should return cases matching either filter criterion independently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The custom filter logic field was entered as filter one AND filter two instead of filter one OR filter two.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The logic string had been typed manually rather than selected from the guided builder, and the typo went unnoticed since the resulting report still returned a plausible-looking, non-empty result set.

RESOLUTION
The filter logic was corrected to use the OR operator between the two filter lines.

VALIDATION
The corrected report's row count matched the sum expected from running each filter criterion independently and removing overlap.

column1: A dashboard viewed by an executive shows different totals than the same dashboard viewed by an analyst, both with equivalent access
column2:
CONTEXT
A shared dashboard runs its underlying reports as the viewing user, intended to reflect each viewer's own record-level access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two users who should have identical visibility into the underlying data see materially different totals on the same dashboard component.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Users with equivalent record access should see matching totals on the same dashboard component.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One user's total is consistently lower, suggesting a sharing or role difference not accounted for by the assumption that their access is equivalent.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A comparison of the two users' permission sets found a subtle difference in one sharing group membership that had not been considered part of their otherwise matching profiles, though the exact record set this excludes has not been fully enumerated.

RESOLUTION
The affected user's sharing group membership was corrected to match the intended access level, while a full audit of similarly configured users is still underway to catch other discrepancies.

VALIDATION
The corrected user's dashboard total now matches the comparison user's, though the broader audit has not yet confirmed no other users are affected.

column1: A scheduled report's timezone setting does not match the recipient's timezone, so the labeled date range is misleading
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled report labeled as covering the previous business day is emailed each morning to a distribution list spanning two regional offices in different time zones.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Recipients in the second office reported that the report's previous-day label does not match the data actually included for their local business day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The report's labeled date range should be unambiguous regardless of a recipient's own time zone.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report's day boundary is calculated using the report owner's time zone, shifting the actual included window relative to the second office's business day.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The report had originally been built for a single office and the time zone dependency was never surfaced when the second office was added to the distribution list.

RESOLUTION
The report's date filter was changed to use a fixed, clearly labeled range independent of any individual user's time zone, and the email subject now states the range explicitly in coordinated time.

VALIDATION
Recipients in both offices confirmed the explicit date range in the email subject now matches the data included in the attached report.

column1: A report exported to a spreadsheet shows more decimal precision than the same report displayed in the browser, leading to rounding disputes
column2:
CONTEXT
A commission report displays currency totals rounded to two decimal places in the browser view, matching the display format configured on the underlying field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When exported to a spreadsheet, the same totals appear with additional unrounded decimal places, causing recipients to question which figure is correct.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The exported figures should match the rounded figures shown in the browser view.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The export function pulls the field's underlying stored precision rather than its display-formatted value.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This behavior is a documented characteristic of the export function rather than a defect, though it was not previously communicated to the teams relying on exported totals for commission disputes.

RESOLUTION
A formula field that explicitly rounds to two decimal places was added to the report and configured as the export column in place of the raw currency field.

VALIDATION
Ten exported rows using the new formula field matched their browser-displayed totals exactly, and the commission team confirmed no further discrepancy reports since the change.

column1: A joined report's second block resets its own sort order every time the report is refreshed
column2:
CONTEXT
A joined report combines two blocks of related data, with the second block manually sorted by a specific column to support a weekly review meeting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The manual sort applied to the second block reverts to a default order every time the report page is refreshed or reopened.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A manually applied sort order should persist across refreshes for the user who set it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Only the first block's sort order is saved with the report definition; the second block's sort is treated as a session-only preference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a known limitation of joined reports with the platform's current report builder rather than a recent regression, confirmed by testing the same behavior on an older, unrelated joined report.

RESOLUTION
A dedicated summary formula column was added to the second block that encodes the desired sort priority directly into the data, allowing the default sort to consistently produce the intended order.

VALIDATION
Five consecutive refreshes of the report confirmed the second block consistently displays in the intended order using the new formula-driven approach.

column1: A custom summary formula referencing a cross-block value returns a value that predates the report's own last refresh
column2:
CONTEXT
A joined report includes a custom summary formula in one block that references a total calculated in a different block of the same report.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The formula's displayed value occasionally lags behind the current report run, appearing to reflect an earlier refresh.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The cross-block formula should always reflect the values from the current report run.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
On some refreshes the formula displays a value consistent with the prior run rather than the one just generated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The staleness appears correlated with rapid consecutive refreshes, suggesting a caching layer between the two blocks' calculation steps, though this has not been confirmed with certainty.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, users have been advised to wait a few seconds between consecutive refreshes, while the caching behavior is raised with the platform vendor for clarification.

VALIDATION
Ten refreshes spaced several seconds apart consistently showed the correct current value, though rapid back-to-back refreshes still occasionally reproduce the stale value.

column1: A dashboard filter selector shows options that no longer exist after the underlying report's source object changed
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard filter lets viewers narrow results by region, populated from a picklist on the underlying report's source object.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The filter dropdown still lists two region values that were retired from the picklist months ago during a territory restructuring.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The filter's available options should reflect the picklist's currently active values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
