Selecting one of the retired region values returns an empty dashboard with no explanation, since no records carry that value anymore.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dashboard filter's option list had been cached at the time the filter was configured and never refreshed after the picklist was later trimmed.

RESOLUTION
The dashboard filter was reconfigured to rebuild its option list from the current picklist values, removing the two retired regions.

VALIDATION
The filter dropdown now shows only the six active regions, matching the current picklist exactly.

column1: A large export bypassing the dashboard exceeds the row limit and is silently truncated rather than warning the requester
column2:
CONTEXT
An analyst exports the full underlying data behind a large report directly rather than through the dashboard summary view, for use in an external analysis tool.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The exported file consistently contains fewer rows than the report's own displayed row count, with no indication in the file that it was truncated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An export exceeding the platform's row limit should clearly indicate that truncation occurred.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The export silently stops at the platform's row limit and produces a file that looks complete, with no truncation notice included.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The row limit itself is an expected platform constraint, but the export path used by this workflow does not surface any warning when the limit is reached, unlike the standard in-browser export option.

RESOLUTION
The analyst's workflow was switched to use the standard export path, which does display a truncation warning, and the report was also split into smaller date-bounded segments to stay under the row limit.

VALIDATION
A test export using the new segmented approach captured the full expected row count across the combined segments with no truncation.

column1: A trending report shows a sudden data gap for exactly one week that does not correspond to any known outage
column2:
CONTEXT
A weekly trending report tracks case volume over a rolling twelve-month window, normally showing a continuous week-over-week pattern.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One specific week in the trend line shows a near-zero value, dropping sharply below the weeks immediately before and after it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The trend line should reflect actual case volume for every week without unexplained gaps.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected week's value is far lower than the surrounding weeks, though the underlying case records for that week appear to exist when queried directly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Checking the platform's published status history found no recorded incident during the affected week, and no scheduled maintenance is on record for that period either.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been identified and the report continues to show the gap; the underlying case records have not been altered since they still exist independently of the report's calculation.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to rebuild the report's date-bucketing logic for just that one week in isolation to determine whether the gap is a calculation artifact or a genuine data absence.

column1: An email-to-case rule strips inline images from the case description, losing screenshots customers attach directly in the message body
column2:
CONTEXT
Email-to-case processing converts inbound customer messages into case records, storing the message body as plain text in the case description field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers who paste a screenshot directly into their email body lose the image entirely, leaving agents without the visual context it provided.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Inline images should be preserved as case attachments even though the description field itself is plain text.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The processing step discarded inline image content during the conversion to plain text rather than extracting and attaching it separately.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The original email-to-case configuration only handled traditional file attachments, not images embedded directly in the message body, a distinction not considered when the process was first built.

RESOLUTION
The processing step was updated to detect inline images and save them as case attachments alongside the plain-text description.

VALIDATION
Ten test emails with pasted screenshots all produced a case with the image correctly attached and referenced in the description.

column1: A shared mailbox alias occasionally delivers a customer's reply to the wrong case when two cases share a near-identical subject line
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound email matching uses the case number embedded in the subject line to route replies to the correct existing case.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of replies were matched to the wrong case when a customer had two open cases with subject lines differing only by case number, and the matching pattern occasionally captured the wrong one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each reply should route only to the case number actually present in its subject line.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The matching pattern occasionally captured a case number from quoted prior message text further down in the thread rather than the current subject line.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Six misrouted replies were found over two months, all involving customers with multiple concurrent cases and long reply chains containing quoted case numbers from earlier messages.

RESOLUTION
The matching logic was updated to only read the case number from the leading subject line text, ignoring quoted content further in the string, and the six misrouted replies were manually reassigned.

VALIDATION
A test thread with two different quoted case numbers in the body correctly routed to the case number in the actual subject line.

column1: An email template's merge field renders a stale value because it pulls from a report snapshot rather than the live record
column2:
CONTEXT
An outbound email template merges in an account's current tier level, sourced through a formula field that was originally built to reference a cached reporting snapshot for performance reasons.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers occasionally receive emails showing an outdated tier level that does not match their account's current status.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The merged tier level should always reflect the account's current, live value.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula field updates only when the nightly snapshot refreshes, so same-day tier changes are not reflected in emails sent before the next refresh.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The snapshot dependency was intentional when the field was built, but its implications for real-time outbound email accuracy were not fully considered at the time, and how many customers received a stale tier value has not yet been quantified.

RESOLUTION
The template was switched to merge directly from the live tier field for now, while the performance impact of removing the snapshot dependency across other consumers of that field is still being evaluated.

VALIDATION
Ten test emails sent immediately after a tier change now show the current value, though the broader snapshot-dependency review remains open.

column1: A case auto-assignment rule based on email domain misroutes messages from a customer using a personal email address instead of their company domain
column2:
CONTEXT
Case auto-assignment routes inbound support emails to the correct account team based on the sender's email domain matching a known company domain.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A customer who emailed from a personal address instead of their usual company address had their case routed to a generic unassigned queue instead of their dedicated account team.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cases from a known contact should route to the correct team even if sent from an unrecognized email address.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The routing rule matches solely on sender domain and does not fall back to checking whether the sender's address matches an existing contact record by any other means.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The contact record did include the personal email as a secondary address field, which the routing rule simply never checked as part of its matching logic.

RESOLUTION
The routing rule was updated to also check the secondary email field on matching contact records before falling back to the unassigned queue.

VALIDATION
A test email from the same personal address now correctly routes to the customer's dedicated account team.

column1: A quoted-text collapse feature hides part of a customer's message that included a critical detail needed for resolution
column2:
CONTEXT
The case email view automatically collapses quoted prior message text to keep long reply chains readable, showing only the newest reply by default.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An agent missed a critical detail because the customer had added it partway down within what the interface treated as quoted text rather than as new content.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
New content a customer adds anywhere in their reply should be visible by default, not hidden inside a collapsed quote block.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The collapse logic relies on the email client's quoting markers, which one customer's mail client formatted differently, causing genuinely new text to be misclassified as quoted.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The affected mail client's quoting format is a known variant not fully covered by the collapse logic's detection pattern, though how many other mail clients share this variant has not been fully catalogued.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, agents have been advised to always expand quoted sections before closing a case, while the collapse logic's detection pattern is being expanded to cover the additional format.

VALIDATION
The specific mail client's format was reproduced in testing and confirmed to still misclassify content pending the detection pattern update.

column1: An email notification digest batches multiple case updates into one message but only links to the first case mentioned
column2:
CONTEXT
A daily digest email summarizes all case updates a manager's team received that day, listing each case with a short summary line.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Clicking the link on any case entry in the digest other than the first one still opens the first case listed rather than the one actually clicked.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each case entry's link should open that specific case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The digest template used a single shared link variable set from the first case in the loop instead of a per-entry link built from each case's own identifier.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The templating logic that assembles the digest had a loop variable scoping error, reusing the first iteration's link value across all subsequent entries.

RESOLUTION
The template was corrected to build each entry's link from that entry's own case identifier within the loop.

VALIDATION
A test digest with five cases confirmed each entry's link now opens the correct corresponding case.

column1: A bounced delivery notification is filed as a new case instead of being matched back to the original outbound message
column2:
CONTEXT
When an outbound email to a customer bounces, the mail server's bounce notification arrives at the same shared support mailbox used for inbound customer email.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Bounce notifications are being processed as new cases from an unrecognized sender rather than being linked back to the case the original outbound email came from.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A bounce notification should be recognized and logged against the originating case rather than filed as an unrelated new case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The email-to-case logic has no specific handling for the mail server's bounce message format, so it treats the notification like any other inbound email.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly fifteen bounce notifications a month are currently misfiled this way, and a reliable pattern for identifying them has been identified but not yet implemented in the routing logic.

RESOLUTION
Misfiled bounce cases are currently being manually identified and closed each week as a stopgap while the automated bounce-detection pattern is built and tested.

VALIDATION
The manual weekly cleanup has kept the misfiled case backlog from growing, though automated detection has not yet been deployed.

column1: An email signature's disclaimer text pushed the actual message content below the visible preview pane on mobile devices
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound case emails append a standard legal disclaimer below the agent's signature, formatted with generous spacing for readability on desktop email clients.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers reading replies on a mobile device saw only the disclaimer in their preview pane, with the actual response requiring an extra tap to reveal.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The substantive reply content should appear before the disclaimer in any preview context.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The disclaimer was positioned above the reply body in the template's layout rather than below it, an ordering that had gone unnoticed on desktop where the full email is visible at once.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template's original design placed the disclaimer at the top for visibility reasons, without testing how mobile clients truncate long messages in preview panes.

RESOLUTION
The template was reordered to place the reply content first and the disclaimer at the bottom, matching standard email conventions.

VALIDATION
A test reply viewed on three different mobile mail apps now shows the actual response content in the preview pane.

column1: A vacation-responder rule set by an individual agent unintentionally auto-replies to customers on their assigned cases
column2:
CONTEXT
An agent configured a personal out-of-office auto-responder on their individual mailbox while away, separate from the platform's case-management email handling.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers replying to case emails from that agent received an auto-reply instead of their message being processed normally into the case.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Personal auto-responders should not interfere with case email processing routed through the shared support address.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The agent's case-related emails were being forwarded to their personal mailbox as a convenience setting, which is where the personal auto-responder then fired on customer replies.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The forwarding convenience setting was not intended to be used during extended absences, but no policy or technical control currently prevents an agent from leaving it enabled while away.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate step, the forwarding setting was disabled for the returning agent's account, and a reminder was added to the time-off checklist to disable personal forwarding before extended leave.

VALIDATION
A follow-up check confirmed no further auto-replies were sent to customers on that agent's cases after the forwarding setting was disabled.

column1: Encoding differences between the email service and the platform corrupt accented characters in customer names within case records
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound emails from customers with accented characters in their name are processed through the email service before landing as case and contact records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of these records display garbled characters in place of the correct accented letters, though the original email content displays those characters correctly when viewed directly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Accented characters in customer names should display correctly and consistently in resulting case and contact records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Corruption appears inconsistently, affecting some accented names but not others, without an identified pattern distinguishing the two groups so far.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Comparing raw message headers for affected and unaffected emails has not yet revealed a consistent encoding difference between them, and the exact point in the processing pipeline where corruption occurs has not been isolated.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the inconsistent pattern makes it unclear whether the cause lies with the sending mail client, the email service, or the platform's own parsing step.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to capture the raw byte-level message source for both an affected and unaffected email sent from the same customer, if one can be found, to isolate where the encoding diverges.

column1: A duplicate rule's matching criteria treats records with different capitalization as distinct, letting true duplicates through undetected
column2:
CONTEXT
A duplicate rule on the account object matches on company name using an exact-match criterion to flag potential duplicates before a record saves.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two accounts differing only in the capitalization of their company name were both created without the duplicate rule flagging either one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The duplicate rule should treat company names as matching regardless of capitalization differences.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The matching criterion was configured as case-sensitive exact match, so differently capitalized versions of the same name were treated as entirely distinct values.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A search across existing accounts found nineteen other pairs with the same capitalization-only difference that had similarly gone undetected by the rule since it was first configured.

RESOLUTION
The matching criterion was changed to a case-insensitive comparison, and the nineteen existing duplicate pairs were queued for manual review and merge.

VALIDATION
A test pair created with differing capitalization was correctly flagged by the rule after the change.

column1: A record's last-modified timestamp updates from an automated field recalculation, making genuinely stale records appear recently touched
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly batch job recalculates a rollup-style custom field on account records to keep a summary metric current, saving the record even when only that field changes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A report meant to surface accounts with no recent human activity was returning almost no results, since the nightly recalculation refreshed the modified timestamp on nearly every account.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The last-modified timestamp used for staleness reporting should reflect meaningful user or business activity, not routine automated recalculation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Every account touched by the nightly job showed a same-day modified timestamp regardless of whether any user had actually interacted with it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The batch job saved the full record rather than updating only the specific field through a more targeted method, which is what caused the standard modified timestamp to advance.

RESOLUTION
The batch job was changed to update the field through a method that does not advance the standard last-modified timestamp, and a separate custom field now tracks the recalculation time instead.

VALIDATION
The staleness report re-run after the change correctly surfaced accounts with no genuine recent activity, matching a manual spot-check of ten accounts.

column1: A custom button that used to clone a record with its attachments now clones the record only, silently dropping the files
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom clone button on the opportunity object was built to duplicate a record along with its related files, used regularly when setting up renewal opportunities from an existing template.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a recent platform update, cloned opportunities no longer carry over their related files, though the record fields still clone correctly.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The clone action should continue to duplicate related files along with the record itself.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The button's underlying logic relied on a file-cloning behavior that changed with a recent platform release, silently no longer copying attachments.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform release notes confirmed a change to how the default clone action handles the newer file storage model, which the custom button's logic had not been updated to account for.

RESOLUTION
The custom button's logic was updated to explicitly copy related files using the current supported method rather than relying on the old default behavior.

VALIDATION
Five test clones confirmed all related files now carry over correctly to the new opportunity record.

column1: A page layout assignment based on record type stopped applying after a profile consolidation project, leaving some users with the wrong layout
column2:
CONTEXT
Page layout assignments on the case object are configured per combination of profile and record type, and a recent project consolidated a dozen overlapping profiles into three standardized ones.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of users began seeing a generic default layout instead of their team's specific layout after the consolidation went live.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every profile and record type combination should have an explicit layout assignment carried forward through the consolidation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Several profile-and-record-type combinations that existed under the old profiles had no corresponding assignment configured under the new consolidated profiles.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The consolidation project's layout mapping had been built from a checklist that missed three less-common record types not represented in the primary testing scenarios.

RESOLUTION
The three missing layout assignments were added for the new consolidated profiles, matching the intended layouts from the original configuration.

VALIDATION
Test users representing each of the three affected combinations confirmed they now see the correct team-specific layout.

column1: A mass reassignment tool changes record ownership but leaves stale sharing rules from the previous owner still granting access
column2:
CONTEXT
A mass reassignment tool is used periodically to transfer large blocks of accounts between sales territories, updating the owner field directly through a bulk operation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users on the previous owner's team retained visibility into reassigned accounts weeks after the reassignment, through sharing rules that never recalculated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Sharing access should recalculate automatically to reflect the new owner once a bulk reassignment completes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mass reassignment tool updates ownership without triggering a full sharing recalculation, since it uses a bulk API path that bypasses the standard save-triggered recalculation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a known characteristic of the specific bulk API path the tool uses, trading off performance for the deferred recalculation, a tradeoff not previously documented for this tool's users.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, a manual sharing recalculation job is now triggered immediately following every mass reassignment run, while a change to a recalculation-inclusive API path is being evaluated.

VALIDATION
A recent reassignment followed by the manual recalculation job confirmed previous-owner access was correctly removed within the same day.

column1: A rollup field recalculates correctly on edit but not on the deletion of a child record, leaving inflated totals behind
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom rollup field on the account object sums the value of related open orders, recalculating through a trigger-based approach rather than the platform's native rollup summary tool.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deleting an order does not reduce the account's rollup total, so the field overstates open order value for any account that has had an order deleted.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The rollup should recalculate correctly whether a related order is created, edited, or deleted.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The custom trigger logic only fired on insert and update events for the order object, with no corresponding handling for the delete event.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The delete case had been overlooked when the trigger was first built, since order deletions were rare at the time and became more common only after a later process change allowed them.

RESOLUTION
The trigger was updated to also handle delete events, recalculating the rollup accordingly, and all accounts with a deleted order in their history were reprocessed to correct the inflated totals.

VALIDATION
A test deletion confirmed the rollup total decreased by the correct amount immediately after the order was removed.

column1: A required lookup field can be cleared through an API update despite being enforced on the page layout
column2:
CONTEXT
A lookup field linking cases to a parent service agreement is marked required on the page layout, intended to ensure every case is tied to an agreement.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An integration was found to be clearing the field on certain updates, something that would be blocked if attempted through the standard user interface.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The field's required status should be enforced consistently regardless of whether the update comes through the interface or the API.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Page layout-level required settings are enforced only in the user interface, not for updates made through the API, which the integration's periodic sync job used.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is expected platform behavior rather than a defect, but it had not been accounted for when the field was originally marked required only at the layout level; the number of cases with the field cleared this way is still being counted.

RESOLUTION
A validation rule enforcing the field at the database level has been drafted and is pending rollout, which will apply consistently to both interface and API updates.

VALIDATION
The draft validation rule was tested in a sandbox and confirmed to block the integration's clearing behavior; production rollout is pending final review.

column1: A record merge selects the wrong record as the surviving master by default, and the reversal process is manual and error-prone
column2:
CONTEXT
The standard record merge tool defaults to preselecting the most recently created record as the surviving master when merging duplicate contacts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents repeatedly accepted the default selection without checking, resulting in several merges where the older, more complete record was discarded in favor of a sparser newer one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Agents should be prompted to consciously select the correct master rather than relying on a default that may not reflect data completeness.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The default preselection combined with a fast merge workflow led to the default being accepted without review in a meaningful share of merges.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of recent merges found eight cases where the discarded record held more complete data than the surviving one, requiring manual data recovery from field history.

RESOLUTION
The merge screen was reconfigured to require an explicit master selection with no default preselected, and the eight affected records were manually restored using field history.

VALIDATION
A test merge confirmed the screen no longer proceeds until a master is explicitly selected by the user.

column1: A scheduled Apex job intended to clean up stale records also deletes records that were briefly stale due to an unrelated approval delay
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled cleanup job removes draft records that have remained untouched past a defined age threshold, intended to clear out abandoned entries.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of records were deleted by the job while genuinely awaiting a slow approval step, not because they were actually abandoned.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records legitimately waiting on an in-progress approval should not be treated as stale regardless of how long the approval takes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The job's staleness check is based solely on the record's last-modified date, which does not distinguish an abandoned draft from one waiting on a slow approver.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
It has not yet been determined how many records overall have been affected historically, since deleted records are not retained long enough in the recycle bin to fully reconstruct the pattern.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; the cleanup job continues to run on its existing schedule while the approach for distinguishing abandoned from delayed records is being designed.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to temporarily log records the job would delete without actually deleting them, to measure how often an in-progress approval would have been affected.

column1: Two nearly simultaneous edits from different automation sources produce a record state that matches neither source's intended values
column2:
CONTEXT
An opportunity record can be updated by both a scheduled batch process and a real-time flow within the same narrow time window during end-of-day processing.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of records each month end up with a mix of field values that does not match what either the batch process or the flow individually intended to write.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Concurrent updates from different automation sources should resolve to a consistent, predictable final state.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The resulting record shows some fields from the batch process's intended update and others from the flow's, suggesting the two updates interleaved rather than one cleanly following the other.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform's standard locking behavior should prevent this kind of interleaving, but the specific mechanism allowing it here has not been identified from the available transaction logs.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the interleaving mechanism itself is not yet understood well enough to design a targeted correction.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to enable detailed transaction logging for one week specifically covering the end-of-day window to capture a live occurrence with full timing detail.

column1: A multi-year contract's total contract value displays correctly in the quote but the opportunity amount only reflects the first year
column2:
CONTEXT
A multi-year contract quote calculates a total contract value across all years, syncing a summary amount back to the associated opportunity record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The opportunity amount field shows only the first year's value rather than the full multi-year total shown on the quote.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The opportunity amount should reflect the full total contract value for accurate pipeline and forecast reporting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The sync process pulls from a quote field that was originally built for single-year deals and was never extended to sum across multiple contract years.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twenty-two active multi-year opportunities were found with an understated amount, all originating from the same quote template introduced when multi-year deals became more common.

RESOLUTION
The sync process was updated to pull from a new field that correctly totals all contract years, and the twenty-two affected opportunities were corrected.

VALIDATION
A test three-year quote confirmed the opportunity amount now matches the full total contract value shown on the quote.

column1: A discount approval workflow re-triggers from the start whenever any unrelated field on the quote is edited, even after approval was already granted
column2:
CONTEXT
A discount approval workflow requires sign-off once a quote's discount exceeds a defined threshold, evaluated through a process that checks the quote record on every save.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Sales reps making a minor unrelated edit, such as correcting a shipping address, after approval was granted were finding the approval reset and required again.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Editing a field unrelated to the discount should not require re-approval of an already-approved discount.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The approval process re-evaluated on every save regardless of which field changed, treating any edit as grounds to restart the approval requirement.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The process had been built with a save-based trigger rather than a field-change-based one, a simpler but overly broad approach that had not caused visible friction until quote volume increased.

RESOLUTION
The approval process was rebuilt to only re-trigger when the discount percentage or amount field specifically changes.

VALIDATION
A test quote with an unrelated field edit after approval no longer triggered a new approval request, while a discount change still correctly required one.

column1: A price adjustment applied at the order level does not flow back to update the originating opportunity's reported amount
column2:
CONTEXT
Order records are generated from closed-won opportunities, and occasionally a price adjustment is applied directly at the order level to correct a fulfillment-time pricing issue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When such an adjustment is made, the originating opportunity's amount field continues to show the original pre-adjustment figure, skewing closed revenue reporting.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An order-level price adjustment should be reflected back on the originating opportunity's reported amount.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No synchronization exists from order-level changes back to the opportunity, since the standard flow only ever pushes data forward from opportunity to order.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Building reverse synchronization carries a risk of conflicting with the opportunity's own closed-stage locking rules, and a safe approach has not yet been fully designed.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, finance now maintains a manual tracking list of order-level adjustments to apply as a correction factor in revenue reports, while a longer-term synchronization design is evaluated.

VALIDATION
The manual tracking list was cross-checked against finance's own adjustment records for the past quarter and found to capture all known cases.

column1: Territory-based quota credit is calculated using an account's current territory rather than the territory in effect when the deal closed
column2:
CONTEXT
Quota credit for a closed deal is calculated by a nightly job that looks up the account's territory assignment at the time the job runs.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A deal closed before a territory realignment was later credited to the new territory instead of the one that actually owned the deal at close.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Quota credit should reflect the territory assignment in effect at the moment the deal closed, not the account's current assignment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The nightly job recalculates credit using the account's live territory field, so any later reassignment retroactively shifts credit for already-closed deals.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Following the most recent realignment, thirty-one already-closed deals had their credit silently shift to the new territory, creating a quota dispute between two regional teams.

RESOLUTION
The credit calculation was changed to use a territory value captured and locked at the moment of close, and the thirty-one disputed deals were manually corrected to their original territory.

VALIDATION
A test realignment performed in a sandbox confirmed previously closed deals retained their original locked territory credit afterward.

column1: A subscription proration calculation produces a negative line amount when a downgrade and a renewal fall in the same billing cycle
column2:
CONTEXT
Subscription proration logic calculates a partial-period credit or charge whenever a plan change occurs mid-cycle, applied as an adjustment line on the next invoice.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When a downgrade and a scheduled renewal happened to fall within the same billing cycle, the resulting proration line showed a negative total invoice amount.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Combined events within one cycle should still produce a mathematically valid, non-negative total after all proration adjustments.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The proration logic calculated each event's adjustment independently and summed them without checking whether the combined result made sense as a final invoice line.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three customers were affected over the prior quarter, each triggering an invoice that finance had to manually correct before it reached the customer.

RESOLUTION
The proration logic was updated to calculate combined events together as a single adjustment rather than summing independent calculations, and the three historical invoices were confirmed already corrected by finance.

VALIDATION
A test scenario recreating the same downgrade-and-renewal combination produced a correct, non-negative invoice line after the fix.

column1: A deal's close date is changed after quarter-end for a legitimate documentation correction, and it silently shifts historical quota attainment
column2:
CONTEXT
Sales operations occasionally corrects a deal's close date after quarter-end to fix a documentation error, such as a date entered in the wrong format during data entry.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Such corrections silently shift which quarter's quota attainment the deal counts toward, sometimes changing a rep's already-reported results after the fact.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A documentation-only close date correction should be distinguishable from a change that legitimately affects quota attainment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Quota attainment reports recalculate purely from the current close date field with no memory of which quarter a deal was originally reported against.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A way to flag a close date change as documentation-only versus attainment-affecting has been proposed, but it has not yet been built or agreed upon with the sales operations team.

RESOLUTION
As an interim measure, sales operations now manually documents any post-quarter close date change in a shared log for finance to reference, while a proper flagging mechanism is designed.

VALIDATION
The shared log has captured all known post-quarter corrections made so far, though it depends on manual discipline rather than a system-enforced control.

column1: An opportunity split between two sales reps is not reflected in the commission system, which only reads the primary owner
column2:
CONTEXT
Opportunity splits allow credit for a single deal to be divided between two collaborating sales reps, recorded through a dedicated split percentage field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The commission system only reads the opportunity's primary owner field, so the secondary rep on a split deal receives no commission credit at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Commission calculations should honor the split percentages recorded on the opportunity.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The commission system's data feed was built before opportunity splits were adopted by the sales organization and has never been extended to read split data.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Extending the commission system's feed to read split data requires a change on the vendor's side that has been requested but does not yet have a committed timeline.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, finance manually calculates and applies split commission adjustments each period based on an exported list of split opportunities, pending the vendor-side feed change.

VALIDATION
The manual adjustment process was cross-checked against a full quarter of split opportunities and found to correctly account for all of them.

column1: A contract renewal generated a duplicate line item because the renewal template was updated without deactivating the previous version
column2:
CONTEXT
Contract renewals are generated from a template that defines the standard set of line items, recently updated to reflect a new product bundling structure.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several renewals generated shortly after the template update contained a duplicate line item, one from the old template structure and one from the new.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Only the current active template version should be used when generating a renewal's line items.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The previous template version remained active alongside the new one, and the renewal generation process pulled from both instead of the newer one exclusively.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nine renewals generated in the window between the new template's activation and the old one's eventual deactivation carried the duplicate line item.

RESOLUTION
The old template version was deactivated, and the nine affected renewals were corrected to remove the duplicate line before being sent to customers.

VALIDATION
A renewal generated after the deactivation confirmed only a single, correct set of line items from the current template.

column1: A custom rollup meant to sum only active contracts also includes contracts in a terminated status added after the rollup was built
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom rollup field on the account object sums contract value across all contracts considered active, filtered by a defined list of active status values.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A newer terminated-for-nonpayment status, added to the contract object after the rollup was originally built, is being included in the active total.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The rollup should exclude any status representing a terminated contract, including ones added after the rollup's original configuration.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rollup's filter explicitly lists included statuses rather than excluding terminated ones, so a newly added status defaults to being included unless someone remembers to update the filter.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
It has not yet been determined how many accounts currently carry an inflated total due to this gap, since a full recalculation across all accounts has not yet been run.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; the filter still needs to be updated to an exclusion-based approach, and this has not been scheduled.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to run a one-time report identifying every account with a contract in the newer terminated status to estimate how many rollup totals are currently overstated.

column1: Two finance systems reconcile total bookings for most periods but diverge for one specific quarter with no identified transaction-level cause
column2:
CONTEXT
Total bookings figures are independently calculated in the CRM and in a separate finance system, normally matching within an expected small rounding tolerance each quarter.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One specific past quarter shows a divergence between the two systems well outside the normal tolerance, without a specific transaction identified as the cause.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Total bookings between the two systems should reconcile within the normal tolerance for every quarter.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The total divergence for the affected quarter has been quantified, but line-by-line comparison so far has not isolated which transactions account for the gap.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A first-pass comparison of transaction counts between the two systems for the affected quarter matched exactly, suggesting the divergence lies in value rather than record count, though the specific records have not been isolated.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no correction has been made to either system's reported figures for the affected quarter.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is a full transaction-level value comparison between the two systems for the affected quarter, rather than the aggregate comparison performed so far, to isolate the specific divergent records.

column1: A client library caches API metadata at startup and does not pick up a newly added required field until the client restarts
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration client library caches the platform's object metadata once at startup to avoid repeated metadata calls during normal operation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a new required field was added to an object, the client kept submitting records without it and receiving validation errors, even though the client's code had been updated to supply the field.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The client should recognize newly required fields without needing a full restart to refresh its cached metadata.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The cached metadata from before the field was added continued to be used for request validation on the client side, masking the fact that the field was already being sent correctly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client's cache had no expiration or refresh trigger, an intentional design for performance that had not accounted for schema changes happening while the client stayed running for extended periods.

RESOLUTION
A periodic background metadata refresh was added to the client library, running on an interval independent of restarts.

VALIDATION
A test schema change was correctly picked up by a long-running client instance within one refresh interval without requiring a restart.

column1: Concurrent API updates to the same record from two different integrations are both accepted, and the platform's optimistic locking never triggers
column2:
CONTEXT
Two separate integrations occasionally update the same account record within moments of each other, relying on the platform's optimistic locking to prevent one from silently overwriting the other.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A review of conflicting field values found cases where both integrations' updates appeared to have been accepted without either receiving a locking conflict error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A near-simultaneous conflicting update should be rejected with a locking error for one of the two integrations.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Both updates succeeded because they modified different fields on the same record, which the platform's locking mechanism does not treat as a conflict even when the business logic depends on both fields together.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is expected platform locking behavior at the field level rather than a defect, but it had not previously been accounted for in the two integrations' shared assumptions about mutual exclusivity.

RESOLUTION
One integration was updated to read the record immediately before writing and detect a conflicting recent change through an application-level timestamp check rather than relying on platform locking.

VALIDATION
A simulated concurrent update scenario confirmed the application-level check now correctly detects and defers to the other integration's more recent change.

column1: An API consumer's OAuth scope was narrowed during a security review, causing previously working write calls to fail with an unclear permission error
column2:
CONTEXT
A routine security review narrowed a connected app's OAuth scope to remove access believed to be unused, based on a sample of recent API call logs.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An infrequently used but legitimate monthly write process began failing immediately after the scope change, since it fell outside the sampled log window used for the review.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Scope changes should account for infrequent but legitimate usage patterns, not only recent, frequent activity.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The monthly process's write calls began failing with a generic permission error that did not clearly indicate the scope change as the cause.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The sampled log window used for the review covered only two weeks, missing the monthly process entirely, a gap in the review methodology rather than a platform defect.

RESOLUTION
The necessary scope was restored, and the review methodology was updated to check a full quarter of call history before narrowing any connected app's scope going forward.

VALIDATION
The monthly process was manually triggered as a test and completed successfully with the restored scope.

column1: A streaming API subscription silently stops delivering events after an idle period longer than the platform's undocumented connection timeout
column2:
CONTEXT
A subscriber client maintains a long-lived connection to a streaming API channel to receive near-real-time record change events for a downstream dashboard.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During low-activity overnight periods, the connection occasionally drops without the client receiving any disconnect notification, so the dashboard silently stops updating until the next event arrives and fails.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The client should be notified of a dropped connection so it can reconnect promptly rather than appearing idle but actually disconnected.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The connection closes after an extended idle period with no corresponding event or notification sent to the client to indicate the closure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The exact idle timeout duration is not published in the platform's documentation, and it has only been approximately estimated from observed disconnect timing across several occurrences.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the client now sends a lightweight periodic keep-alive query well within the estimated timeout window to prevent the connection from ever reaching the idle threshold.

VALIDATION
The dashboard has not missed an overnight update in the two weeks since the keep-alive query was added, though the platform's actual timeout behavior remains undocumented.

column1: A bulk query job's CSV output uses a different null representation than the same data returned through the REST API, breaking a downstream parser
column2:
CONTEXT
A downstream data pipeline consumes records through both the bulk query API for large historical loads and the REST API for smaller incremental updates.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The parser built for the REST API's null representation broke when applied to bulk query output, which represents empty fields differently in its CSV format.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The parser should either handle both representations or the two APIs should represent null values consistently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The bulk query CSV output uses an empty string for null values while the REST API's structure uses an explicit null marker, a documented but easily overlooked difference between the two interfaces.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The difference is expected and documented in the platform's reference material, but the pipeline's parser had only ever been tested against REST API output during development.

RESOLUTION
The parser was updated to explicitly handle both representations, normalizing them to a single internal null value before further processing.

VALIDATION
A test run against both a bulk query export and a REST API response containing null fields confirmed both now normalize identically.

column1: An API client retries on a 500 error without any backoff, amplifying load on the platform during a brief service degradation
column2:
CONTEXT
An API client was built with a simple immediate-retry policy for server errors, intended to handle occasional transient failures without manual intervention.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During a brief period of elevated platform latency, the client's rapid retries were observed contributing measurably to the load during the degraded window.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The client should back off progressively between retries rather than retrying immediately and repeatedly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The client retried failed calls with no delay at all, so a slow period produced a rapid burst of repeated requests rather than a moderate, spaced-out retry pattern.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A proper exponential backoff policy has been designed and is partially implemented in a test branch, but has not yet been fully validated across all of the client's call paths.

RESOLUTION
An interim fixed delay was added between retries as a quick mitigation while the full exponential backoff implementation is completed and tested.

VALIDATION
The fixed delay was confirmed in testing to reduce retry burst intensity substantially, though the more adaptive backoff implementation is not yet complete.

column1: A picklist field's API-returned values do not reflect a recent restriction of allowed values, so the consumer still submits now-invalid options
column2:
CONTEXT
An external ordering system queries the platform's picklist metadata periodically to populate its own dropdown of valid shipping methods before submitting an order.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After several shipping methods were retired on the platform side, the external system continued offering them as options, and submissions using them failed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The external system's dropdown should reflect the platform's currently valid picklist values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The external system's metadata refresh interval was longer than assumed, so it continued using a picklist snapshot from before the retirement for several days.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The refresh interval had been configured conservatively for performance reasons years earlier and was never revisited as the picklist began changing more frequently.

RESOLUTION
The external system's refresh interval was shortened, and a fallback was added so a submission using a retired value returns a clear, specific error rather than a generic failure.

VALIDATION
A test submission using a deliberately retired value now returns a clear error identifying the invalid shipping method by name.

column1: A composite request exceeding the subrequest limit fails with a count that does not match the consumer's own tally of subrequests sent
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer batches several related operations into a single composite API request to reduce the number of individual API calls made per transaction.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A composite request that the consumer counted as within the documented subrequest limit was rejected for exceeding it, with the platform's reported count higher than the consumer's own tally.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The platform's reported subrequest count should match what a consumer would reasonably calculate from the request they constructed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The platform appears to count certain nested operations as multiple subrequests internally, though this has not been fully confirmed against documentation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A support case has been opened with the platform vendor to clarify exactly how nested operations are counted toward the subrequest limit, and a definitive answer is still pending.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the consumer's batching logic now applies a conservative margin below the documented limit while the exact counting behavior is clarified.

VALIDATION
Requests built with the conservative margin have not been rejected in the two weeks since the change, though the precise counting rule is still unconfirmed.

column1: An API consumer's polling interval was tuned for the old data volume and now falls behind as record volume grew, creating a growing backlog
column2:
CONTEXT
An external reporting tool polls the platform every fifteen minutes for newly created records, a fixed interval set when record volume was substantially lower than it is today.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The tool's processing of each poll's results now takes longer than the fifteen-minute interval itself, so polls begin overlapping and the backlog of unprocessed records grows.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The polling interval should be sized appropriately for current record volume so each poll's processing completes before the next one begins.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Overlapping polls led to duplicate processing attempts on some records and an accumulating queue of records not yet reflected in the downstream report.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Record volume for the polled object had grown roughly threefold since the interval was originally configured, a gradual change that had not prompted a corresponding review of the polling configuration.

RESOLUTION
The polling interval was widened and the tool was changed to track its own last-processed timestamp precisely, avoiding overlap regardless of future volume growth.

VALIDATION
The backlog was fully cleared within a day of the change, and no further overlap has occurred in the two weeks since.

column1: A specific combination of query filters occasionally returns a duplicate row for the same record within a single result set
column2:
CONTEXT
An API consumer runs a query combining a relationship filter with a sort on a related object's field, normally returning one row per matching record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
On a small fraction of executions, the exact same query returns the same record twice within a single result set, with no change to the underlying data between runs.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The query should consistently return exactly one row per matching record regardless of how many times it is run.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The duplicate appears intermittently rather than consistently, and re-running the identical query moments later often returns the correct single row.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The intermittent nature has made the duplicate difficult to reproduce on demand, and no consistent pattern in timing, data state, or query variation has been identified so far.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been identified and no fix has been applied; the consumer currently deduplicates results client-side as a temporary safeguard.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to capture the platform's internal query execution identifier on every occurrence to give the platform vendor a specific trace to investigate.

column1: A question using a relative date term the assistant doesn't recognize falls back to showing all-time data without flagging the substitution
column2:
CONTEXT
The natural-language assistant translates relative date phrases like this month or last week into corresponding date range filters for the generated query.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question using a less common relative date phrase produced an answer covering all-time data instead of the intended narrower range, with no indication the phrase was not understood.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An unrecognized date phrase should be flagged to the user rather than silently defaulting to no date filter at all.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assistant's date-parsing logic failed closed by omitting the date filter entirely rather than surfacing a clarification request.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of recent query logs found several other uncommon date phrasings that triggered the same silent fallback, none previously reported since the resulting answers still looked plausible.

RESOLUTION
The date-parsing logic was updated to respond with a clarification request whenever a date phrase cannot be confidently parsed, rather than silently dropping the filter.

VALIDATION
The previously silent phrasings now correctly prompt a clarification question in a follow-up test of ten sample queries.
column6: Unrecognized Date Term Falls Back Silently

column1: A comparison question between two custom objects returns results even after one of the objects was deprecated and hidden from the schema
column2:
CONTEXT
A comparison question type joins two custom objects to compare a metric across them, built when both objects were actively used and visible in the schema.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After one of the two objects was deprecated and hidden from general schema visibility, the comparison question continued returning results referencing it as if still current.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question referencing a deprecated, hidden object should be declined with an explanation rather than answered as if the object were still active.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assistant's cached understanding of the schema had not been refreshed since deprecation, so it still considered the hidden object queryable.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The assistant's schema cache refresh had been scheduled but had not yet run at the time the deprecation took effect, leaving a stale view in place longer than intended.

RESOLUTION
The schema cache was refreshed immediately, and the refresh schedule was tightened to run promptly after any object visibility change is detected.

VALIDATION
The same comparison question now correctly declines to answer and explains that one of the referenced objects is no longer available.

column1: A question that should return zero results instead returns a null-valued row that display code renders as a confusing blank entry
column2:
CONTEXT
An aggregate question, such as counting records matching a rare combination of filters, is expected to return either a count of zero or an empty result set when nothing matches.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
For a specific class of aggregate questions, the generated query instead returns a single row with a null value rather than a proper zero or empty result.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A question with no matching records should present clearly as zero or no results.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The display layer renders the null-valued row as a blank line in the answer, which users have interpreted as a formatting glitch rather than a legitimate answer of zero.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The underlying query behavior producing a null row for this aggregate pattern is understood, but the fix requires a change to the display layer's handling of aggregate results that has not yet been scheduled.

RESOLUTION
A short-term wording change was added so a null-valued aggregate result now displays with explanatory text noting it likely represents zero, pending the proper display layer fix.

VALIDATION
The explanatory wording was confirmed to appear correctly in five test questions producing the null-row pattern.
column6: Null Row Instead Of Zero Results

column1: Two nearly identical phrasings of the same business question about renewals reliably produce different SOQL query shapes and different answers
column2:
CONTEXT
Two members of the renewals team asked what appeared to be the same question about upcoming renewal count, phrased with slightly different wording.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The two phrasings consistently produced different generated queries and different resulting counts, despite both intending to ask about the same set of renewals.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Semantically equivalent phrasings of the same business question should produce the same or clearly comparable answers.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One phrasing implicitly included a status filter the other did not, a distinction the assistant applied inconsistently based on subtle wording cues.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing ten variations of the same underlying question found four distinct implicit filter combinations being applied depending on specific wording choices.

RESOLUTION
The renewals question pattern was rebuilt with an explicit, documented default filter applied consistently regardless of minor wording variation, with the assistant now stating the filter it applied.

VALIDATION
The same ten previously divergent phrasings now all produce the same count and each explicitly states the filter applied.

column1: A question involving a formula field returns the formula's default value rather than its calculated value in certain edge cases
column2:
CONTEXT
A question asking about a record's discount tier relies on a formula field that calculates the tier based on several underlying deal attributes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
For records where one of the formula's underlying fields was blank, the assistant's answer showed the formula's defined default value rather than acknowledging the calculation could not run.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A record where the formula cannot meaningfully calculate should be flagged rather than presented as if it resolved normally to the default.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query read the formula field's stored value directly, which is indistinguishable at the query level from a genuinely calculated default result.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twelve records were confirmed to have a blank underlying field producing the same value as the formula's actual default, making the two cases visually identical in any answer.

RESOLUTION
The question pattern was updated to also check the underlying fields the formula depends on and note when one is blank, rather than presenting the formula's value alone.

VALIDATION
Re-running the question against the twelve affected records now correctly flags the blank underlying field alongside the formula's default value.
column6: Formula Default Instead Of Calculated Value

column1: The assistant answers a permission-restricted question by silently querying with elevated access rather than respecting the asking user's own visibility
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant executes generated queries using a dedicated service account with broad read access, intended only to simplify query construction across the full schema.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A user without visibility into a restricted compensation object was able to receive an answer summarizing data from that object, since the underlying query ran under the broader service account rather than the user's own permissions.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should only return data the asking user would themselves be permitted to see.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No permission check was performed comparing the asking user's actual access against the objects and fields referenced in the generated query before returning the answer.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The affected user's session was reviewed and the query traced to a single instance; access to the compensation object through the assistant was disabled immediately, and the security team was engaged to assess broader exposure.

RESOLUTION
As immediate containment, the assistant was restricted from querying the compensation object and several other sensitive objects, pending a proper per-user permission check in the query execution path.

VALIDATION
A repeat of the original question from the same account now returns a permission-denied response instead of an answer, confirmed across three restricted objects.

column1: A multi-part question is only partially answered, with the assistant addressing the first part and silently dropping the second
column2:
CONTEXT
Users occasionally combine two related questions into a single message, such as asking for a count and also asking for the average value in the same sentence.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The assistant answered only the first part of such combined questions, with no acknowledgment that a second part had been asked.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both parts of a clearly combined question should be answered, or the assistant should explain that only one part could be addressed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The question-parsing step extracted a single primary intent from the message and discarded the secondary request without any note to the user.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A sample of twenty combined questions from recent logs found this pattern occurred in the large majority of cases, with the second part silently dropped every time.

RESOLUTION
The question-parsing step was updated to detect multiple distinct intents in a single message and answer each one, or explicitly note when only a subset could be addressed.

VALIDATION
Re-running the same twenty combined questions after the update produced answers to both parts in every case.

column1: A generated query's implicit row limit truncates results for a legitimately large answer set without informing the user of the truncation
column2:
CONTEXT
Generated queries include a default row limit intended to keep typical answers fast and readable, applied uniformly regardless of the question's actual expected result size.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question legitimately expecting several thousand matching records returned only the default limit's worth of rows, presented as if it were the complete answer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A truncated result should be clearly labeled as partial, with an indication of the actual total matching count.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The answer presented the limited row count with no language distinguishing it from a genuinely complete result set.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Adding a full count query alongside the limited result query is technically straightforward but has a meaningful performance cost for very large objects that has not yet been fully evaluated.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, questions likely to exceed the row limit based on the object and filter combination now include a generic caution note that results may be incomplete, while a proper count-based labeling approach is evaluated.

VALIDATION
The caution note was confirmed to appear on ten test questions known to exceed the row limit, though it does not yet state the actual total count.

column1: A rounding question about win rates gives a different answer depending on whether the assistant computes the percentage before or after rounding intermediate values
column2:
CONTEXT
A win rate question divides closed-won count by total closed count and presents the result as a percentage, a calculation that can be sensitive to when rounding is applied.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The same underlying data produced two different percentage answers on separate occasions, differing by a small but noticeable margin.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The same underlying data should consistently produce the same win rate percentage regardless of when the question is asked.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It is not yet confirmed whether the assistant is rounding intermediate counts inconsistently or whether the underlying data itself changed slightly between the two occasions.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both possibilities remain open, since the two occasions were far enough apart in time that some underlying records could plausibly have changed status in between.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no change has been made to the calculation logic, since altering the rounding behavior without confirming the actual cause risks addressing the wrong issue.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to ask the identical question twice within the same minute against a frozen data snapshot to rule out underlying data change as the explanation.

column1: An unusually phrased question about historical account ownership returns results attributing current ownership incorrectly to a past owner
column2:
CONTEXT
A question asking who owned a specific account at a past point in time relies on historical field tracking data rather than the account's current owner field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
For one unusually phrased version of this question, the answer named a past owner even for a time period after that owner's assignment had ended.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A historical ownership question should correctly bound the named owner to the actual period they held the account.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The generated query appears to have matched the wrong historical tracking record for the requested date, though the exact matching logic responsible has not yet been isolated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The historical tracking data itself was confirmed accurate by a direct check, narrowing the likely cause to how the generated query selects among multiple historical records for a given date, though this has not been fully traced.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the specific query-matching defect has not been isolated well enough to correct with confidence.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to log the full set of historical records the generated query considers for this question pattern, to see exactly which one it selects and why.

column1: A migrated picklist field mapped multiple legacy values to the same target value, collapsing distinctions the business still needs
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration mapping table translated a legacy status field's many granular values into a smaller, simplified set of target picklist values to reduce clutter.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A reporting team found that two legacy statuses tracked separately for compliance purposes had been merged into the same target value, losing a distinction they still needed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The migration mapping should preserve any legacy distinction still required for business or compliance reporting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping table was built primarily for a sales-facing simplification goal, without a review from the compliance reporting team that depended on the finer distinction.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly four hundred migrated records lost the specific distinction, with no way to recover it from the migrated data alone since the collapse happened at mapping time.

RESOLUTION
The original legacy values were recovered from the archived source export and used to re-populate a new field preserving the distinction, run alongside the simplified target field.

VALIDATION
A sample of fifty recovered records was cross-checked against the archived source and confirmed to match the original legacy value exactly.

column1: A batch of migrated records inherited a default currency instead of their original transaction currency because the source export omitted the currency column
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration batch covering several years of historical transactions relied on a source export that was expected to include each transaction's original currency code.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of migrated records showed the organization's default currency instead of the foreign currency the original transaction was actually recorded in.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated transaction should retain its original recorded currency.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The source export for one particular legacy region omitted the currency column entirely, causing the migration tool to fall back to the configured default for those records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Approximately eleven hundred records from the affected region were confirmed to have the incorrect default currency, identified by cross-referencing a separate archived report that did include currency detail.

RESOLUTION
The eleven hundred records were corrected using the currency values recovered from the separate archived report, and the export process for any future migration batches was updated to explicitly require the currency column.

VALIDATION
A sample of one hundred corrected records was verified against the archived report and matched exactly.

column1: A migrated hierarchy of parent-child records lost its ordering, so child records display in an arbitrary sequence instead of their original order
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration moved a hierarchy of ordered child line items under their parent records, where the original system's display order carried business meaning such as a specific sequence of process steps.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The migrated child records display in whatever order the migration tool happened to insert them, unrelated to their original meaningful sequence.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migrated child records should display in their original, meaningful order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No field was migrated to explicitly capture the original sequence, since the target object's default display relied on creation order, which the migration tool did not control precisely enough to preserve it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The source export did include an implicit row order that corresponded to the correct sequence, but this had not been mapped to any field during migration and was only usable if reprocessed from the original export.

RESOLUTION
A new explicit sequence number field was added, populated by reprocessing the original export's row order, and the display was configured to sort by this new field.

VALIDATION
A spot check of twenty parent records confirmed their child items now display in the correct original sequence.

column1: A migration script's deduplication step ran before a required enrichment step, so duplicate detection compared incomplete records and missed true duplicates
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration pipeline enriches incoming records with a standardized company identifier from a reference lookup before running deduplication logic that relies partly on that identifier.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A post-migration audit found duplicate accounts that should have been caught, tracing back to the pipeline's step order having deduplication run before enrichment completed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deduplication should run only after all fields it depends on, including the enriched identifier, are fully populated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records compared for duplication during the affected run were missing the enriched identifier, so pairs that should have matched on it were treated as distinct.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The pipeline's step order had been changed during a performance optimization pass without recognizing the dependency between the two steps, affecting one migration run before being caught.

RESOLUTION
The pipeline's step order was corrected to enrich before deduplicating, and the affected run's records were reprocessed through deduplication with the identifier properly populated.

VALIDATION
Reprocessing identified and merged sixty-three true duplicate pairs that had been missed in the original run.

column1: A record's owner field migrated correctly but its associated team membership records did not migrate, breaking downstream sharing
column2:
CONTEXT
Account sharing in the target system depends on both the owner field and separate team membership records that grant additional collaborators visibility.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Migrated accounts show the correct owner, but the additional team members who should also have visibility do not, since their membership records were not part of the original migration scope.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Team membership records should migrate alongside the owner field to preserve the original sharing intent.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The migration project's original scope focused on the primary owner relationship and did not account for the separate team membership object.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The source system's team membership data does exist in an archived export, but mapping it to the target system's equivalent object has not yet been fully designed, since the two systems model team membership somewhat differently.

RESOLUTION
A first batch of the most active accounts' team memberships has been manually recreated as an interim step, while the full mapping design for the remaining accounts continues.

VALIDATION
The manually recreated batch was confirmed to restore expected visibility for the reviewed accounts, though the majority of accounts still await the full migration.

column1: Migrated records reference a legacy status value that has no equivalent in the target picklist, and they display with a blank status
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration mapping table translates legacy status values to the target system's picklist, built from a list of status values believed to cover the full legacy set.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of migrated records display with a completely blank status field, since their legacy value was not present in the mapping table used during migration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every migrated record should resolve to a defined target status, even if that requires a documented catch-all mapping for less common legacy values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping table had been built from a sample of the most common legacy values and missed several rare ones that appeared only in older archived records.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twenty-two records were found with an unmapped legacy status, all originating from a period predating the current status taxonomy used by the rest of the migrated data.

RESOLUTION
The mapping table was extended to cover the rare legacy values, and the twenty-two affected records were reprocessed to receive their correct target status.

VALIDATION
All twenty-two records were confirmed to display a defined, correct status after reprocessing.

column1: A source system's soft-deleted records were migrated as active because the export did not include the deletion flag
column2:
CONTEXT
The legacy source system marks removed records with a soft-deletion flag rather than physically deleting them, intending such records to be excluded from any downstream export.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of records that had been soft-deleted in the legacy system appeared as normal active records after migration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
