Soft-deleted legacy records should be excluded from migration entirely, or at minimum clearly marked as inactive in the target system.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The export query used for this migration batch did not include the deletion flag as a filter condition, an omission specific to this batch's export configuration.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly ninety records were confirmed to be soft-deleted in the source system but present as active in the migrated target, identified by cross-referencing the source system directly.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate step, the ninety identified records were deactivated in the target system, while the export configuration for any remaining migration batches is being corrected to include the deletion flag filter.

VALIDATION
The ninety records were confirmed deactivated, and a re-export using the corrected filter for a small test batch showed zero soft-deleted records included.

column1: A staged cutover left a subset of records temporarily writable in both the legacy and target systems, and a handful of records were edited in both, creating conflicting versions
column2:
CONTEXT
A phased cutover plan kept the legacy system writable for a transition period to allow users time to adjust, while the target system was also live and accepting edits.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of records were edited independently in both systems during the overlap window, leaving two divergent versions with no clear way to determine which should be considered authoritative.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The overlap window should either prevent dual edits or provide a clear mechanism to reconcile conflicting versions when they occur.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No dual-write detection existed during the overlap period, so the conflicting edits were only discovered afterward through a manual comparison.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Six records were confirmed to have conflicting versions, and for two of them it is not yet clear which system's edit reflects the user's actual final intent.

RESOLUTION
The four records with a clear authoritative edit were resolved in the target system, while the remaining two are being followed up on directly with the users who made the edits.

VALIDATION
The four resolved records were confirmed correct by the respective record owners; the two remaining records are still pending user confirmation.

column1: A migration validation script only sampled the first and last one thousand records of each object, missing formatting errors concentrated in the middle of one large file
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration validation script checks a sample of records from each migrated object rather than every record, sampling from the beginning and end of each source file for practicality.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of formatting errors concentrated in the middle portion of one unusually large source file was missed entirely by the sampling approach and only surfaced through a later user report.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The validation approach should reliably catch formatting errors regardless of where in a large file they happen to be concentrated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The errors were clustered in a middle section that the beginning-and-end sampling strategy never touched, an artifact of how that particular source file happened to be assembled.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly one hundred forty records in the middle section had the formatting error, all from a specific export batch appended into the middle of the larger file.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the affected section was manually re-validated and the records corrected, while a random-sampling approach across the full file is developed to replace the beginning-and-end method.

VALIDATION
The corrected records passed validation, and a manual pass of the remaining large files found no similar clusters elsewhere.

column1: A post-migration reconciliation job flags legitimate business-driven differences as migration errors, creating alert fatigue for the team reviewing it
column2:
CONTEXT
A post-migration reconciliation job compares migrated records against the legacy source on a recurring basis to catch any lingering migration discrepancies.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A growing share of the job's flagged discrepancies turn out to be legitimate differences from normal business activity occurring after migration, rather than actual migration errors.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The reconciliation job should distinguish genuine migration errors from expected post-migration business changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The team reviewing flagged discrepancies has begun spending most of its time dismissing false positives, and it has not yet been determined how to reliably tell the two categories apart programmatically.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of a week's flagged discrepancies found the large majority were legitimate post-migration changes, but no consistent field or pattern has been identified that cleanly separates them from genuine errors.

RESOLUTION
No change has been made to the reconciliation job's logic yet, since a reliable distinguishing pattern has not been found and an overly broad exclusion risks hiding real migration errors.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to tag a full week of flagged discrepancies by hand with their true category, building a labeled dataset to analyze for a distinguishing pattern before changing the job's logic.

column1: A flow's decision element compares text values with mismatched case, so an otherwise matching condition silently fails to branch as expected
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow on the lead object routes leads to a specialist queue when a source field equals a specific text value entered by a web form integration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Leads from the web form stopped routing to the specialist queue after the form vendor changed how it capitalizes the source value.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The routing condition should match the source value regardless of letter case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The decision element's equals comparison is case-sensitive, so the newly capitalized value no longer matched the condition text exactly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The vendor's change was not communicated in advance, and forty-one leads over one week were routed to the default queue instead of the specialist queue, delaying their initial follow-up by nearly two days on average.

RESOLUTION
The condition was rebuilt using a case-insensitive text comparison, and the forty-one misrouted leads were manually reassigned to the specialist queue with a note explaining the delay.

VALIDATION
Test leads submitted with three different capitalizations of the source value all routed correctly to the specialist queue, and the vendor confirmed no further capitalization changes are planned.

column1: A subflow's output variable is never actually returned to the calling flow because the subflow ended through an alternate exit path that skips the return assignment
column2:
CONTEXT
A subflow calculates a shipping estimate and assigns it to an output variable before ending, called from a parent flow that uses the estimate to populate an order field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Orders occasionally save with a blank shipping estimate even though the subflow appears to run without any error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The parent flow should always receive the calculated estimate from the subflow when it completes successfully.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The subflow has a secondary exit path for a rare edge case that ends the interview before the output variable assignment element is reached.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The edge case, an order with no shippable line items, triggers the alternate exit and was not considered when the output assignment was originally placed near the end of the main path.

RESOLUTION
The output variable assignment was moved earlier so both exit paths set it, with a default value of zero for the edge case.

VALIDATION
Ten test orders including the edge case scenario all returned a defined shipping estimate value to the parent flow.
column6: Subflow Output Lost On Alternate Exit

column1: A scheduled flow paused during a full sandbox refresh resumes with references to since-deleted sandbox-specific records
column2:
CONTEXT
A long-running scheduled flow pauses partway through processing and waits for a follow-up condition before resuming, running in a sandbox used for automation testing.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the sandbox was refreshed from production, a previously paused flow interview resumed and immediately failed referencing a record that no longer existed post-refresh.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear what the correct handling should be when a sandbox refresh invalidates a paused flow's referenced records.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The paused interview resumed automatically and threw an unhandled reference error rather than failing gracefully or being cleared by the refresh.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
It has not yet been determined whether sandbox refreshes are expected to clear paused flow interviews or whether this is a known gap in the refresh process.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; the interaction between sandbox refreshes and paused flow interviews has not been resolved.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to open a case with the platform vendor asking for documented behavior on paused flow interviews across a sandbox refresh, since none could be found.
column6: Paused Flow References Deleted Sandbox Data

column1: A flow's collection-filter element silently returns an empty collection when the source collection itself was never initialized on one specific entry path
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow filters a collection of related tasks down to overdue ones, with the source collection normally populated by an earlier get-records element.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
When the flow is entered through a specific update-only path, the filter step returns an empty result even for records with genuinely overdue tasks.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The filter should operate on a properly populated source collection regardless of which entry path triggered the flow.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The update-only entry path skips the get-records element that populates the source collection, so the filter always operates on an empty variable.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The get-records element was only wired into the create path when the flow was first built, and the later addition of the update path did not replicate it.

RESOLUTION
The get-records element was added to the update path as well, though a broader review of whether other elements are similarly missing from that path is still in progress.

VALIDATION
Test records entered through the update path now correctly populate the filtered overdue task collection, pending the wider element review.

column1: A record-triggered flow evaluates entry conditions against the record's pre-update image even when configured to run after the update, confusing two developers debugging it
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow configured to run after a save includes an entry condition checking whether a status field equals a specific value.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two developers separately reported the flow not firing on records where the status had just been changed to the qualifying value.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An after-save entry condition should evaluate against the record's new, saved values.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The entry condition had been built referencing the flow's stored prior-value variable instead of the current record variable, evaluating against the old status.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The condition was copied from an earlier before-save version of the flow during a rebuild, and the variable reference was never updated to match the new after-save context, a gap that went unnoticed since the flow still fired correctly on a second, unrelated save.

RESOLUTION
The entry condition was corrected to reference the current record variable instead of the prior-value variable, so the flow now evaluates against the record's actual saved state.

VALIDATION
A test record updated to the qualifying status now correctly triggers the flow on the first save, matching the behavior both developers had originally expected.
column6: Entry Condition Evaluated On Old Values

column1: A get-records element in a flow returns a randomly ordered result set, so a first-record assumption downstream picks a different record on each run
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow retrieves all open cases for an account and uses the first record in the resulting collection to populate a summary field, assuming a consistent retrieval order.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The summary field occasionally reflects a different case than expected when the flow is re-run against the same unchanged data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The first record used by the flow should be consistent and predictable across runs against the same data.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The get-records element had no explicit sort order configured, so the platform's default retrieval order is not guaranteed to be stable.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is expected behavior when no sort order is specified, a detail not accounted for when the flow was originally built around a first-record assumption.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, an explicit sort by creation date was added to the get-records element, giving a stable and intentional definition of first record.

VALIDATION
Ten repeated runs against the same account now consistently selected the same case as the first record.

column1: A flow triggered by a formula field change does not fire because the formula recalculates without generating a detectable field-level change event
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow is configured to fire when a formula field crosses a risk threshold, with the formula recalculating automatically whenever an underlying input field changes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The flow does not fire even when the formula's displayed value clearly crosses the threshold after an underlying field update.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should detect and act on a qualifying change in the formula field's calculated value.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Record-triggered flows evaluate field-change conditions against the record's stored field values at save time, and formula fields are not stored, so no change event exists for the flow to detect.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a documented platform characteristic of formula fields rather than a defect, but it had not been accounted for when the flow was originally designed around the formula field directly.

RESOLUTION
The flow's entry condition was rebuilt to evaluate the same underlying input fields the formula depends on, rather than the formula field itself.

VALIDATION
A test update to the underlying input field crossing the threshold now correctly triggers the flow.

column1: Two versions of the same flow are simultaneously marked active for different record types after a bulk deployment, and one record type is now running outdated logic
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow was updated and redeployed through a bulk metadata deployment that included several unrelated components alongside the flow's new version.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records of one record type continued behaving according to the flow's prior logic while another record type correctly used the new version.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All record types the flow applies to should run against the same, current active version.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The deployment activated the new flow version but a record-type-specific override elsewhere in the org still pinned one record type to the prior version number.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The override had been set months earlier for an unrelated testing purpose and was never removed, a detail the deployment process had no visibility into.

RESOLUTION
The record-type-specific override was removed, and the deployment checklist now includes a step to search for any version-pinning overrides before activating a new flow version.

VALIDATION
Records of the previously affected record type were confirmed to run the current flow version in a follow-up test.

column1: A flow's numeric rounding element rounds up for currency fields but rounds down for plain number fields, producing inconsistent totals across two related figures
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow calculates both a currency total and a related unit-count figure from the same underlying line item collection, rounding each to a whole number for display.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The two rounded figures occasionally imply a different underlying value than each other, confusing users who expect them to be mathematically consistent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Rounding behavior should be consistent, or the discrepancy in edge cases should at least be explainable.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The currency field's platform-level rounding convention differs from the plain number field's, a difference not previously noticed since it only produces a visible discrepancy at specific fractional values.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This appears related to differing default rounding conventions between the two field types, though it has not yet been confirmed whether this is documented platform behavior or an inconsistency worth escalating.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the flow now applies an explicit consistent rounding formula to both figures rather than relying on each field type's default.

VALIDATION
Ten previously inconsistent test cases now produce matching rounded figures, though the underlying field-type rounding difference itself remains unconfirmed.

column1: A time-based scheduled path built around a specific hour breaks silently after clocks shift for daylight saving time
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled path on a record-triggered flow fires a reminder exactly two hours after a case is created, calculated using the org's default time zone.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reminders sent in the days immediately following a daylight saving time change arrived either an hour early or an hour late.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The two-hour reminder offset should remain accurate regardless of daylight saving time transitions.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The scheduled path's offset calculation does not appear to consistently account for the time change during the transition window, though the exact internal mechanism has not been confirmed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The misalignment was only observed in the days immediately surrounding the transition and self-corrected afterward, making it difficult to reproduce on demand outside that window.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the reminder offset was padded with an extra buffer during the week of any known time change, reviewed manually twice a year ahead of each transition.

VALIDATION
The buffered offset produced correctly timed reminders through the most recent transition, though the underlying calculation issue itself remains unresolved.
column6: Scheduled Path Breaks After Time Change

column1: A middleware queue processes messages strictly first-in-first-out across all record types, so a burst of low-priority updates delays a handful of urgent account creates behind it
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware queue processes all inbound integration messages in strict arrival order regardless of record type, feeding both routine updates and urgent new account creations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A large batch of routine product updates delayed several urgent new account creations by over an hour, since the queue had no concept of priority.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Urgent record types like new account creation should not be blocked behind a large batch of lower-priority updates.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The queue's single-lane design processes every message in the order received, with no mechanism to reorder by message type.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The queue was originally designed when message volume was low enough that ordering delays were negligible, an assumption that no longer held once batch update volume grew.

RESOLUTION
The queue was split into a fast lane for account creation messages and a standard lane for routine updates, processed independently.

VALIDATION
A repeat of the same batch scenario showed account creations completing within two minutes regardless of the routine update volume in the standard lane.

column1: An integration's retry logic treats a validation error the same as a transient error, endlessly retrying a record that will never succeed until manually removed
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration's retry mechanism reattempts any failed record on a fixed schedule, originally designed around transient network and timeout failures.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A record failing due to a genuine data validation error was retried hundreds of times over several days with no chance of ever succeeding.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A validation failure should be distinguished from a transient failure and routed to manual review rather than retried indefinitely.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retry logic checks only whether a call failed, not the failure's error category, so validation and transient errors are handled identically.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Six other records were found in the same endlessly retrying state, all failing on validation errors that retrying could never resolve, together accounting for several thousand wasted retry attempts over the preceding month.

RESOLUTION
The retry logic was updated to inspect the error type and route validation failures directly to a manual-review queue instead of the retry schedule, stopping the wasted attempts immediately.

VALIDATION
The six affected records stopped retrying and appeared in the manual-review queue as expected after the change, and retry volume for the integration dropped noticeably the same day.

column1: A partner's outbound feed occasionally sends the same record twice within the same file under two different batch identifiers, and the integration's deduplication only checks within a single batch
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner's nightly feed occasionally splits a single day's records across two batch identifiers within the same file due to an internal batching quirk on the partner's side.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of records were created twice because the same record appeared in both batch identifiers within one file, and deduplication only compared records inside the same batch.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deduplication should catch a repeated record regardless of which batch identifier it was tagged with within the same file.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The deduplication check keyed off batch identifier as a scoping boundary, so records with matching content but different batch tags were never compared.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Fourteen duplicate records were found over one month, all traced to the partner's batching quirk rather than any issue with the source data itself.

RESOLUTION
The deduplication check was widened to compare across all batches within the same file, and the fourteen duplicates were merged.

VALIDATION
A follow-up file containing the same cross-batch duplication pattern was correctly deduplicated on the next scheduled run.

column1: A field mapped to sync a picklist value uses the value's label from the partner system, which does not match the API name expected on the receiving side after a recent picklist restructure
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration mapping translates a partner system's status label directly into the corresponding picklist value on the receiving side, previously a reliable one-to-one match.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a picklist restructure changed several API names while keeping display labels similar, incoming records began failing with an invalid picklist value error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The mapping should resolve to the correct API name regardless of label changes on either side.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping table stored the receiving side's old API name, which the restructure had changed even though the visible label looked unchanged.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The restructure's change log was not cross-checked against the integration's mapping table before the restructure was deployed, and other mapping tables sharing the same picklist have not yet been audited.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate fix, the mapping table for this integration was updated with the new API names, while a broader audit of every other mapping table referencing the same picklist is still pending.

VALIDATION
A batch of previously failing records was resubmitted and processed successfully, though the wider mapping audit has not yet confirmed no other integration shares the same gap.

column1: An integration user's session times out mid-batch during an unusually long-running sync, and the partial batch is neither fully committed nor cleanly rolled back
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly sync job processes a large batch of records under a single long-lived integration session, normally completing well within its timeout window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
On an unusually large run, the session timed out partway through, leaving some records synced and others not, with no clear boundary recorded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear whether the correct behavior should be a full rollback or a resumable checkpoint, since this scenario had not been previously planned for.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The job's logging does not clearly indicate which records processed before the timeout, making the partial state's exact boundary hard to determine after the fact.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A manual record comparison against the source system is underway to establish which records synced before the timeout.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the scope of the partial batch is not yet established well enough to safely reconcile it.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to complete the manual comparison and then design batch checkpointing so a future timeout has a clear, recoverable boundary.
column6: Session Timeout Mid-Batch Leaves Partial State

column1: A newly onboarded partner was mistakenly granted access to a shared integration queue meant for a different partner, and its records intermixed with existing traffic for several hours before being separated
column2:
CONTEXT
A shared integration queue was originally intended for a single partner, with access controlled through a configuration entry identifying the authorized partner system.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During onboarding of a new, unrelated partner, its integration was mistakenly pointed at the existing shared queue instead of a newly provisioned one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each partner integration should write only to its own dedicated queue.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Records from both partners intermixed in the shared queue for several hours before the misconfiguration was noticed during a routine volume check.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The intermixed records were traced by partner-specific identifier fields on every record, allowing them to be cleanly separated, though onboarding had no step verifying queue assignment before go-live.

RESOLUTION
The new partner was repointed to its own dedicated queue, the intermixed records were separated and reprocessed, and onboarding now includes an explicit queue-assignment verification step.

VALIDATION
A post-separation audit confirmed all records were correctly attributed to their originating partner with no remaining cross-contamination, and the next partner onboarded followed the updated checklist without incident.
column6: Wrong Partner Granted Shared Queue Access

column1: A middleware step normalizes phone numbers to a specific country format, corrupting numbers already correctly formatted for other supported countries
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware normalization step reformats inbound phone numbers to a consistent format, originally built and tested against a single country's numbering pattern.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Phone numbers from other supported countries are being reformatted incorrectly, stripping or misplacing digits that do not fit the original country's pattern.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The normalization step should correctly format phone numbers for every supported country, not only the one it was originally built for.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Numbers from at least three other countries come out with visibly incorrect formatting, though the full list of affected countries has not yet been confirmed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The normalization logic uses a single hardcoded pattern rather than a country-aware set of rules, a limitation not apparent until international volume grew.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, normalization has been disabled for the three confirmed affected countries, passing their numbers through unformatted, while a country-aware rule set is developed.

VALIDATION
Numbers from the three affected countries now arrive unmodified rather than corrupted, though proper formatting for them is not yet implemented.

column1: An integration health-check monitor reports the connection as healthy even though the underlying data sync has been silently failing for several days
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration health-check monitor pings the partner endpoint on a fixed schedule and reports the connection as healthy whenever the ping succeeds.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The monitor showed a healthy status throughout a multi-day period during which the actual data sync had been failing for an unrelated authentication reason.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The health check should reflect the actual success of data synchronization, not just basic connectivity to the endpoint.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The ping check only confirmed the endpoint was reachable, which remained true even while every actual sync call was failing on an expired credential.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No sync had completed successfully in four days, a gap only discovered when a downstream team noticed stale data, not through the monitor itself.

RESOLUTION
The health check was rebuilt to also verify a recent successful sync timestamp rather than connectivity alone, and the expired credential was renewed.

VALIDATION
A simulated authentication failure now correctly flips the health check to unhealthy within one monitoring cycle.
column6: Health Check Blind To Sync Failures

column1: A field sync depends on a lookup that was recently converted to a master-detail relationship, and the sync's original field-level permission no longer applies under the new relationship type
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration writes to a child object field through a lookup relationship, relying on a field-level permission granted specifically for that relationship type.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the lookup was converted to a master-detail relationship as part of an unrelated data model change, the integration began failing with a field access error.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration's write access should continue functioning across the relationship type change, or the change should have been coordinated with integration owners.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The master-detail conversion altered how field-level access is inherited on the child object, and the integration user's original permission grant no longer covered the field under the new model.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The data model change had been reviewed for functional impact but not specifically for its effect on the integration user's field-level permissions.

RESOLUTION
The integration user's permission set was updated to explicitly grant access under the new master-detail model.

VALIDATION
A test write from the integration succeeded immediately after the permission update, with no further access errors observed.
column6: Field Permission Gap After Relationship Conversion

column1: Two integrations independently create the same external record when a shared trigger condition briefly overlaps during a batch window
column2:
CONTEXT
Two separately maintained integrations both listen for the same qualifying record condition to create a corresponding record in two different downstream systems.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of records triggered both integrations within the same brief batch window, and one of the two downstream systems ended up with a duplicate record.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each integration should create its downstream record independently without either one being duplicated due to the other's timing.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear whether the duplication originates from one integration re-triggering itself or from an unexpected interaction between the two separate integrations.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Both integration teams have reviewed their own logic in isolation and found no obvious defect, leaving the interaction between the two as the remaining unexplored area.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no fix has been applied, since neither integration team's individual logic review has explained the duplication so far.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is a joint session between both integration teams to trace a single occurrence end to end across both systems' logs simultaneously.

column1: A permission set assignment expiration date was set but the platform does not automatically revoke access once that date passes, leaving temporary access active indefinitely
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission set was assigned to a contractor with an expiration date entered on the assignment, intended to grant access only for the duration of a short engagement.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A routine access review found the contractor's access still active more than two months after the entered expiration date had passed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Access should be automatically revoked once the assignment's expiration date passes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The expiration date field is informational only and does not trigger automatic removal of the underlying permission set assignment.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No misuse of the extended access was found in the audit trail, but the assumption that the expiration date was self-enforcing had not been previously verified by any team.

RESOLUTION
The contractor's access was revoked immediately upon discovery, and a scheduled job was built to automatically remove any permission set assignment past its entered expiration date.

VALIDATION
A test assignment with a past-dated expiration was correctly removed by the new scheduled job within one run cycle.

column1: A scheduled report export job that bypasses row-level sharing began emailing its output to a broader distribution list than intended, reaching users who lack access to the underlying records
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled export job runs under a system-level context that bypasses row-level sharing, generating a daily attachment of sensitive case records for a small finance distribution list.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An unrelated distribution list consolidation project added several general finance staff to the list, and the export began reaching users without direct record-level access to the underlying cases.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The export's recipient list should be reviewed against actual record-level access whenever the underlying distribution list changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The consolidation project changed the distribution list without anyone flagging that the export depended on its membership matching a narrower access group.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Delivery logs confirmed the broadened list received nine deliveries over three weeks before being caught during a routine review, with no evidence the attachments were forwarded further.

RESOLUTION
The recipient list was immediately narrowed back to the original access-matched group, and a dependency note was added documenting the export's reliance on it.

VALIDATION
A follow-up delivery to the corrected list was confirmed to exclude all users without underlying record-level access, verified against current sharing rules.

column1: A security review found an integration user account with an unused but still-active API-only login enabled from years earlier, alongside its still-valid credential
column2:
CONTEXT
A periodic security review inventories all active integration user accounts and their associated credentials against a list of currently used integrations.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One integration user account was found with API-only login enabled and a valid credential, but no corresponding active integration could be identified as still using it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every active integration account should map to a currently used integration, with unused accounts deactivated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The account remained active and credentialed years after the integration it was believed to support was decommissioned, since no offboarding step existed for retired integrations.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Login history showed no successful authentication using the account in over a year, consistent with it being genuinely dormant rather than quietly still in use.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate precaution, the account's credential was rotated and its login was restricted pending a short confirmation window, rather than deactivating it outright in case an undocumented dependency exists.

VALIDATION
No failed login attempts or dependency reports surfaced during the confirmation window, and full deactivation is scheduled once the window closes.

column1: A custom Apex class runs with elevated sharing settings and was found to be callable from an unauthenticated context due to a missing access check
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom Apex class supporting a public-facing form runs without sharing enforcement to allow the form to create records on behalf of anonymous visitors.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A code review found the class had no explicit check limiting which fields or record types an anonymous caller could specify beyond what the form's interface normally sends.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The class should validate and constrain anonymous input regardless of what the form's interface is designed to send.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No unauthorized use was found in a review of recent submissions, but the class's lack of server-side validation means it currently relies on the form as the only control.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A full input-validation layer has been scoped but not yet built, since the fix requires coordinating with the form's data model to define the correct allowed value ranges.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, request logging was added to flag any submission with an unexpected field combination for manual review, while the full validation layer is developed.

VALIDATION
The interim logging has flagged zero anomalous submissions in the two weeks since deployment, though the underlying validation gap remains open.
column6: Elevated Apex Class Missing Access Check

column1: An emergency break-glass administrator account used during an incident was not deactivated afterward, and its use was not logged with a required justification
column2:
CONTEXT
A break-glass administrator account exists for emergency use during incidents when normal administrative access is unavailable, intended to be activated, used, and deactivated with a logged justification each time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A post-incident review found the account had been activated during a recent outage but never deactivated afterward, and no justification had been logged.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The break-glass account should be deactivated immediately after its emergency use concludes, with justification logged at time of activation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The account remained active for eleven days after the incident was resolved, with no record explaining why it had been activated in the first place.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The engineer who activated the account confirmed it was used only for the incident's legitimate remediation steps, but the process had no automated reminder to deactivate it afterward.

RESOLUTION
The account was deactivated immediately upon discovery, and an automated alert was configured to notify security whenever the break-glass account remains active more than one hour.

VALIDATION
A test activation confirmed the new alert fired correctly within the one-hour window.

column1: A recently rotated API credential was found still cached and in active use by a legacy scheduled job that had not been included in the rotation communication
column2:
CONTEXT
A routine credential rotation was performed for a shared integration account, with the rotation communicated to all known consuming systems ahead of time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A legacy scheduled job continued authenticating successfully using what should have been the old, rotated-out credential value, days after the rotation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All consumers of the rotated credential should either use the new value or fail authentication after rotation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been determined how the legacy job is still succeeding with the old credential, since the platform's own records indicate the credential was fully rotated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team has been engaged and is treating this as an active investigation; whether the job is using a cached value, a secondary undocumented credential, or something else has not been established.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and the legacy job has been temporarily disabled as a precaution while the credential behavior is investigated.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to enable verbose authentication logging on the shared integration account to capture exactly which credential value the job presents on its next attempt.

column1: A dashboard shared externally through a public link exposed underlying record-level detail beyond the intended aggregate view
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard summarizing aggregate case volume was shared through a public link for an external stakeholder presentation, intended to show only chart-level totals.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A team member testing the public link found that clicking into a chart component revealed the underlying individual case records with customer-identifying detail.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A publicly shared dashboard should expose only its aggregate view, with no drill-through to underlying record detail.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The public link inherited the dashboard's normal drill-through behavior, which is enabled by default and had not been disabled before sharing.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Access logs for the public link showed only the internal team member's test click, with no evidence of external access to the drill-through view before it was disabled.

RESOLUTION
The public link was disabled immediately upon discovery, and a reissued link was configured with drill-through explicitly turned off before being shared again.

VALIDATION
The reissued public link was tested and confirmed to show only the aggregate chart view with no drill-through option available.
column6: Public Dashboard Link Exposed Record Detail

column1: An audit of login history found repeated failed login attempts against several service accounts originating from an unexpected external network range
column2:
CONTEXT
A routine login history audit reviews failed authentication attempts across all account types on a recurring schedule.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The audit found a cluster of failed login attempts against three service accounts originating from a network range not associated with any known legitimate integration.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Login attempts against service accounts should originate only from known, expected network ranges.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
All attempts failed, and no successful login from the unexpected range was found in the same period, but the source of the attempts has not been identified.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team was engaged immediately and opened an active investigation; the three service accounts' credentials were rotated as a precaution while the source of the attempts is traced.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate containment step, login IP restrictions were applied to the three affected service accounts limiting access to their known legitimate ranges, pending full resolution of the investigation.

VALIDATION
No further login attempts from the unexpected range have succeeded or been observed against the restricted accounts since the containment was applied.
column6: Failed Login Attempts From Unexpected Range

column1: A permission set group inherited a broader object permission than any of its individual member permission sets intended, due to how the platform combines permission set groups
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission set group was assembled from several individual permission sets, each independently reviewed and approved for a narrow, specific scope of access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the combined permission set group granted delete access on an object that no individual member permission set granted on its own.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A permission set group's combined access should not exceed the union of its individual members' intended grants.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One member permission set granted delete at the object level while another restricted it at the record-type level, and the platform's combination logic resolved the conflict in favor of the broader grant.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This combination behavior is a documented characteristic of how permission set groups resolve overlapping settings, but it had not been accounted for during the group's original review.

RESOLUTION
The overly broad member permission set was corrected to remove the object-level delete grant, relying solely on the more specific record-type-level setting.

VALIDATION
The combined permission set group was retested and confirmed to no longer grant delete access beyond the intended record types.
column6: Permission Set Group Broader Than Members

column1: A departing employee's personal device retained an active mobile session that was not remotely revoked as part of the standard offboarding checklist
column2:
CONTEXT
The standard offboarding checklist deactivates a departing employee's platform user record and is assumed to also terminate any active mobile app session on their device.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A departing employee's mobile app was found still able to access cached case data several days after their user record was deactivated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deactivating a user record should also terminate any active session on a mobile device tied to that account.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been confirmed whether the cached session genuinely allows continued live access or only displays previously cached data with no live connection.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team has been notified and is assessing scope; the mobile app vendor's documentation on session revocation after deactivation has not yet been fully reviewed.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since it is not yet confirmed whether this represents live access or only stale cached data requiring a different remediation approach.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to test the same scenario on a controlled device to determine whether deactivation terminates the live session or only blocks new data retrieval.
column6: Mobile Session Not Revoked At Offboarding

column1: A report's date-range filter uses equals-this-fiscal-quarter but the org's fiscal year settings were changed mid-year, and the report continues using the old fiscal boundary definition
column2:
CONTEXT
A quarterly performance report filters records using a relative equals-this-fiscal-quarter date range, which depends on the org's configured fiscal year start month.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the fiscal year start month was changed mid-year for a business reorganization, the report continued to show records from the old quarter boundaries for several days.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The relative fiscal quarter filter should immediately reflect the newly configured fiscal year settings.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report's cached filter definition did not refresh automatically when the org-wide fiscal year setting changed, continuing to use the prior boundary calculation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three other reports relying on the same relative fiscal filter were found showing the same stale boundary, all resolved once each report was manually reopened and resaved.

RESOLUTION
All four affected reports were resaved to pick up the new fiscal year setting, and a note was added to the fiscal year change checklist reminding teams to resave dependent reports.

VALIDATION
The reports were confirmed to reflect the new fiscal quarter boundaries immediately after resaving.
column6: Stale Fiscal Boundary After Settings Change

column1: A scheduled dashboard refresh silently fails for one specific component whenever the underlying report returns exactly zero rows, leaving the previous run's chart displayed indefinitely
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard component displays a chart of open escalations by team, refreshed automatically each morning from its underlying report.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
On mornings when no team had any open escalations, the component continued displaying the prior day's chart instead of an empty or zero state.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The component should refresh to reflect a genuine zero-row result just as reliably as any non-zero result.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The component's refresh logic silently skipped updating its cached chart image whenever the report returned no rows, an edge case not handled by the refresh routine.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This occurred on four mornings over two months, each time going unnoticed until a viewer questioned why escalations shown did not match what they knew to be true.

RESOLUTION
The refresh routine was updated to explicitly render a zero-state chart when the report returns no rows, rather than skipping the update.

VALIDATION
A test report forced to return zero rows now correctly refreshes the dashboard component to a clear zero-state chart.

column1: A report folder's sharing settings were copied from a template folder that granted broader edit access than intended, letting unauthorized users modify a widely distributed report
column2:
CONTEXT
A new report folder was created by copying settings from an existing template folder to save setup time, intended to be restricted to a small analytics team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several users outside the analytics team were found to have edit access to reports in the new folder, tracing back to broader sharing inherited from the template.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The new folder's sharing should have been reviewed and scoped down rather than inheriting the template's broader settings.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The template folder had been configured for a different, larger audience, and its sharing settings carried over unchanged when used as a starting point.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No unauthorized edits to the widely distributed reports were found in version history, but the excess access had existed for roughly three weeks before being caught.

RESOLUTION
The folder's sharing was corrected to the intended narrow analytics-team scope, and new folders created from a template now require an explicit sharing review before publishing.

VALIDATION
A follow-up access check confirmed only the intended analytics team retains edit access to the folder.

column1: Two report subscribers viewing an identical dashboard link at the same time see different currency conversion rates applied to the same figures
column2:
CONTEXT
A multi-currency dashboard converts figures to each viewer's personal currency setting, sourcing exchange rates from the org's dated currency conversion table.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two viewers with the same personal currency setting, looking at the identical dashboard link at the same time, reported different converted totals.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Viewers with the same currency setting should see identical converted totals for the same dashboard at the same time.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One viewer's converted total matched a slightly older exchange rate than the other, suggesting some form of caching inconsistency, though this has not been fully confirmed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The dashboard rendering pipeline includes a caching layer whose refresh timing relative to exchange rate updates has not yet been fully mapped.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the exchange rate table's update process was moved to run at a fixed time with more buffer before the dashboard's own refresh window, reducing the overlap risk.

VALIDATION
No further discrepancy has been reported in the two weeks since the timing adjustment, though the underlying caching interaction has not been fully diagnosed.
column6: Divergent Currency Rates For Same Dashboard

column1: A summary formula referencing a picklist's sort order breaks after the picklist values were reordered, silently changing which value the formula treats as first
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom summary formula identifies the earliest stage a deal reached in a reporting period by referencing the picklist's defined value order rather than a dedicated sequence field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the stage picklist's values were reordered to reflect an updated sales process, the formula began identifying a different, incorrect stage as earliest.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The formula's notion of earliest stage should remain accurate regardless of picklist value reordering, or should be built on a definition not tied to display order.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula's logic implicitly relied on the picklist's positional order, an undocumented dependency that broke silently the moment the order changed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The picklist reorder had been reviewed for its direct effect on the sales process but not for its indirect effect on formulas depending on value order.

RESOLUTION
The formula was rebuilt to reference an explicit stage-sequence custom field instead of the picklist's display order, removing the hidden dependency.

VALIDATION
Ten historical deals were re-checked against the rebuilt formula and confirmed to show the correct earliest stage.

column1: A report built with a custom date field shows records one day off for entries created near midnight, inconsistent with the same records shown correctly in a native date field
column2:
CONTEXT
A report groups records by a custom date field derived from a datetime value, alongside a native date field on the same object used for comparison.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records created within roughly an hour of midnight occasionally appear grouped under the following day in the custom field's grouping but the correct day in the native field.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both date representations should group a given record under the same calendar day.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The custom field's derivation formula converts the underlying datetime to a date using a fixed time zone offset, while the native field uses the viewing user's own time zone.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a known difference in how formula-derived dates versus native date fields handle time zone conversion, not previously surfaced since it only affects records near the midnight boundary.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the report was changed to group by the native date field instead of the custom formula field for any calendar-day-level analysis.

VALIDATION
A sample of ten previously misgrouped near-midnight records now group under the correct day using the native field.
column6: Custom Date Field Off By One Day Near Midnight

column1: A report's summary formula referencing a custom hierarchical account field pulls the value from the immediate parent account rather than the ultimate top-level parent for multi-level hierarchies
column2:
CONTEXT
A report includes a summary formula referencing a custom field meant to capture an account's ultimate top-level parent in a multi-level hierarchy, used to roll up enterprise customer metrics.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
For accounts nested three or more levels deep, the formula returned the immediate parent's value instead of the true top-level parent, understating the consolidated metric.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The formula should resolve to the ultimate top-level parent regardless of how many intermediate levels exist.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula only traversed a single parent level, a limitation that went unnoticed since most hierarchies in the org are only two levels deep.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Eighteen enterprise hierarchies three or more levels deep were found affected, each understating its consolidated metric by referencing an intermediate parent instead of the top-level one.

RESOLUTION
The formula was replaced with a custom rollup field maintained by a batch job that walks the full hierarchy depth, correctly resolving to the top-level parent regardless of nesting.

VALIDATION
The eighteen affected hierarchies were recalculated using the new rollup field and verified against a hand-traced walk for three of the deepest cases.
column6: Matrix Grand Total Double-Counts Shared Row

column1: A dashboard filter dependent on a custom field-level security setting silently omits data for viewers who lack visibility to the filtering field itself, without any error indicating the omission
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard filter lets viewers narrow results by a custom region field, with each report run as the viewing user according to their own field-level access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A viewer without field-level access to the region field saw an empty dashboard with no indication that the filter itself was the reason.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A viewer lacking access to a filtering field should see a clear message explaining the limitation rather than a silently empty result.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The filter attempted to apply against a field the viewer could not see, which resolved to no matching records rather than an error or explanation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three other users were found to share the same restricted field-level access and would have encountered the identical silent empty result.

RESOLUTION
The dashboard now detects when a viewer lacks access to the filtering field and displays an explanatory message instead of an empty chart, though this does not restore data access itself.

VALIDATION
A test using one of the three affected accounts confirmed the message now appears, though those users still cannot see filtered results without a separate access change.
column6: Filter Field Visibility Silently Omits Data

column1: A historical trending report's data appears to reset every time the report's underlying report type is edited, even for unrelated cosmetic changes
column2:
CONTEXT
A historical trending report accumulates snapshot data over time based on a custom report type, used to track case volume trends across many months.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An unrelated cosmetic edit to the report type's label caused the trending report's accumulated historical data to appear to reset to empty.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Cosmetic changes to a report type should not affect previously accumulated historical trend data.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The trending report's snapshot storage is keyed internally to the report type's identifier in a way sensitive to certain metadata changes, which the label edit inadvertently triggered.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is a known platform sensitivity around historical trend report type edits, confirmed by reproducing the same reset behavior on a test report type in a sandbox.

RESOLUTION
The report type's label was reverted, which restored visibility into the previously accumulated data, and a guidance note was added warning against any future edits to trend-tracked report types.

VALIDATION
After reverting the label, the trending report's full historical data range was confirmed visible again.
column6: Trend Data Resets On Report Type Edit

column1: An analytics snapshot job that populates a historical trending object stopped running after a scheduled job limit was reached by unrelated jobs, and nobody was notified
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled analytics snapshot job runs nightly to populate a historical trending object used for long-range volume reporting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The snapshot job stopped running for two weeks, discovered only when a trend report showed a flat, unchanging line for that period.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The snapshot job should either run reliably every night or generate a visible alert if it cannot be scheduled.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The org's total count of scheduled jobs reached a platform-imposed limit due to unrelated jobs added by other teams, silently preventing the snapshot job from being rescheduled each night.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
It is not yet confirmed which specific unrelated jobs pushed the org over the limit, since several teams have independently scheduled jobs without a shared inventory.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet; the snapshot job remains unscheduled while the full inventory of scheduled jobs across the org is being compiled to identify what to consolidate or remove.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to complete the org-wide scheduled job inventory and identify enough low-value jobs to remove to free capacity for the snapshot job to run again.
column6: Snapshot Job Silently Stopped By Job Limit

column1: A case email thread displays messages sent from two different support queues as if from a single continuous conversation, confusing agents about which team owns the reply
column2:
CONTEXT
A case transferred between two support queues retains its full email thread history, displaying all messages together in one continuous conversation view.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents in the receiving queue could not tell which messages were sent by the original queue versus their own team, leading to duplicate or contradictory replies.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each message in the thread should clearly indicate which queue or team sent it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The thread view displayed sender name and timestamp but no queue attribution, a detail not included when the view was originally designed for single-queue cases.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of recently transferred cases found several instances of agents unknowingly duplicating a reply already sent by the prior queue, occasionally sending conflicting information to the same customer within minutes of each other.

RESOLUTION
The thread view was updated to display the originating queue name alongside each message's sender and timestamp, giving receiving agents immediate context before replying.

VALIDATION
A test transfer between two queues confirmed each message in the resulting thread now clearly shows its originating queue, and a follow-up agent survey confirmed the change resolved the confusion.

column1: An email routing rule based on keyword matching in the subject line misclassifies a billing question as a technical case because it happened to include a technical product name
column2:
CONTEXT
An email routing rule scans the subject line for keywords associated with technical issues and routes matching messages to the technical support queue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A billing inquiry that happened to mention a technical product name in its subject line was misrouted to the technical queue instead of billing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Routing should reflect the actual nature of the inquiry rather than incidental keyword overlap.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The keyword match triggered purely on the product name's presence, without considering the surrounding context of the message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of routing history over one month found nine similar misclassifications, all involving a product name that also happens to resemble a technical keyword, each adding an unnecessary handoff delay before reaching the correct billing team.

RESOLUTION
The routing rule was refined to exclude the ambiguous keyword when it appears alongside common billing-related terms, and the nine misrouted cases were manually reassigned to billing.

VALIDATION
A test email combining the product name with billing language now correctly routes to the billing queue, and a batch of historical subject lines was replayed with no new misclassifications.
column6: Keyword Routing Misclassifies By Product Name

column1: A templated email's conditional merge logic shows a blank section instead of the intended fallback text when the referenced record field is empty
column2:
CONTEXT
An outbound email template includes a conditional section meant to display a fallback message whenever a specific case field is left blank.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers with a blank field received an email with a visibly empty section instead of the intended fallback message.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear whether the template's conditional check is faulty or whether the field is populated with an unexpected non-blank placeholder upstream.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The conditional logic does not trigger the fallback for the affected records, but a spot check found the field genuinely empty, ruling out the simplest explanation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The template's conditional syntax has been reviewed against documentation with no obvious error found, leaving the exact evaluation behavior for this field type unconfirmed.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the conditional check appears correctly written and the actual point of failure has not been isolated.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to send test emails with the field set to several different blank-like values to determine which value the check fails to catch.
column6: Missing Fallback Text On Blank Field

column1: Case creation from a forwarded email captures the forwarding employee as the contact instead of the original customer named in the forwarded content
column2:
CONTEXT
An internal employee occasionally forwards a customer's email to the support mailbox on the customer's behalf when the customer cannot reach the mailbox directly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Cases created from such forwarded emails list the forwarding employee as the contact rather than the original customer named in the forwarded message.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Case creation should recognize the original sender named within a forwarded message body as the contact when a forward pattern is detected.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Case creation always attributes the contact based on the immediate sender's address, with no logic to parse forwarded content for the original sender.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Building reliable parsing of forwarded message headers across different email client formats has proven more complex than initially expected and is still being evaluated.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, employees forwarding on a customer's behalf are now asked to note the customer's name and email in the forward's own message body for agents to manually correct.

VALIDATION
The manual correction process has been used successfully for the forwarded cases received since the workaround was introduced, pending a proper automated parsing solution.

column1: An email attachment virus-scanning step occasionally times out on larger legitimate files, silently dropping the attachment rather than delivering it or flagging the failure
column2:
CONTEXT
Inbound email attachments pass through a virus-scanning step before being saved to the case, with the step normally completing well within its allotted time for typical file sizes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers submitting larger legitimate diagnostic files found their attachments missing from the resulting case with no explanation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A scan timeout should be surfaced as a clear failure rather than resulting in a silently dropped attachment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
When the scan exceeds its time allotment on a larger file, the email-to-case process proceeds without the attachment and without logging the timeout as an error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The scanning vendor has confirmed larger files can occasionally exceed the current timeout, but has not yet provided a clear timeline for increasing the allotted scan time.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, a note is now automatically added to any case where a scan timeout is detected, alerting the agent that an attachment may be missing.

VALIDATION
The interim note was confirmed to appear correctly in five test cases with deliberately oversized attachments, though the underlying timeout limit remains unchanged.
column6: Virus Scan Timeout Drops Large Attachments

column1: A support mailbox's spam filter began quarantining legitimate customer replies after a filter rule was tightened following an unrelated phishing incident
column2:
CONTEXT
The support mailbox's spam filter rules were tightened organization-wide following an unrelated phishing incident detected in a different mailbox.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several legitimate customer replies to open cases began landing in quarantine instead of reaching the support mailbox after the filter change.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Spam filter tightening applied for an unrelated incident should not quarantine legitimate ongoing case correspondence.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The tightened rule flagged replies containing quoted prior message content with embedded links, a pattern common in legitimate case threads but also resembling certain phishing patterns.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nineteen legitimate replies were found in quarantine over three days, all sharing the quoted-link pattern that triggered the tightened rule, delaying resolution on several already-aging cases.

RESOLUTION
An exception was added for the support mailbox exempting quoted-thread replies to known open cases from the tightened rule, and the nineteen quarantined replies were released and delivered to their cases.

VALIDATION
No further legitimate replies were quarantined in the week following the exception, confirmed by a manual review of the quarantine log alongside the security team that had requested the original tightening.
column6: Spam Filter Tightening Quarantined Legitimate Replies

column1: An email-to-case setup creates a new case for every reply in a thread instead of appending to the existing case, after a change to how the thread identifier is generated
column2:
CONTEXT
Email-to-case matches inbound replies to an existing case using a thread identifier embedded in the message, generated by the email service handling inbound mail.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the email service updated how it generates thread identifiers, replies stopped matching their existing case and instead created a new case each time.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Replies to an existing case thread should continue appending to that case regardless of changes on the email service's side.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The matching logic expected the identifier in a specific format that the email service's update changed, breaking the match for every affected message.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly two hundred duplicate cases were created over two days before the pattern was identified and traced to the email service's update notes.

RESOLUTION
The matching logic was updated to support the new identifier format, and the duplicate cases were merged back into their original threads.

VALIDATION
A test reply using the new identifier format correctly appended to its existing case rather than creating a duplicate.
column6: Thread Identifier Change Breaks Case Matching

column1: A case comment made through email erroneously overwrites the case description field instead of appending as a separate comment, due to a misconfigured field mapping
column2:
CONTEXT
Replying to a case by email is expected to add a new comment to the case's activity history without altering any other field on the record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of case replies instead overwrote the case description field with the reply content, erasing the original description.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An email reply should always append as a separate comment and never modify the case description field.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been determined what distinguishes the affected replies from the many that behave correctly, since no consistent pattern has been found in message format or case type.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of the field mapping configuration found no obvious rule that should map reply content to the description field, leaving the exact trigger condition unclear.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the specific mapping condition causing the overwrite has not been isolated with confidence.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to capture the full raw email payload for the next occurrence to compare it directly against a normal reply and identify what differs.

column1: Emails sent to an internal distribution list as part of case escalation are rejected by the mail server because the distribution list exceeds an unexpected recipient limit
column2:
CONTEXT
A case escalation notification is configured to email a large internal distribution list covering every member of a support leadership group.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Escalation emails began bouncing back as undeliverable after the distribution list grew past a recipient count the mail server apparently does not support for a single list.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Escalation notifications should be delivered successfully regardless of how large the target distribution list grows.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mail server enforces an undocumented recipient limit on flattened distribution lists that the notification's list had grown past following recent leadership additions.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The mail server administrator confirmed the limit after being consulted, since it was not previously known to the team managing the escalation notification, and several escalations had gone unnoticed by leadership as a result.

RESOLUTION
The single large distribution list was split into two smaller regional lists, both included on the escalation notification, keeping each list comfortably under the confirmed limit.

VALIDATION
A test escalation notification successfully delivered to both smaller lists with no bounce errors, and the mail server administrator confirmed the new list sizes leave adequate headroom for future growth.

column1: A customer satisfaction survey email is sent automatically upon case closure, but fires again on a subsequent unrelated reopen-and-reclose cycle for the same case
column2:
CONTEXT
A satisfaction survey email is automatically triggered whenever a case's status changes to closed, intended to capture feedback once per resolved issue.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers whose case was reopened for a minor follow-up and then closed again received a second survey email for what they considered the same original issue.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A survey should ideally be sent once per genuinely resolved issue, not once per closure event if the case was reopened for a minor follow-up.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The trigger fires on every transition into closed status with no memory of whether a survey was already sent for that case.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Distinguishing a genuinely new issue reopening from a minor follow-up reopening would require a judgment call not currently captured anywhere in the case data.

RESOLUTION
As an interim measure, the trigger was updated to suppress a second survey if the case was reopened and reclosed within twenty-four hours, covering the most common minor follow-up pattern.

VALIDATION
The twenty-four-hour suppression correctly blocked a duplicate survey in test cases within that window, though longer-cycle reopens can still trigger a second survey.

column1: A record type's default field values differ from its page layout's field order, so a value auto-populates into a field agents don't expect to see prefilled
column2:
CONTEXT
A record type's default field values were configured separately from its page layout, with a default priority value set that agents did not realize was active.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents repeatedly submitted records with an unintended priority value because the default was not visually obvious given where the field appears on the layout.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Default field values should be clearly visible or intuitively placed so agents notice and can override them if needed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The priority field sits near the bottom of the layout, far from the top fields agents typically focus on, so the pre-filled default went unnoticed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of records created over one month found roughly thirty with the unintended default priority still in place, requiring correction.

RESOLUTION
The default value was removed, requiring agents to explicitly select a priority, and the field was moved higher on the layout for visibility.

VALIDATION
The thirty affected records were corrected, and no new records with the previously unintended default have appeared since the change.

column1: A custom object's sharing model was changed from private to public read-only as part of an unrelated project, and nobody flagged the broader visibility change for review
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom object storing sensitive contract terms had a private sharing model, changed to public read-only during an unrelated project intended only to simplify a different object's configuration.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A quarterly access review found the contract terms object visible to the entire organization rather than the intended small contracts team.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A sharing model change affecting a sensitive object should be explicitly reviewed and approved before deployment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The change was bundled into a larger deployment package covering several objects, and the specific impact on this one sensitive object was not individually called out for review.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The change had been active for approximately five weeks, and access logs showed no evidence of the broader visibility being exploited during that window.

RESOLUTION
The sharing model was reverted to private immediately upon discovery, and the deployment review checklist now requires explicit sign-off for any sharing model change on a designated sensitive object.

VALIDATION
A follow-up access check confirmed only the contracts team retains visibility into the object.

column1: A related list's row limit silently hides additional related records beyond the configured display count, with no indication more records exist
column2:
CONTEXT
A related list on the account page shows the account's open opportunities, configured to display a fixed number of rows for page load performance.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users working with accounts that have more open opportunities than the display limit were unaware additional opportunities existed, since no view-more indicator was present.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The related list should indicate when additional records exist beyond the displayed rows.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The related list component's current configuration does not include a view-all link for this particular layout placement, unlike the platform's default behavior elsewhere.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The component's configuration options for enabling a view-all link were found to be limited for this specific placement, and a full alternative component may be needed to fully resolve it.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the related list's row limit was increased to a higher count that covers the large majority of accounts, while a more complete component-level fix is evaluated.

VALIDATION
The increased limit was confirmed to cover ninety-five percent of affected accounts based on a review of open opportunity counts, though a small number may still exceed it.
column6: Related List Hides Records Beyond Limit

column1: A record's autonumber field skipped a large block of numbers after a failed bulk import, and the gap was mistaken by a downstream audit as evidence of deleted records
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom object uses an autonumber field as a human-readable reference number, incremented sequentially with every record creation attempt including failed ones.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
