The flow's running context should be predictable and reflect the owner the business process actually intends.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The flow evaluates the owner field at its own execution point, which can differ from the owner at the time the record was originally saved.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Reordering the transaction's automations so reassignment always happens after this flow looks like the likely fix, but a full order-dependency audit is still in progress.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the flow now captures the owner value into a separate variable at the start of the transaction, reducing the risk of mid-transaction reassignment.

VALIDATION
Ten test transactions with the reassignment automation confirmed the captured value matches the intended context, though the full audit remains open.

column1: A middleware connector cached OAuth scopes at startup, so after an admin narrowed a connected app's scopes the connector kept operating with the cached broader permissions until restarted
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware connector authenticates once at startup and caches the resulting OAuth scope for the remainder of its running session, refreshing only on restart.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An admin narrowed the connected app's granted scopes for security reasons, but the running connector continued performing actions the narrowed scope should have blocked.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A scope change should take effect for a running connector without requiring a manual restart.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The connector's cached authorization token carried the original broader scope until its own expiration, unaffected by the admin's change to the connected app definition.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The connector continued writing to a field the narrowed scope was meant to block for six hours, until its cached token expired naturally.

RESOLUTION
The connector was restarted immediately to force reauthorization, and its configuration was changed to refresh its token on a fixed short interval instead of only on restart.

VALIDATION
A repeat scope narrowing test confirmed the connector picked up the change within the new refresh interval without requiring a manual restart.
column6: Cached OAuth Scope Outlives Admin Change

column1: Two integrations writing to the same custom object through separate Bulk API jobs scheduled seconds apart cause row-locking failures that go unretried
column2:
CONTEXT
Two independently scheduled integrations each run a Bulk API job against the same custom object, historically scheduled far enough apart to avoid overlapping.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A scheduling change brought the two jobs within seconds of each other, and a subset of records in each job began failing with row lock errors that were never retried.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Overlapping jobs touching the same records should either avoid contention or have failed rows automatically retried.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Neither job's error handling distinguishes a lock contention failure from any other failure, so locked rows are logged as failed with no automatic retry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rescheduling the two jobs further apart is the simplest fix, but the teams owning each integration have not yet agreed on new timing that fits both of their constraints.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, failed rows from lock contention are now manually resubmitted after each job run while the scheduling negotiation continues.

VALIDATION
Manual resubmission successfully cleared all lock-related failures in the three most recent runs, though the underlying overlap has not yet been eliminated.
column6: Concurrent Bulk Jobs Cause Lock Failures

column1: A middleware field mapping was built against a sandbox describe call's field order, causing a positional mapping bug that only appeared after the production deployment
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware integration was configured using a field mapping tool that captured field order from a sandbox describe call, then mapped incoming data positionally rather than by field name.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After deployment to production, several fields arrived with values that clearly belonged to a different field, though the same mapping worked correctly in the sandbox.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Field mapping should be unaffected by any difference in field order between environments.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Production's describe call returned fields in a different order than the sandbox, and the positional mapping shifted several values into the wrong fields.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Thirty-seven records were confirmed to have received misaligned field values before the pattern was caught during a data quality spot check.

RESOLUTION
The mapping was rebuilt to reference fields by API name rather than position, and the thirty-seven affected records were corrected from the original source data.

VALIDATION
A test load using the name-based mapping produced correctly aligned values regardless of field order returned by the describe call.

column1: An external object definition was not updated after a field was added to the source, so new field data is silently unavailable when users query the external object
column2:
CONTEXT
An external system publishes changes to a data source that the org queries through an external object, with field definitions expected to track the source schema.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A field recently added to the source system does not appear on the external object, and users querying it have no way to know the data exists elsewhere.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether external object definitions should update automatically or through manual review whenever the source schema changes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The external object still only exposes fields defined when it was originally configured, with no indication additional source data exists.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The team owning the source schema and the team maintaining the external object have been connected, but a governance process to keep them in sync has not been agreed.

RESOLUTION
No change has been made yet, since the process for keeping external object definitions in sync with source schema changes has not been decided.

VALIDATION
The next step is to agree on a governance process between both teams, after which the missing field can be added.
column6: External Object Missing New Source Field

column1: A partner's UPSERT keyed on a non-unique External ID field created a random update-instead-of-create race after an upstream data quality issue let two source records share the same identifier
column2:
CONTEXT
A partner integration performs upsert operations keyed on an External ID field that had not been marked as enforcing uniqueness at the platform level.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two unrelated source records sharing the same external identifier, caused by an upstream data quality issue on the partner's side, began alternately overwriting each other on every sync.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The External ID field should have prevented two records from ever sharing the same identifier in the first place.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Without a uniqueness constraint, both source records matched the same target record on upsert, with whichever synced last overwriting the other's data.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The partner's upstream data quality issue was confirmed as the origin of the duplicate identifier, affecting exactly one pair of records identified through the sync's own error pattern.

RESOLUTION
The External ID field was reconfigured to enforce uniqueness, causing the second colliding record to fail loudly instead of overwriting, and the partner corrected the source duplicate.

VALIDATION
A test upsert using two records with a duplicate identifier now fails with a clear uniqueness error instead of silently overwriting.
column6: Non-Unique External ID Causes Update Race

column1: A middleware connected app's certificate-based authentication failed after a Hyperforce migration because the trusted IP allowlist still referenced the legacy instance's IP ranges
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware platform authenticates using a certificate-based flow combined with a trusted IP allowlist restricting which network ranges may present that certificate.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Following an infrastructure migration of the Salesforce instance, the integration began failing authentication even though the certificate itself remained valid and unchanged.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Authentication should continue working across an infrastructure migration that does not change the certificate or the middleware's own network location.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The trusted IP allowlist still referenced the legacy instance's outbound IP ranges, which changed as part of the migration, blocking otherwise valid authentication attempts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The migration's own documentation did note a change to published IP ranges, but the integration's allowlist had not been cross-referenced against it before cutover.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate step, the allowlist was updated with the new IP ranges, while a broader review of other integrations with similar IP-based restrictions is still underway.

VALIDATION
Authentication succeeded immediately after the allowlist update, though the broader review of other affected integrations has not yet completed.
column6: Certificate Auth Broke After Hyperforce Migration

column1: A nightly bulk extract using PK Chunking had one chunk boundary land exactly on a record being reparented at that moment, causing it to appear in two chunks' results
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly integration extract uses PK Chunking to split a large bulk query into smaller sequential chunks based on record identifier ranges.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A downstream reconciliation occasionally found one record counted twice in a single night's extract, though the underlying data was not actually duplicated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Each record should appear in exactly one chunk's results regardless of concurrent changes happening during the extract.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A record whose identifier sat exactly on a chunk boundary was being reparented at the same moment the chunk query executed, causing it to satisfy both adjacent chunks' filter conditions briefly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This occurred only once in three months, consistent with the narrow timing window required for a record to be mid-update exactly at a chunk boundary during extraction.

RESOLUTION
The downstream reconciliation step was updated to deduplicate on record identifier before processing, absorbing this rare boundary condition without requiring a change to the extract itself.

VALIDATION
A simulated boundary-timing collision in a test environment confirmed the reconciliation step now correctly processes the record only once.
column6: PK Chunk Boundary Duplicated A Record

column1: A CRM-to-ERP integration broke for a newly enabled second currency because the middleware's currency ISO code validation list was never updated after multi-currency activation
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware integration validates currency ISO codes against a static internal list before forwarding records to the ERP system, originally built when the org supported one currency.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a second currency was activated for a new market, every record using that currency began failing the middleware's validation step.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The middleware's currency validation should stay in sync with whichever currencies are active in the source org.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The static validation list had never been revisited since initial setup, so it rejected any currency code beyond the original single entry.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The multi-currency activation project's rollout checklist did not include a step to notify integration owners of the new currency being enabled.

RESOLUTION
The validation list was updated to include the new currency code, and the multi-currency activation checklist now includes an integration-notification step for future currency additions.

VALIDATION
A batch of previously failing records in the new currency processed successfully through the middleware after the validation list update.

column1: An org-to-org integration between two Salesforce instances using external objects failed after one org's API version deprecated a field the other org's mapping depended on
column2:
CONTEXT
Two separate Salesforce orgs are connected through an external object integration, with one org's field mapping depending on a field exposed by the other org's API.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the providing org upgraded to a newer API version that deprecated the depended-on field, the consuming org's external object began returning that field as blank.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The consuming org's mapping should be updated in coordination with any deprecation affecting a field it depends on.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The providing org's API version upgrade proceeded without cross-checking which external consumers still depended on the deprecated field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A replacement field was identified in the providing org's newer API version, confirmed to carry equivalent data through a side-by-side comparison of both fields.

RESOLUTION
The consuming org's mapping was updated to reference the replacement field, and a cross-org deprecation notification step was added to the providing org's API upgrade checklist.

VALIDATION
The external object was confirmed returning correct data through the replacement field, verified against ten sampled records.

column1: A middleware queue worker crashed and restarted mid-message, and because the integration lacks an idempotency key, message replay after restart created a duplicate case
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware queue worker processes inbound support messages one at a time, creating a corresponding case for each message, without any idempotency key to detect a repeated message.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A worker crash and automatic restart during message processing resulted in the same message being processed twice, creating two cases for one inbound request.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided how message replay after a crash should be safely handled without an idempotency mechanism already in place.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The queue's own retry mechanism resubmitted the message after the crash with no way for the worker to recognize it had already been partially processed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Only this single occurrence has been found so far, and the platform team is assessing whether an idempotency key can be added without disrupting the existing message format.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since adding an idempotency mechanism requires a message format change still under evaluation.

VALIDATION
The next step is to finalize the message format change with the platform team, after which idempotent replay handling can be implemented and tested.

column1: A nested public group's membership granted unintended access to a restricted permission set group after an unrelated group was added as a member for an unrelated reporting need
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission set group's assignment rule targets members of a specific public group, which itself contains another public group nested within it for reporting convenience.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found users in the nested group had inherited elevated permissions never intended for them, since the assignment rule targets group membership transitively.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Permission set group assignments should be reviewed for transitive nested group membership before being configured.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The nested group had been added purely to simplify a reporting share, with nobody considering its effect on the outer group's permission set assignment.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Eleven users in the nested group had held the elevated permission for approximately one month, with no evidence of misuse found in the audit trail during that window.

RESOLUTION
The nested group was removed from the outer group immediately, and a separate group was created for the original reporting share to avoid future permission entanglement.

VALIDATION
A follow-up permission audit confirmed the eleven users no longer hold the elevated permission while retaining their intended reporting access.
column6: Nested Group Grants Unintended Permission Access

column1: A refreshed sandbox retained production-masked customer contact details visible to external developers because the org's data masking policy was not applied before developer access was granted
column2:
CONTEXT
A sandbox refresh pulls a full copy of production data, with an org policy requiring a data masking job to run before any external developer is granted access to that sandbox.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An external development team was granted access to a freshly refreshed sandbox before the masking job had completed, briefly exposing live customer contact details.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Sandbox access provisioning should be blocked until the required masking job confirms completion.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Access provisioning and the masking job were scheduled as two independent steps with no dependency enforced between them, so access was granted first.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Access logs showed the external team queried a small number of contact records during the roughly two-hour exposure window before masking completed.

RESOLUTION
The masking job was rerun immediately and access was briefly suspended during the rerun, and provisioning is now explicitly gated on masking job completion.

VALIDATION
A subsequent sandbox refresh confirmed access provisioning correctly waited for the masking job's completion signal before proceeding.

column1: A muted permission in a permission set group blocked access that an individual member permission set was supposed to grant, silently denying a subset of users
column2:
CONTEXT
A permission set group combines several individual permission sets, one of which includes a muting configuration intended to suppress a specific permission from a different member set.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users assigned the group could not access a feature that one of the member permission sets was specifically built to grant, with no error explaining why.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The muting configuration should only suppress the permission it was explicitly intended to mute, not an unrelated one granted elsewhere in the group.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The muted permission's underlying identifier overlapped with the unrelated feature's permission in a way not anticipated when the muting was configured.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Reconfiguring the muting to target only the intended permission requires rebuilding part of the permission set group's structure, which has not yet been scheduled.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, affected users were given the needed feature access through a separate, individually assigned permission set outside the group in the interim.

VALIDATION
The individually assigned permission set was confirmed to restore the needed access for all affected users, pending the group's structural rebuild.

column1: An Apex controller running without sharing returned records a user could not otherwise open, exposing detail beyond the user's own record-level access
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom Lightning component's Apex controller was built without sharing enforcement to simplify a cross-object lookup used in a search feature.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A user reported seeing a record referenced in search results that they could not open when clicking through, since the underlying record was outside their sharing access.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Search results should only reference records the searching user actually has access to view.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The without-sharing controller queried across the full object regardless of the running user's access, surfacing record names and identifiers the user should never have seen.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The exposure was limited to record names and identifiers in search results, with no further field-level detail exposed, confirmed by reviewing the controller's query fields.

RESOLUTION
The controller was rebuilt to enforce sharing, filtering search results to only records the running user can access.

VALIDATION
A test search by a user with restricted access confirmed results no longer reference records outside their sharing visibility.

column1: Protected identifiers were found written in clear text to an integration log field that was not covered by the org's field-level encryption policy
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration writes a diagnostic log entry to a custom object for troubleshooting failed sync attempts, including the payload that was sent.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the logged payload includes a protected identifier in clear text, on an object not covered by field-level encryption.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet decided whether the fix should redact the identifier before logging or bring the log object under encryption, since both carry tradeoffs.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Log entries have accumulated the identifier in clear text for an unknown period, since retention has not yet been fully audited.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team is treating this as an active investigation into the scope of historical exposure while a remediation approach is evaluated.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the remediation approach is still under evaluation and existing entries have not been purged or encrypted.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to determine the full historical volume of affected entries so security can finalize a remediation plan.
column6: Protected Identifiers Logged In Clear Text

column1: A pilot permission left assigned to all internal users after a feature trial ended allowed validation rules to be bypassed org-wide
column2:
CONTEXT
A feature pilot temporarily granted all internal users a permission that allows bypassing certain validation rules, intended to be removed once the pilot concluded.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review months after the pilot ended found the bypass permission still assigned to every internal user, well beyond its intended temporary scope.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A pilot-scoped permission should be automatically or explicitly removed once its trial period concludes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The pilot's rollback plan covered feature configuration but did not include a step to revoke the temporary permission grant.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of validation rule bypass activity during the extended window found a small number of records saved that would normally have been blocked, none appearing malicious.

RESOLUTION
The bypass permission was revoked from all internal users immediately, and pilot rollback checklists now explicitly require reviewing any temporary permission grants.

VALIDATION
A follow-up permission audit confirmed no internal user retains the bypass permission, and validation rules now correctly block the previously bypassed records.

column1: A departed employee's integration token continued to authenticate successfully for several days after their user record was deactivated
column2:
CONTEXT
A departing employee had personally generated an API token for a lightweight scripting tool, separate from the org's managed integration accounts.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the token still authenticating successfully several days after the employee's user record was deactivated as part of standard offboarding.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Deactivating a user record should immediately invalidate any personally generated tokens tied to that account.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Investigation into why the token remained valid past deactivation is still underway, since this behavior was not expected given the platform's documented deactivation handling.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team has opened a case with the platform vendor to understand why token invalidation did not occur immediately upon deactivation as expected.

RESOLUTION
As an immediate containment step, the token was manually revoked and the account's session was forcibly terminated, pending the vendor's explanation of the underlying behavior.

VALIDATION
The manually revoked token was confirmed to no longer authenticate, though the platform vendor's root-cause explanation for the delay is still pending.

column1: Files shared through public links remained reachable without a login even after the underlying record's sharing was revoked
column2:
CONTEXT
Users can generate a public link for a file attached to a record, intended to expire or become inaccessible once the underlying record's sharing is revoked.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found several public file links remained fully accessible without login even after the associated record's external sharing had been revoked weeks earlier.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A public file link should become inaccessible once the record it was shared from no longer permits external sharing.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Public file links are generated independently of the record's own sharing state and do not automatically revoke when that sharing changes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Fourteen stale public links were found still active across several revoked records, none showing evidence of recent external access in available logs.

RESOLUTION
The fourteen links were manually revoked, and a scheduled job was built to cross-check active public file links against their record's current sharing state weekly.

VALIDATION
The scheduled job's first run correctly identified and flagged a newly revoked record's still-active public link for manual follow-up.
column6: Public File Links Outlived Record Sharing Revocation

column1: Access to a sensitive object cannot be logged natively by the platform, so a custom automation records access attempts but misses access made through report exports
column2:
CONTEXT
A sensitive custom object requires access logging for compliance, but native event monitoring does not cover this object type, so a custom Apex trigger logs direct record views instead.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A compliance audit found access through report exports is not captured by the custom logging, since exports do not pass through the trigger's logging path.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All access to the sensitive object, including through report exports, should be captured in the compliance log.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The custom trigger only fires on direct record view and query events, with no equivalent hook for report export activity.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A platform event monitoring feature that would cover export activity exists but requires an additional license the org does not currently hold.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, report access to the object was restricted to a small named group whose activity is reviewed manually, while the licensing gap is evaluated.

VALIDATION
The restricted group's manual review process was confirmed functional at the current small group size, though it does not scale as a permanent solution.
column6: Native Access Logging Gap For Sensitive Object

column1: Several users reported password reset messages they did not request, and neither a targeted attack nor a system malfunction has been confirmed as the cause
column2:
CONTEXT
The platform's standard self-service password reset flow sends a reset email whenever a request is submitted through the login page.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Five users across unrelated teams reported receiving a password reset email within the same week without having requested one themselves.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Password reset emails should only be sent in response to a genuine user-initiated request.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Login history shows a reset request was indeed submitted for each affected account, but the originating IP addresses do not match any known pattern shared across the five cases.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The security team has been engaged and is treating this as an active investigation into whether this reflects a coordinated attempt or five unrelated triggers.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no fix has been applied; affected accounts have had their sessions reviewed with no evidence of a successful takeover found so far.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to correlate the five originating IP addresses against threat intelligence feeds and check for any shared browser fingerprint across the requests.

column1: A custom summary formula performing division inside a matrix report's row grouping divides by the row's own subtotal, producing a misleading percentage on the grand total row
column2:
CONTEXT
A matrix report includes a custom summary formula that divides a subcategory total by its row's overall subtotal to show a percentage breakdown within each grouping.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The grand total row displayed a percentage that made no logical sense, since the formula divided the grand total's own subtotal by itself in a way that did not match the per-row logic.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The grand total row should either compute a meaningful equivalent percentage or leave the calculation blank rather than showing a misleading figure.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula's denominator reference resolved differently at the grand total level than at each individual row grouping, an inconsistency not caught during the report's original build.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing confirmed the formula works correctly at every row level and only produces the misleading figure at the grand total row.

RESOLUTION
The formula was rebuilt with an explicit check suppressing the percentage calculation at the grand total level, showing it as not applicable instead.

VALIDATION
The corrected report now shows a clear not-applicable marker at the grand total row while row-level percentages remain accurate.
column6: Grand Total Formula Divides By Own Subtotal

column1: A dashboard component built on a report with a cross filter behaved correctly in the report builder preview but returned different results embedded on a Lightning page
column2:
CONTEXT
A report using a cross filter to exclude records with no related child records was embedded as a chart component directly on a Lightning record page.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The embedded chart consistently showed a higher record count than the same report's preview in the report builder, despite both supposedly running the identical report definition.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An embedded report chart should return the same results as the report itself run through the standard report builder.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The embedded component's rendering context evaluated the cross filter using a slightly different default scope than the report builder's preview, including some records the cross filter should have excluded.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This rendering-context difference was reproduced consistently on a second, unrelated report using the same type of cross filter embedded the same way.

RESOLUTION
The cross filter was rebuilt using an explicit relationship-based filter instead, which produced consistent results in both the report builder and the embedded component.

VALIDATION
Record counts from the embedded component and the report builder preview now match exactly after the filter rebuild.
column6: Cross Filter Behaves Differently When Embedded

column1: An analytics snapshot object ran before a related field's formula was fixed, so historical snapshots permanently retain the old buggy calculated value after the fix
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled analytics snapshot job captures a calculated field's value nightly into a historical trending object, independent of any later changes to the calculation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a known calculation bug in the formula field was fixed, trend reports built on the snapshot object show a sudden discontinuity at the fix date instead of a smooth trend.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether historical snapshots should be recalculated retroactively or the discontinuity simply documented and left as-is.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Snapshots taken before the fix permanently retain the old buggy value, since the object stores a captured value rather than a live formula reference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Recalculating historical snapshots would require reconstructing the old formula's inputs for each historical date, which may not be fully possible given data retention.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since retroactive recalculation's feasibility is unconfirmed and no alternative approach has been decided.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to determine how far back the inputs needed for recalculation are still available in the underlying data.

column1: A report folder migrated between two Salesforce orgs during a merger retained its original report type mappings, and several reports silently return zero rows post-merger
column2:
CONTEXT
During a post-merger org consolidation, a report folder was migrated from the acquired org into the parent org along with its existing reports and their report type references.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several migrated reports began returning zero rows in the parent org, despite the underlying data existing and matching what the original reports showed in the acquired org.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Migrated reports should either resolve to an equivalent report type in the new org or clearly indicate they cannot be resolved.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type references pointed at object relationships that exist differently in the parent org's schema, silently returning no matches rather than an error.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nine reports were confirmed affected, all sharing the same underlying custom report type that had no direct equivalent in the parent org's object model.

RESOLUTION
A new report type was built in the parent org matching the intended relationship structure, and the nine reports were rebuilt against it.

VALIDATION
All nine rebuilt reports were confirmed to return the same row counts as their original versions in the acquired org.
column6: Migrated Report Folder Lost Valid Report Types

column1: A custom report type field showed a calculated value different from the same field viewed directly on the record, because the report type's field reference resolved against a stale cached schema
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom report type references a formula field, with the report type's own metadata expected to reflect the formula's current calculation logic.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A report using this report type displayed a value that differed from the same field viewed directly on individual records, despite both supposedly reading the same formula.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The report should always reflect the formula field's current calculation logic, matching what is shown on the record.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type's field reference resolved against a describe schema cached before a recent edit to the formula, still applying the formula's prior logic within the report.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Resaving the report type's field list forced a schema refresh that resolved the discrepancy, confirming the stale cache as the cause.

RESOLUTION
The report type was resaved to refresh its cached schema, and a note was added to the deployment checklist to resave dependent report types after any formula field edit.

VALIDATION
The report's displayed values now match the record-level formula output exactly after the resave.
column6: Report Type Cached Stale Formula Schema

column1: A currency dashboard filter set to corporate currency silently reverted to personal currency for viewers whose personal currency setting was bulk-updated by an unrelated onboarding script
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard's currency filter is configured to display figures in the org's corporate currency regardless of each viewer's individual personal currency setting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of viewers began seeing figures in their own personal currency instead of the corporate currency after an onboarding script bulk-updated new users' personal currency field.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The dashboard's corporate currency filter should override any individual viewer's personal currency setting consistently.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The specific personal currency value the onboarding script assigned interacts with the dashboard filter in a way that causes it to revert to personal currency, a combination not previously tested.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The interaction has been reproduced in a sandbox for the specific currency value the script assigns, but why this particular value triggers the reversion is not yet understood.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the onboarding script was changed to assign a different default personal currency value that does not trigger the issue, avoiding new occurrences.

VALIDATION
New users onboarded since the script change no longer experience the reversion, though the underlying interaction for the original currency value remains unexplained.
column6: Bulk Currency Update Broke Dashboard Filter

column1: A report scheduled with a relative last full week date filter produced a different week boundary than expected after a locale policy change altered the org's first day of week setting for new users
column2:
CONTEXT
A weekly scheduled report uses a relative last full week date filter, with the week boundary determined by the org's first day of week locale setting.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two cohorts of report subscribers began seeing non-comparable week boundaries after a locale policy change altered the default first day of week for newly created users.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All subscribers to the same scheduled report should see the same week boundary regardless of their individual locale settings.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The relative date filter resolves using each viewing user's own locale setting rather than a single fixed definition, so the two cohorts calculated different week boundaries.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twelve newer subscribers had the updated locale default while the remaining older subscribers retained the original setting, explaining the split.

RESOLUTION
The report's date filter was rebuilt using an explicit fixed date range calculated by a formula field rather than the locale-dependent relative filter.

VALIDATION
All subscribers, regardless of locale setting, now see identical week boundaries in the report after the rebuild.

column1: An aggregate report grouped by a picklist field with dependent picklist relationships double-listed a renamed legacy value because old records still reference the prior label internally
column2:
CONTEXT
An aggregate report groups cases by a picklist field, with one value having been renamed as part of a terminology update earlier in the year.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The report showed two separate rows for what should be a single grouping, one for the old label and one for the new, splitting what users expected as one combined total.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records using the old and new labels for what is functionally the same picklist option should group together as one bucket.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rename created a value with a new underlying reference while older records retained their original stored reference, and the report groups strictly by that stored reference.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly six hundred older records were confirmed still carrying the prior stored reference, all predating the rename.

RESOLUTION
A batch update was run to migrate all older records to the new picklist value's stored reference, consolidating the grouping going forward.

VALIDATION
The report now shows a single combined row for the renamed value, confirmed by comparing the new total against the sum of the two prior rows.

column1: A top N report configured with a row limit interacted unexpectedly with a bucket field, limiting records before bucketing was applied rather than after
column2:
CONTEXT
A report groups records into custom buckets and is configured with a row limit intended to show only the top several buckets by total value.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The displayed top buckets did not match a manual recount of the full dataset, since some individually large records were excluded by the row limit before their bucket's total could be fully calculated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The row limit should apply after bucketing and totaling, so the buckets shown genuinely represent the largest totals across the full dataset.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report builder applies the row limit to underlying records first, then buckets and totals only the records that survived the limit, understating some buckets.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This ordering is a documented characteristic of how the report builder processes row limits relative to bucket fields, not a configurable option.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the row limit was removed and a summary formula filter used instead to approximate the top buckets after full bucketing.

VALIDATION
The workaround's results were cross-checked against a full recount and found accurate, though it requires periodic manual threshold adjustment.

column1: A scheduled report refresh and a live dashboard refresh used different as-of-timestamp semantics for a today filter, producing different day boundaries for the same nominal date
column2:
CONTEXT
A report filtered to show today's activity is both scheduled to run at midnight and separately viewable live on a dashboard throughout the day.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The scheduled midnight run and the dashboard viewed the following morning showed subtly different figures for what both were labeled as the same day.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Both the scheduled run and the live dashboard view should resolve today to the same calendar day boundary.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The scheduled run evaluated today at the moment it fired, capturing the tail end of the prior day, while the live dashboard evaluated today fresh each time it was viewed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This is consistent with how relative date filters behave at the exact moment of evaluation, a distinction not previously considered significant.

RESOLUTION
The scheduled run's trigger time was shifted from midnight to a few minutes after, reducing but not eliminating the chance of landing exactly on the ambiguous boundary during a delayed run.

VALIDATION
The next several scheduled runs after the shift matched the dashboard's live figures, though a delayed run could still theoretically reproduce the original mismatch.
column6: Scheduled And Live Refresh Disagree On Today

column1: A macro that inserts a canned response into a case email also silently cleared a previously set case priority field, since the macro's action list included an outdated field reset step
column2:
CONTEXT
A support macro combines inserting a canned email response with a series of quick field updates, built when the team's priority-handling process worked differently than it does today.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents running the macro on an already-prioritized case found the priority field reset to its default value every time, undoing manual triage work.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The macro should only perform the field updates still relevant to the current process, not reset fields unrelated to its intended action.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
An old field reset step included when the macro was first built had never been removed as the team's process evolved around it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of macro usage over one month found this specific macro run over two hundred times, with the priority reset affecting every qualifying case.

RESOLUTION
The outdated field reset step was removed from the macro, leaving only the canned response insertion and the fields still relevant to the current process.

VALIDATION
Ten test runs of the updated macro on already-prioritized cases confirmed the priority field remained untouched.

column1: Omni-Channel routing assigned overflow email cases to an agent skill that no longer matched any active agent after a team reorganization removed the last agent with that skill
column2:
CONTEXT
Omni-Channel routing directs overflow email cases to a specific skill-based queue when primary queues are full, historically staffed by a small dedicated specialist team.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A team reorganization reassigned the last agent holding that specialist skill, and overflow cases began queuing indefinitely with no agent able to receive them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Overflow routing configuration should be reviewed whenever a reorganization changes which agents hold a routed-to skill.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The routing configuration had no dependency check against current skill staffing, so it continued directing cases to an effectively empty destination.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Thirty-one overflow cases queued unassigned for up to six hours before the pattern was noticed through a stalled-case alert.

RESOLUTION
The overflow routing was updated to target a currently staffed skill, and the thirty-one queued cases were manually assigned.

VALIDATION
A simulated overflow surge confirmed cases now route to agents holding the updated skill with no unassigned queue buildup.

column1: A Knowledge article auto-suggested to agents replying by email referenced a product that was discontinued, and the suggestion engine has no mechanism to exclude retired articles
column2:
CONTEXT
An email reply suggestion feature recommends relevant Knowledge articles to agents based on the case subject and body, drawing from the full published article library.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Agents repeatedly saw a suggested article referencing a discontinued product, since the article remained published for archival reasons but was never flagged as retired to the suggestion engine.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The suggestion engine should exclude articles marked as referencing retired products from its recommendations.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No retirement flag exists on individual Knowledge articles distinct from their published status, so the engine cannot distinguish an archival-only article from an actively relevant one.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Adding a distinct retirement flag to the Knowledge article data model has been scoped but requires a broader content governance decision still under discussion.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the specific article was manually excluded from the suggestion engine's index, while the broader retirement-flag capability is still being designed.

VALIDATION
The excluded article no longer appears in suggestions for matching cases, though other retired articles remain unaddressed pending the broader fix.

column1: An email-to-case Apex trigger processing inbound messages hit a governor limit only during a promotional campaign's reply surge, silently failing to create cases for the excess messages
column2:
CONTEXT
An email-to-case Apex trigger performs several lookups per inbound message to determine routing, normally well within governor limits at typical daily message volume.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During a promotional campaign that generated an unusually large reply surge within a short window, a batch of inbound messages failed to create cases at all.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The trigger should handle any realistic volume of inbound messages within a single transaction without silently failing.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The surge pushed a batch of messages processed in one transaction past the trigger's per-transaction query limit, causing that batch to fail without generating cases.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Forty-seven messages from the surge window were confirmed lost, identified by cross-referencing the mail server's delivery log against created cases.

RESOLUTION
The trigger was rebuilt to batch its lookups more efficiently, and the forty-seven lost messages were manually recreated as cases from the mail server log.

VALIDATION
A simulated surge matching the original campaign's volume processed successfully through the rebuilt trigger with no lost messages.
column6: Governor Limit Hit Only During Reply Surge

column1: A subset of outbound case emails sent through a newly configured secondary sending domain show as delivered in the platform but never arrive in recipient inboxes
column2:
CONTEXT
A secondary sending domain was recently configured to handle a portion of outbound case email volume, alongside the original primary sending domain.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several customers reported never receiving replies that the platform's own delivery tracking marked as successfully delivered through the secondary domain.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Messages marked as delivered by the platform should reliably reach the recipient's inbox.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been determined whether the messages are being silently filtered by recipient mail providers or whether the platform's delivered status is inaccurate for this domain.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The secondary domain's authentication records have been reviewed and appear correctly configured, leaving the exact point of failure between platform and recipient inbox unconfirmed.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the point of failure has not been isolated between the platform, the domain's reputation, and recipient-side filtering.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to send test messages through the secondary domain to mailboxes at several major providers and inspect the full delivery headers for filtering signals.
column6: Secondary Domain Emails Report Delivered But Missing

column1: A case emailed to a shared queue mailbox and later reassigned to an individual agent's personal queue lost its original thread history because the two queues use separate email routing addresses
column2:
CONTEXT
Cases can be reassigned from a shared queue mailbox to an individual agent's personal queue mailbox as part of a specialized escalation process, with each queue using its own dedicated email address.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customer replies sent after such a reassignment landed as a new, disconnected case instead of continuing the original thread, since replies still targeted the original shared queue address.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A reassigned case should continue receiving replies at whichever address the customer last corresponded with, linking back to the same case.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The reassignment process changed the case's owning queue but did not update the reply-to address embedded in prior outbound messages already in the customer's inbox.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nine cases over one month were confirmed split into disconnected threads following this specific reassignment pattern.

RESOLUTION
The reassignment process was updated to send a follow-up message from the new queue's address referencing the original case, and the nine split cases were manually merged.

VALIDATION
A test reassignment followed by a customer reply confirmed the reply now correctly threads to the reassigned case.
column6: Reassignment Across Queues Broke Thread Continuity

column1: An email parsing rule intended to extract an order number from the subject line also matches an unrelated numeric pattern in some customers' email signatures, misattributing cases to the wrong order
column2:
CONTEXT
An email-to-case parsing rule extracts an order number from the subject line using a pattern match, used to automatically link the resulting case to the correct order record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of customers whose email signature includes a numeric employee identifier in a similar format caused the parsing rule to misattribute their case to an unrelated order matching that number.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The parsing rule should only match a genuine order number, not an incidentally similar numeric pattern elsewhere in the message.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rule scans the full message body rather than restricting its match to the subject line, where the order number is reliably placed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Tightening the rule to scan only the subject line risks missing legitimate order numbers some customers include only in the body.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, misattributed cases are flagged for a quick manual order verification step before any order-specific automation acts on them.

VALIDATION
The manual step caught and corrected six misattributed cases in its first two weeks, while the parsing rule itself remains unchanged.

column1: An outbound email template's merge field for a multi-currency amount displayed the wrong currency symbol when the record's currency differed from the template owner's personal currency
column2:
CONTEXT
An outbound email template merges in an invoice amount field from a multi-currency-enabled object, with the template itself owned by a specific administrator user.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Customers with an invoice in a currency different from the template owner's personal currency setting received an email showing the correct number but the wrong currency symbol.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The merged amount should always display with the symbol matching the record's actual currency, not the template owner's personal setting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The merge field's formatting resolved against the template owner's personal currency display preference rather than the record's own currency field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This was confirmed as a formatting-only issue, since the underlying numeric amount itself was always correct regardless of the displayed symbol.

RESOLUTION
The template was rebuilt to reference a formula field that explicitly renders the amount with its own record-level currency symbol.

VALIDATION
Test emails generated for records in three different currencies now each display the correct corresponding currency symbol.
column6: Merge Field Uses Template Owner's Currency Symbol

column1: A case's email activity timeline shows messages sent through a mobile app appearing minutes before their actual send time due to a device clock synchronization gap
column2:
CONTEXT
The mobile support app allows agents to send case emails from the field, logging each message's timestamp based on the device's own local clock rather than server time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several case timelines showed a mobile-sent message appearing to predate an earlier server-timestamped message, since the sending device's clock had drifted ahead of actual time.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Message timestamps on the case timeline should reflect actual send order regardless of an individual device's clock accuracy.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mobile app trusts the device's local clock at the moment of composition rather than the server's receipt time when logging the activity.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A permanent fix requires changing the mobile app's timestamp logic to use server time, which is planned for an upcoming app release not yet scheduled.

RESOLUTION
As a partial mitigation, agents were advised to verify their device's clock synchronization settings, reducing but not eliminating the frequency of drift-caused misordering.

VALIDATION
Reported timeline ordering issues dropped after the device guidance was distributed, though the underlying app logic still needs the planned server-time fix to fully resolve it.
column6: Mobile App Timestamps Predate Actual Send

column1: A small number of outbound emails sent through a quick action are missing their attachment even though the attachment was confirmed present at the moment of sending
column2:
CONTEXT
An email quick action lets agents attach a file and send a case update in one step, normally including the attachment reliably in the outbound message.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A handful of emails sent this way arrived at the customer with no attachment, despite the sending agent confirming the file was selected before clicking send.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear whether the attachment is being dropped during composition, during the send process, or somewhere in mail delivery.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The case's own activity record shows the attachment as logged, but the actual outbound message the customer received did not include it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The discrepancy between the logged activity and the actual delivered message suggests the gap occurs after logging but before or during transmission, though this has not been confirmed.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the exact point where the attachment is lost has not been isolated.

VALIDATION
The next diagnostic step is to capture the raw outbound message payload at the mail relay for the next occurrence to determine whether the attachment was ever actually transmitted.
column6: Quick Action Emails Occasionally Drop Attachment

column1: Records archived to a Big Object no longer appear in standard list views, and users searching for older activity history get no results with no indication the records moved
column2:
CONTEXT
An archival process moves activity records older than a defined age into a Big Object to reduce storage on the standard object, intended to remain queryable through a dedicated archive page.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users searching for older activity through the standard list view interface found nothing, with no indication the records had moved to a different storage location entirely.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Users should be able to discover that older records exist in the archive, even if standard list views cannot display Big Object data directly.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The dedicated archive page existed but was not linked from anywhere users would naturally look, so most users were unaware it existed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A support ticket review found repeated confusion from users assuming archived records had been deleted rather than relocated.

RESOLUTION
A banner and direct link to the archive page were added to the standard list view whenever a date filter would have included archived records.

VALIDATION
User testing confirmed the new banner successfully guided five test users to locate archived records they previously could not find.
column6: Big Object Archive Invisible To List Views

column1: A validation rule referencing a $User merge field threw an error whenever a record was queue-owned instead of user-owned, since queue ownership has no corresponding user fields
column2:
CONTEXT
A validation rule references a $User field to compare the current user's department against a record's assigned department, intended to run only for user-owned records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records placed in a queue rather than assigned to an individual user began failing to save with an unclear error whenever this validation rule evaluated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The validation rule should either skip queue-owned records cleanly or evaluate them using logic that does not depend on individual user fields.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rule's underlying reference resolved to a null or unexpected value for queue ownership, since queues do not carry the same user attributes the rule depended on.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This had not surfaced previously because queue ownership was rarely used for this object until a recent process change routed more records through queues.

RESOLUTION
The validation rule was rebuilt with an explicit check to bypass the department comparison entirely whenever the record is queue-owned.

VALIDATION
Ten test records placed in a queue now save successfully, while user-owned records continue to enforce the original department check.
column6: Validation Rule Fails On Queue-Owned Records

column1: A Path component's key fields configuration referenced a field that was later made read-only for a profile, so users on that profile see the Path but cannot use it to update the guiding fields
column2:
CONTEXT
A Path component guides users through a record's stages, configured with key fields intended to be updated directly from within the Path interface.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users on a specific profile could see the Path and its stages but could not update the key field through it, after that field was made read-only for their profile in an unrelated access change.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The Path's key field configuration should stay coordinated with field-level security changes affecting the profiles using it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field-level security change was made without checking whether any Path component depended on that field remaining editable for the affected profile.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Reverting the field-level security change would undo an intentional access restriction made for an unrelated compliance reason, so a different approach is needed.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, a distinct field was added specifically for Path-driven stage updates, left editable for the affected profile, decoupled from the original restricted field.

VALIDATION
Users on the affected profile confirmed they can now progress through Path stages using the new dedicated field without regaining edit access to the original restricted one.
column6: Path Key Field Made Read-Only For Profile

column1: A dynamic related list filtered by record type was never updated when a new record type was introduced, so qualifying records of the new type never appeared on it
column2:
CONTEXT
A dynamic related list on the account page displays related opportunities filtered to specific record types relevant to the account's business line.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A new opportunity record type introduced for an expanded product line never appeared on the related list, even for accounts clearly qualifying for it.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The related list's filter should be reviewed and updated whenever a new record type is introduced that should logically appear there.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The related list's filter explicitly lists included record types rather than excluding irrelevant ones, so a newly added type defaulted to being excluded.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The record type rollout checklist for the new product line did not include a step to review dependent related list filters across the org.

RESOLUTION
The related list's filter was updated to include the new record type, and the rollout checklist now includes a related-list filter review step.

VALIDATION
A test account with an opportunity of the new record type now correctly displays it on the related list.
column6: Dynamic Related List Missed New Record Type

column1: A skinny table built to speed up a heavily filtered list view went stale after a bulk field update, since skinny tables are not refreshed by certain bulk update paths
column2:
CONTEXT
A skinny table was configured on a high-volume object to speed up a heavily filtered list view, mirroring a subset of fields for faster querying.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After a large bulk field update ran through a specific loading tool, the list view continued showing outdated values for hours despite records being correctly updated.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The skinny table should refresh promptly to reflect any bulk update to its mirrored fields.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The bulk update path used bypassed the standard synchronization trigger that normally keeps the skinny table current, a known characteristic of that path.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform vendor confirmed this is expected for the specific loading path used and recommended a manual refresh request after any large bulk update.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the team now submits a manual skinny table refresh request after any large bulk update through the affected path.

VALIDATION
The manual refresh resolved staleness within the expected turnaround in the two most recent updates, though the trigger gap remains a platform limitation.
column6: Skinny Table Stale After Bulk Update

column1: Two duplicate rules with different match criteria both fire on the same save, but the platform's alert only surfaces the first rule's matches, hiding a second, more relevant duplicate
column2:
CONTEXT
Two duplicate rules are active on the account object, one matching on company name and one matching on a combination of billing address fields, both intended to run on every save.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A user reported creating a duplicate that the address-based rule should have caught, but only the name-based rule's unrelated, less relevant matches appeared in the alert.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
When multiple duplicate rules find matches on the same save, all relevant matches from every rule should be surfaced to the user.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The duplicate alert interface displays only the first rule's matches by evaluation order, silently suppressing a second rule's matches on the same save.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This was confirmed as a documented interface limitation rather than a rule configuration error, reproduced consistently across several test scenarios with two active rules.

RESOLUTION
The two rules were consolidated into a single rule with combined match criteria, ensuring all relevant matches surface together in one alert.

VALIDATION
A test record matching both original criteria sets now shows all relevant duplicate matches in a single consolidated alert.

column1: Users switching between two Lightning apps see two different page layouts for the same record with different visible fields, since the app-specific page assignment was configured inconsistently
column2:
CONTEXT
Lightning App Builder allows a record page to be assigned per app, and two apps used by overlapping teams each have their own assignment for the same record page.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users working across both apps for the same record type saw a different set of visible fields depending on which app they were in, causing data entry confusion.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Teams sharing the same record type across multiple apps should see a consistent layout unless a deliberate difference is intended.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The two apps' page assignments were configured independently by different admins at different times, with no coordination on which fields appear.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Consolidating to a single shared assignment is the long-term fix, but it requires reconciling each app's distinct workflow needs, not yet fully scoped.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the two assignments were manually aligned to show the same core fields, while full consolidation is scoped separately.

VALIDATION
A side-by-side comparison confirmed the core fields now match between the two apps, though each retains a few app-specific fields pending consolidation.

column1: A mass update using a data loading tool's insert-null-values option on an update operation blanked several fields that were intentionally left off the update mapping
column2:
CONTEXT
A mass update was performed through a data loading tool with an option enabled that inserts null values for any field present in the source file but left blank for a given row.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several fields that had been intentionally excluded from the update's column mapping were blanked out on thousands of records after the load completed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Fields excluded from the update's mapping should remain untouched, regardless of the insert-null-values setting.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The operator misunderstood the setting's scope, believing it only applied to mapped columns left blank rather than also affecting how the tool interpreted the overall operation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review confirmed exactly which fields and how many records were affected by cross-referencing a pre-load backup export taken as routine practice.

RESOLUTION
The affected fields were restored from the pre-load backup export, and the team's data loading checklist now explicitly calls out reviewing this setting before every mass update.

VALIDATION
A sample of five hundred restored records was spot-checked against the backup export and confirmed to match exactly.
column6: Insert Null Values Blanked Unmapped Fields

column1: Apex-managed sharing recalculated by a nightly batch job silently excluded records created on weekends due to a bug in the batch job's scope query date logic
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom object's sharing is calculated by a nightly Apex batch job using Apex-managed sharing, with the job's scope query selecting records created since its last successful run.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users found they had no sharing access to records that were confirmed to have been created over a weekend, despite the batch job running successfully every night since.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The batch job's scope query should include every record created since its last run, regardless of the day of the week.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The scope query's date boundary calculation had an off-by-one error specific to how it handled the gap across a weekend, permanently excluding weekend-created records from ever being scoped.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Eighty-three records created on weekends over the prior two months were confirmed to have never had their sharing calculated.

RESOLUTION
The scope query's date logic was corrected, and a one-time run was triggered specifically targeting the eighty-three previously missed records.

VALIDATION
The eighty-three records were confirmed to have correct sharing access after the targeted run, and two subsequent weekends processed correctly.
column6: Batch Job Scope Query Excludes Weekend Records

column1: A report-based automation written before Person Accounts were enabled applies Contact-only field logic to Person Account records, corrupting a subset of them
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled automation was originally written to process standard Contact records using field logic specific to that object, before Person Accounts were later enabled in the org.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of Person Account records, which share underlying Contact-like fields, are processed by the same automation and end up with corrupted field values.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been determined whether the automation should be modified to handle Person Accounts correctly or excluded from processing them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The automation's query does not distinguish Person Accounts from standard Contacts, applying logic that assumes a field configuration only true for Contacts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The full scope of corrupted records has not yet been determined, since isolating which field changes came from this automation requires further log analysis.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the automation continues running while the scope of already-corrupted records is assessed.

VALIDATION
The next step is to cross-reference the automation's execution log against Person Account field history to scope affected records before deciding on a fix.
column6: Automation Applies Contact Logic To Person Accounts

column1: A CPQ discount schedule referencing a tiered pricing table was updated for new deals but not retroactively for in-flight quotes, so quotes started before the update calculated against stale tiers
column2:
CONTEXT
CPQ discount schedules reference a shared tiered pricing table, updated periodically as part of routine pricing strategy changes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of quotes already in progress when the pricing table was updated continued calculating discounts against the prior tiers instead of picking up the new values.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
In-flight quotes should recalculate against the current pricing table whenever it changes, or should be clearly flagged as using a locked prior version.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The discount schedule's values were snapshotted onto the quote at creation time and never refreshed, a detail not communicated to the sales team when the pricing update went out.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Nineteen in-flight quotes were confirmed using the stale tiers, all created in the two weeks before the pricing update.

RESOLUTION
The nineteen affected quotes were manually regenerated against the current pricing table, and the pricing update communication process now explicitly flags in-flight quotes for review.

VALIDATION
The nineteen regenerated quotes were confirmed to reflect current pricing tiers, verified against the updated table directly.
column6: In-Flight Quotes Used Stale Pricing Tiers

column1: An Order Management flow did not carry forward a contract's negotiated payment terms onto orders generated from contract renewal, defaulting every renewal order to standard terms
column2:
CONTEXT
Orders generated automatically from a contract renewal are expected to inherit the original contract's negotiated payment terms field, alongside several other contract-level attributes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance found that renewal orders consistently showed standard payment terms regardless of what had been individually negotiated on the original contract, causing invoicing discrepancies for several accounts.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A renewal order should inherit the same negotiated payment terms as the contract it renews, matching the customer's original agreement.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The renewal order generation logic mapped most contract fields but had never included the payment terms field in its mapping since the object was first built.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twenty-six renewal orders over the prior quarter were confirmed to have incorrectly defaulted terms, requiring manual correction with affected customers and their account teams.

RESOLUTION
The payment terms field was added to the renewal order generation mapping, and the twenty-six affected orders were corrected and reissued to the customers involved.

VALIDATION
A test renewal from a contract with non-standard terms now correctly carries those terms onto the generated order, confirmed against the original contract record.
column6: Renewal Orders Default To Standard Payment Terms

column1: A revenue schedule for a ramped subscription miscalculates year two's recognized revenue because the schedule template assumes a flat quantity across the full term
column2:
CONTEXT
A revenue recognition schedule is generated from a template that spreads a subscription's total value evenly across its term, built before ramped subscriptions with increasing quantity per year existed as a product option.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A ramped subscription's year two revenue was recognized using the same flat monthly amount as year one, understating year two and overstating year one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The schedule should recognize revenue proportional to each year's actual contracted quantity for a ramped subscription.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The template has no concept of a quantity change mid-term, spreading the contract's total value evenly regardless of the ramp structure.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Building a ramp-aware schedule template is a larger effort than a quick fix and has been scoped as a proper project with finance, not yet started.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, ramped subscriptions are now flagged for manual schedule adjustment by finance until the ramp-aware template project is completed.

VALIDATION
The manual adjustment process was applied successfully to the three ramped subscriptions closed since the issue was found, pending the template project.

column1: Forecast category updates based on stage, but a separate Apex trigger firing after the standard update silently overwrites it back to the old value
column2:
CONTEXT
Forecast category automatically updates based on opportunity stage through standard platform behavior, with a separate custom Apex trigger also firing on stage change for an unrelated notification purpose.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Forecast rollups intermittently showed opportunities at their previous forecast category despite the stage having clearly advanced.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The forecast category should reflect the current stage after any stage change completes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The custom trigger executed after the standard forecast category update and re-saved the record using a cached prior value, inadvertently reverting the category.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The custom trigger's re-save was an unintended side effect of how it captured the record's state at the start of the transaction rather than after the platform's own update.

RESOLUTION
The custom trigger was updated to re-query the record's current forecast category immediately before its own save, avoiding the stale overwrite.

VALIDATION
Ten test stage advancements confirmed forecast category now correctly reflects the new stage after both automations complete.

column1: A CPQ approval process re-evaluates against list price after a quote is cloned for renewal, ignoring that the clone inherited an already-approved discount, triggering unnecessary re-approval
column2:
CONTEXT
A CPQ approval process checks a quote's discount against list price whenever the quote is saved, intended to catch new discounts requiring sign-off.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Quotes cloned from an already-approved original for a straightforward renewal re-triggered the same approval requirement, even though the discount itself was unchanged and previously approved.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A cloned quote carrying forward an already-approved discount should not require re-approval for the same unchanged discount.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The approval process has no memory of a discount's prior approval status once cloned onto a new quote record, treating every clone as entirely new.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Hundreds of straightforward renewals were found triggering unnecessary approval requests monthly, adding meaningful delay to routine renewal processing.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, a flag was added that CPQ administrators can set on a clone to bypass re-approval when the discount is verifiably unchanged from the approved original.

VALIDATION
The bypass flag correctly skipped re-approval for fifty test renewal clones with unchanged discounts, while a clone with a modified discount still triggered approval as expected.

column1: A report type built before dated exchange rates were enabled still uses the static corporate exchange rate for historical figures, producing quietly wrong historical currency conversions
column2:
CONTEXT
The org uses dated exchange rates for accurate historical conversion, enabled some time after a specific custom report type had already been built using the default conversion.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance found historical figures in reports built on this older report type do not match figures from newer reports using dated rates for the same period.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether the older report type should be rebuilt or retired in favor of dated-rate-aware reports.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type's conversion behavior predates dated exchange rates and continues using the static corporate rate regardless of close date.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Several other reports were found still built on this same older report type, so the scope of affected figures is broader than assumed.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the rebuild-versus-retire decision has not been made and the full list of dependent reports is still being compiled.

VALIDATION
The next step is to finish compiling the list of dependent reports so finance can decide whether to rebuild or retire the report type.
column6: Report Type Ignores Dated Exchange Rates

column1: A custom rollup summarizing total contract value walked up an account hierarchy using the Parent Account field, but a territory reorganization reassigned rollups to the wrong ultimate parent
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom rollup on the account object sums total contract value across an entire account hierarchy, calculated by walking up the standard Parent Account field to the ultimate top-level parent.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A territory reorganization project reparented several accounts for unrelated territory reasons, and the rollup silently reassigned their contract value totals to a different ultimate parent as a side effect.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
