A change to account hierarchy for territory purposes should not silently redistribute financial rollup totals without review.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The rollup recalculates automatically on any Parent Account change, with no distinction between a territory-driven reparenting and a genuine corporate hierarchy change.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Seven top-level parent accounts saw their rollup totals shift as a direct side effect of the territory project, confirmed by comparing rollup values before and after the reorganization.

RESOLUTION
A separate hierarchy field dedicated to financial rollups was introduced, decoupled from the territory-driven Parent Account field, and the seven affected totals were corrected.

VALIDATION
The corrected rollups were manually verified against the original pre-reorganization hierarchy and confirmed to match.
column6: Territory Reorg Silently Reassigned Rollup Totals

column1: A rep working an opportunity in a second currency inadvertently selected a price book entry priced in the wrong currency, and no validation caught the mismatch before the quote was sent
column2:
CONTEXT
Price book entries are maintained separately per active currency, and opportunities can be worked in any currency enabled for the org.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A rep working a foreign-currency opportunity accidentally added a price book entry priced in a different currency, and the quote was sent to the customer before anyone caught the mismatch.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether a hard validation block or a softer warning is the appropriate response to a currency mismatch at the point of entry.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
No validation currently exists comparing a selected price book entry's currency against the opportunity's own currency before allowing it to be added.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Product and sales operations are discussing whether a hard block could interfere with legitimate cross-currency use cases that exist for certain international deals.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the appropriate validation approach is still under discussion between product and sales operations.

VALIDATION
The next step is to finalize whether a hard block or warning is appropriate, after which the corresponding validation can be built and tested.
column6: No Validation On Price Book Currency Mismatch

column1: A partner referral commission calculation requires the partner tag before a deal reaches a specific stage, but a bulk stage-advancement tool pushed referred deals past that stage before tagging, losing eligibility
column2:
CONTEXT
Partner referral commission eligibility requires a partner tag to be applied to the opportunity before it reaches a specific pipeline stage, enforced by the commission calculation logic.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A bulk stage-advancement tool used during a pipeline cleanup effort pushed several referred deals past the eligibility stage before their partner tags had been applied.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Bulk pipeline operations should not inadvertently cause legitimate partner referrals to lose commission eligibility.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The bulk tool advanced stages purely based on age and activity criteria, with no awareness of the partner tagging dependency tied to commission eligibility.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Six referred deals were confirmed to have lost eligibility under the current logic, all traced to the same bulk cleanup run.

RESOLUTION
The six deals were manually flagged as eligible with a documented exception approved by sales operations, and the bulk tool was updated to exclude opportunities pending partner tag application.

VALIDATION
The six deals' commission eligibility was confirmed corrected, and a repeat bulk run excluded all opportunities pending a partner tag as intended.
column6: Bulk Stage Advancement Skipped Partner Tagging

column1: A custom object tracking one-time setup fee revenue events was never included in finance's month-end reconciliation report, so several months of fee revenue went unreported in leadership dashboards
column2:
CONTEXT
One-time setup fees are tracked on a custom object separate from standard opportunity revenue, introduced after the finance team's month-end reconciliation report was already built.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Finance discovered during a manual cross-check against source contracts that several months of one-time fee revenue never appeared in leadership dashboards built from the reconciliation report.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The reconciliation report should include every revenue-generating object relevant to the business, including the custom fee-tracking object.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The reconciliation report was never updated to include the newer custom object, since its introduction was not communicated to the team maintaining the report.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Five months of one-time fee revenue were confirmed missing from leadership dashboards, with the total now calculated separately for a corrective adjustment.

RESOLUTION
The reconciliation report was updated to include the fee-tracking object, and the five months of missing revenue were added as a one-time adjustment to leadership dashboards.

VALIDATION
The corrected dashboards were reviewed and confirmed by finance to match the manually calculated total, though the adjustment required a one-time manual entry rather than automated backfill.
column6: One-Time Fee Revenue Excluded From Reconciliation

column1: A consumer using the Tooling API to read custom field metadata got a response omitting a property the REST API includes for the same field, causing a schema misclassification
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration reads custom field metadata through the Tooling API at startup to build an internal schema cache used for validating outbound data before sending it.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A specific field type consistently caused the integration's schema cache to misclassify the field's expected data format, leading to validation errors on otherwise valid data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The Tooling API response should include enough information to correctly classify every field type the integration needs to handle.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The Tooling API's response for this field type omitted a property that the standard REST API's describe call includes, which the integration's classification logic depended on.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Comparing the two APIs' responses for the same field side by side confirmed the specific missing property and its presence in the REST API alternative.

RESOLUTION
The integration's schema cache builder was updated to supplement Tooling API metadata with a REST API describe call specifically for this field type.

VALIDATION
A test integration run against fields of this type now classifies them correctly and passes validation for genuinely valid data.
column6: Tooling API Field Metadata Omits Property

column1: An integration using JWT bearer flow continued working in a cached token state for hours after certificate rotation, then failed all at once when the cached token expired
column2:
CONTEXT
An external system authenticates using a JWT bearer flow against a certificate configured in the org, with the client caching its resulting session token for reuse.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the certificate was rotated, the integration appeared unaffected for hours before failing entirely once its cached token expired, delaying detection of the rotation timing.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A certificate rotation's effect should be immediately visible rather than masked by a long-lived cached token.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The client's caching behavior is intentional for performance, but was not designed with certificate rotation monitoring in mind.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The client vendor confirmed the caching is by design and offers no way to detect an underlying certificate change before the token naturally expires.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the rotation process now includes a manual token cache clear on the client immediately after rotation, avoiding the masking delay.

VALIDATION
The most recent rotation using the manual clear step showed immediate, correctly timed failure and recovery, though an automated solution is still pending.
column6: Cached Token Masked Certificate Rotation Timing

column1: A consumer relying on the includeDeleted parameter to track deletions missed records that were hard-deleted through a data management tool bypassing the recycle bin entirely
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer's deletion-tracking logic queries with the includeDeleted parameter to detect records that moved to the recycle bin since its last check.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of records deleted through a data management tool that performs a hard delete never appeared in the consumer's deletion tracking, since they never passed through the recycle bin.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The consumer's deletion tracking should account for the possibility of records being hard-deleted rather than only soft-deleted through the recycle bin.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Hard deletes bypass the recycle bin entirely, and the includeDeleted mechanism the consumer relies on has no visibility into records removed this way.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Sixty-three records hard-deleted through the data management tool over one month were confirmed missing from the consumer's deletion tracking.

RESOLUTION
The consumer's deletion tracking was supplemented with a periodic reconciliation pass comparing full record counts against its own last-known set, catching hard deletes indirectly.

VALIDATION
The reconciliation pass correctly identified the sixty-three previously missed deletions when run retroactively against the affected period.

column1: A platform event resubscription assumed contiguous replay IDs, but an event bus trimming operation created a gap that caused the consumer's resume logic to silently skip a window of events
column2:
CONTEXT
A platform event subscriber resumes from its last processed replay ID after any disconnection, built on the assumption that replay IDs form a contiguous sequence.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Following a platform-side event bus trimming operation, the resume logic silently skipped a window of events whose replay IDs fell within the resulting gap.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet clear what the correct behavior should be when a gap exists, since trimming is expected but the consumer has no way to detect it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The subscriber resumed from its last known replay ID with no indication a gap existed between that ID and the next available event.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform vendor confirmed trimming can create such gaps under normal retention policy but offers no way for a consumer to detect one occurred.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since no reliable mechanism currently exists to detect a replay ID gap from the consumer side.

VALIDATION
The next step is to work with the platform vendor to determine whether a gap-detection mechanism can be added to the subscription API.
column6: Replay ID Gap Silently Skipped Events

column1: A custom Apex REST endpoint was refactored to return a wrapper class with pagination metadata instead of a plain list, and consumers not notified of the version bump failed schema validation
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom Apex REST endpoint originally returned a plain list of records, refactored to return a wrapper object including pagination metadata alongside the same record data.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of consumers that had not been notified of the change began failing schema validation, since their parsers expected the original plain list structure.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A breaking change to a custom endpoint's response structure should be communicated to every known consumer before deployment.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The endpoint's consumer registry was incomplete, missing two integrations that had been built directly against it without formally registering as consumers.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The two unregistered consumers were identified once their failures were traced back to the endpoint change, confirming the registry gap as the root communication failure.

RESOLUTION
The two consumers were updated to handle the new wrapper structure, and the consumer registry was audited and completed to prevent a similar communication gap.

VALIDATION
Both updated consumers were confirmed processing the new response structure correctly, and the completed registry was cross-checked against actual endpoint traffic.

column1: An outbound Apex callout routed through a configured proxy with a smaller request size limit than Salesforce's own outbound limit failed silently for larger callouts with no error surfaced back
column2:
CONTEXT
Outbound Apex callouts to an external service are routed through a configured network proxy, which enforces its own request size limit independent of the platform's outbound limit.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of larger callouts, still within the platform's own size limit, failed at the proxy with no error information returned to the calling Apex code.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A callout blocked by the proxy's size limit should surface a clear error rather than failing in a way indistinguishable from other failure types.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The proxy silently drops oversized requests without an informative response, and the Apex code's generic error handling could not distinguish this from other network issues.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The network team confirmed the proxy's size limit as the cause after correlating callout payload sizes against failure timing, though changing the proxy's own limit is outside this team's control.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the Apex code now checks payload size before sending and splits any callout exceeding the proxy's limit into smaller sequential requests.

VALIDATION
Ten previously failing large callouts now complete successfully using the split-request approach.
column6: Proxy Size Limit Silently Drops Large Callouts

column1: A scope-narrowing change intended for one integration's authorization flow was accidentally applied to a Connected App shared with a second, unrelated integration
column2:
CONTEXT
Two separate integrations were both configured to use the same Connected App, requesting different OAuth scopes at their own individual authorization time.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A scope-narrowing change intended only for the first integration's authorization request was mistakenly applied to the Connected App's default scope setting, affecting the second integration's next token refresh.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A scope change intended for one integration's authorization flow should not affect a different integration sharing the same Connected App.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The change was made at the Connected App's default scope level rather than scoped to the specific authorization flow, since the two integrations' shared use of the app was not accounted for.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The second integration's next token refresh failed with a permission error immediately after the change, tracing directly back to the default scope modification.

RESOLUTION
The default scope was reverted, and the two integrations were migrated to their own dedicated Connected Apps to prevent future cross-impact.

VALIDATION
Both integrations were confirmed authenticating successfully with their own independent scopes after the migration.
column6: Scope Change Accidentally Affected Shared App

column1: A REST API consumer's long-running extract held a queryLocator open across a period of significant underlying data change, and the resulting locator expiration error aborted the entire extract
column2:
CONTEXT
A REST API consumer paginates a large extract using a queryLocator, normally completing well within the locator's validity window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An unusually long-running extract held its locator open long enough to hit expiration, and the consumer's retry logic had no specific handling for this error, aborting the entire extract rather than resuming.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A locator expiration during a long extract should be handled gracefully, resuming from a safe point rather than discarding all progress.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The consumer's generic retry logic treated the locator expiration the same as any other transient error, retrying the same expired locator rather than starting a fresh query from the last known position.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The consumer's own logs confirmed it had already successfully processed most of the extract before the expiration discarded that progress entirely.

RESOLUTION
The consumer's retry logic was updated to specifically detect locator expiration and restart pagination from the last successfully processed record's position.

VALIDATION
A simulated long-running extract forced past the expiration window now correctly resumes and completes rather than aborting.

column1: A Salesforce Connect external object displayed blank records rather than an error when the external system timed out during a spike in callout volume, misleading users
column2:
CONTEXT
An external object surfaces data from an outside system through Salesforce Connect, normally displaying that data reliably under typical callout volume.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
During a spike in Salesforce Connect callout volume, some external object records displayed with entirely blank fields rather than any indication that the underlying request had timed out.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A timeout retrieving external object data should be surfaced to the user as an error rather than displayed as if the record genuinely has no data.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The default rendering behavior for a failed external object retrieval falls back to blank fields rather than an explicit error state.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The pattern was reproduced in a sandbox by artificially throttling the external system, confirming the blank-field fallback as the platform's default behavior under timeout.

RESOLUTION
A custom Lightning component was built to replace the default external object display, explicitly showing an error state when the underlying callout fails or times out.

VALIDATION
The custom component was tested under a simulated timeout and correctly displayed an error message instead of blank fields.
column6: External Object Shows Blank Instead Of Error

column1: A consumer using Bulk API 2.0 assumes job completion means all data loaded, but the monitoring only checks job-level status and misses individually failed records within an otherwise complete job
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer loads data through Bulk API 2.0 and monitors job completion status to confirm a load finished successfully, without separately checking the job's failed-records file.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A load reported as complete actually had a subset of individual records fail, but these failures went unnoticed since the consumer's monitoring only checked the overall job-level status.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The consumer's monitoring should also check for individually failed records within a job reported as complete.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The monitoring script was originally built to check job-level status only, before individual record failure rates became noticeable enough to warrant deeper checking.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of recent job history found several prior loads with a small percentage of individually failed records that had gone completely unnoticed until now.

RESOLUTION
The monitoring script was updated to also retrieve and check the failed-records file for every completed job, alerting on any non-empty result.

VALIDATION
The updated monitoring correctly flagged a subsequent load's failed records, though a backfill to identify all historically missed failures is still in progress.
column6: Job-Level Status Masks Individual Record Failures

column1: A schema context retrieval step truncates custom field descriptions after a fixed character count, so questions relying on longer business-specific descriptions get an incomplete understanding of the field
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant retrieves field-level metadata, including custom field descriptions, to interpret business terminology in questions, passed through a fixed-length context window.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question relying on a lengthy custom field description explaining a nuanced business rule was answered incorrectly, since the description had been cut off mid-explanation.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should retain enough of a field's description to correctly interpret the rule it explains, or flag when truncated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retrieval step truncated the description at a fixed character count regardless of whether the cut point fell in essential context.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Seven fields across the schema were found with descriptions long enough to be truncated at the current limit.

RESOLUTION
The truncation limit was raised for these seven known fields through a manual override, but the fixed limit itself remains unchanged for any other field that may grow long enough to be truncated later.

VALIDATION
The original question was re-asked and now correctly reflects the full rule, though the underlying fixed limit has not been generally resolved.

column1: A question phrased using a business acronym recently redefined by a different team for an unrelated purpose caused the assistant to build a query using its old, now-incorrect definition
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant maintains a glossary of business acronyms and their corresponding field or filter mappings, used to interpret shorthand terms in user questions.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A team redefined an existing acronym for a new, unrelated purpose, and questions using that acronym continued resolving to the old, now-incorrect mapping.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant's glossary should stay current as acronym meanings evolve across the business.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The glossary has no process for detecting or flagging when a term's meaning has changed, relying entirely on manual updates that had not yet occurred for this acronym.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Establishing an ongoing process for glossary maintenance requires identifying an owner across business teams, which has not yet been assigned.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the specific acronym's mapping was manually corrected, while a broader glossary governance process is still being defined.

VALIDATION
The corrected acronym now resolves to its new meaning in test questions, though the broader governance gap for future redefinitions remains open.

column1: The assistant returned an artificially low count for a manager-role question because it did not account for role hierarchy inheritance when estimating visible records before running the query
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant runs generated queries under the asking user's own permissions, and for certain question types pre-estimates an expected result size to decide whether to warn about a large answer.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A manager asking about records visible to their team received an unusually low count, inconsistent with their actual role-based visibility into subordinates' records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The pre-estimate and the actual query should both correctly reflect role hierarchy inheritance for a manager's visibility.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The pre-estimate step used a simplified visibility calculation that did not account for role hierarchy, though the actual underlying query did, creating a mismatch between the warning and the real answer.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The pre-estimate logic was built before role hierarchy inheritance was added as a supported access model, and was never updated to match.

RESOLUTION
The pre-estimate logic was rebuilt to use the same role-hierarchy-aware visibility calculation as the actual query.

VALIDATION
A repeat of the manager's original question now shows a pre-estimate consistent with the actual returned count.
column6: Role Hierarchy Not Considered In Visibility Estimate

column1: A question asked right at a scheduled nightly data refresh window occasionally returned a partial answer reflecting mid-refresh data, since the assistant has no awareness of the refresh timing
column2:
CONTEXT
A nightly data refresh job updates a large reporting object over a multi-minute window, during which some records reflect the new data and others momentarily still reflect the old.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of questions asked during this window returned an answer that was internally inconsistent, mixing pre-refresh and post-refresh values in the same response.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should avoid answering from data mid-refresh, or should indicate that a refresh is in progress.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assistant has no visibility into when the nightly refresh job is running and queries live data without any awareness of that job's state.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The refresh job's own status is tracked in a custom object that the assistant was not previously configured to check.

RESOLUTION
The assistant was updated to check the refresh job's status object before answering questions against the affected reporting object, briefly deferring if a refresh is active.

VALIDATION
A test question submitted during a simulated refresh window now correctly waits and answers using fully refreshed data.

column1: The assistant's query generation correctly quotes string literals but fails to escape an apostrophe in a filter value, causing a malformed query surfaced as a generic failure
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant builds SOQL query filters from business names and other free-text values extracted from a user's question, wrapping string literals in quotes as required.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question referencing a business name containing an apostrophe produced a malformed query that failed with a generic error message giving no indication of the actual syntax problem.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should properly escape special characters like apostrophes within string literals before constructing the query.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The query construction step quoted the literal but did not escape an embedded apostrophe, breaking the string boundary and producing invalid syntax.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing five other business names containing apostrophes reproduced the same malformed query pattern consistently.

RESOLUTION
The query construction step was updated to properly escape apostrophes and other special characters within string literals before building the query.

VALIDATION
All five previously failing test names now produce valid, correctly escaped queries that return the expected results.

column1: A follow-up question referencing the same time period after an initial question used a custom fiscal period is answered using standard calendar periods instead
column2:
CONTEXT
A user asked an initial question using a custom fiscal period defined for their business unit, followed by a related question referencing the same time period without restating it explicitly.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The follow-up question was answered using standard calendar period boundaries instead of carrying forward the custom fiscal period from the initial question.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant's conversation context should carry forward a custom fiscal period selection to a directly related follow-up question.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The context tracking mechanism currently only carries forward object and filter selections, not the specific date period type used.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Extending context tracking to include period type is a larger change to the conversation state model that has not yet been scheduled for development.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the assistant now explicitly asks the user to confirm which period type applies whenever a follow-up question references a time period ambiguously.

VALIDATION
Ten test follow-up questions now correctly prompt for period confirmation rather than silently defaulting to calendar periods.
column6: Follow-Up Loses Custom Fiscal Period Context

column1: A question comparing two custom objects joined only through a junction object generated a query that omits records where the junction relationship is populated on only one side
column2:
CONTEXT
Two custom objects relate to each other only through a junction object, with some legitimate records having the junction populated on just one side during a multi-step business process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A comparison question joining the two objects through the junction silently excluded records where the relationship was only partially populated, undercounting valid relationships.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The generated query should account for partially populated junction relationships rather than silently excluding them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The standard join pattern the assistant generates assumes both sides of the junction are always populated together, which does not hold for records still mid-process.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rebuilding the join pattern to correctly handle partial population requires a more complex query structure that has not yet been fully validated for performance at scale.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, questions involving this specific junction object now include an explanatory note that mid-process records may be undercounted, pending the query rebuild.

VALIDATION
The explanatory note was confirmed to appear correctly, though the underlying undercounting itself has not yet been resolved.

column1: A user asking about their team's records had the term team resolve to a broad, stale public group instead of the user's actual direct reports
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant interprets the word team in a question by resolving it to the asking user's public group membership, a mapping decision made when the assistant was first built.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A manager asking about their team's records received results including many people no longer on their team, since their public group membership had not been updated to match a recent org change.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Team should resolve to the user's actual current direct reports rather than a potentially outdated group membership.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The public group used for this mapping is maintained manually and had not been updated to reflect several recent reporting line changes.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Role hierarchy data was found to accurately reflect current direct reports, offering a more reliable source than the manually maintained public group.

RESOLUTION
The team interpretation was rebuilt to resolve against role hierarchy direct reports instead of the manually maintained public group.

VALIDATION
The original manager's question now correctly returns only their current direct reports' records.
column6: Team Resolved To Stale Public Group

column1: The assistant occasionally answers using data from a field recently deprecated and hidden from page layouts but not removed from the schema, giving an answer based on a field the business no longer considers valid
column2:
CONTEXT
A field was recently deprecated as part of a data model cleanup, hidden from all page layouts but left in the schema to avoid breaking dependencies before full removal.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question phrased in a way that matched this deprecated field's name returned an answer based on it, though the business no longer considers it a valid source of truth.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether the assistant should exclude all deprecated fields automatically or require explicit flagging.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assistant's schema awareness has no concept of deprecated status distinct from a field simply existing in the schema.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The cleanup project maintains its own list of deprecated fields, which has not yet been connected to the assistant's schema retrieval.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since connecting the two systems' field status information has not been scoped as a project.

VALIDATION
The next step is to scope a connection between the deprecation list and schema retrieval so deprecated fields can be excluded.

column1: The assistant generates a LIMIT clause for a some-examples question but the response text does not clarify the results are a partial subset, misleading users into treating it as complete
column2:
CONTEXT
A question asking to see some examples of matching records is answered with a small limited subset, intended as a representative sample rather than a complete list.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several users acted on the returned subset as though it represented the complete result set, leading to decisions based on incomplete information.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The response should clearly indicate when it shows a partial sample rather than the complete matching set.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The response text presented the limited results with no language distinguishing a sample from a complete answer.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
User feedback specifically cited this ambiguity as a source of confusion in a review of recent negative feedback submissions.

RESOLUTION
The response template for example-style questions was updated to explicitly state the sample size and the actual total matching count.

VALIDATION
Ten example-style test questions now clearly display both the shown sample size and the true total count in the response.
column6: Example Response Doesn't Flag Partial Coverage

column1: Two External ID fields on different objects were both marked case-insensitive unique, and a batch of records with case-only differences in their identifiers silently linked to the wrong parent during migration
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration used External ID fields on two related objects to resolve parent-child relationships during load, with both fields configured as case-insensitive unique identifiers.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A batch of child records linked to the wrong parent after migration, traced to source identifiers differing only in letter case that the case-insensitive matching treated as identical.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records with genuinely distinct source identifiers, even differing only by case, should never resolve to the same parent unless truly intended to match.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The case-insensitive uniqueness setting caused two source systems' differently cased but distinct identifiers to collide during the relationship-resolution pass.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Forty-four child records were confirmed linked to an incorrect parent, all traced to eleven case-collision pairs in the source identifiers.

RESOLUTION
The External ID fields were reconfigured to case-sensitive uniqueness, and the forty-four affected child records were relinked to their correct parents.

VALIDATION
A sample of the relinked records was cross-checked against the original source data and confirmed correctly matched.
column6: Case-Insensitive External ID Linked Wrong Parent

column1: Field history tracking enabled before migration generated a misleading trail showing every migrated field as changed from blank, cluttering the object's real audit history
column2:
CONTEXT
Field history tracking was enabled on a custom object before a large migration load, intended to capture genuine post-migration changes for compliance purposes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The migration itself generated an enormous field history trail showing every migrated field as changed from blank to its loaded value, burying genuine subsequent changes in noise.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Field history tracking should ideally capture only genuine post-migration business changes, not the migration load itself.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Tracking was left enabled during the load with no consideration for the volume of history entries a full data load would generate.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Several hundred thousand history entries were generated by the load alone, confirmed by comparing entry timestamps against the migration window.

RESOLUTION
The migration-generated history entries within the load window were bulk-purged using a supported data management process, leaving only genuine subsequent history.

VALIDATION
A post-purge review confirmed the object's field history now starts cleanly from the first genuine post-migration change.

column1: An unusually wide custom object hit a Bulk API 2.0 automatic batch size where a small number of records exceeded a row size limit and were silently skipped without appearing in any error file
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration wave used Bulk API 2.0's automatic batch sizing to load a custom object with an unusually large number of fields, normally handled without issue at typical row widths.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A small number of the widest records were missing from the target entirely after the load, despite the job reporting successful completion with no errors logged.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Any record that fails to load, for any reason, should appear in the job's error file.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected records exceeded an internal row size limit at a point in processing that occurs before the loader's own error logging step, so the failure was never recorded anywhere.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform vendor confirmed this as a known gap for a specific combination of field count and batch sizing, without an immediate fix timeline.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the widest object's migration batches were manually resized smaller than the platform's automatic sizing to stay safely under the row size limit.

VALIDATION
A reload using the manually resized batches successfully loaded all previously missing records with no silent skips.
column6: Wide Object Records Skipped Below Error Logging

column1: Early-migrated currency records display as plain numbers without a currency symbol because the migration ran before a new field's currency-type formatting was applied
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom currency field was added to support a migration, with its currency-type formatting applied shortly after the field's creation rather than before the first migration batch ran.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records migrated in the earliest batch display their monetary values as plain numbers without a currency symbol, inconsistent with later batches migrated after the formatting was applied.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
All migrated records should display consistent currency formatting regardless of which batch loaded them.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The field's display format is a metadata setting that only affects rendering, not stored data, so records loaded before the setting was applied simply inherited the format once it existed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing confirmed the underlying numeric values were always correct and only the display formatting had lagged, resolved automatically for existing records once the field setting was applied.

RESOLUTION
The currency-type formatting was applied to the field, which immediately corrected display for all previously migrated records without requiring any data change.

VALIDATION
A spot check of ten early-batch records confirmed they now display the currency symbol correctly alongside later-batch records.
column6: Currency Formatting Missing On Early Records

column1: A subset of legacy records had been migrated once already years earlier by a forgotten prior effort, so their createdDate reflects that earlier migration rather than true original creation
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration script preserves historical order by relying on the source system's createdDate field, assumed to reflect each record's true original creation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of records showed a createdDate inconsistent with other historical evidence, eventually traced to a previously forgotten migration effort years earlier that had already touched those same records.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Historical trend reports relying on createdDate should reflect true original creation, not an intermediate migration event.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The earlier forgotten migration had reset createdDate to its own load time for the records it touched, a fact undocumented anywhere the current migration team could find.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Roughly three hundred records were identified as likely affected based on a suspicious clustering of createdDate values, though not every affected record has been individually confirmed.

RESOLUTION
A separate true-creation-date field was populated from an older archival source for the confirmed subset, while the remaining suspected records are still being individually verified.

VALIDATION
The confirmed subset's true creation dates were cross-checked against the archival source and found accurate, though full verification of all suspected records is ongoing.

column1: A two-pass migration linking opportunities and contact roles left a subset of contact roles pointing at a placeholder opportunity that was never cleaned up after the real opportunity loaded
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration loaded contact roles before their linked opportunities existed, using a two-pass process where contact roles first attach to a placeholder opportunity, then get relinked once the real one loads.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A subset of contact roles were found still pointing at their original placeholder opportunity, never relinked during the second pass as intended.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every contact role should be relinked to its real opportunity by the end of the two-pass process, with no placeholder links remaining.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The second pass's relinking query missed contact roles where the real opportunity's identifier used a formatting variant not covered by the query's matching logic.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
One hundred and seventy-eight contact roles were confirmed still linked to placeholder opportunities, all sharing the same identifier formatting variant.

RESOLUTION
A corrective batch job was run with matching logic covering the missed formatting variant, relinking all affected contact roles to their real opportunities.

VALIDATION
All one hundred and seventy-eight contact roles were confirmed relinked correctly, verified against the original source relationship data.
column6: Placeholder Opportunity Links Never Cleaned Up

column1: Field-level encryption enabled partway through a migration left records loaded before the change unencrypted at rest while later records are encrypted, creating an inconsistent compliance posture
column2:
CONTEXT
A large object's field-level encryption was enabled partway through an extended migration effort, intended to apply going forward without disrupting the migration already in progress.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A compliance review found records loaded before encryption was enabled remain unencrypted at rest, creating an inconsistency the compliance team was not previously aware of.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been decided whether all pre-encryption records should be retroactively encrypted or handled through a different compliance accommodation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Enabling field-level encryption does not automatically encrypt already-existing data, only data written afterward, a platform characteristic not accounted for in the migration's original plan.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The compliance team is assessing whether retroactive encryption is required or whether a documented exception is acceptable, since retroactive encryption may have its own data risks.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the compliance team's assessment of the appropriate remediation path is still in progress.

VALIDATION
The next step is to await the compliance team's determination, after which either a retroactive encryption pass or a documented exception can be finalized.

column1: A migration mapping a legacy multi-value tag field into individual boolean flags only accounted for the eight most common combinations found in the test sample, silently dropping tags for less common combinations
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration mapped a legacy multi-value tag field into several individual boolean flag fields on the target, built and tested against a sample of the most common tag combinations in the source.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A post-migration audit found roughly three percent of records had one or more tags silently dropped, all using combinations not present in the original testing sample.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The mapping should correctly handle every tag combination present in the full source dataset, not only the ones covered by the testing sample.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The mapping logic only explicitly handled the eight combinations found during testing, silently ignoring any tag not part of one of those combinations.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
One hundred sixty-two records were confirmed to have at least one dropped tag, spanning eleven untested combinations found in the full dataset.

RESOLUTION
The mapping logic was rebuilt to handle each tag independently rather than by combination, and affected records were reprocessed with tags restored.

VALIDATION
All one hundred sixty-two affected records were confirmed to have their full original tag set after reprocessing, verified against source data.
column6: Uncommon Tag Combinations Dropped In Mapping

column1: A migrated record's owner was set to an active user whose default division differs from the division implied by the record's data, causing it to appear in cross-division reports inappropriately
column2:
CONTEXT
The org uses a multi-division structure, and migrated records were assigned an owner based on a name-matching process against active users, without considering each user's assigned division.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A data governance review found a subset of migrated records owned by a user whose division did not match the division implied by the record's own business data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A migrated record's owner should belong to the same division as the record's data to maintain the org's data segregation policy.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The name-matching process used during migration selected the first active user matching a legacy owner name, without checking division alignment.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Fifty-two records were confirmed with a division-mismatched owner, all resolved to the same small set of commonly duplicated legacy owner names.

RESOLUTION
The fifty-two records were reassigned to the correct division-matched user identified through a corrected name and division matching pass.

VALIDATION
A follow-up governance review confirmed all fifty-two records now show an owner correctly aligned with their division.
column6: Owner Division Mismatch Violates Segregation Policy

column1: A phased cutover's read-only mode flag on the legacy system was expected to block all writes during the freeze window, but a small number of records changed anyway with no source yet identified
column2:
CONTEXT
A phased migration cutover used a read-only mode flag on the legacy system to prevent any writes during the final synchronization window before cutover completed.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A post-cutover comparison found a small number of legacy records with a modification timestamp inside the freeze window, despite the flag reportedly blocking all writes.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet confirmed whether the flag has a gap for a specific write path, or whether the timestamps reflect something other than an actual change.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The affected records' current values appear consistent with pre-freeze data, but the modification timestamp itself cannot yet be explained.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The legacy system's own audit log for the freeze window has been requested to determine what process, if any, touched these records.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no fix applied, since it is not yet clear whether this reflects a genuine freeze gap or a logging artifact.

VALIDATION
The next step is to review the legacy audit log for the freeze window once received, to identify what process modified the records.

column1: A screen flow's embedded Lightning web component fires its custom event before an asynchronous data load finishes, so the flow advances to the next screen showing incomplete data
column2:
CONTEXT
A screen flow embeds a custom Lightning web component that fetches related record data asynchronously and fires a completion event once the flow should advance to the next screen.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users occasionally advanced to the next screen before the component's data had actually finished loading, seeing a summary built from partial data.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow should only advance once the component's asynchronous load has genuinely completed.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The component fired its completion event as soon as the fetch request was issued rather than waiting for the response to resolve, a timing bug in the component's own code.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The issue was intermittent, appearing only when the fetch took longer than usual, which correlated with periods of higher overall platform load.

RESOLUTION
The component was corrected to fire its completion event only inside the fetch response handler, guaranteeing data availability before the flow advances.

VALIDATION
Twenty test runs under artificially slowed network conditions confirmed the flow now waits correctly every time before advancing.
column6: Custom Component Event Fires Before Load Completes

column1: A record-triggered flow's entry condition checks whether a field changed, but evaluates the record image from before an Apex trigger in the same transaction updates that field, missing the change
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow's entry condition checks whether a field changed on save, intended to catch updates made either directly by a user or by an Apex trigger earlier in the same transaction.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The flow consistently failed to fire when the change originated from the Apex trigger rather than a direct edit, even though the field's final saved value clearly differed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The flow's change detection should reflect the field's actual final value at save time, regardless of which automation set it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The entry condition evaluated against the record's state before the trigger's update within the same transaction, missing the later change.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This traced to the specific order in which the platform evaluates flow entry conditions relative to earlier trigger execution in the same save.

RESOLUTION
The Apex trigger was refactored to make its field update in an earlier phase of the transaction, ensuring the flow evaluates the trigger's final value.

VALIDATION
Ten test saves where only the trigger changed the field now correctly fire the flow every time.

column1: A flow orchestration stage assigned to two approvers in parallel completed as soon as the first approver responded, though the business process required both approvals before proceeding
column2:
CONTEXT
A flow orchestration process includes a stage assigned to two approvers in parallel, intended to require sign-off from both before the process advances to the next stage.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The orchestration advanced to the next stage as soon as either approver responded, skipping the second approver's review entirely.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The stage should only complete once both assigned approvers have responded.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The stage was configured with a completion condition based on any response rather than all responses, a configuration option that had been overlooked during setup.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Reconfiguring the stage to require all responses is possible, but doing so for records already mid-process requires careful handling to avoid orphaning in-flight approvals.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, new orchestration instances now use the corrected all-responses configuration, while a small number of already in-flight instances are being manually tracked to completion.

VALIDATION
Five new test instances confirmed the stage now correctly waits for both approvers, while in-flight instances are being resolved individually.
column6: Orchestration Advanced On First Of Two Approvals

column1: A record-triggered flow calling a subflow inside a loop hits the platform's per-transaction subflow invocation limit only on the one day each month a scheduled batch process triggers thousands of qualifying records at once
column2:
CONTEXT
A record-triggered flow loops over line items and calls a subflow once per item, normally well within the per-transaction subflow invocation limit at typical daily volumes.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
On the one day each month a scheduled batch advances thousands of qualifying records at once, a subset of transactions hit the subflow invocation limit and failed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet decided whether to restructure the flow to avoid per-item subflow calls or to throttle the monthly batch process instead.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Transactions with an unusually high line item count on batch day exceed the limit, while the same records processed individually any other day never approach it.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The batch process's owning team and the flow's owning team have been connected, but neither has proposed a specific design change yet.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the two teams have not agreed on whether to redesign the flow or throttle the batch process.

VALIDATION
The next step is a joint design session between both teams to scope an approach before the next monthly run reproduces the failure.
column6: Subflow Invocation Limit Hit Only On Batch Day

column1: A middleware connector's shared connection pool across multiple client orgs let a slow query from one client exhaust available connections, delaying an unrelated client's sync with no visibility into the cross-tenant cause
column2:
CONTEXT
A middleware platform serves multiple client orgs through a shared connection pool, intended to balance resource usage efficiently across all tenants.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
One client's integration experienced intermittent sync delays with no apparent cause on their own side, since nothing in their own configuration or data volume had changed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
One tenant's slow query should not be able to delay an unrelated tenant's sync through the shared pool.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A different client org's unusually slow query was holding connections from the shared pool long enough to occasionally starve the affected client's own sync attempts.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The middleware vendor confirmed the shared pool architecture after being provided timing logs showing the delays correlating with the other client's known slow query window.

RESOLUTION
The vendor moved the affected client to a dedicated connection pool, isolating it from the other tenant's query performance.

VALIDATION
Sync timing for the affected client has been consistent for two weeks since the dedicated pool was provisioned, with no further unexplained delays.

column1: An integration correctly mapped a picklist field's values but was never updated when the picklist was converted from single-select to multi-select, so it now writes only the first selected value and drops the rest
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration writes a picklist field's value from an external system, built and tested when the field was single-select, mapping one source value to one target value.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the field was converted to multi-select to support a new business requirement, the integration continued writing only a single value, silently dropping any additional selections.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The integration should write all selected values for a multi-select field, not just the first.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The integration's mapping logic was never updated for the field's new multi-select structure, since the conversion project did not include a review of dependent integrations.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rebuilding the mapping to handle multiple values requires coordinating an updated data format with the external system, which has not yet been scheduled.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the integration currently writes only the primary value while a semicolon-delimited multi-value format is negotiated with the external system's team.

VALIDATION
The single-value workaround was confirmed stable and non-disruptive for current records, though full multi-value support remains pending.
column6: Integration Unaware Of Single To Multi-Select Change

column1: A retried failed integration record was resubmitted using a payload built from a stale in-memory cache rather than a fresh read, so the retry succeeded but overwrote a legitimate intervening update
column2:
CONTEXT
An integration's retry mechanism resubmits a failed record using the payload originally constructed at the time of the first attempt, cached in memory for efficiency.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A record legitimately updated by a user between the original failed attempt and the eventual retry was overwritten back to its older, cached state once the retry succeeded.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A retry should use current source data rather than a payload captured before an intervening legitimate change.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The retry mechanism was built to reuse the exact original payload for simplicity and consistency, without considering that source data could change during the retry delay.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Four records were confirmed to have been overwritten this way, all involving a retry delay long enough for a user to make an intervening edit.

RESOLUTION
The retry mechanism was rebuilt to re-fetch current source data immediately before resubmitting, rather than reusing the original cached payload.

VALIDATION
A test scenario with an intervening edit during the retry delay now correctly reflects the updated data rather than the original stale payload.

column1: A Platform Encryption key rotation caused a batch job querying an encrypted field with an unsupported operator to silently return incomplete results instead of erroring, undetected until a compliance report looked short
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom Apex batch job queries an encrypted field using a comparison operator, run routinely as part of a monthly compliance reporting process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Following a routine encryption key rotation, the compliance report's record count dropped noticeably without any error being logged anywhere in the batch job.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A query against an encrypted field using an operator the platform does not support for encrypted data should fail loudly rather than silently returning a partial result.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The specific comparison operator used has limited, order-sensitive support for encrypted fields that can behave differently across a key rotation, silently narrowing the matched result set.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform vendor confirmed the operator's behavior with encrypted fields is inherently order-dependent in a way not previously documented clearly to the team.

RESOLUTION
The batch job was rebuilt to use a supported operator for encrypted field comparisons, and the compliance report was rerun for the affected period.

VALIDATION
The rerun report's count matched an independent manual count for the same period, confirming the fix captured the previously missed records.
column6: Encrypted Field Query Silently Incomplete Post-Rotation

column1: An admin granted Modify Metadata permission to a support-tier profile to unblock one task, and its broader implications were not realized until an audit found unauthorized flow edits made by a support user
column2:
CONTEXT
An admin granted the Modify Metadata permission to a support-tier profile temporarily to allow one specific configuration task, without fully considering its broader scope.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A later security audit found a support user on that profile had used the permission to make unrelated edits to an active flow, outside the original task's intent.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Broad configuration permissions should be scoped narrowly and reviewed before being granted to a non-administrative profile.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The permission's scope extends far beyond the single task it was granted for, and no review process caught this before or after the grant.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The unauthorized edits were found to be a well-intentioned but unauthorized attempt to fix an unrelated issue, not malicious, though still outside change control.

RESOLUTION
The permission was revoked from the support-tier profile, the flow edits reverted, and a temporary permission set with an expiration date issued for the original task instead.

VALIDATION
A follow-up audit confirmed the profile no longer holds the broad permission, and the flow's edit history now reflects only authorized changes.
column6: Modify Metadata Grant Enabled Unintended Flow Edits

column1: A Connected App's IP relaxation setting configured to relax restrictions for mobile convenience inadvertently allowed API access from any network for all users assigned that app, not just the intended mobile client
column2:
CONTEXT
A Connected App used by a mobile client was configured with a relaxed IP restriction setting, intended to accommodate mobile users on varying cellular and wifi networks.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A security review found the relaxation applies to any API access using that app's credentials, not scoped specifically to the mobile client it was intended for.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
IP relaxation should ideally be scoped narrowly enough to avoid broadening access for any other consumer of the same Connected App.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The setting applies at the Connected App level as a whole, with no finer-grained scoping available to target only the mobile client.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
No evidence of unauthorized access exploiting the broadened scope was found in login history, but the exposure has existed since the app was first configured.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, a separate dedicated Connected App was provisioned exclusively for the mobile client, while the original app's setting is tightened back to standard restrictions.

VALIDATION
The mobile client was confirmed functional against the new dedicated app, with the original app's tightening scheduled pending a compatibility check.
column6: IP Relaxation Setting Too Broad For App

column1: A scheduled Apex job running as an automated process user retained full object permissions from a permission set that was supposed to have been narrowed months earlier, since the org's permission review script only checks named individual users
column2:
CONTEXT
A periodic permission review script checks named individual users' permission set assignments against an approved access list, intended to catch any excess access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A scheduled Apex job running under the platform's automated process user retained a broad permission set that had been intentionally narrowed for every named user months earlier, but never for this automated context.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The permission review process should cover automated process contexts, not only named individual users.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The review script's query specifically filtered for user records matching named individuals, excluding the automated process user by its own design.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A review of the automated process user's actual usage confirmed the broad permissions were unused beyond the narrowed permission set's scope, with no evidence of misuse.

RESOLUTION
The automated process user's permission set was narrowed to match the intended scope, and the review script was updated to include automated and system contexts.

VALIDATION
The scheduled job was confirmed still functioning under the narrowed permissions, and the updated review script now covers the automated process user.
column6: Automated Process User Missed By Permission Review

column1: A scheduled report running in a specific user's context stopped after that user's license changed to a limited type, silently losing access to a report type the license doesn't support
column2:
CONTEXT
A scheduled report runs under a specific named user's context and license, relying on that user's continued access to the underlying custom report type.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The scheduled report silently stopped delivering results after the running user's license type was changed to a more limited one during a cost-optimization review.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A license change affecting a user who owns scheduled reports should trigger a check for reports that would be broken by the change.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The limited license no longer supported the custom report type, causing the schedule to silently fail without generating any visible error or notification.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The schedule had been failing for three weeks before subscribers noticed the missing reports, since no failure notification was configured for this schedule.

RESOLUTION
The schedule was reassigned to run under a user with an appropriate license, and a failure notification was configured for this and other scheduled reports.

VALIDATION
The reassigned schedule delivered successfully on its next run, and a deliberately induced failure confirmed the new notification fires correctly.
column6: Report Owner License Downgrade Broke Schedule

column1: A dashboard table component sorted by a formula field re-sorts unexpectedly after each refresh because the formula's ties are broken using row insertion order, which is not stable across refreshes
column2:
CONTEXT
A dashboard table component displays records sorted primarily by a formula field, with several records frequently sharing the same formula result value.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Users noticed the table's row order shifted unpredictably between refreshes even when no underlying data had changed, making it hard to track specific records visually.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Records with tied formula values should sort in a consistent, predictable order across refreshes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The platform breaks ties using an internal row ordering that is not guaranteed stable between separate query executions, so tied records reshuffled on each refresh.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Testing confirmed the instability specifically affects records sharing an identical formula value, while uniquely valued records sorted consistently every time.

RESOLUTION
A secondary sort on a stable unique field was added after the formula field, giving tied records a consistent, predictable secondary ordering.

VALIDATION
Ten consecutive refreshes after the secondary sort was added showed identical row ordering each time.
column6: Unstable Tie-Breaking Reorders Table Each Refresh

column1: A dynamic dashboard shows different filter options to different viewers because the filter's picklist values are sourced from records the viewing user has access to, rather than the full picklist definition
column2:
CONTEXT
A dynamic dashboard filter offers a dropdown of region values, populated by querying distinct values currently present in records the viewing user can access.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two users comparing notes on the same dashboard found they saw different sets of available filter options, since their respective record access differed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The filter's available options should be consistent for every viewer, reflecting the full picklist definition rather than each viewer's own visible record subset.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The filter's option list was built by querying distinct values from accessible records rather than referencing the picklist's defined value set directly.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
This was confirmed as the filter's original design choice, intended to avoid showing an option with zero matching accessible records, an unintended tradeoff for consistency.

RESOLUTION
The filter was rebuilt to source its option list directly from the picklist definition, showing every defined region regardless of individual record access.

VALIDATION
Two users with different record access now see identical filter options, confirmed through a side-by-side comparison.
column6: Filter Options Vary By Viewer's Record Access

column1: An aggregate query joining two objects through a polymorphic lookup field returns inconsistent totals because the report type's join logic only follows one of the possible target object types
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom report type joins task records to their related parent through a polymorphic lookup field, which can point to either of two different object types depending on the task.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Aggregate totals in the report undercounted tasks whose polymorphic lookup pointed to the second, less common target object type.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The report type's join should correctly follow the polymorphic lookup regardless of which target object type a given task points to.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The report type was originally built and tested primarily against the first, more common target type, and its join logic does not fully account for the second.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Rebuilding the report type to fully support both target types requires platform capabilities that only partially support this join pattern.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, a supplemental report was built for the second target type, with totals from both reports combined manually until a fuller solution exists.

VALIDATION
The combined manual total was cross-checked against a direct record count and confirmed accurate, though a single unified report remains unavailable.
column6: Report Type Join Misses Polymorphic Target

column1: Einstein Activity Capture automatically logged inbound customer emails as activities while a separate email-to-case rule also created a case-linked email record, producing two copies of every message
column2:
CONTEXT
Einstein Activity Capture was recently enabled org-wide to automatically log email correspondence as activities, alongside an existing email-to-case rule that separately creates case-linked email records.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Every inbound customer email began appearing twice on the case timeline, once through activity capture and once through the existing email-to-case process.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A single inbound email should appear once on the case timeline, regardless of how many features are configured to log it.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Activity capture and the email-to-case rule operate independently with no awareness of each other, both logging the same message as a separate record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The activity capture rollout did not account for its overlap with the existing email-to-case process already logging the same correspondence.

RESOLUTION
Activity capture's scope was narrowed to exclude the mailbox addresses already covered by the email-to-case rule, eliminating the overlap.

VALIDATION
Ten test inbound emails after the scope change each appeared exactly once on the case timeline.
column6: Activity Capture And Case Rule Both Log Email

column1: A List Email send to a large segment was rejected midway through delivery after crossing an org-wide daily email allocation shared with all other outbound email features, with no advance warning of the shared limit
column2:
CONTEXT
A List Email campaign was sent to a large customer segment, drawing from the same org-wide daily email allocation shared with case correspondence and other outbound automation.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The campaign stopped partway through sending once the shared daily allocation was exhausted, and no case correspondence could be sent for the remainder of the day either.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A large planned campaign send should be checked against the shared daily allocation in advance, or scheduled to avoid disrupting other outbound email.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The campaign was sent without checking its size against the remaining daily allocation, consuming nearly all of it and blocking unrelated case correspondence.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The marketing team sending the campaign was unaware the daily allocation was shared with support case correspondence rather than being a marketing-specific limit.

RESOLUTION
The campaign was rescheduled to send in smaller batches across several days, and marketing was briefed on the shared allocation for future large sends.

VALIDATION
The rescheduled batched send completed fully across three days with no further disruption to case correspondence.
column6: List Email Hit Shared Daily Allocation

column1: A case's email thread displays messages in the wrong order when a customer's reply arrives through a different regional mail relay with measurable propagation delay relative to the agent's own reply
column2:
CONTEXT
Case email threads display messages ordered by their received timestamp, normally reliable since messages typically arrive close to when they were sent.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A customer's reply sent shortly after an agent's message occasionally displayed before the agent's message, since the customer's mail relay in a different region introduced a noticeable propagation delay before the message was actually received.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Thread ordering should reflect the true chronological order messages were sent, not solely when each happened to be received.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The received timestamp used for ordering does not account for relay propagation delay, which varies enough between regions to occasionally invert the visible order.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The delay was measured at up to several minutes for the specific regional relay involved, enough to occasionally invert ordering for closely timed messages.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, agents in affected regions were advised to check the full message headers when thread order looks suspicious, while a sent-timestamp-based ordering change is evaluated.

VALIDATION
The workaround guidance was distributed to affected teams, though the underlying ordering logic itself has not yet been changed.
column6: Regional Mail Relay Delay Reorders Thread

column1: A custom hierarchy field referencing the same object for a management chain created a circular reference after a bulk reassignment, and validation rules meant to catch loops were disabled during the bulk load
column2:
CONTEXT
A custom hierarchy field on the employee object references another record of the same object to represent a management chain, with a validation rule normally preventing circular references.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A bulk reassignment performed with validation rules deliberately disabled for load performance created a two-record loop where each referenced the other as their manager.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A circular reference should never be possible regardless of whether validation rules are active during a given load.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
With validation disabled for the bulk operation, nothing prevented the two records from being updated to reference each other in the same load.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The loop caused a rollup report walking the management chain to fail with a recursion error, which is how the circular reference was first discovered.

RESOLUTION
The loop was manually broken by correcting one record's reference to the actual intended manager, and the bulk load process now includes a mandatory post-load circular reference check.

VALIDATION
The post-load check was run against the corrected data and confirmed no circular references remain anywhere in the hierarchy.
column6: Bulk Load Created Circular Hierarchy Reference

column1: A Flow Orchestration process managing a multi-step record review left several records in an ambiguous in-review state after an orchestration version was deactivated mid-flight for records still actively progressing through it
column2:
CONTEXT
A Flow Orchestration process manages a multi-step review, with several records actively progressing through its stages when a newer version was activated to replace it.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Deactivating the prior orchestration version left records that were mid-process in an ambiguous state, neither continuing under the old version nor picked up by the new one.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
In-flight records should either complete under their original orchestration version or be cleanly transitioned to the new one.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Deactivation stops new work from entering the old version but does not affect or transition already in-flight instances, leaving them stalled with no active version driving them forward.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Eight records were confirmed stalled in this ambiguous state, identified by comparing the orchestration's own instance log against expected active-record counts.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the eight stalled records were manually advanced through their remaining review steps outside the orchestration tool, while a version-transition procedure is designed for future orchestration updates.

VALIDATION
All eight records were confirmed to have completed their review manually, though a proper transition mechanism for future version changes remains to be built.

column1: A list view filtered using My Territory scope returns different record counts for two users nominally on the same territory because one user's territory assignment carries an end date in the past that was never cleaned up
column2:
CONTEXT
A list view uses a My Territory filter scope to show records relevant to the viewing user's territory, based on the user's active territory assignment record.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Two users believed to be on the same territory saw different record counts on the identical list view, with one seeing noticeably fewer records than expected.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Users genuinely assigned to the same active territory should see consistent counts on the same My Territory filtered list view.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
One user's territory assignment carried an end date in the past, technically making it inactive even though the user still considered themselves on that territory.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The stale end date traced back to a territory realignment project months earlier that left the field populated as a placeholder rather than genuinely ending the assignment.

RESOLUTION
The stale end date was cleared from the affected user's assignment, and a query was run to identify and correct any other similarly stale assignments.

VALIDATION
The corrected user's list view now matches their territory peer's count, and no other stale end dates were found in the follow-up query.
column6: Stale Territory End Date Skews My Territory Filter

column1: A Compact Layout's highlighted field references a formula field that occasionally throws a display error for a specific data combination, and because the error occurs at render time rather than save time, records save fine but are unreadable on the detail page
column2:
CONTEXT
A Compact Layout's highlighted panel displays a formula field summarizing a record's status, calculated from several underlying fields at render time rather than stored on save.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Records with a specific rare combination of underlying field values saved successfully but then displayed an error in place of the highlighted panel whenever the record's detail page was opened.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A formula calculation error should not prevent a user from viewing the rest of the record's detail page.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The formula's calculation fails for the rare combination in a way that breaks the Compact Layout's entire highlighted panel rendering rather than failing gracefully for just that field.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Twelve records with the rare combination were identified, and the formula's specific division-by-zero condition triggering the error was isolated through testing.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the formula was wrapped with a conditional check to avoid the division-by-zero condition, showing a placeholder value instead of erroring for the twelve affected records.

VALIDATION
