All twelve previously broken records now display their detail page correctly with the placeholder value shown in the highlighted panel.
column6: Compact Layout Formula Error Blocks Record View

column1: A CPQ co-terminated subscription amendment's proration calculation double-counted a mid-term price increase that had already been separately invoiced, overstating the amendment's additional charge
column2:
CONTEXT
A CPQ co-termination amendment process prorates a subscription's remaining value when a mid-term change occurs, aligning the new term's billing with the original contract's anniversary date.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
An amendment following a mid-term price increase that had already been invoiced separately calculated an additional charge that effectively billed the increase a second time.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The proration calculation should account for value already invoiced through an earlier mid-term change, not recalculate from the original unmodified contract value.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The proration logic recalculated from the subscription's original baseline value, unaware that a separate mid-term increase had already been applied and billed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three amendments over the prior quarter were confirmed to have this double-counting issue, all involving a subscription with a mid-term price change in its history.

RESOLUTION
The proration logic was updated to check for and net out any already-invoiced mid-term changes before calculating the amendment's additional charge, and the three affected amendments were corrected.

VALIDATION
A test amendment on a subscription with a mid-term increase now correctly nets out the already-invoiced amount, verified against a manual calculation.

column1: A sales spiff calculation reads an opportunity's total amount field, including a one-time services fee the spiff program explicitly excludes, since a recurring-revenue-only field was introduced after the program launched
column2:
CONTEXT
A sales spiff program pays an incentive based on recurring revenue only, explicitly excluding one-time services fees, calculated by a formula reading the opportunity's total amount field.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Reps closing deals with a significant one-time services fee component received a spiff payout larger than the program intended, since the total amount field includes both revenue types combined.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The spiff calculation should read only the recurring-revenue-specific field introduced after the program launched, excluding one-time fees entirely.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The spiff formula was never updated to reference the newer recurring-revenue-only field, continuing to use the original combined total amount field from before that field existed.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Identifying every historical spiff payout affected by this over-calculation requires cross-referencing each closed deal's fee breakdown, a reconciliation still in progress with finance.

RESOLUTION
The spiff formula was updated to reference the recurring-revenue-only field going forward, while the historical overpayment reconciliation with finance continues separately.

VALIDATION
New spiff calculations since the formula update correctly exclude one-time fees, though the historical overpayment reconciliation has not yet concluded.
column6: Spiff Calculation Includes Excluded Services Fee

column1: An automated churn-risk score recalculating nightly from support case volume spiked for otherwise healthy accounts because bulk-reassigned cases during a team restructuring were counted as new case creation
column2:
CONTEXT
An automated churn-risk score recalculates nightly based partly on an account's recent support case volume, intended to flag accounts with a genuine rise in support activity.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several healthy accounts saw their churn-risk score spike sharply after a support team restructuring bulk-reassigned existing cases to new owners, with no actual increase in support activity.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A case reassignment should not be counted the same as a genuinely new case being created for churn-risk purposes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The churn-risk calculation counted any case with a recent last-modified date as recent activity, and the bulk reassignment's mass update touched every reassigned case's last-modified timestamp.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Forty-one accounts were confirmed to have an artificially inflated score directly attributable to the bulk reassignment's timing.

RESOLUTION
The churn-risk calculation was updated to use case creation date rather than last-modified date for measuring recent activity, and the forty-one affected scores were recalculated.

VALIDATION
The forty-one recalculated scores returned to levels consistent with the accounts' actual support history, confirmed by comparing against the un-reassigned case creation timeline.
column6: Bulk Reassignment Miscounted As New Case Volume

column1: A consumer authenticating via External Credential under the newer named credential model failed after the referenced legacy integration user was deactivated during an access cleanup, surfacing a generic connection error
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer authenticates through an External Credential configured under the newer named credential model, referencing a specific integration user as its authentication principal.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The integration began failing entirely after the referenced integration user was deactivated during an unrelated access cleanup effort, with the resulting error giving no indication of the actual cause.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
An authentication failure caused by a deactivated principal should surface a clear, specific error rather than a generic connection failure.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The error returned to the consumer was a generic connection failure message, giving no indication that the underlying issue was specifically the principal's deactivation.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The access cleanup effort's review process did not check whether any deactivated user was still referenced as a named credential's authentication principal.

RESOLUTION
The integration user was reactivated with restricted login access, and the access cleanup process now includes a check for named credential principal references before deactivating any user.

VALIDATION
The integration resumed functioning immediately after reactivation, and a test deactivation of an unrelated referenced user was correctly flagged by the updated cleanup check.

column1: A REST API consumer's client-side certificate pinning broke after the platform's TLS certificate was renewed with a new issuing authority as part of routine infrastructure maintenance
column2:
CONTEXT
A REST API consumer implements certificate pinning for additional security, originally configured to pin the specific certificate rather than its issuing authority.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
All API calls from the consumer began failing immediately after a routine TLS certificate renewal on the platform side replaced the previously pinned certificate.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A routine certificate renewal using a different but still trusted issuing authority should not break a properly configured pinning implementation.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The consumer's pinning was implemented against the specific certificate rather than the issuing authority, a brittle approach not designed to tolerate routine renewal.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform's certificate renewal was routine and expected, with the consumer's own pinning implementation identified as the actual point of failure.

RESOLUTION
The consumer's pinning configuration was rebuilt to pin against the issuing certificate authority rather than the specific leaf certificate, tolerating future routine renewals.

VALIDATION
A test connection using the updated pinning configuration succeeded, and the consumer's team confirmed understanding of the more resilient pinning approach going forward.
column6: Certificate Pinning Broke On Routine Renewal

column1: An External Service defined from an OpenAPI specification stopped generating one specific action after the source specification file exceeded a size limit during a routine update, failing silently in Flow Builder
column2:
CONTEXT
An External Service was defined from a partner's OpenAPI specification, generating a set of callable actions usable directly within Flow Builder.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
After the partner added new endpoints to their specification during a routine update, one specific previously working action silently disappeared from Flow Builder with no error shown.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Regenerating an External Service from an updated specification should either include every valid action or clearly report which ones could not be generated.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The updated specification file exceeded an internal size limit for External Service generation, silently truncating the processed definition and dropping the one action that fell past the cutoff.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The platform vendor confirmed the size limit exists but does not currently surface a warning when a specification is truncated during generation.

RESOLUTION
As a workaround, the partner's specification was split into two smaller files, each generating its own External Service comfortably under the size limit.

VALIDATION
Both resulting External Services, including the previously dropped action, now appear correctly available in Flow Builder.
column6: OpenAPI Size Limit Silently Dropped One Action

column1: A consumer's API usage regularly spikes above its allocated limit only on the first business day of each month, correlating with a batch reporting process, but the platform's usage logs don't break down calls by originating feature
column2:
CONTEXT
A consumer's API usage regularly spikes close to or above its allocated monthly limit specifically on the first business day of each month, coinciding with a known internal batch reporting process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The team owning the consumer application cannot determine which report or process is responsible for the spike, since usage logs only show aggregate call volume.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It has not yet been determined whether the application needs better internal instrumentation or whether usage logs should offer a finer-grained breakdown.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The platform's usage logs report total call volume per consumer without any breakdown by originating feature or code path.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
The consumer team has ruled out several known monthly processes through manual code review, but has not identified the responsible one.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since the specific responsible process within the application has not been identified.

VALIDATION
The next step is to add call-tagging instrumentation within the application to attribute API calls to specific processes ahead of the next cycle.
column6: Monthly Spike Cause Unidentified In Usage Logs

column1: A question about total pipeline value returned a figure that appeared doubled because the assistant did not recognize that opportunity records were intentionally split across two currency-denominated records representing one deal
column2:
CONTEXT
One business unit models certain deals using two separate opportunity records, one per currency, when a single deal spans two currencies, a pattern unique to that unit's process.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A total pipeline value question summed both currency-split records as if they were two distinct deals, roughly doubling the reported value for affected opportunities.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The assistant should recognize the currency-split modeling pattern and treat the two linked records as one deal for total value purposes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The assistant's standard aggregation logic has no awareness of this business unit's specific modeling convention, treating every opportunity record as an independent deal.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A linking field connecting the two split records to their shared parent deal identifier already exists but was not previously used in any aggregation logic.

RESOLUTION
The pipeline aggregation logic was updated to deduplicate on the shared parent deal identifier before summing, correctly counting split-currency deals once.

VALIDATION
A repeat of the original question now returns a total matching a manual reconciliation against the business unit's own deal tracking spreadsheet.
column6: Split-Currency Deal Modeling Doubled Pipeline Total

column1: The assistant's confidence score is calculated from query execution success alone, so a syntactically valid but semantically wrong query matching the wrong object is reported with high confidence despite being incorrect
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant displays a confidence indicator alongside each answer, currently calculated based on whether the generated query executed without error.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A question resolved to the wrong object due to ambiguous phrasing still executed successfully and was shown with high confidence, misleading the user into trusting an incorrect answer.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The confidence indicator should reflect the likelihood the answer is semantically correct, not merely whether the query ran without a syntax or execution error.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
A query can be syntactically valid and execute successfully while still answering a completely different question than the one intended, and the current confidence calculation cannot distinguish this case.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A sample of twenty answers with known object-selection ambiguity found high confidence displayed regardless of whether the resolved object was actually correct.

RESOLUTION
The confidence calculation was updated to also factor in the object-selection step's own certainty score, lowering confidence when object ambiguity was present.

VALIDATION
The same twenty test questions now show noticeably lower confidence specifically for the cases where object selection had been ambiguous.

column1: A question asking for this fiscal year to date produces a different answer depending on whether it is asked before or after the nightly sync the assistant's fallback data source uses when a live query times out
column2:
CONTEXT
The assistant normally answers from live data, falling back to a nightly-synced secondary source only when a live query exceeds its timeout, a mechanism most users are unaware exists.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
The same fiscal-year-to-date question produced two different totals on separate occasions, with no indication a fallback source might have been used for one of them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet decided whether the assistant should avoid the fallback for this question type or clearly disclose when a fallback answer was used.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Whether a question hits the live query timeout and falls back appears inconsistent, depending on live query performance at the moment asked.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Confirming which occasion used the fallback requires internal logging that was not retained long enough to review after the discrepancy was reported.

RESOLUTION
No fix has been applied yet, since it has not been confirmed how often this question type actually triggers the fallback.

VALIDATION
The next step is to add persistent logging of fallback usage per question type to measure frequency before deciding on a fix.
column6: Fallback Data Source Produces Inconsistent Answers

column1: A middleware ETL tool's retry logic resubmitted a batch after a partial timeout without deduplicating against records already committed, loading roughly two percent of one wave's records twice with different internal IDs
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration wave used a middleware ETL tool's built-in retry logic to automatically resubmit a batch that experienced a partial timeout during loading.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A post-migration audit found roughly two percent of the wave's records existed twice in the target, each copy with a different internal identifier, traced to the automatic retry.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
A retried batch should only load records that were not already successfully committed by the original attempt.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The tool's retry logic resubmitted the entire batch without checking which individual records had already committed before the timeout occurred.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Three hundred eleven duplicate record pairs were identified by matching on the source system's own unique identifier, confirming the retry as the cause.

RESOLUTION
The duplicate pairs were merged, keeping the earlier-created copy, and the ETL tool's retry configuration was changed to use a supported idempotent resubmission mode.

VALIDATION
A test batch deliberately interrupted mid-load and then retried using the idempotent mode produced no duplicate records.

column1: A migrated object's autonumber field was seeded to continue from the highest known legacy identifier, but a subsequent discovery of an even higher identifier in an overlooked archival table caused a collision months later
column2:
CONTEXT
A migrated object's autonumber field was seeded at cutover to continue counting upward from the highest legacy identifier found across the source system's primary tables.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Months after cutover, a separate project surfaced an archival table that had not been included in the original identifier survey, containing a higher legacy identifier than the seed value assumed.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
The autonumber sequence should never collide with any legacy identifier still considered relevant for reference purposes.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
As the autonumber sequence advanced over time, it eventually reached and collided with the higher archival identifier, creating a naming conflict for a newly created record.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A full inventory of every legacy table, including rarely accessed archival ones, is still being compiled to determine whether other undiscovered higher identifiers exist.

RESOLUTION
As an interim step, the autonumber sequence was manually advanced past the newly discovered archival identifier, while the full legacy table inventory continues.

VALIDATION
No further collisions have occurred since the manual advance, though the inventory needed to fully guarantee no future collision is still in progress.
column6: Autonumber Collided With Overlooked Archive Table

column1: A separate audit comparing migrated data against the live source system found records missing that the migration's own reconciliation never flagged, and the cause has not yet been isolated
column2:
CONTEXT
A source system's export tool generates the file used for migration, with reconciliation comparing the loaded record count against the export file's own row count.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
A separate audit comparing migrated data against the live source system found records missing that reconciliation never flagged, since the export file never contained them.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
It is not yet confirmed whether the export tool silently dropped these records or whether they were excluded earlier in extraction.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The missing records share no single obvious characteristic identified so far, so the exact point of exclusion has not been isolated.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
A sample of missing records is being compared field by field against successfully exported records to look for a distinguishing pattern.

RESOLUTION
No cause has been confirmed and no fix applied, since the export tool's exclusion behavior has not yet been isolated.

VALIDATION
The next step is to complete the field-by-field comparison and, if no pattern emerges, request export logging from the source vendor.

column1: A migration mapped a legacy assigned-team field to a Salesforce Group, but several of the largest legacy teams silently truncated to the platform's maximum group membership size during a separate group-membership load step
column2:
CONTEXT
A migration mapped a legacy assigned-team field to a corresponding Salesforce Group, with group membership loaded through a separate step after the groups themselves were created.

ISSUE OR REQUEST
Several of the largest legacy teams were found with fewer members in their migrated group than the legacy system showed, with no error raised anywhere in the migration process.

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Every legacy team member should be preserved in the corresponding migrated group regardless of the team's original size.

ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
Salesforce Groups have a maximum membership size smaller than several of the largest legacy teams, and the separate membership load step silently stopped adding members once that limit was reached.

INVESTIGATION AND FINDINGS
Six legacy teams were confirmed to have exceeded the platform's maximum group size, each missing members proportional to how far over the limit they were.

RESOLUTION
The six affected teams were restructured into multiple linked subgroups to accommodate their full membership within the per-group limit.

VALIDATION
A member count comparison for all six restructured teams confirmed every legacy team member is now represented across their subgroups.
column6: Largest Legacy Teams Truncated At Group Size Limit
